# manuscript-guard — design

Status: design agreed 2026-08-03. All eight phases are built, and what has been added since
is described where it belongs. A statement written from now on says which kind of evidence
below it rests on; much already here does not, and some of it is judgement or the author's
decision, which is neither. What remains is listed under Known gaps.

That list is load-bearing and has to be kept true. It drifted once — it went on claiming
five guideline licences were unconfirmed after they had been read, and went on describing
two defects that had been fixed — which is the same failure the toolkit exists to catch one
level down. Correct it in the same commit as the code, or it becomes a rumour.

## What a claim rests on

A statement about the toolkit rests on one of four kinds of evidence, and says which; a
choice or a judgement is neither, and says so:

1. **A deterministic test is green in CI.** Most of what this document says of a gate rests
   on this: its corruption cases, the generated inputs and their broken rules, the
   differential readings. It proves the gate does what the test holds on the inputs the
   test has, and no more.
2. **A measurement on real inputs**, with its date, the inputs, and what it found, negative
   results included. Some are recorded where they belong (`audit` on a submitted paper; a
   clone of the project whose input digests failed). Two would measure the toolkit as a
   whole. The review panel read against defects already known has been run once, on the
   example's own manuscript and not on a real paper ("What the panel finds of the defects
   we know"). How often G6 fires on clean text written by people has been measured once,
   on 384 biomedical research articles of 2010 to 2022, and its rate thresholds set from it
   ("The AI-writing lint measures rate, not presence"); no text written by a model was read.
3. **The author used it on a real manuscript.**
4. **Someone else did.**

Tested, committed, reviewed, merged and released are different statements as well. A review
of a pull request is no test; a release on PyPI is no use.

The test of the whole toolkit is a measurement, not a claim: on real projects, are critical
problems found before submission, by the tool or by the person it sends the author to? It
has not been measured. The two above would be first steps, and real users the
next.

**Defaults taken, not decided by the author.** Where the author was asked to choose and did
not, and a default was taken, it is recorded here with its date, in those words, so that a
default is never read as a decision. None has been taken. Two choices put to the author are
open: the model for the paid evaluation runs, which wait unrun, and which gates and
commands have run on the author's real manuscript, for the README's "Status".

## What this is

A toolkit for writing scientific manuscripts in which **every number is traceable to a
source**. It is not a paper. It is the machinery Basile Chrétien will use for subsequent
papers, released publicly under MIT so other scientists can use it.

It ships in two layers:

- a **pip package** (`manuscript-guard`) holding the deterministic gates, the build
  pipeline and the Zotero client. Runs anywhere, including CI, with no LLM involved.
- a **Claude Code plugin** holding the skills, agents and hooks that help draft, verify
  and review.

The split is deliberate and load-bearing. The guarantees belong to the deterministic
layer; an agent may help you write a sentence but never decides whether the manuscript is
clean. A user who does not use Claude Code still gets the guarantee.

### Non-goals

- Writing any particular paper.
- Replacing Zotero, pandoc or the analysis language.
- Requiring R. The toolkit is language-agnostic about the analysis and only requires the
  results contract; R and Python helpers exist for convenience.

## The core invariant

Every number in a deliverable resolves to exactly one of four classes:

| Class | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `results` | a key in the machine-written results file | the cohort size |
| `literature` | a key in the literature ledger, backed by a stored source | a prevalence quoted from a published cohort |
| `convention` | a writing or statistical convention on a reviewed allowlist | `p < 0.05`, `95% CI` |
| `structural` | not a claim at all | `Table 2`, a publication year, a dose inside a drug name |

The check runs in **both directions**:

1. no numeric token in any deliverable may be unclassified;
2. no display value produced by the analysis may lack a bound claim, or be explicitly
   marked as not quoted.

Direction 1 alone lets a stale number hide somewhere nothing looks. Direction 2 alone
produces the failure recorded in the predecessor project, where a registry bound 28 of 236
values and still reported "all clear". Both together are what makes "no stale number" a
property of the build rather than a hope.

### Why the check runs on the source, not the output

The classifier reads the manuscript **source**, where bindings are still visible as
`{{results.x}}` placeholders, rather than the rendered output where every number looks
alike. That turns the check into something almost trivially strong:

> In manuscript source, a bare numeric literal is a defect unless it is a recognised
> convention or structural reference.

There is no matching of numbers against a backing set, and therefore none of the
coincidental-match weakness that made the predecessor's checker near-vacuous — it measured
that 100% of integers up to 100 were already "backed" by something, somewhere. Here a
results-derived number cannot be written as a literal at all: it is either a placeholder or
a build failure.

Two rules support it. Results are **never hand-written** — one machine-generated file
stamped with script, git SHA, input hashes and timestamp. And the build **refuses to run
when the script that wrote the results, or an input that script declared, has changed
since**, which is what makes "the latest results are always used" mechanical rather than
a habit. Changed is by digest, not by date. A module the script imports counts only where
it is listed among the inputs (Known gaps).

## Empirical findings (verified 2026-08-03 on the author's machine)

These were tested, not assumed, and they determine the architecture.

- **pandoc + `zotero.lua` produces a .docx with live Zotero citations.** Real
  `ADDIN ZOTERO_ITEM CSL_CITATION` field codes, built by querying the running Zotero
  through Better BibTeX's JSON-RPC. Confirmed in Word: Zotero adopts the citations after
  Document Preferences, and the file is not reported as corrupt.
  **Consequence: Markdown is the permanent source of truth and the .docx is a disposable
  build artifact.** No surgical patching, no md/docx drift.
- `zotero.lua` emits no `ZOTERO_PREF` properties and no `ZOTERO_BIBL` field for .docx (it
  does for .odt), so a Word build had live citations, no reference list, and a style dialog on
  the first Refresh. `build/zotero_word.lua`, run after it on a live build, now adds both: the
  bibliography field where the manuscript writes a `refs` div (or at the end), and the
  preferences for the target journal's `references.csl`. Verified in Word 16 with Zotero
  9.0.6 on a 57-reference manuscript: Refresh formatted every citation in the preset style
  without a dialog, filled the bibliography, and Add/Edit Citation worked on the document.
  (Narrative `@key` citations also produced no field at the time of the first note; that
  was fixed with `author-in-text: true` — see "The build" below.)
- **Zotero's local API (`/api/`) is disabled** on this machine — returns
  `403 Local API is not enabled`. Not needed: **Better BibTeX's JSON-RPC works** and
  returns CSL-JSON including citation keys.
- **Zotero replies HTTP/1.0 with a close-delimited body.** .NET's HTTP client rejects this
  (`response ended prematurely`); Python's `urllib` handles it. All Zotero access must go
  through Python, never PowerShell.
- **The agent tool sandbox blocks localhost.** Any step touching Zotero needs the sandbox
  disabled, which has consequences for how hooks are written and permissioned.
- **Never ask Better BibTeX for the whole library.** `item.search("")` serialises every item
  as CSL: 51 s for 4,688 items (Better BibTeX 9.0.64), against G7's 20 s budget, so G7 passed
  or failed on how busy Zotero was. G7 now asks `item.pandoc_filter` about the cited keys
  (0.2 s; an unresolvable key comes back with the number of items carrying it, 0 or a
  duplicate count) and finds pinned items with one condition search,
  `item.search([["extra", "contains", "Citation Key:"]])` (0.7 s).
- **A pinned key comes back as `citation-key: xyz`**, in the CSL `note`, although it is typed
  in Extra as `Citation Key: xyz`. `item.search` keeps that line; `item.pandoc_filter` and
  `item.export` strip it, so they cannot tell pinned from unpinned.
- **Word does not carry a paragraph's identifier when it cuts the paragraph** (Word 365,
  driven over COM on the example's build, 2026-09-24). The identifier is an empty bookmark,
  and Word leaves an empty bookmark where it stood. With Track Changes on, it stays in the
  moved-from copy; without, it moves onto the next paragraph. That is the first paragraph
  of what it cuts: the bookmarks of the paragraphs after it go with them (2026-09-28).
  Text pasted or typed at the
  start of a paragraph, Enter included, goes in behind that paragraph's bookmark. And
  pandoc's reference document sets `w:doNotTrackMoves`, so a move made with Track Changes on
  came back as a deletion and an unrelated insertion. See "A move, the way Word makes one".
- Environment: Zotero 9.0.6, Better BibTeX installed, `Zotero.dotm` in Word's STARTUP,
  pandoc 3.9.0.2, Word 16, R 4.3.3–4.6.0, Python 3.12.3.

## Structure

### The toolkit repository

```
manuscript-guard/
  src/manuscript_guard/
    contracts/     # schemas for results, ledger, authors, paper
    gates/         # one module per gate; deterministic, no LLM
                   #   includes journal.py and reporting.py: the guideline checkers
    build/         # md -> docx/pdf, zotero.lua, CSL, tables, figures
    zotero/        # BBT JSON-RPC client, citation-key pinning checks
    panel/         # model providers reading the review panel; no gate imports it
    literature/    # stored sources, quote and value verification
    reporting/     # recipe-driven checklist transcription
    text/          # masking, tokenising, placeholders, docx and code readers
    data/          # the shipped convention, structural and term rules
    profiles/      # shipped, read-only: checklist recipes, journal profiles
    paths.py       # what is shipped vs what a project writes; see the note below
  r/manuscriptguard/   # mg_emitter() -> results fragment with provenance
  .claude-plugin/   # marketplace.json: the repository is its own plugin marketplace
  plugin/
    skills/  hooks/
  profiles/        # the *workspace*, not shipped data: downloaded guideline documents
    reporting/     #   and the profiles transcribed from them. Gitignored.
  example/         # synthetic pharmacovigilance study: demo and test fixture
  tests/
```

The two `profiles/` directories are not a duplication. Shipped and read-only data travels
inside the package so a wheel carries it; documents a user downloads and profiles built from
them are written into the project being worked on, never into `site-packages`. Keeping both
in one root-level directory is what made `manuscript-guard fetch` fail on every installed
copy — see the note under "What an adversarial review found".

### What it scaffolds into a paper project

```
<paper>/
  paper.yaml            # target journal, English variant, reporting guideline
  authors.yaml          # author block, CRediT roles, funding, competing interests
  analysis/             # R or Python; its only output of record is results.json
  results/results.json  # machine-written, never hand-edited, provenance-stamped
  literature/
    sources/            # PDFs and abstracts, filed by citation key
    ledger.yaml         # verified extracted values, each keyed and quoted
  manuscript/*.md       # prose with {{results.x}} / {{lit.y}} and [@citekey]
  manuscript/supplementary/*.md   # the same, built as its own document
  figures/              # scripts that may read results.json and nothing else
  build/                # docx/pdf artifacts, gitignored
  AGENTS.md             # the rules of the project, for any agent working in it
```

`AGENTS.md` is there because the skills and the hooks reach an agent only where they were
installed, and several agent tools read that one file at a project's root on their own. It
holds what the guarantee rests on, on one short page: machine-written files are not edited,
`check` runs before a build, and nobody but `check` decides that the manuscript is clean. It
is worded to hold in any project at any time, because it is written once: a finding is never
typed, though a convention, a pointer, a label or a name is; `check` decides for the stage
the project declares; and for how to install the skills it points to the README without
saying what the README holds for which tool. Where it does not hold, Known gaps says so. It
names no agent tool. Like every file of the scaffold it is never written over an existing
one; where a repository already has an `AGENTS.md` that does not mention the toolkit, `init`
prints the rules to add, because an agent there would otherwise read rules that say nothing
of `results/`. It is advice to the reader and enforces nothing: the gates do that.

`manuscript/supplementary/` is read by every gate that reads prose — a fabricated number in a
supplementary table is still fabricated, and a supplement nobody checks is the obvious place
to put one — and excluded from the two places that mean the main text specifically: the
journal's word and display-item limits, and the count the title page declares to the editor.
It builds as `supplementary.docx` and reaches the pack as its own file. A directory rather
than a declaration, matching how figures and results already work, and because a heading can
be renamed without anyone noticing what left the submission.

A document of its own also comes back from a co-author on its own. `import` compared every
returned document with a fresh build of the paper, so an edited `supplementary.docx` reported
every paragraph of the paper as deleted in Word and applied none of its own edits. The source
stamp cannot tell the two documents apart: both are built from the same sources and carry
the same one. The paragraph identifiers can, because each names its source file. A document
whose identifiers all come from `manuscript/supplementary/` is compared with a fresh build of
the supplement, and one whose identifiers all come from the paper with a build of the paper.
One carrying both is refused: neither build accounts for it. Word drops the identifier of a
single paragraph it pastes, so only two or more paragraphs pasted across bring one along. A
document carrying none is refused too when the project has a supplement, since it could be
either. Whether there is a supplement is read from the source files: a supplement of
headings and tables carries no identifier, and read from the identifiers it was taken for no
supplement, so its document was compared with the paper.

`authors.yaml` is structured rather than prose because journals want more than name and
affiliation: CRediT roles per author, corresponding-author contact block, equal-
contribution groups, ORCID, funding and competing interests. One validated file fills the
title page, the declarations section and the submission form, and the submission gate
refuses to build while a required field is empty. A human-readable Markdown version is
rendered from it.

## The gates

All deterministic, all runnable in CI without Claude.

| | Gate | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| G1 | Results freshness | a results file whose script, or an input that script declared, has changed since it was written; a dataset's date pinned to other data than the results were computed from |
| G2 | Number classification | a numeric token is unclassified, or a display value has no bound claim |
| G3 | Figures | a number in a figure's output or in its source is not traceable to results |
| G4 | Journal profile | word counts, structure, reference style, required statements |
| G5 | Reporting checklist | a checklist item is unaddressed |
| G6 | AI-writing lint | banned constructions and cadence tells; words to the reviewers left in the paper |
| G7 | Citation integrity | unpinned or unresolvable citation key; literature claim with no stored source |
| G8 | Cross-artifact consistency | a quantity differs between abstract, results, table and figure |
| G9 | Methods drift | analysis code changed since the Methods text was last reconciled; per step, a step or the text pointing at it changed since the pair was read |
| G10 | Figure review | a figure has no current review, or its review raised concerns |
| G11 | Panel review | no review round, a stale review, a file nobody read, or an unanswered major finding |
| G12 | Methods appropriateness | the analysis plan does not answer the question asked |
| G13 | Response to reviewers | a point unanswered, or a claimed revision that did not happen |
| G14 | Abbreviations, terms, spelling and notation | never: it warns when an abbreviation is used before it is defined, defined twice, defined for nothing or never defined, when the manuscript uses a term its author gave up for another, when a word is in the spelling of the English the paper does not declare, when a P value, an interval or a percentage is written in two ways, and when a number runs into its unit |
| G15 | Models and their variables | a model of an outcome its kind is not for, a variable entered as another kind than it was declared, a reference or a level other than the declared one, an undeclared variable, a fit that did not converge or has a level without events, rows dropped and never stated (warnings: few events for each coefficient, an ordinal variable entered as a trend, a model the Methods name and the analysis did not fit) |
| G16 | The data and their dictionary | at submission: a dictionary nothing was checked against, an entry or a rule no count covers, counts neither the Methods nor the supplement bind (warnings before; a variable the analysis uses with no entry warns, from the analysis stage) |

Plus one code that belongs to no gate: `gate-errored`, raised when a gate itself throws. It
is in no stage's deferral list and so fails everywhere, because a checker that could not
check is not a pass. Where what the gate threw is the project's own error about a file it
reads, a review record that is not UTF-8 for one, the finding carries that sentence, which
names the file, and does not call it a bug.

And one for the manuscript itself: `manuscript-unreadable`, for a manuscript file whose text
cannot be had, because it is not UTF-8 or the system will not open it. Each gate that reads
the manuscript stops at such a file, so it is reported once for each file, at the file and
the line, with the gates that did not run. The other gates report as usual. It fails at
every stage too. Outside `check`, a command that reads the manuscript's text says the same
sentence and exits 2. Of those, the dry run of a review panel is the one that does not: it
decodes the files itself, names the file and exits 2, with neither the byte and the line nor
the encoding. `review` reads only the bytes, for the digest, and the note after an edit reads
the text with the bytes it cannot decode replaced; neither says anything of the encoding.

And two that `check` takes from the build, under `BUILD`, without making a document. One is
the shapes the build would refuse, read from the sources. The other is TeX in the text that
the Word writer would leave out, `tex-in-the-text`. For that one `check` runs pandoc, once
for the paper and once for its supplement, on the text the build would hand it, and reports
what the build refuses, in the build's sentence, at the file and the line. It fails from
`drafting` on, and the build's warning of a layout command, `tex-does-nothing`, comes with
it. Like the reading of a PDF, this finding depends on a program outside the package, and
on its version, as the build does: a pandoc that reads a line otherwise than the one CI
pins reports otherwise, in `check` and in the build alike. Where pandoc is not on PATH,
`check` does not judge TeX in the text. Its exit code is that of a pass, and it says so
once, in a note: `tex-not-judged`, whose severity is `info` and whose code is its own, with
the count `documents_read_for_tex` at 0. Every other gate runs as usual. `check` gives
pandoc ten seconds for each document and then stops it: a document pandoc has not read by
then, one it cannot read, and a pandoc that cannot be run are each that same note, for that
document.

**Tables and figures are generated from results, never hand-authored.** Tables are emitted
by code from `results.json`; figure scripts may read `results.json` and nothing else. This
closes the hole that, in the predecessor project, let a wrong count reach Table 1 and
survive every check.

## Decisions

| Question | Decision |
|---|---|
| Repository scope | Reusable toolkit; no paper |
| Markdown ↔ Zotero docx | Markdown authoritative, docx regenerated with live citations |
| Enforcement | Hard fail on any unclassified number |
| Analysis stack | R for statistics, Python for tooling; analysis language pluggable |
| Packaging | pip package plus Claude Code plugin |
| Worked example | Synthetic pharmacovigilance disproportionality study |
| Review panels | Composition derived from field and journal; second panel blinded to round one |
| Licence | MIT |
| Reporting guidelines in v1 | STROBE, RECORD, RECORD-PE, CONSORT, SPIRIT, PRISMA, TRIPOD, ARRIVE |
| Tables and figures | Both generated from results; hand-authoring forbidden |
| Author voice | No personal voice to match; generic scientific register |
| English variant | User-configurable, overridden by the journal profile |
| Abstract-only sources | Recorded and flagged in reports; not grounds for failing a build |

## Build order

1. ~~**Contracts.**~~ **Done.** Skeleton, packaging, CI. Schemas for results, ledger,
   attested, authors, paper. An emitter in Python and R with provenance stamping. Gate G1.
2. ~~**The number guarantee.**~~ **Done.** Placeholder syntax and substitution,
   numeric-token classifier, convention allowlist, figure-literal extraction,
   cross-artefact consistency. Gates G2, G3, G8, with the corruption harness below.
3. ~~**Build pipeline.**~~ **Done.** pandoc with `zotero.lua` for live citations, an
   offline mode using the committed `.bib`, emitted tables, figure placement, and gate G7.
4. ~~**Literature ledger.**~~ **Done.** Sources filed by citation key, quote and value
   verified against the stored source, attestations restricted to people, and a skill for
   Chrome-driven retrieval.
5. ~~**Compliance.**~~ **Done.** Journal profiles and reporting checklists as retrieved
   data, with gates G4 and G5 and two retrieval skills. See the note below on why no
   official checklist ships.
6. ~~**Writing quality.**~~ **Done** apart from the pre-analysis design gate. AI-writing
   lint (G6) derived from the Wikipedia essay, methods-drift detection (G9), and skills for
   both.
7. ~~**Review panels.**~~ **Done.** Recorded panels, review records as the contract, a
   blinded second round, and severity that depends on whether a submission is being built.
8. ~~**Example and public documentation.**~~ **Done.** The submission pack, the
   pre-analysis design gate carried over from phase 6, and the worked example throughout.

Phases 1 and 2 carry the guarantee; everything after is additive.

## Provenance depth of literature values

Every literature value carries one of three depths:

| Depth | Meaning | Requires |
|---|---|---|
| `full-text` | extracted from a stored full text | stored source file, locator, verbatim quote |
| `abstract-only` | extracted from a stored abstract | stored abstract file, verbatim quote |
| `user-attested` | the author read a source the toolkit could not retrieve | attester, date, locator, statement |

`full-text` and `abstract-only` live in `literature/ledger.yaml`. **`user-attested` values
live in their own file, `literature/attested.yaml`**, so that the set of numbers resting on
human attestation rather than a stored artefact is trivially auditable — by a co-author, a
reviewer, or the author six months later. Both files feed the same `lit.` namespace, and
G7 reports the three depths separately. Abstract-only status is flagged but never fails a
build; a `user-attested` entry missing its attester or statement does fail.

## A pointer names what the document carries

"As Table 4 shows" is a number like any other, and G2 let it through as a cross-reference:
the rule read the word and whatever digits followed it. So "In step 1204 reports were
excluded, as Table 4000 and Figure 9 show" passed whole, a count hidden behind "step" and
two pointers at nothing. The example called its two tables "Table 2" and "Table 3" from the
day its first table moved to the supplement as Table S1, and nothing said so: the build
prints a table's caption as written and numbers nothing. LaTeX refuses a `\ref` to a label
nobody defined; G2 now does the same for a pointer typed as text. Each finding fails from
the internal-review stage, Basile's choice on 2026-10-14: while the draft is written its
tables move and are numbered again.

What the document carries is counted only where the count is known, Basile's choice on
2026-10-15. A kind, tables or figures, of one document, the main text or the supplement, is
checked where every one of them is placed by its binding, `{{table.<key>}}` or
`{{figure.<key>}}`, counted in the order the files print. "Table 3" names the main text's
third table; "Table S1", "Supplementary Table 1", "Supplemental Table 1", "eTable 1",
"Extended Data Table 1", "Appendix Table 1" and "Table 1 in the Supplement" the supplement's
first. A pointer to one there is not is `pointer-to-nothing`, a list read whole ("Tables 1
and 2", "Figures 2–4", "Tables S1–3" being S1 to S3), and a list joined by a word only after
a plural: "Table 2 and 3 patients" is one pointer. Where a document places one of a kind by
hand (a pipe, grid, simple or multiline table, a caption line, an image, raw HTML) or none
by its binding, as a paper whose figures go to the journal as files of their own does, its
pointers to that kind are not checked, and one note says so (`pointers-unchecked`). The
first version counted tables and images written by hand as well; its review found correct
papers failed by every form of either it did not count, and by figures sent as files.
Those a paper sends to the journal as files of their own, cited in the text and placed
nowhere in it (a flow chart drawn by hand beside a forest plot that is bound), are declared
in `paper.yaml`, `displays: {figures_as_files: 1}` and its three siblings for tables and the
supplement, Basile's choice on 2026-10-15: they are counted with the bound ones, numbered
with them, and have to be cited in order like them. A pointer that opens its paragraph and
ends in a stop or a colon ("**Table 2.** Counts") is a caption typed above a table and no
citation of it; one that opens a line inside a paragraph ends a sentence. The main text's tables and figures are held to
what ICMJE asks for: each cited (`display-not-cited`), and first cited in the order they
are numbered (`cited-out-of-order`). "Number tables consecutively in the order of their
first citation in the text" and "Be sure that each table is cited in the text", from
icmje.org, Preparing for Submission, read 2026-10-14; it says the same of the figures'
order and gives the supplement no rule, so none is applied to it.

The words that point at nothing a gate can check, a step, a panel, a box, an item, take a
small number only: up to 20, as `categorical-label` does, and an item up to 99, since a
checklist runs to 27 items. "Step 1204" is a count. A list after a plural is read as
pointers by G2 too, where only its first number was before: "Tables 1 and 2 show" left its
2 unbound.

## A pointer the build numbers

A typed pointer can only be checked. It goes stale every time a table moves, and the author
renumbers it by hand once G2 says so. LaTeX's `\ref`, and the cross-references of MyST
(Jupyter Book) and pandoc-crossref, print the number from a label instead. Jupyter Book was
looked at on 2026-10-20 for ideas, and this is the one taken: its executed inline expressions
would run code at build time, and its web and JATS outputs are not what journals take. The
label is the key the display is placed by already, so nothing new is declared:
`{{ref.table.baseline}}` prints "Table 2" where `{{table.baseline}}` is the second table the
main text places, and "Table S1" where it is the supplement's first. The count is G2's
(`gates/pointers.py`, `display_numbers`), so the gate and the build cannot disagree about
it: one document at a time, its files in the order the build prints them. Move the table and
every mention follows, and a mention cannot point at a table that is not there.

Basile's choices of 2026-10-20, each asked with the alternatives:

- **Two forms.** `{{ref.table.key}}` prints the pointer whole. `{{num.table.key}}` prints the
  number alone, "2" or "S1", for a list or a range the author writes: "Tables
  {{num.table.a}} and {{num.table.b}}". A list binding that wrote the "and" itself was the
  other choice, and it would have decided the serial comma and the dash for every paper. A
  num is held to the words before it: G2 reads the text with each binding printed, and a num
  that the pointer around it reads as another kind or the other document ("Figure
  {{num.table.a}}", "Supplementary Table {{num.table.a}}" for a table of the main text), or
  that no pointer word stands before, is `pointer-word-mismatch`. That fails from the
  internal review, as a typed pointer's findings do: the words go stale as the table moves,
  the way a typed number does. A ref is held the same way, so "Supplementary
  {{ref.table.a}}" is refused too.
- **The journal's form.** How a pointer is written is the target journal's: the profile's
  `pointers:` gives a form for each kind of each document, "eTable {n}", "Fig. {n}",
  "Supplementary Table {n}", quoted under `pointers.<kind>` like any rule of the page. Where
  it gives none: Table {n}, Figure {n}, Table S{n}, Figure S{n}. A num prints the word of the
  form that holds the number, so "S1" under "Table S{n}" and "1" under "eTable {n}". A form
  G2 does not read back, whole, as a pointer to that kind of that document is
  `pointer-form-unread`, from the start: a ref printed in it would be a pointer G2 could not
  hold to anything.
- **Exact numbers only.** Where a document also places a kind by hand, or sends some to the
  journal as files of their own (`displays:`), where a bound one falls among them is not
  known, and a ref to that kind of that document is `ref-number-unknown`. So is a ref to a
  key placed twice, which has two numbers. These fail from the drafting stage, since the
  build would have nothing to print, and the build refuses them too. Numbering the files
  after the placed ones was the other choice, and it is wrong for the usual case, a flow
  chart drawn by hand that is Figure 1.

A ref to a key nothing places, or one that names no kind (`{{ref.baseline}}`), is
`unresolved-binding`, as a value's typo is. G2 reads a printed ref as a citation where it
stands, so the main text's tables are cited in order and each one cited
(`cited-out-of-order`, `display-not-cited`) with refs and typed pointers mixed; it is never
`pointer-to-nothing`. The build, the annotated copy (green, labelled with the key and the
display it was counted from), `render`, the text a review panel is sent, the response to the
reviewers, the copy of the manuscript a revision round keeps as submitted and the abstract
for the journal's portal print the same number (`revision.displays`); the response round
looked for a quoted sentence in text that still read `{{ref.` until round 1 of #378.
`explain` lists each ref with what it prints and from which display.

In Word, the number a ref prints is a binding like any other: the marked build bookmarks it,
and a co-author who changes "Table 2" to "Table 3" has the paragraph refused, with "'Table 2'
comes from ref.table.two_by_two, numbered where the build places it". A paragraph that is
only a ref gets an identifier, as one that is only a value does. `reworded` reads a ref as a
binding, so a pointer typed and then bound is not a rewording.

`bind --pointers` turns typed pointers into refs, a list's numbers into nums, each only where
the binding prints what is typed, character for character: "Table S1" under "Table S{n}", not
"Supplementary Table 1", which would print as "Table S1". A range that names a number it does
not write ("Tables 1-3") is not offered. With `--apply` the example's every pointer is bound
and its build prints what it printed before.

### A caption carries its display's number

Basile's third choice of 2026-10-20: the build prints an emitted table's caption after the
table's number, "Table 2. Reports by drug group.", from the same count and in the journal's
form, and a table that emits no caption gets its number alone as one. The analysis cannot
know the number, which depends on where the text places the table. A figure's caption is a
paragraph the author writes under it, and opens with `{{ref.figure.forest}}.`, which prints
"Figure 1." and is styled as a caption by the build as a typed "Figure 1." always was.

A caption the analysis numbered already, "Table 2. Baseline ...", "Table 2 Baseline" or
"**Table 2.** Baseline", is printed as it is: adding the number again would print "Table 2.
Table 2.", in every paper that numbered its own captions before. So is the emitted caption
of a table that has a caption typed beside it, as a paragraph or a heading set straight
above it, which was how a paper numbered its tables before refs: the typed caption prints
the number (round 1 of #381 found both printed twice). A caption between two tables is the
caption of the one it names, and the other keeps its number (round 2). A typed caption's
number is set off by a stop, a colon, the end of its bold or a dash between spaces: "Table 2
shows the counts." above a table is a sentence. G2 holds an emitted caption's number to the
table's, and so it holds a caption typed beside a display: the block directly under a
figure placed by its binding, or directly above or under a table, when it opens with a
pointer that cites nothing there (a caption, or a heading). One that names no display it
stands beside, typed or printed by a ref, is `caption-names-another`, failing from the
internal review as the other pointer findings do; a block between two tables is the caption
of whichever it names. A heading with prose between it and the table, as the example's
supplement writes "## Table S1. Code lists", captions nothing and is not held.

## The corruption harness

The claim "no stale number" is worth exactly as much as the evidence that the gate catches
one. `tests/test_corruption.py` is therefore adversarial rather than illustrative.

Its headline test takes **every binding in the example manuscript, one at a time, and
replaces it with the literal value it currently resolves to** — then requires that
manuscript to fail. This is the hardest form of the problem, because at the moment of
corruption the number on the page is still *correct*; it is stale only in waiting. A
checker that compares numbers against a backing set passes every one of them. This one
fails every one, because in source a results-derived number may not be a literal at all.
As of the first build: 14 distinct bindings, 14 caught.

The rest of the harness covers the other routes a number goes wrong: a hand-edited results
file, changed or deleted input data, a modified analysis script, a typo in a binding, a
malformed binding, a declared value nothing quotes, a hand-authored table, an edited
figure, a figure script that stopped reading results, one quantity emitted under two names,
and near-miss conventions such as `p < 0.37` that a laxer allowlist would wave through.

**A check that read nothing says so.** A gate that passes having read nothing is the same
failure as one that misses a number, and it happened three ways at once: `audit --strict` of
an empty paper printed "0 numeric tokens" and exited 0; `bind` said "every number in the
manuscript is accounted for" of a folder with no Markdown in it; and a manuscript kept as
`.qmd`, under `_drafts/` or behind a mistyped `paths.manuscript` failed `check` only through
the results it left unquoted, 21 findings that named everything but the folder, and passed
at the design and analysis stages. Now `audit --strict` fails a paper it read no number in,
`bind` refuses a manuscript it cannot read (exit 2), and G2 reports `manuscript-empty`, one
G0 finding that names the folder, the pattern it read and what it found there instead, in
place of the unquoted results; it fails from the drafting stage. `tests/test_reads_nothing.py`
holds every gate and every subcommand in a table: what it reads, its count, and what it does
when it reads nothing, a finding, an exit code, or a written reason why nothing is fine. A
new gate or command is not in the table and fails that test until someone decides.

## Decisions taken during construction

- **The digest of a results fragment is a `.sha256` sidecar, not a field inside it.**
  Hand-editing the one file the toolkit trusts was otherwise detected by nothing. A field
  inside the fragment would require canonical-JSON agreement between Python and R, which
  float formatting alone will break; "hash the bytes you just wrote" is the same operation
  in every language. This detects accidents, not adversaries, and is documented as such.
- **`display` is resolved at emit time and written into the fragment.** Any consumer in any
  language reads one field and gets the string the prose will show.
- **Axis ticks are declared per figure in a `<name>.guard.yaml` sidecar.** A figure
  legitimately contains numbers that are neither results nor prose conventions. Declaring
  them per figure keeps the exemption small and visible instead of weakening G3 globally.
- **A figure script that ignores the results fails only when its figure prints numbers.**
  A flow diagram has no reason to read results; a figure with numeric annotations whose
  script never opens the results file is drawing them from somewhere unverifiable.
- **The scaffold omits optional fields rather than writing them empty**, so the first
  `check` on a new project reads as a to-do list of real work.

## Figures get three checks, not one

A figure is the easiest place for a stale number to survive: rendered once, looked at
rather than read, and never touched by a prose check. So it is checked three ways.

**The rendered output.** Numeric text in the figure's text layer must match a results
display string or classify as prose would. Axis ticks are declared per figure in
`<name>.guard.yaml`.

**The source.** The classifier runs over the figure script itself, because output checking
alone leaves a hole that is invisible from either side: a script that reads the results
*and also* types one annotation passes the output check, since the typed number equals the
right value today, and passes any script-level check, since the script does read the
results. Two rules apply. Numbers inside string literals are judged exactly as prose, so
`"95% CI"` passes and `"ROR 3.84"` does not. Numbers in code are judged by syntactic
position: a number under a presentation parameter or inside a plotting call is layout,
anything else is a candidate claim. The context comes from a small two-language lexer that
tracks the bracket stack, so `scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2))` gives each number the
chain `c > breaks > scale_y_log10` and one lookup settles it.

The presentation list is deliberately narrow. `x`, `y`, `n` and `digits` are **not** on it,
because allowing bare coordinates would allow `data.frame(x = c(1, 2, 3))` — data typed
into a figure script, which gets its own error message.

**The marks the script computes.** Labels drawn from the results say nothing about the marks.
`sns.barplot` draws a bootstrap 95% interval of the mean unless told not to, with no seed;
`stat_summary` draws a mean and its standard error, `geom_smooth` a fitted line and its
band, `geom_jitter` a jitter from a seed drawn at random. None of these passes through the
results file: the interval drawn can differ from the one the text quotes, it ignores the
clustering the analysis accounted for, and where it is random it changes at every render,
so the figure's review goes stale each time. The script itself does the same when it takes
a spread with numpy's `std`, which divides by n where pandas and R divide by n - 1, samples
rows, draws at random with no seed, or drops the rows with a missing value. Each such call
in `data/figure_estimates.yaml`, with what it does as its library's own reference page says,
is a warning (`figure-estimates`) unless an argument turns it off (`errorbar=None`), its
seed or divisor is given (`seed=`, `ddof=`), a seed set in the script settles a random one,
or the figure's `<name>.guard.yaml` gives a reason under `allow_estimates`.

**A human or model reading the picture (G10).** Gate G10 requires a current review record
per figure. See below.

## Reading the figure

Some errors in figures are invisible to every parser. A truncated axis that makes a small
difference look decisive. A legend naming a series the plot no longer contains. A caption
describing the figure the author meant to make. Every number can trace to the results and
the picture can still mislead.

So the reading is delegated to a model or a person, and `figures/<name>.review.yaml`
records it: who reviewed it, when, seven required checks, findings, and a verdict. G10
enforces what can be enforced mechanically — that a review exists, covered all seven checks,
and applies to the figure as it now stands. **It cannot verify that the review was any
good.** Same bargain as `literature/attested.yaml`.

Two details worth stating plainly, because both were overstated here before.

A per-check `note` is *optional* in the schema, though the schema's own description explains
why it should not be ("a check marked ok with no note is indistinguishable from a check
nobody performed"). It is left optional deliberately — requiring prose produces prose — but
it means the record can be thinner than this paragraph once implied.

And G10 does more than check that the record exists: it reads each finding's own `severity`
and applies it, so a finding recorded as `fail` fails the run and the same observation
recorded as `info` does not. G11 does the same with `severity: major`. That is what "the
record is the contract" means, and it is the one place a model's output can change a
verdict — worth naming, since the README's deterministic-code claim is otherwise absolute.

Two normalisations make review currency workable. Render timestamps and randomly generated
element ids are excluded from the digest, so re-rendering an unchanged figure keeps its
review current while a real change invalidates it. Without that, every build would mark
every review stale, and an author would learn to ignore the gate.

The worked example earned this the hard way. Its first review returned `concerns`: the
manuscript said Figure 1 showed the estimate "against the comparators" and the figure had
one row. Every other gate passed it, because every number in the figure was correct. The
sentence was what was wrong.

## The journal shortlist is a record

The journal-profile skill had the agent propose three to five journals and the author
choose, and said to record the shortlist and the decision in the project without naming a
file or a shape. `journals/shortlist.yaml` is that record, held to a schema
(`contracts/schemas/shortlist.schema.json`):

* the author's criteria, asked for first and written down with who stated them and when:
  the article type, open access and a funder's mandate, the APC budget, speed, the indexing
  required, the audience, and how strong the author judges the contribution, which is their
  statement and never an agent's grade;
* the candidates, each claim made of one with its source URL and the date it was read, the
  recent papers like this one that justify the fit, and the honest risk;
* the ranking and its reasons, the decision and who made it, and the history of earlier
  choices, which is what the skill reads again after a rejection.

Whether a journal is one the registries know follows the pattern of `lookup`: an opt-in
command asks, the answers are kept dated, and `check` reads them offline.
`lookup --journals` asks the NLM Catalog (through E-utilities: ESearch on `<issn>[IS]`,
ESummary's `currentindexingstatus`) whether each ISSN's journal is currently indexed for
MEDLINE, and DOAJ (its search API, version 4) whether it is listed. It sends an ISSN and
nothing of the manuscript. Each answer is kept in `journals/lookups/<issn>.yaml` with the
digest of what it says. G4 warns when the target journal, found among the candidates by its
profile or by the profile's name, is not currently indexed for MEDLINE on any of its ISSNs
(`journal-not-in-medline`), and when it is open access and DOAJ lists it on none
(`journal-not-in-doaj`). With no target journal set, the journal the decision chose is read.
A target journal that is none of the candidates is said in a note
(`journal-target-not-shortlisted`): the decision is not taken for it, since it may name
another journal (round 1 of #321). Being listed is evidence against a predatory journal, not
proof, and a sound one can be outside them; the author can say why in the candidate
(`outside_medline`, `outside_doaj`), and the warning is then a note that quotes them. Neither
ever fails (decided 2026-10-15). A record that is missing or edited, or an answer that did
not come, is no evidence either way: a note (`journal-not-looked-up`). A journal ranked or
chosen that is not among the candidates is a warning (`shortlist-unknown-journal`), and so is
a shortlist that breaks its schema.

Finding the journals that publish papers like this one is the skill's work, not the
command's: a journal-name estimator that takes a title and an abstract, and PubMed. Both are
asked by the agent, with the author's knowledge, and each claim is recorded with its source
and date. The command never sends the manuscript's text anywhere.

## A figure file meets the journal's artwork guide

A journal states the formats it takes, the resolution each kind of figure needs at the width
it prints, the largest file and the longest legend. These were free text in a profile's
`notes`, and the first anyone heard of them was the portal refusing the upload. A profile
now carries them under `figures:`, read from the journal's own artwork guide, with the date
it was read and whether every value was found on it (`confirmed`). G4 holds each figure the
manuscript places to them: its formats (`figure-format`), a raster's resolution at the width
it prints for its kind (`figure-resolution`), its printed height (`figure-height`), the size
of each file (`figure-file-size`), and the paragraph that labels it (`legend-words`). A
raster drawn much larger than it prints is said too (`figure-shrinks`): a figure drawn 165 mm
wide and printed at 89 mm prints the 10 pt text a plotting library draws at 5.4 pt, though
its resolution passes. The size of a raster is read from its own header, PNG, JPEG or TIFF,
with the standard library.

An SVG figure is scaled to the width it prints at, and its text and lines with it, so its
smallest text and its thinnest line are held to the journal's least at that width
(`figure-text-small`, `figure-line-thin`), and a text anchored outside what it shows, its
`viewBox`, is said to be cut off (`figure-text-clipped`). Each text's size and each line's
width is read from the SVG (`gates/figure_svg.py`): set on the element, by the figure's own
stylesheet (svglite strokes every black line there, Illustrator sets sizes through
classes) or inherited, in units whatever unit it is written in, SVG's 16 where none is
set, an em or a percentage of the size around it. It is carried through every transform around the element, a `<use>`
read where it is used and nothing in `<defs>` where it is defined, and a `<tspan>` is a text
of its own, as a sub- or superscript is drawn. A text's size is its height through the
transforms, the length its upright takes: under `scale(2, 0.5)` a text is half its size,
turned a quarter it is twice it. A line is widened by the square root of the transforms'
determinant. The printed size is that, times the printed width over the `viewBox`'s; where
no width is given, at the figure's own width, a width with no unit read as pixels.

A PDF figure is held the same way, read with the standard library (`gates/figure_pdf.py`):
its objects where they stand and inside object streams, its streams where they are
Flate-compressed, which is how plotting libraries write them. A text's size is the size
`Tf` sets, through the text matrix (`Tm`, `Td`), every `cm` around it and a form's
`/Matrix`, as the height that takes on the page; a line's width is the `w` it is stroked
at, through the same, and a path only filled is no line. A form draws with the line width
and the font size of what draws it, as matplotlib's markers do, and a page's content
streams draw as one. The printed size is that times the printed width over the page's: its
CropBox where it has one, else its MediaBox, its height where `/Rotate` turns it a quarter.
A text in a composite (Type 0) font is measured and not quoted, since its bytes may be
glyph numbers. And each font the page uses is said where it is Type 3
(`figure-font-type3`), which matplotlib writes unless `pdf.fonttype` is 42 (its
`rcParamsDefault` says 3, read on 3.9.0), or where its file is not in the PDF
(`figure-font-not-embedded`), as R's `pdf()` leaves Helvetica: a printer then sets the text
in a font of its own.

A figure's print width and kind are in its `<name>.guard.yaml` (`print_width_mm`, `kind`).
Without them the narrowest width the journal prints at is taken, so that a resolution found
too low is too low at any width, and the kind is halftone. A figure placed only in the
supplement is held to the profile's `supplementary:` rules where it has them. All of it is a
warning, and a note where the journal applies the rules only once the paper is accepted
(`applies_from: acceptance`).

## A figure says what it shows to a reader who cannot see it

A screen reader reads a picture's alternative text and nothing else of it, and more
journals ask for one with each figure, in the manuscript's file or in a box of the portal.
The build placed every figure as `![](path)`, so every document it made went out with none.

A figure's alternative text is written once, in its `<name>.guard.yaml` under `alt:`, beside
its print width and kind (decided 2026-10-21, against a line in the manuscript and a field of
the figure review: the first is a convention the round trip would have to learn, the second
the reviewer's words and not the author's). It may quote values by binding, as prose does,
and G3 holds it as G2 holds prose (`gates/figure_alt.py`): a number in it bound to nothing
that is not a convention, a label or a declared term fails from drafting
(`figure-alt-number`), so a value typed into it is stale in waiting as it would be in a
sentence, and a binding that prints no value fails with it (`figure-alt-binding`). A figure
with none is a note while drafting, a warning from internal review, and a failure at
submission where the journal's profile requires one (`figures.alt_text: required`); a text
longer than the profile's `alt_text_max_chars`, counted as printed, warns. The check reads
the stage itself, since the policy table gives a code one stage to fail from and this one
warns before it fails. A figure the supplement places is held to the same, and written
into `supplementary.docx` as the paper's are into `manuscript.docx`; a rule under the
profile's `figures.supplementary` replaces the main one for a figure only the supplement
places, as every artwork rule of G4 does.

The build writes it as the picture's description. Pandoc makes an image alone in its
paragraph a figure and prints its description under it as a caption, so the image is placed
in a span of the class `mg-figure`, `[![text](path)]{.mg-figure}`, where it is not alone and
no caption is printed (pandoc 3.9.0.2: a span holding the image, with its description, is
written with `descr` set and nothing printed; `![](path){alt="..."}` leaves `descr`
empty). The text is written with every ASCII punctuation mark escaped and its white space
folded to single spaces, so that pandoc reads none of it as markup: a property in
`tests/test_properties.py` holds that pandoc reads back each text drawn, with every mark of
emphasis, a link, a citation, maths, raw HTML and a comment in it, as exactly the text, and
two broken rules fail it. `figure_caption.lua` knows a figure's paragraph by that span as
well as by a bare image. `submit` writes every figure's text, as printed, into
`alt-text.md`, and a double-blind build looks for the authors in each picture's
description and title as it does in the text.

Since the build prints it, an HTML comment in the text is read like the rest of it, not
hidden as in prose (round 1 of #387), and only ASCII white space is
folded, so a no-break space typed in it stays. It is held as the prose is in more than its
numbers: a parameter or a release the analysis declares, typed into it, fails as G2 fails it;
the document's stamp covers it, so editing it makes a built document stale; a count bound in
it is held to the data custodian's minimum; and a result it quotes from a synthetic run is
said. A journal that applies its artwork rules from acceptance gets a note for a missing one,
as G4 gives, and so does a text too long.

Whether the text says what the figure shows is not checked by any gate. The figure review
reads it under `readable-and-accessible`, and the figure-review skill says how to write one.

## A figure's colours stay apart for every reader

About one man in twelve and one woman in two hundred of European descent see colour with a
deficiency, most of them red and green nearer than others do. A figure whose two series are
told apart by colour alone can be one series to them, and to anyone reading it printed in
grey. The figure review asked whether "any information depends on colour alone", a question
a reviewer answers by eye, for one kind of vision, their own.

So G3 reads each colour a figure the manuscript places paints its marks in, from the figure
itself (`gates/figure_colours.py`, decided 2026-10-21): from its SVG, every fill and stroke
as the element, its stylesheet or its groups set it, `currentColor` the `color` it inherits,
laid over white at the opacity it is drawn at, its own and its groups' multiplied
(`gates/figure_svg.py`); from its PDF, every path filled or stroked and every text shown,
in the colour `rg`, `g`, `k`, their stroking twins or `sc` and `scn` set, at the opacity of
its graphics state, `q` and `Q` saving and restoring them, a form drawing in its drawer's
(`gates/figure_pdf.py`). A text's colour is kept apart and not compared: text rarely tells
one series from another, and black text beside a dark mark confuses no data. A raster is
not read: its colours blend at every edge of every mark, and guessing which are the marks'
is a heuristic that would warn of colours nobody chose. A figure with no SVG or PDF is
said to be unread (`figure-colours-unread`, a note).

Each pair of the colours is taken through what each dichromacy makes of it, Machado,
Oliveira and Fernandes's model at full severity (IEEE TVCG 2009; the matrices of their
Table 1, applied to linear RGB as colorspacious and R's colorspace apply them), and through
grey, the grey of the same relative luminance. Two colours are far enough apart where their
CIEDE2000 difference is at least 10. No standard sets that number: about 2 is the least an
observer sees between large patches side by side, a figure's lines and points need far more
(Szafir 2018), and Adobe's Leonardo passes a simulated pair at 11. A pair at least 10 apart
to normal vision and less than 10 after is said: `figure-colours-confused` for a deficiency,
a warning and never a failure; `figure-greyscale-confused` for grey, a note, and a warning
where the journal's profile says its figures print in grey (`figures.print: greyscale`) or
the figure's guard file asks (`greyscale: true`). Basile chose both on 2026-10-21. A pair
already less than 10 apart to normal vision is not said, since no deficiency made it so.

**A figure that draws a continuous scale is not compared.** A colormap, or points coloured
by a variable, has neighbours just over 10 apart, and grey, which keeps lightness alone, or a
deficiency, which takes chroma away, brings them under it: every such figure warned (round 1
of #398). Which of a figure's colours are a scale's shades and which a series' is not known
from the colours, and each rule tried for it was wrong one way or the other: leaving a scale
out took in a series near one of its shades (round 2: tab:red beside a heat map in reds, and
tab:green with it, went unsaid); comparing a series with the shades compared two scales with
each other, and two series near one scale's shades still went uncompared (the round on the
fix). Basile chose to narrow the check to what it can decide (2026-10-21): a figure whose
colours chain within 10 of one another, three or more, greys apart, and run through 10 of
lightness or more, is said to draw a scale (`figure-colours-scale`, a note), and its colours
are not compared; nor are a figure's of more
than 300 colours (`figure-colours-many`), since finding a scale among them takes time in their
square. Its review looks at it, and a scale and its series drawn as figures of their own have
the series compared. The two conditions on a chain keep an ordinary figure compared: greys
chain easily (a panel's background, its grid, a legend's frame) and are never confused with
one another; and the light bands of several series, each laid over white at one opacity,
chain by hue at one lightness, where a colormap runs through it (the round on the
narrowing: tab:red, tab:orange and tab:olive at 0.1 are 6.6 and 7.1 apart).

Where two series are told apart by more than colour, a line style or a label on each line,
the figure's guard file says so under `allow_colours`, the pair (or one colour of it) and
the reason, and the warning is a note that quotes it.

A figure the supplement places is read and compared as the paper's are (Basile, 2026-10-21:
the supplement is held to the main text's rules). A `print` under the profile's
`figures.supplementary` replaces the main one for a figure only the supplement places, so a
journal that prints the paper in grey and puts its supplement online in colour is said so.

The implementation is the standard library's (`colour.py`): sRGB's transfer function and
matrix, CIELAB under D65, CIEDE2000 as Sharma, Wu and Dalal write it out, and the three
matrices. `tests/test_colour.py` holds CIEDE2000 to the 34 pairs Sharma, Wu and Dalal publish,
in both orders, and the simulation to what colorspacious, which implements Machado's model on
its own, makes of four colours. Okabe and Ito's eight have no pair any deficiency makes one,
and matplotlib's default red and green, 72 apart, are under 5 apart with deuteranopia: the
model says what the literature says of both.

## Palettes are other people's, and each says what the check makes of it

A figure's colours are its author's choice, and the toolkit never draws the figure. What it
can do is hand the author palettes by name and say, for each, what the colour check makes
of it (decided 2026-10-21: every palette of the collections asked for, derived, with Python
and R helpers, a `palettes` command and a `figure-design` skill).

**The palettes.** MetBrewer, MoMAColors, NatParksPalettes, PNWColors and wesanderson, the
artists' and photographers' palettes Basile asked for; Okabe and Ito's eight; ColorBrewer's
schemes, each for every number of classes it offers; viridis, magma, inferno and plasma;
cividis; and Crameri's scientific colour maps, version 8: 260 palettes. Each collection's
licence was read at its source before any colour was copied (CC0, MIT, Apache 2.0 and
Battelle's BSD-style licence all allow it with their notices), and each is credited in
ATTRIBUTION.md with its notice beside the data, `data/palettes_LICENSES.txt`.

**Derived, never typed.** `tools/derive_palettes.py` reads each collection's colours from its
own file at a pinned commit, refusing a file whose SHA-256 is not the one written beside it,
as the spelling list is derived from VarCon: the R lists of MetBrewer, MoMAColors,
NatParksPalettes, PNWColors and wesanderson, ColorBrewer's JSON export, the CC0 source of
viridis, PNNL's cividis table and cmcrameri's copy of Crameri's tables. It writes the licence
file from the collections' own licence files the same way. Only Okabe and Ito's eight colours
are typed, as the numbers their page publishes. With the files in a folder named by
`MANUSCRIPT_GUARD_PALETTE_SOURCES`, a test derives both files again and compares them byte for
byte. The R package carries the same two files, held equal by a test.

**What the check makes of each** (`palettes.assess`), written into the file when it is
derived and recomputed by a test, so a change to the check that changes a verdict has the
file derived again: for a set of colours, how many of them, taken as its collection takes
them for that many, stay at least 10 apart (CIEDE2000) to normal vision, for every reader
with protanopia, deuteranopia or tritanopia, and in grey; for every palette, whether its
lightness runs one way, turns once or neither, judged at eleven points along a continuous
map (its 256 colours, rounded to 8 bits, step back and forth by a fraction of a unit), and
whether each deficiency keeps that. Beside it, what the collection claims where it claims
anything. MetBrewer calls Archambault colour-blind friendly; three of its colours stay 10
apart for every reader. Both are shown, and the skill says both.

**Taking n colours** follows each collection's own rule, so a palette here gives what its
own package gives: ColorBrewer's scheme of n, and for fewer than its smallest scheme of
three, n evenly spaced along that one, its two ends for two, where `scale_colour_brewer`
takes the first two, one arm and the middle of a diverging scheme; MetBrewer's, MoMAColors', NatParksPalettes' and
PNWColors' colours whose rank in the palette's order is at most n, in the palette's
sequence (`met.brewer`'s `palette[[1]][which(palette[[2]] %in% c(1:n))]`); otherwise the first
n; and n evenly spaced along a continuous map. More than a set has is refused, and `ramp`
interpolates, in a straight line through sRGB as R's `colorRampPalette` does (a channel that
falls on a half may round the other way). Python: `palettes.colours`, `cycle`, `use`,
`cmap`, and `figure_style`, matplotlib settings sized to the target journal: its width, its
smallest text and thinnest line or more (7 pt and 0.5 pt where the journal's least is less),
and fonts kept as text in an SVG and embedded in a PDF, as G3 and G4 read them. R:
`mg_palette`, `mg_palettes`, `scale_colour_mg`, `scale_fill_mg`, `mg_theme` and
`mg_figure_size`, from the same file.

**Choosing** is the author's, with the `figure-design` skill: it proposes two or three
layouts for the figure's kind and two or three palettes for the number of colours it needs,
says which every reader can read, offers an artist's palette the check does not pass only
with that said, and applies the choice to the author's script. `manuscript-guard palettes`
lists and filters (`--kind`, `--colours`, `--safe`, `--collection`) and shows one with its
licence (`--show`). With `--colours n`, `--safe` holds the n colours the palette gives, a
continuous map's evenly spaced along it, apart for every reader, as G3 holds a figure of n
classes (rounds 2 and 3 of #406: PuOr's seven and viridis's seven do not stay apart, though
PuOr's ten do and viridis runs one way). The check that counts is still G3's, on the
rendered figure, the supplement's figures as the paper's.

## The journal's citation style is used by every build

A profile names the journal's citation style as the CSL style repository and Zotero name it
(`references: {csl: the-lancet}`). Only the live build used it, by handing the name to
Zotero. The offline build, which is what CI and a co-author without Zotero get, formatted in
pandoc's default style unless `--csl` named a file. `manuscript-guard style` now fetches the
style once from the repository's own files and keeps it in the project, under
`profiles/journals/styles/`. A name is asked for at the repository's root, where its
independent styles are, and then under `dependent/`. A name with `.csl`, a file's, is
refused with the name to give instead, and G4 says the same (round 1 of #322: it was asked
for as `vancouver.csl.csl`). A dependent style holds no formatting of
its own and names the style it formats like (`<link rel="independent-parent">`), so that
style is fetched from the root and kept beside it. A record, `<name>.yaml`, holds each
file's address, the SHA-256 of its bytes, the licence it names, the day, and the style's
citation format.

An offline build without `--csl` formats with the stored style, and `--csl` still wins. The
folder of whatever style the build is given is put on pandoc's resource path after the
working directory, because pandoc looks there for a dependent style's parent, by its name,
before it would fetch it: an offline build of a stored dependent style opens no connection.
A live build hands the same name to Zotero, as before, so both format alike where Zotero
has the style installed. G4 warns where the profile names a style and the project holds no
copy (`journal-style-not-stored`); where a stored file is not what was fetched
(`journal-style-changed`), which the build then does not use; and where the style's
citation format, the dependent style's own or else its parent's, disagrees with the
profile's `numbered:` (`journal-style-format`). The styles are the CSL project's, under
CC BY-SA 3.0, and live in the author's project: nothing of them is in this package, and the
tests write their own.

## The build

The .docx is regenerated from Markdown every time and never edited or patched. That is what
makes a stale number impossible rather than merely unlikely: nothing is ever carried across
by hand, so there is nothing to forget.

Two modes, and the choice is a fact about the machine rather than a preference:

- **live** — pandoc with Better BibTeX's `zotero.lua`, which queries the running Zotero and
  writes real `ADDIN ZOTERO_ITEM CSL_CITATION` fields that Word's Zotero plugin adopts.
  Verified end to end: both bracketed `[@key]` and narrative `@key` produce fields, the
  latter only once `author-in-text: true` is set in the generated front matter, which is
  the second of the two chores the first pipeline test uncovered.
- **offline** — pandoc `--citeproc` against a committed `literature/references.bib` and a
  CSL style. Citations become formatted text rather than live fields. This is what a
  co-author without Zotero gets, and what CI builds with, and it is why the `.bib` is
  committed rather than exported on demand. `manuscript-guard sync-bib` rewrites the `.bib`
  from Zotero, containing exactly the keys the manuscript cites.

`zotero.lua` is fetched and cached under `build/.cache/` rather than vendored: it belongs to
Better BibTeX and tracks its behaviour, so a pinned copy would go stale.

After a live build the document is reopened and its Zotero fields counted, because the
filter fails quietly when Zotero is closed — the result looks fine until someone clicks
Refresh in Word and every citation vanishes.

CI installs the pandoc version pinned as `MANUSCRIPT_GUARD_REQUIRE_PANDOC` in
`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, and with that variable set the test suite refuses to start
unless that pandoc is on PATH. Until it did, no test job had pandoc: every test that needs
it skipped on every job, and none failed for want of it.

**Tables are emitted, not written.** `em.table(...)` puts a table in the results fragment,
`{{table.key}}` places it, and the build renders a pipe table. A hand-typed table is the
most reliable place for a stale number to survive: long, dull to re-read, never diffed. An
emitted table nothing places is a coverage failure, exactly like an unquoted value.

**Figures are placed, captions are prose.** `{{figure.key}}` resolves to the rendered file,
preferring raster or PDF over SVG because Word's SVG support is uneven and a journal's
production system is worse. The caption stays in the manuscript as ordinary prose, so it is
checked like prose and can carry bindings.

**A line of dashes opens no block.** Below the front matter, pandoc may read a line of
dashes with a line directly under it as the start of YAML metadata, when the lines under it
are a mapping, or of a table, and prints no heading from either. YAML there is merged over
the build's header with the later value winning, so a `title:` in it replaced paper.yaml's
on the title page; and the gates, reading prose, took the closing rule for a setext
underline, so `note: |` over an indented `Methods`, or `Methods` alone in a one-cell table,
under `## Results` headed the paragraph after, and `p < 0.001` in it passed as the alpha
chosen in advance. Both of pandoc's readers were modelled in the heading scan first, along
with what the build's bookmarks do to them, and two rounds of review each found the model
and the build printing different headings, the second round's worst caused by the first
round's fix. So the shape is refused instead (`rule-opens-a-block`), by `check` and by the
build.

The refusal first exempted the underline of a setext heading, and that exemption was a model
of its own. Four reviews each found titles the heading scan took and pandoc did not: a div's
fence, an HTML tag, LaTeX, a table's row, indented code, and a line continuing a paragraph,
a quotation or a list item (the first); a comment on the line above, which pandoc reads as
no break (the second); a table placeholder with spaces in its braces or after other text
(the third); and a comment after the underline, a comment whose last line looks like a
heading, a listing pandoc does not make, and an `===` underline pandoc does not read above
the title (the fourth, with four false passes through `check` and the build). The fourth
also found the rule's other side open: `# Methods` or a quotation over `---` and a blank
line is a setext heading to pandoc, made before the `#` heading or the quotation. So a line
of dashes now passes only between blank lines, where pandoc reads nothing but a thematic
break, and a heading is written with `#`. Nothing in `example/`, the scaffold or the skills
underlines a heading with dashes; `===` has no dashes to misread and is untouched. A line in
code, a comment or the front matter is not read, and a comment that closes on the line is
taken off in front of it, as pandoc reads on from its `-->`. The fifth review found pandoc
starting a block partway along a line, behind an HTML tag or comment, a TeX command, or a
list, definition or footnote marker, and reading the dashes after it as YAML; dashes ending
a line that opens with any run of such markers, block-level HTML tags (pandoc's list, and
the tags it takes for a block or inline as it finds them), comments, processing
instructions, or TeX commands with their groups, are refused wherever they stand, outside a
quotation, and so is the same after a comment that closes on the line. Three dashes at
least: two are an en dash, and a list item that is one opens nothing. Inline markup,
`m<sup>2</sup> ---` or `[drug]{.smallcaps} --`, starts no block and is prose (the sixth and
seventh reviews). The eighth found four more of pandoc's block tags (`applet`, `area`,
`frameset`, `isindex`), and the pattern reading one line more ways than one: a roman
numeral that was a letter too, a comment running on across later ones, a TeX command's
name stopping at any letter, and an optional argument that was a footnote's marker, so a
line of a few hundred markers took minutes. Each now reads a line one way, and the dashes
are split off from the end of the line before the rest is matched. The eighth round's fix
took every `[^` after a command for a footnote's marker, and the ninth found pandoc taking
`\newpage[^1]` whole, the YAML under it read. A bracket is a command's argument before its
groups, colon or not: `\newpage[^1]: ---` is the command and then text, no footnote's
marker. After a group a bracket is text, and `\vspace{1em}[^x] ---` opens no block; the
review of #65's fix-only round found it refused, and it passes now.

**The build asks pandoc.** Every shape in those refusals was found by a review, a round at a
time, and the fifth still found five that put another title on the title page, and shapes
no refusal of a single file can see: a comment the heading scan misreads, and a comment or
a fence carried from one file into the next. So before it writes the document, the build
reads it with pandoc (`build/reading.py`) and refuses (`MisreadError`, exit 1) when the
metadata of the whole text differs from that of the build's header alone, or when the
headings pandoc makes differ from those the gates read in the sources. Nothing there lists
shapes, so most shapes nobody has found yet are caught too. Each heading the gates read is
paired with the one at the same index in the same file with its values put in, and
compared by that title, so `{{results.dose}}mg` reads as `50mg`; a file whose headings
change in number or level when its values go in is refused (see Known gaps for values
that move one). A placeholder used to match any text instead, and the eighth review
found a title that was only a placeholder matching whatever heading pandoc made at its
level, so two misreads that cancelled passed. The titles are read by pandoc as well, each a
numbered paragraph of its own behind a lead made new each build: compared as written,
`$\beta_{1}$`, `HbA~1c~`, `&amp;`, a comment or a footnote in a title split into other words
than pandoc's, and the sixth review found each refused. One pandoc makes no paragraph of,
block HTML in it, is compared in its own words, where the seventh review found it switching
the check off for every heading of the document. Raw markup and footnotes print no words in
a heading. A heading in a quotation, a note or a figure is left out on both sides, the
gates reading none there by design; one in a list, a definition or a table is the
document's, and the seventh round's leaving those out too passed `1. # Results` with a
claim under it, which the gates read under the heading before (the eighth). Such a heading
matches none the gates read, and always refuses: the ninth review found `- # Methods`
standing in for a `# Methods` the gates misread straight under a line of text, the claim
between passing under the wrong heading. The header's metadata is read on its own: read
with the titles and the definitions they refer to, a footnote's definition holding a YAML
block set a title there too, and the whole text matched it (the eighth). The definitions
are copied from the text the gates do not take for code or a comment (`scannable`), and
when the header or the titles cannot be read on their own while the document can, the
build refuses (see Known gaps for a definition in a `<pre>`): the
ninth review found a commented-out footnote holding broken YAML failing that run, which
switched the check off. The lists are aligned, so a refusal names the heading, with the
file and line of one the gates read. Pandoc's reading is walked without recursion, and a
document nested too deep for Python's JSON reader, two thousand divs, is refused.

It costs two more runs of pandoc's reader a document, three with listings, and one on the
header, kept for the next document with the same header. It guards the document, not
`check`: a source the build refuses can still pass `check`, and a number a misread hides
from G2 without touching
metadata, headings or listings is not compared. A refused build removes the document the last one
left in build/, which is not this source's, so that it is not sent or packed; a refused
supplement fails `build` and `submit` like the paper, and `submit --document` refuses a pack
missing either, taking the supplement beside the document, or else the one in build/. It
refuses a document inside build/submission/ too, which the new pack replaces: the ninth
review found `--document build/submission/manuscript.docx` deleted before it was copied. Two
builds go without asking: `import`'s, since the document it rebuilds has already been sent,
and refusing there stranded it with the co-author holding it; and the annotated copy, marked
up for the author to read, whose marks the annotator has pandoc check as it makes them
(#76).

**The header comes from `paper.yaml`, and a manuscript's front matter prints nothing.** The
build strips every source file's YAML block and writes a header of its own with the title,
short title and keywords from `paper.yaml`. A `title:` in the manuscript is compared with
that one and a disagreement warned about (`two-titles`): by `check` at every stage, and by
`build` and `submit` before the document is made. It is read there as YAML reads it, and
the two are compared with their spaces and line breaks folded. An `abstract:` there is
refused,
by G2 and by the build alike (`front-matter-abstract`), as a block pandoc cannot read is
(`front-matter-unreadable`). G2 reads it, because pandoc prints one, and until 2026-09-26
the build dropped it without a word: the abstract was checked, then left out of the
document, and the word count, which follows the build, let a journal's abstract limit pass
on 0 words. It is refused rather than printed because everything else here already finds
an abstract by its heading: the word count, G4's structured-abstract headings, and the
paragraph identifiers the Word import maps edits back with. Printed from the header, each
would have needed a second place to look, and a co-author's edit to it in Word would have
had no source paragraph to go back to.

The abstract is found by reading the block as pandoc does, with the loader that decides
the block is front matter, and not with G2's reader, which finds a value by its key line.
Read G2's way, a quoted key (`"abstract":`), a quoted value opened on the key's line and
continued below it, or a flow mapping passed `check` and was dropped by the build, though
pandoc prints each of them; and `abstract: null` or `abstract: # to do` was refused,
though pandoc prints nothing for either. Merge keys are followed, because pandoc honours
them: an abstract merged in with `<<: *base` prints. A key is known by its text, as pandoc
knows it, so `"<<": *base` merges too, although PyYAML tags only a plain `<<` as a merge.
Each mapping is visited once, since a chain of mappings each merging the one before it
