twice doubles the work of expanding them with each line, and 614 bytes of such front
matter once held `check` for 38 seconds. An abstract pandoc reads as empty is let through,
and so is a key named `abstract` inside another mapping, which pandoc does not take for
the abstract. Any other value, a number or `yes`, is refused rather than guessed about.
PyYAML's composer and pandoc 3.9 were compared on each of these spellings, and on a
duplicated key, where both keep the last.

## LaTeX manuscripts

Status: designed 2026-10-20. Built: the first half of step 1, the format, the reader's file
list, `two-formats`, `other-format-file` and `not-read-in-latex`; step 2, the scanner and
its mask; step 3, the include tree and its refusals under BUILD; and step 4, the bindings,
G2 but for its pointers to tables and figures, the custodian's counts and G1's synthetic
inputs, held to the example by its LaTeX twin, and the values file with G1's hold on it. Where the design depends on
what LaTeX does, the pull request that relies on it checks the statement against TeX Live and
MiKTeX and records the measurement. On the author's machine, 2026-10-20: MiKTeX 24.4 and
latexmk 4.88, with pdfLaTeX, LuaLaTeX, XeLaTeX, BibTeX and Biber on PATH.

Not yet checked against the program it is about, each in the step that relies on it (the
design's reviews named them, Basile chose to settle them there):
- the natbib and biblatex commands listed, with their capitalised and starred forms (step 5);
- MiKTeX's switch that turns its package installer off, and whether it honours `TEXMFHOME`
  (step 9);
- the commands pandoc writes under `link-citations`, and whether it still wraps a section in
  `\hypertarget` (step 11);
- how Overleaf resolves `\input` and figure paths (step 10, for the submission folder: no
  Overleaf project could be had to measure it in step 4, whose values file writes a figure's
  path from the entry file's folder, `../figures/forest.pdf`, as pdfLaTeX finds it);
- whether `check` writes nothing in a LaTeX project as it writes nothing in a Markdown one
  (each step that moves a gate).

LaTeX is used in two ways, built together. It is a source that an author writes and the gates
check. It is also an output: the journal's `.tex` and a PDF, built from a Markdown source.

Decided by Basile on 2026-10-20:
- Source and output are built together.
- The gates read `.tex` through a reader of our own, not through pandoc's LaTeX reader.
- A binding is one command, `\mg{namespace.key}`, defined in a values file that the tool
  writes and that is committed.
- A command the reader does not know has its name blanked and its arguments read.
- pdfLaTeX compiles unless the journal's profile names another engine.

Taken as defaults, and open to change:
- the letters, digits and signs in maths are read by G2, as Markdown's are;
- comments are removed from the submission copy;
- the LaTeX twin of the example lives under `tests/data/`;
- a `.bbl` is sent only where the profile asks for one;
- a project mixing the two formats is refused.

Two things are settled by measurement in the pull requests that need them: how Overleaf
resolves paths, and how CI installs TeX Live.

### One format to a project

The format is read from the entry file, `manuscript/main.md` or `manuscript/main.tex`, and
nothing declares it in paper.yaml. A declaration would be a second place to say what the
folder already says, and the two could disagree. A project holding both entry files is refused
(`two-formats`, G0), and fails at every stage as `manuscript-unreadable` does. So is a file of
the other format anywhere the gates read (`other-format-file`). Left alone, it would be text
that no gate reads and no build prints. The supplement is in the project's format, its entry
`manuscript/supplementary/main.tex`. With one format, each document has one build pipeline.

### The reader is chosen once

`text/reader.py` holds a `Reader` protocol and `reader_for(project)`. That returns the Markdown
reader, or a LaTeX reader built once per run from the include tree. The Markdown reader wraps
the functions the gates call today and changes nothing they return. The proof is the
old-against-new test, with no entry in `differential_expected.yaml`. The reader is an object
rather than a dispatch on the suffix, for two reasons. A LaTeX file is not read alone: the
headings in force where `main.tex` inputs it decide how its numbers are judged. And the citation
reader is sometimes handed a path that is not the manuscript's, as `data_statement.cited_in`
hands it the `.bib`.

| Reader | Markdown today | Read by |
|---|---|---|
| `files(main_text_only)`, `printed_order` | `gates/numbers.py` | about 30 modules, through `source_files` |
| `mask(text)` | `masking.mask` | G2, G5, G6, G8, G14 |
| `words(text)` | `language._hidden` | G14, G15 |
| `uncommented(text)` | `masking.blank_comments` | G2, G7's quotations, G9 |
| `headings(text, path)`, `sections(text, path)` | `heading_index`, `split_sections`, `footnote_index` | G2, G4, G5, G9, G15 |
| `listings(text)` | `fenced_blocks` | G2's code check |
| `bindings(text)` | `placeholders.parse` | G1's synthetic inputs, G2 and the custodian's counts, G4's figure files, G8, G9, G15, the build |
| `substituted(text, values)` | `placeholders.substitute` | G8, G9, G13, `submit`'s response letter and abstract |
| `citations(text, path)` | `zotero.find_citations` | G6, G7, `lookup` |
| `count(text, abstract_title)` | `sections.measure` | G4, the title page |
| `table_at(text, offset)` | a row opening with a pipe | G2's `hand-authored-table` |
| `printed_view(text)` | `scannable` | G4's required statements |
| `refusals(path, text)` | `refused_shapes` | `check` under BUILD, the build |

Every view but `substituted` keeps the source's length and line breaks, so a finding from any of
them names the `.tex` line. `substituted` is the text with the values put in, as `substitute` gives
it today, and the gates that read it place a finding as they place one today. In LaTeX it writes
each display with TeX's ten specials escaped and nothing else changed, so a `%` in `12.5%` does
not start a comment and a `<` stays one character for G8's P. The response letter, which stays
Markdown, takes the display as it is. G13 looks for a response's quote in the reader's prose
view of the substituted text, where `~` is a space, commands are blanked and every escape, the
author's or the display's, is the character it stands for.

The gates that read no part of the manuscript but its file list change only through
`source_files`: G1's freshness, G3's figure checks, G10, G11 (its digests then cover the
`.tex` files) and G12. G1's synthetic-input check reads bindings and moves with them. The analysis
plan stays Markdown.

The gates that read the manuscript move to the reader one at a time, G1's synthetic-input check
among them. Until a gate has moved, it reads nothing of a LaTeX project and says so in one
finding, `not-read-in-latex`, naming the gate. That finding fails from `submission`; before then
it is shown as a note, as any finding not yet due is. Each pull request then ships on its own,
and a half-taught `check` cannot pass a submission. `tests/test_reads_nothing.py` gets a row
for each such gate. The commands not yet moved refuse a LaTeX project with a sentence and exit
2: every command that reads the manuscript only as Markdown, `explain`, `bind`, `reworded`,
`checker` and the panel's prompt among them (step 1, `_MARKDOWN_COMMANDS`), and `audit`
given a `.tex`, which it holds apart since it reads no project. A hook stops nothing, and the
hooks are taught in step 12.

### What the LaTeX reader reads

The reader lives in `text/latex/`, apart from `text/tex.py`, which reads TeX inside Markdown:
- `commands.py` is the closed table of what each known command takes, and what each argument
  is;
- `mask.py` scans a file as it reads it, under TeX's default category codes, and gives the
  masked text and the first refusal (step 2);
- `structure.py` and `cite.py` answer the reader's other questions (steps 3 and 5).

It is one pass, linear in the file.

Its contract is `mask`'s: the same length, line breaks kept, and what is not prose replaced by
NUL. Two additions keep the length:
- A sign that TeX prints as a space is a space: `~`, `\,`, `\ `, `\quad`, and `&` and `\\` in a
  table. So `Table~2` meets the rule that reads `Table 2`.
- An escaped character is that character at the backslash's place, followed by a NUL. So
  `95\%` reads as `95%`, one atom.

| Read as prose | Blanked |
|---|---|
| the body, `\begin{document}` to `\end{document}`, and the files input from it | the preamble of `main.tex` and the files input from it, except what the next row reads |
| in the preamble, `\title`'s argument, read as the title in Markdown's front matter is and compared with paper.yaml's (`two-titles`); an abstract, read under Abstract; `\thanks`'s outside `\author`, read as a footnote is; the arguments of `\AtBeginDocument`, `\AtEndDocument`, `\AddToHook` and `\AfterEndPreamble`, read as the body is, or as the package is in an author's package | the author block, `\author` with what it holds, which is what authors.yaml holds for a Markdown project and G2 does not read; `\date`, which a Markdown build never prints (a known gap) |
| the arguments of text commands: `\emph`, `\textbf`, `\footnote`, `\caption` and its short form, `\section` and its kin, `\href`'s text | command names and braces; `\label`, `\ref` and its kin, `\url`, `\href`'s address, `\includegraphics` |
| a citation's notes, as Markdown's prefix and suffix are read | citation keys |
| the letters, digits and signs in maths, in subscripts and superscripts too, as Markdown's `mask` keeps them in `$x_1 = 10^{-8}$` | maths' commands, braces and delimiters |
| `\verb` and `\texttt`, read as a code span is | `verbatim`, `Verbatim`, `lstlisting`, read by G2's code check as fenced blocks are |
| table cells | a `tabular`'s column specification, `\multicolumn`'s first two arguments, rules |
| the arguments, optional ones too, of a command not in the table | comments (an unescaped `%` to the end of the line, the `comment` environment, a plain `\iffalse` block to its `\fi`, or to its `\else`, whose branch is read), the layout commands `text/tex.py` knows, everything after `\end{document}`, bindings whole |

**Maths** is hidden from `words`, so G14 and G15 never read it as words. Its digits and signs
stay in `mask`, as they do in `$...$` in Markdown today, because blanking `$\beta = 0.42$` would
let a typed estimate pass G2. That keeps the agreement test's promise below: the digits the PDF
prints are the ones `mask` keeps, `$10^{-8}$` and `$R^2$` among them. Markdown's `mask` keeps
`\beta` and the braces as well, and the LaTeX one blanks them, so `10^{-8}` reads as `10^`, a
NUL, `-8` and a NUL. How G2's tokenizer reads such a power is settled in step 4 by corruption
cases on maths, and held by the agreement test from step 9.

**A command not in the table** has its name blanked and its arguments read. This errs towards
findings, as `masking.py` already does: a command the table lacks shows up as an unclassified
number such as `2em`, never as a hidden claim.

**Includes.** `\input` and `\include` are followed from `main.tex`, depth first, and that
order is `printed_order`.
- A path resolves as TeX resolves it: from the entry file's folder, not from the folder of the
  file that includes it, with `.tex` added to a path that has none.
- The import package's `\import{folder}{file}` names the file in that folder of the
  manuscript's, and `\subimport{folder}{file}` the file in that folder under the one the file
  it stands in was imported from, as the package resolves them. An `\input` in an imported
  file is looked for in the entry file's folder, then in the folder the file was imported
  from, which the package adds to LaTeX's path. The submission folder writes the file in
  where the command stands, and looks for a picture an imported file names in the same two
  folders (2026-10-23: an Elsevier template's `\import{./}{intro}` was refused, and every
  section read as a file nothing inputs).
- Each file is read on its own, so a finding names that file's line.
- A file starts in the state its `\input` stands in. One input from the body is body, and one
  input from the preamble is preamble. The headings in force there stand before the file's first
  character (`Source.under`, and `Source.chain_at` at any point of the file), so `p < 0.05` in a
  file input under `\section{Methods}` is read under Methods. So does the environment that
  encloses the `\input`: a file input inside `abstract` is abstract, and one inside a `tabular`
  is table cells. A heading of a file input reaches the text after its `\input`, as LaTeX
  prints it.
- An `\input` in a comment, in a plain `\iffalse` block or in the `comment` environment is no
  input. A file named only there is one that nothing inputs, below.
- A package file in `manuscript/`, such as `\usepackage{macros}` with
  `manuscript/macros.sty` beside the entry file, is followed as a file input from the preamble.
  A class file is not: a journal's `.cls` is shipped beside the entry file and is not the
  author's.
  It is read as LaTeX reads a package, with `@` a letter. Its definitions are then read where
  they are written, below. In it, and in the preamble, both branches of a conditional other than
  a plain `\iffalse` block are read, since a package tests what is loaded. A package found
  anywhere else is not the author's and is not read. `mgvalues.sty` is excluded by name: the
  tool writes it, its definitions are the bindings, and `check` compares it with what `values`
  would write.
- Refused:
  - a path that is not written out in full, or, in the body, not written in braces: in the
    preamble TeX's `\input macros` names the file by the name up to a space (2026-10-27);
  - a path outside `manuscript/` or under a `_` folder;
  - a missing file, or a cycle. A bare name input from the preamble that `manuscript/` does not
    hold, such as `\input{glyphtounicode}`, is the distribution's and is passed over, as a
    package is, and so is TeX's form without braces there, `\input glyphtounicode`;
  - `\InputIfFileExists`, and the import package's `\inputfrom` and
    `\includefrom` and their `sub` forms, and its starred `\import*` and `\subimport*`;
  - a command that prints a file no gate reads: `\lstinputlisting` and its kin,
    `\verbatiminput`, csvsimple's `\csvautotabular` and `\csvreader`, pgfplotstable's
    `\pgfplotstabletypeset` with a file name, datatool's `\DTLloaddb` and its displays, and
    pdfpages' `\includepdf`. A table is bound with `\mg{table.key}` instead.
- A `.tex` file that nothing inputs is still read, as every `.md` file is, and warned about
  (`tex-not-input`). It is read as body under no heading, where definitions, `\makeatletter`
  (after which `@` is a letter) and conditionals are accepted as in the preamble, since such a
  file may be a set of macros left out.
- A `.tex` file that a class or a package the paper loads inputs is the class's, and is not
  read at all (2026-10-23: a journal's class, kept in a folder of its own beside the paper,
  inputs a list of the publisher's journals from that folder, which the paper never inputs,
  and its numbers, abbreviations and words reached the gates as loose main text). A class or
  a package counts where the manuscript holds it, found as LaTeX finds it from the entry
  file's folder: the class `\documentclass` names, each package a file of the tree loads, the
  author's among them, and what those load in turn with `\RequirePackage`, `\usepackage` or
  `\LoadClass`. Each is read for its loads and nothing else: `\input` with braces or without,
  `\@input` and `\InputIfFileExists`, by a path written out in full, outside a comment and
  outside a definition's body. A load inside the body of `\newcommand`, `\renewcommand`,
  `\providecommand`, `\DeclareRobustCommand`, `\def`, `\gdef`, `\edef`, `\xdef`, LaTeX's
  `\@namedef`, `\protected@edef` and `\protected@xdef`, etoolbox's `\csdef` and
  `\newrobustcmd` and their kin, xargs' `\newcommandx`, expl3's `\cs_new:Npn`,
  `\cs_set:Npn` and `\cs_gset:Npn` in their `x`, `e`, `c`, `_protected` and `_nopar` forms
  and without the `p` (round 2 of #445), `\newenvironment` and the document commands
  and environments (`\NewDocumentCommand` and its kin), at any depth inside it, runs where
  the command is used, and its file is printed there: it stays loose, read and warned of
  (round 1 of #445: a package's `\newcommand{\abstracttext}{\input{abstract}}` made the
  paper's abstract the package's, read by no gate). A body runs from the brace past the
  command's name, its options and, for TeX's forms, its parameter text, to the brace that
  closes it, or to the end of the file where none does; a defining command copied with
  `\let` defines nothing. A file one inputs is read for its loads too, and is the class's in
  turn. A file the paper inputs as well is the paper's, read where the paper inputs it
  (`structure._theirs`). The rule follows what a class
  inputs, not where its files are kept: a file of the author's in the class's folder that
  nothing inputs is loose and warned of, as any other is. `structure._classes`;
  `Document.classes` lists them.
- A `.tex` file that holds a document of its own, a `\begin{document}` the reader reaches
  when it reads the file as an entry file, is another document and never part of the one
  whose folder holds it (2026-10-23: a paper's supplement, kept as a second document beside
  `main.tex`, was read as its main text, and so was another paper left in the folder). It
  fails BUILD at every stage, `tex-second-document`, at that `\begin{document}`, and no
  gate reads it. A `\begin{document}` in a comment, a listing or an `\iffalse` block opens
  none. Some files that show one are not second documents, and are read as files nothing
  inputs, loose and warned of, as before (round 1 of #445). One is a picture in the
  `standalone` class, which the paper prints, placed by `\includestandalone` or as the PDF
  compiled from it: it failed BUILD at every stage. So is a part in the `subfiles` class,
  `\documentclass[../main.tex]{subfiles}`, which the paper places by `\subfile` (round 2).
  Either, placed by its command, is read where the command stands, past its preamble, under
  the heading and inside the environments in force there, and is not loose (2026-10-27,
  `structure._placed`). The last is a file the reader refuses in
  its preamble before it reaches a `\begin{document}`: it keeps that refusal and is read
  past it, where it was refused as a second document at its first character and not read.
  The supplement is the document at `supplementary/main.tex`, as the Markdown
  supplement is what `supplementary/` holds: a second document there is refused too. It is
  refused rather than taken for the supplement because a file names no document it is,
  and a title that says "Supplementary" is a guess, where the folder is not; it is refused
  rather than passed over with a warning because, like a file of the other format, it would
  be text no gate reads and no build prints (`other-format-file`).

**Environments.**
- In `figure` and `table`, the caption is prose, and a typed number in a `tabular` is
  `hand-authored-table`.
- `equation`, `align`, `gather` and `multline`, their starred forms, `\[`, `$$` and `\(` are
  maths.
- `abstract`, or `\abstract{…}`, opens a section titled Abstract for every reader, so the
  counts, G4 and G5 find it as they find `# Abstract`. One in the preamble is read as prose
  there, as `\title`'s argument is, since a class such as PNAS's prints it from there. This
  design first refused it, as an `abstract:` in Markdown's front matter is refused. Round 2
  of #385 found that this failed such a class, and failed `\let\oldabstract\abstract`, which
  only names the command. Where a class does not print it, the compile fails (step 9).
- A class's front matter in the body is passed over, as Markdown's YAML header is: Elsevier's
  `frontmatter` and BMC's `fmbox`, with the title, the authors and the addresses they hold,
  and a list of keywords, `keyword`, `keywords` or `IEEEkeywords`. An abstract in the front
  matter, inside environments only, BMC's `abstractbox` among them, is read as one outside
  it is, and so are Elsevier's `highlights`, the paper's claims with its numbers, and
  `graphicalabstract` (round 1). So are the commands the major classes give the front matter, each argument
  blanked: addresses and affiliations (`\address`, `\affiliation`, `\affil`), notes on the
  authors (`\cortext`, `\fntext`, `\email`, `\corresp`), `\keywords`, and Wiley's, Oxford's
  and Springer's issue, dates and running heads (`\Volume`, `\Issue`, `\DOIsuffix`,
  `\pagespan`, `\Receiveddate`, `\copyrightyear`, `\titlerunning` and the rest of
  `FRONT_MATTER_COMMANDS`). An author may define one of these again, as an article's
  preamble often defines `\keywords`: it is then the author's command, here and in every
  file of the tree, read as an unknown command is, as it was before the table held it
  (round 1: an author's `\journal` printed text that was hidden) (Basile, 2026-10-23, after
  an Elsevier and a Wiley template, whose title, addresses and issue were read as main
  text). The title is still read where it stands outside the front matter, in the preamble
  as before.
- The title page the classes write outside such an environment is passed over too, each
  arity read from the class (2026-10-23, after 17 papers from arXiv): `\title`'s option,
  the running head's short title in Springer's `sn-jnl` and amsart and an option list in
  Elsevier's CAS classes, `\title [mode = title]{...}`, a space before it as LaTeX allows;
  Springer's `\author*`, the corresponding author's; CAS's option list after the author's
  name and after an address, `\author{...}[orcid=...]` (`O{} m O{}` in `cas-common.sty`),
  its marks, `\cormark[1]`, `\fnmark`, `\tnotemark` (`O{}`), its CRediT roles, `\credit`,
  a note with no mark and the running heads (`m`); elsarticle's `\fnref`, `\corref` and
  `\tnoteref`; and acmart's CCS concepts, the `CCSXML` environment, which the class
  excludes as the comment package's, read to its `\end` and blanked as `comment` is, and
  `\ccsdesc[300]{...}` with its weight (`\ccsdesc[2][100]`). The XML is the publisher's
  metadata and no note of the author's, so the submission folder keeps it, where it takes a
  comment's text out.
- A TikZ picture, `tikzpicture`, is passed over, its options, coordinates, styles and paths,
  as `\includegraphics` passes over a picture's file; so are `\tikzset`, `\pgfplotsset` and
  the old `\tikzstyle{name} = [...]`, which style it (2026-10-23: their sizes and shifts,
  `minimum size=1em`, `xshift=-4cm`, were numbers of the text). What the picture prints as
  text is read as prose where it stands (`text/latex/pictures.py`; round 1 of #443: passed
  over whole, a flow diagram's `\node[draw] {Reports screened (n = 4371)};` was seen by no
  gate): a node's text, the braces after `\node` or after `node` in a path, past the node's
  name, options and `at (x,y)`; a label's and a pin's, `label={[red]above:Text}` or
  `pin=above:Text`, past its options and its angle, to the first colon as TikZ reads it;
  `node contents=`; a `matrix of nodes`, its cells; pgfplots' `xlabel`, `ylabel`, `zlabel`,
  `title` and `legend entries`, and the text of `\addlegendentry` and `\legend`. A text
  without braces runs to the next comma, bracket or
  brace of its options, or its line's end, and is read as typed. A picture is found to its
  first `\end{tikzpicture}` outside a comment, and a file input inside one is read as one.
  In a definition's body, where an environment is otherwise text expanded at each use, a
  picture whose `\end` stands in the same body is a picture there, as a command that draws
  a circled letter holds one.
- An environment not in the table is read as an unknown command is, and so is its body.

**Definitions.** A `\newcommand`, `\renewcommand`, `\providecommand`,
`\DeclareRobustCommand`, `\def` or `\DeclareMathOperator`, or one of xparse's definers, whose
argument specification is read for the defaults it prints, is read where it is written, and
its body is prose there, in the preamble
too, and in a package file of the author's (above). So `\newcommand{\n}{4100}` is one
unclassified number, at its definition. The parameter tokens `#1` to `#9` in a body are blanked.
A use of the macro is read as an unknown command is: its name is blanked and its arguments are
read. So with `\newcommand{\ci}[2]{95\% CI #1--#2}`, the `95` is found at the definition and
each number of `\ci{1.2}{3.4}` at the use. Nothing is
expanded, because an expansion is text at a place the file does not hold, with no offset to
give a finding.

A length in a definition's body, typed as TeX reads one with its unit against its number, in
a unit TeX measures the page in and a paper does not, `pt`, `sp`, `dd`, `em`, `ex` or `mu`,
is layout: G2 lets it through as `tex-length`, `\def\bibhang{24pt}` and `\lower.5ex`
(2026-10-23, after two papers from arXiv whose preambles gave 24pt and .5ex as numbers). The
reader reads the body as before, and the classifier decides, given the bodies' spans by the
file's read (`_Read.layout`, `Classifier.scan(..., layout=...)`), so `check`, `explain` and
`bind` judge the number alike. In the text a length is a number like any other, since
"24pt" may be a scale's points. TeX's big points, Cicero and picas are a paper's base pairs,
cubic centimetres and parsecs, `500bp`, `20cc`, `8pc`, and are numbers anywhere, as are
millimetres, centimetres and inches, which may be the paper's own measure (round 1 of #443).

A `\def` with delimited parameters, `\def\x#1.{...}`, is read where it is written, its
parameter text blanked and its body read as any body is. A use of it is refused where the
document prints what it makes, in prose, maths or a printed argument, since what it takes
there is not known, and in a hook's body, which LaTeX runs where it stands; in a blanked
argument, the preamble, a comment or another definition's body it prints nothing, and is
let be. The parameter text is read as TeX reads it: the spaces after a control word are
skipped, and a comment to its line's end with the next line's spaces, so `\def\x {...}` and
a `\def\x%` whose body opens the next line delimit nothing (round 1). The definition may
stand in another file of the tree or in the author's package, so a tree that holds one is
read a second time, each file told of it. A parameter of a definition inside a body is
doubled, `##1`, and is a parameter all the same. `\let` of a command the reader reads to
another it reads the same way is read as before: `\let\footnote=\endnote`, with the
endnotes package, prints each note at the end, and its text is the same prose. Not between
headings, citations or cross-references, whose one form prints a level, a kind of citation
or a name, `\let\chapter\section` (round 1). Let to anything else, the command is defined
again (Basile, 2026-10-23, after two journals' templates: the first two were refused at the
definition, and the rest of each file read as typed).

A `\def` whose parameter text holds no parameter, only what must follow each use,
`\def\eg/{e.g.\@}`, takes nothing: a use prints the body, a text the definition holds, and
what follows it, the `/`, is TeX's, passed over as a run of spaces is one space and a line
break, not a blank line, a space. A use it does not follow is refused where it prints, as a
use of delimited parameters is, since TeX stops there: `\def\bSig\mathbf{\Sigma}`, then
`$\bSig$`. The spaces after a control word in the parameter text are no token, as at a use,
so `\def\x\relax /{a}` is followed by `\relax/` (round 1 of #442). The tree tells each file
of these too (2026-10-23: a paper's package of such shortcuts, `\eg/` and `\wm/` among them,
was refused at the first use).

`\providecommand` of a command that is defined defines nothing, so one of a command the reader
reads is read as before, in the preamble and in the body. A command that a package gives
and LaTeX does not, siunitx's `\unit`, `\num`, `\qty` and the rest (`PACKAGE_COMMANDS`), is
the reader's only where a file of the tree loads a package that gives it, siunitx, units for
`\unit` or physics for `\qty`; elsewhere an author's definition of it makes it the author's
command in every file of the tree, read as an unknown command is, as the front matter's
commands are above (2026-10-23: an article's own `\unit` for a unit vector, with no
siunitx, was refused as defined again).

TeX looks for an argument past spaces and one line break, and past a comment with its line's
break and the next line's spaces, as many lines of comments as there are, but not past a blank
line, which ends the paragraph. The reader does the same, and records each comment so passed
(2026-10-23: pandoc's `\newenvironment{CSLReferences}[2] % #1 hanging-indent`, its body on
the next line, was read as a group, and a brace after it closed nothing).

A reference list typed in `thebibliography` is often BibTeX's `.bbl` pasted in, whose header
tests what is loaded and defines what the style needs: natbib's
`\expandafter\ifx\csname urlstyle\endcsname` and `\providecommand{\url}`, REVTeX's
`\makeatletter` and its `\providecommand \@ifx`. In such a list's header, from its `\begin` to
its first `\bibitem`, the reader reads a conditional as in the preamble, both branches, and
accepts `\makeatletter`, `@` a letter to the list's end, where TeX's group puts it back;
`\expandafter` and `\csname`; and `\catcode` and the rest of what changes how characters are
read in a definition's body only, where it prints nothing. In its entries each is refused as
in the body (round 1 of #442). REVTeX's `\citenamefont` and harvard's and apacite's
`\citeauthoryear`, the labels of its entries, are no citations anywhere in the list; a
citation in an entry, `\bibitem{a} See \citeA{b}`, is one, and one the reader does not know is
refused there as elsewhere (2026-10-23: three papers' lists were refused at their header, and
with the span of the list unrecorded, G6, the pack and the blind check read it as text).

A command whose name holds `cite` is a citation's: one the reader does not know is refused
where it prints, since its keys would not reach G7, however the name holds it, `\citeZ`,
`\mycite`, `\mycitep`, `\maincite`. Not where the name opens with an English word that cites
nothing, `\excite`, `\recited`, `\solicited`, `\elicited`, `\anthracite`, `\plebiscite`: such
a word inside a name is no word of it, and `\maincite`, which holds "incite", is refused (round
2 of #442). Nor in IEEE's `\IEEEcompsocitemizethanks`, named whole (2026-10-23: it was refused). The reader
knows natbib's and biblatex's commands, biblatex's multi-citations `\footcitetexts` among
them, and apacite's and chicago's, read from their `.sty`: `\citeA`, `\citeNP`,
`\citeauthorNP`, `\citeyearNP`, `\shortcite` and `\fullcite` with their `A`, `NP`, `author`
and `authorNP` forms, `\nocitemeta`, and chicago's `\citeN`, `\citeANP`, `\shortciteN` and
`\shortciteANP`. apacite's prenote in angle brackets, `\citeA<see>[p.~3]{key}`, is read as a
citation's note (round 1 of #442: a rule that read only a name's start and end let
`\shortciteNP` and `\mycitep` pass unread, their keys hidden from G7).

Refused:
- a definition, in a file of the author's, of any command the reader reads, `\mg` among them,
  but `\abstract`, which the reader read as an unknown command before it opened a section and
  which an author restyles, pandoc's `\citeproc` and `\citeproctext`, which its template
  defines, `\providecommand` of one, and a package's command where no package that gives it
  is loaded (above);
- a use of a command defined with delimited parameters, where it prints (above), and a use
  that what its parameter text holds does not follow;
- anything that changes how characters are read: `\catcode`, `\makeatletter` in the body,
  `\csname`, `\expandafter`, and `babel` with a language whose shorthands make a character
  active, but in a reference list's header (above);
- in the body, any conditional but a plain `\iffalse` block and `\ifthenelse`, a command whose
  branches are its arguments and are both read, and those of a reference list's header.

**Characters.**
- `--` and `---` stay as typed, as in Markdown.
- ``` `` ``` and `''` read as typographic quotation marks, the mark first and a NUL after it, in
  every view the reader gives, so G7's quotations, which read `uncommented`, find a quotation.
- An accent command or `\-` inside a word cannot be written in place without a NUL that splits
  the word, so that word is hidden from `words`. G14 says, once a file, how many words it did
  not read and why: the file is UTF-8, so type the letter.
- An `inputenc` other than `utf8` is refused, but in a tree whose files are all ASCII, which
  reads the same in each encoding inputenc knows. A file of ASCII that sets one is accepted
  and the tree refuses it there where another of its files is not ASCII, since TeX reads
  every file of the tree in that encoding (2026-10-23: a paper's `latin9` was refused in a
  file of ASCII).

**Refused.** Each refusal is a finding under BUILD that fails at every stage, as `unclear-fence`
does. Beyond those above, `tex-unbalanced` covers a group, an environment or maths left open or
closed twice. Past a refusal the rest of the file is read as prose, so that nothing the reader did
not understand is hidden.

### Bindings

| Markdown | LaTeX |
|---|---|
| `{{results.key}}`, `{{lit.key}}` | `\mg{results.key}`, `\mg{lit.key}` |
| `{{table.key}}` | `\mg{table.key}`, the tabular; the caption is the float's `\caption`, prose as a figure's is |
| `{{figure.key}}` | `\mg[options]{figure.key}`, `\includegraphics` of the rendered file |
| `{{method.step}}` | `\mg{method.step}`, which prints nothing |

One command carries the namespace inside its braces, as `{{results.key}}` does, so a paper
moves from Markdown to LaTeX by a direct rewrite. `bindings` returns the `Placeholder` records
that `parse` returns, so every gate that reads bindings reads these unchanged. The whole
command is NUL in `mask`, so a typed number is found and a bound one is not.
- A near spelling, an unclosed brace, or a namespace or key outside the grammar is
  `malformed-placeholder`.
- A binding in a comment is not read.
- A binding in `verbatim` would print as typed, and is refused.
- A binding in the number argument of `\num` or `\SI` is refused, because siunitx parses a
  number, and a value's display string is formatted text.

**The values file.** `manuscript-guard values` writes `mgvalues.sty` beside each entry file.
- It defines `\mg` and one entry per key: values and tables with LaTeX's specials escaped,
  figure paths relative to its own folder.
- Its first line names the results file by its digest.
- The entry file loads it with `\usepackage{mgvalues}`, and the `.tex` then compiles in any
  editor with the values filled in.
- A key it does not define prints `??` and the key, with a LaTeX warning, as an undefined
  `\ref` prints `??`. `check` already fails it (`unresolved-binding`).
- The file is committed, so a co-author's editor has it.

`check` writes nothing. It compares the file with what `values` would write, and fails a
difference from `drafting` (`values-file-stale`, `values-file-missing`), since a PDF compiled
from a stale file shows the old number.

**Escaping** is a closed table in `build/latex_values.py`. It covers:
- the ten specials;
- `<`, `>` and `|`, written with `\ensuremath`, since pdfLaTeX's default OT1 encoding prints a
  typed `<0.001` as `¡0.001`;
- for pdfLaTeX, the characters that values carry: −, –, ±, ×, ≤, ≥, ·, the no-break and thin
  spaces, and Greek letters, the mathematical ones also with `\ensuremath`. A `$...$` would
  close the maths that a binding stands in, as in `$p = \mg{results.p}$`.

A value holding any other character outside Latin-1 is refused, not guessed at: it is left
out of the file, so `\mg` prints `??` for it and LaTeX warns, and G1 says so
(`value-not-printable`) where a document binds it; one nothing binds stops nothing. A dash is
written as a command, and two hyphens apart, so that no dash TeX joins from them takes a
minus sign after it. The pull request that builds the table compiles each entry under OT1
and T1 and compares the printed text with the value.

**The submission copy** replaces each binding with what the file defines for it and writes
`\usepackage{mgvalues}` as `\usepackage{graphicx}`, which the values file loads, so it needs
no macro file (step 10).

### Citations

`text/latex/cite.py` returns the `CitationUse` records that `find_citations` returns.
- **Read:** `\cite` and `\nocite`; natbib's `\citep`, `\citet`, `\citealt`, `\citealp`,
  `\citeauthor`, `\citeyear`, `\citeyearpar` and `\citenum`; biblatex's `\parencite`,
  `\textcite`, `\autocite`, `\footcite`, `\smartcite` and `\supercite`, and their
  multi-citation forms with global and per-group notes; the capitalised and starred form of
  each.
- **Notes:** one optional argument is the postnote, and two are the prenote and the postnote,
  which natbib and biblatex agree on.
- **Keys** are split at commas, and each record carries its key's own line and offset.
- **Narrative:** `narrative` is true where the authors' names are printed in the sentence
  (`\citet`, `\citealt`, `\textcite`, `\citeauthor`), and false otherwise, `\cite` included.
- **The rest:** `\nocite{*}` cites every entry of `references.bib`, as LaTeX does. Any other
  command whose name holds `cite` is refused.

### The build of a LaTeX source

`build/latex.py` compiles with latexmk. It runs with:
- `-norc`, so nobody's configuration runs;
- the engine the profile names, pdfLaTeX by default;
- `-interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error -file-line-error`;
- `-no-shell-escape`, since TeX Live's restricted shell escape is on by default, and the reader
  refuses `minted` and anything else that needs one.

It compiles a copy in `build/latex/`, with a fresh `mgvalues.sty` and
`literature/references.bib`; `build` never writes in `manuscript/`. Under TeX Live it sets
`openout_any=p`, so nothing is written outside the copy, and `openin_any=p`, so no file is read
by a path that leaves it. Files found through TeX's own search paths are still read. So
`TEXINPUTS` names the copy before the standard trees, and `TEXMFHOME` points at an empty
folder, so that an author's own folder of packages is not searched. Both settings are measured
under TeX Live and MiKTeX in step 9.
Under MiKTeX it turns the package installer off and names a missing package rather than
fetching it mid-build. The log is read: an error is a `BuildError`, with its file and line
mapped back to the source, and an undefined citation or reference fails at `submission`. The
numbered headings LaTeX wrote to the `.aux` file, as its `\@writefile{toc}` lines, are compared
with the reader's, and a difference is refused (`MisreadError`), as pandoc's headings are
compared. The `.aux` is read rather than the `.toc`, which LaTeX writes only for a document
with `\tableofcontents`.

latexmk and one engine are needed for a PDF. Without them `build` says so and exits 2, `check`
runs every gate as usual, and the tests that need LaTeX skip. CI installs a pinned TeX Live and
sets `MANUSCRIPT_GUARD_REQUIRE_LATEX`, with which `tests/conftest.py` refuses to start unless
that TeX Live is there.

**The journal profile** gets an optional `latex:` block, each rule quoted from the journal's
page:
- `class` and `class_options`;
- `bibliography`: `bibtex` with a `bst`, or `biblatex` with a `style`;
- `engine`;
- `files`: the class and style files the journal hands out, fetched once into
  `profiles/journals/latex/<slug>/` with their address, SHA-256 and licence, as CSL styles are.
  None of them ships with the package.

G4 warns where `\documentclass`, `\bibliographystyle` or biblatex's `style=` differ from the
profile.

**The submission folder.** `submit` writes `build/submission/latex/`:
- `manuscript.tex`, flattened, with the values written in and the comments removed, since a
  comment can hold a draft and its old numbers;
- `references.bib` with only the cited keys, and the `.bbl` (step 10 packs it always);
- the figures, with their paths rewritten;
- the journal's files (not yet: no command fetches them);
- the PDF, which step 10 puts at the pack's root, beside the other documents.

The folder is then compiled alone, in an empty directory, and refused if it needs anything
outside itself.

**Word counts** are the reader's, and the rule is printed with the count, as for Markdown.
They count the prose of `words` and the headings, with the abstract apart. Floats and display
maths are not counted, and an inline formula is one word.

### LaTeX out of Markdown

`build --latex` assembles the document as the Word build does, then runs `pandoc -t latex`.
It passes:
- the profile's class, and its template where the profile keeps one;
- `--natbib` or `--biblatex` as `bibliography:` says, or citeproc with the CSL where it says
  neither;
- the title, keywords and authors from paper.yaml and authors.yaml, as template variables.

The result is compiled and packed by the code above, and checked three times:
1. The gates read the Markdown, as today.
2. The LaTeX reader reads the body pandoc writes without the template (`-t latex` without
   `--standalone`) under the author's rules, and refuses what it refuses. Raw TeX that the Word
   writer drops (`tex-in-the-text`) reaches the `.tex` and takes effect, so a definition or an
   `\input` in it is caught here. The template is the profile's or pandoc's, not the author's.
3. The digits the reader's `mask` keeps in that body must be the ones G2 read in the source's
   body, with the bound values put in, in order. A difference refuses the build. The title
   page, which the template writes from paper.yaml and authors.yaml wherever the class puts
   it, and the source's front matter are on neither side. The
   commands pandoc writes for layout are in the reader's table with the arguments that are not
   prose: both of `\setcounter`'s, a column's width in `\real{0.33}`, and the anchor of
   `\hypertarget`, whose second argument is the content it wraps and is read. Where citeproc
   writes the citations and the reference list as text, they are left out of the comparison,
   found by the commands pandoc wraps them in, which it writes under `link-citations`; the build
   passes it. If pandoc's output does not mark them, `build --latex` refuses a profile that
   names neither natbib nor biblatex, rather than compare digits it cannot place. Which commands
   pandoc writes is measured in that pull request, against the pinned pandoc.

### Tests

- **The twin.** `tests/data/latex/manuscript/` is the example's manuscript in LaTeX. A fixture
  runs it against the example's analysis, results, figures and fictional citekeys. A test holds
  the twin and the example to the same bindings and headings, and to equal G2 counts, so the
  twin has no `\thanks`; the citations join the comparison when the citation reader does.
- **Corruption cases.** Each manuscript case in `tests/test_corruption.py` is to run on the twin
  too, with each `\mg` replaced by its value. G2's cases run on it from step 4, and each other
  gate's join them as the gate moves; until then a gate's Markdown cases stand for it. Further
  cases:
  - a key mistyped, and a binding cut short;
  - a number in a `tabular`, a `\footnote`, a caption, a postnote, a `\newcommand` body and an
    input file;
  - `$p<0.05$` under Results;
  - a stale `mgvalues.sty`, and a missing input;
  - a key not in the `.bib`;
  - a required section renamed, and an abstract over its limit;
  - each refusal.
- **Generated inputs.** `tests/generated.py` gets `latex_texts()`, drawn from a pool as `texts()`
  is:
  - words, and numbers as LaTeX writes them: `95\%`, `$p<0.05$`, `3--5`, `Table~\ref{t}`;
  - citations with notes, bindings, labels, `\verb` spans, comments and URLs;
  - openers and closers never paired: `\begin{verbatim}`, `\end{equation}`, `{`, `$`, `\[`,
    `\iffalse`, `\input{`;
  - the bare signs `\`, `%`, `&`, `#`, `^`, `_` and `~`.
- **Readings and properties.** `tests/readings.py` names `latex mask`, `latex words`,
  `latex sections`, `latex bindings`, `latex citations`, `latex refusals` and `latex check`.
  `tests/test_properties.py` holds of them what it holds of Markdown:
  - nothing raises;
  - the length and every line break are kept;
  - what is planted in prose, a heading, a footnote, a caption, maths or a note is found, there;
  - nothing planted in a comment, a key, a label, a binding, the preamble, a listing or after
    `\end{document}` is found;
  - nothing past a refusal is hidden.
- **Broken rules.** `BROKEN` gets at least these, and each must fail under a dozen seeds:
  - an escaped `%` opens a comment;
  - a comment runs past its line;
  - maths is blanked whole;
  - a citation's notes are blanked;
  - a group closes at the first brace;
  - `\verb` takes only `|` as its delimiter;
  - the preamble ends at the first `\begin`;
  - an input file starts under no heading;
  - a file named only by an `\input` in a comment is not read;
  - a macro's use hides its arguments.
- **Old against new.** In the pull request that adds a `latex` reading, the base lacks it, so
  the reading is passed over and written on the job's page; from the next pull request on, it is
  compared. The first pull request leaves every Markdown reading unchanged.
- **LaTeX itself.** `tests/test_latex_agreement.py` does for LaTeX what
  `test_pandoc_agreement.py` does for pandoc. It compiles a fixed number of generated files the
  reader does not refuse, and the digits the PDF prints must be the ones `mask` keeps. A
  LuaLaTeX callback writes the digits out page by page.

### Known gaps, from the start

- `babel` with a language whose shorthands make a character active is not refused yet (step
  2): a shorthand changes letters, not digits, so it is left to step 7, which reads words.
- Only the first refusal of a file is reported: past it the file is read as prose, and the
  next is found once the first is put right.
- A file whose only `\begin{document}` stands in a `\verb`, a listing or an `\iffalse` opens in
  the preamble; refused, it keeps that reading, and what stands before the refusal is blanked.
- A `.tex` file in a Markdown manuscript is not refused, as a Markdown file in a LaTeX one is
  (`other-format-file`): a project written before LaTeX was read may keep a `.tex` beside its
  Markdown for pandoc's header, and refusing it would fail a paper that passed. It is read by
  no gate. Whether to warn of it is left for later.
- The hooks are not refused with the commands: a hook never stops the tool that called it.
  The submission refusal and the status line run the gates, so they see `not-read-in-latex`
  as `check` does; the note on a saved file reads only Markdown, and says nothing when a
  `.tex` is saved (round 2 of #370), until step 12 teaches the hooks.
- On a LaTeX project, `sign` of an id that stands nowhere lists G15's ids among those that
  stand, though `sign` refuses them there; and `review --suggestions --design`, a misuse, is
  told LaTeX is not read rather than that `--suggestions` stands alone (round 2 of #404).
- An author's macro is not expanded where it is used, so a word its body prints there is in no
  sentence that G6 or G14 reads; its body is read once, at the definition.
- An `\input` records the environments open around it, not the command whose argument it is
  in, so `\title{\input{title}}` reads `title.tex` as preamble, blanked, though LaTeX prints it
  (round 1 of #385).
- A command whose body uses one defined with delimited parameters, or one let to it, is not
  refused where it is used, though LaTeX prints that use there: only the delimited
  command's own uses are. One defined again without delimited parameters is still
  refused where it prints (2026-10-23).
- A note let to the endnotes package's, `\let\footnote=\endnote`, is read where it is
  typed, under the heading in force there, though LaTeX prints the notes together at the
  end of the document (2026-10-23).
- The import package's `\inputfrom`, `\includefrom` and their `sub` forms are refused, not
  followed (2026-10-23).
- `\let\include\input`, which an author writes to drop `\include`'s page breaks, is refused:
  the submission folder would write the file in between the `\clearpage`s TeX no longer
  prints. A file input from inside a definition is read as one nothing inputs, warned of,
  and the commands it defines with delimited parameters reach no other file, so a use of
  one is not refused (2026-10-23, the fix-only round of part 1).
- A file a class inputs by a path it builds, `\input{\@journal-names}`, or a class that is
  not UTF-8, which the reader cannot read, leaves the file to be read as one nothing inputs,
  warned of (`tex-not-input`); a path in a class's `\iffalse` block or in a branch it does
  not take counts as input. A file the class's file list or the author's package inputs is
  not read at all, so a command it defines is not known to the reader (2026-10-23).
- A class's definition is found by its command's name, not by expanding the class: a
  LaTeX definition whose name is built, `\expandafter\newcommand\csname x\endcsname{...}`
  (TeX's `\def` so written is seen), or a defining command the class renamed with `\let`
  and uses under that name, is not seen as a definition, and a load in it counts as the
  class's. So does a load kept in a token list or a box, expl3's `\tl_set:Nn` or
  `\sbox`, which is stored, not defined, and a load in the code of an expl3 function other
  than the `\cs_new`, `\cs_set` and `\cs_gset` forms, `\prg_new_conditional:Npnn` say; a load in a
  hook, `\AtBeginDocument`
  or `\DeclareOption`'s code, counts as the class's too, since it runs whether or not the
  paper asks for it. A body whose braces do not balance, such as one with a brace changed
  by `\catcode`, runs to the end of the file, so the loads past it stay loose and warned of
  (rounds 1 and 2 of #445). xargs' `\providecommandx` is not read as a definition, and a
  defining command copied with expl3's `\cs_new_eq:NN` or `\cs_set_eq:NN` is taken for one,
  its next braced group for a body; the generated folders plant the TeX and LaTeX forms,
  and the expl3 and xargs forms are held by unit tests alone.
- A `standalone` picture or a `subfiles` part the paper places nowhere, and a document of
  its own that the reader refuses in its preamble, are read as files nothing inputs, under
  no heading and warned of: a second document refused before its `\begin{document}` fails
  BUILD by that refusal rather than as a second document, its preamble and its body read as
  loose main text (round 1 of #445). One the paper places by `\includestandalone` or
  `\subfile` is read where it stands (see "Closed since"), with these limits: its preamble
  is passed over whole, so a command it defines is not known in its body, where TeX would
  not know it either, nor in the paper's other files (round 1 of #452: one defined with
  delimited parameters had main's own command of that name refused). Under `standalone`'s
  `subpreambles` option a picture's preamble is kept and run where the picture is placed,
  and the reader passes it over all the same, so the submission folder's packed source
  loses what that preamble defines or loads, which the compile of the packed source then
  catches. A file the command places that is in neither class is read as an
  `\input` of it, and its own `\documentclass` is refused; an `\includestandalone` of a
  picture whose `.tex` the folder lacks is taken for the image compiled from it and passed
  over; and the submission folder writes the picture's body in the command's place, so the
  command's options, a width or a scale, do not size it there (2026-10-27).
- A file a class inputs, and a document of its own, are left out of each document, but not
  out of the manuscript's file list (`Reader.files`): G11's digests, the review panel's
  prompt and G12's reading of the manuscript's text as typed still take them in (2026-10-23).
- A supplement kept as a second document beside `main.tex` is refused, not read as the
  supplement: the author moves it to `supplementary/main.tex`, and its paths to pictures and
  inputs with it, since a path resolves from its entry file's folder (2026-10-23).
- An appendix's tables and figures are the supplement's to G2 only: G4 still counts one
  placed with a binding toward the journal's limit on the main text's display items. An
  appendix that numbers its own, `\renewcommand{\thetable}{S\arabic{table}}` after
  `\setcounter{table}{0}`, is still counted on from the main text's, so a pointer typed to
  its "Table S1" is read as one to the supplementary document's, and one to "Table A1" is
  read as no pointer. So is an appendix a class numbers apart: elsarticle's `\appendix`
  prints "Table A.1", and a "Table 3" typed for the appendix's first table after two in
  the main text is taken as pointing at it. An `\appendix` in an author's macro opens no
  appendix where the macro is used, so a table there cited first is out of order to G2.
  Springer's and BMC's headings for files sent apart are read; a journal's other wording
  for a supplement's heading is not (2026-10-23, round 1). A heading that is the word alone,
  "Supplement", is taken for the supplement's even in a trial of a dietary supplement
  (round 2). A reference list a supplement holds of its own, biblatex's `refsection` or
  a typed `thebibliography` printed before its tables, ends the part there, and the tables after it are the main
  text's (the fix-only round).
- A distribution's package shipped beside the entry file, as an arXiv source often ships
  `natbib.sty`, is read as the author's, and refused at the first construct the reader
  does not read, natbib's `\csname`. Taken out of `manuscript/`, it is the
  distribution's again (2026-10-23).
- A file input past a refusal in the file that inputs it, from inside a definition, or from
  `\AtBeginDocument{\input{x}}` is not followed. It is warned of as `tex-not-input`, whose
  message says no `\input` the reader follows names it, and is read under no heading (round 1
  of #385).
- A file input from the preamble by a path with no folder that `manuscript/` lacks,
  `\input{settings.tex}` or `\input settings` too, is taken for the distribution's and
  passes; the compile finds it missing (step 9) (rounds 1 and 2 of #385). In the body,
  TeX's `\input name` without braces is refused as before: only the preamble's is followed
  (2026-10-27).
- After `\renewcommand{\abstract}` or `\let\abstract\relax`, `\abstract{…}` still opens a
  section titled Abstract, though LaTeX prints what the author defined (round 2 of #385).
- The Abstract an abstract opens stays in force to the next heading of its level, so text
  between `\end{abstract}` and the first `\section` stands under Abstract, in the preamble's
  case as in the body's. No gate reads LaTeX's headings yet; the counts, G4 and G5 close it
  where the abstract ends (`Reading.abstracts`) when they move (round 3 of #385).
- In the preamble, `\g@addto@macro\abstract{…}` or `\pretocmd\abstract{…}` reads the group
  after `\abstract` as an abstract, and so is one in the branch of a conditional that is not
  taken, both read there (round 3 of #385).
- G2 holds a LaTeX manuscript's typed pointers to what a float's `\caption` numbers (step
  13). A supplement's numbering is taken to be Table S1, as in Markdown, whatever its
  `\thetable` prints; a typed "Figure 1a" points at Figure 1, `\subfloat`'s letters unread; a
  pointer typed in a float's caption or a `\captionof`'s is not read; and a label defined
  twice names the first display it labels. A range of cross-references is read where a dash
  joins two, where "to" does after "Tables", "Figures" or "Figs." typed before the first or
  before a list it ends, or in a `\crefrange`, as `pointers.py` reads a typed one: "to" after
  a plural a command of the author's prints, `\Figs~\ref{a} to~\ref{b}`, and `\ref{a},
  \dots, \ref{b}` cite their ends only, so a display between them first cited later is said
  out of order; a range whose ends are more than 50 apart, of two kinds, or of the main text
  and the supplement cites its ends only. Unlike Markdown's, the join may have a line's end
  on either side, which TeX reads as a space (corpus round, 2026-10-23, and fix round 1). A
  group of the subfloat package, `subfigures` or `subtables`, is one display however its
  floats' captions are written, and a group that is not closed leaves its floats numbered
  each. Where a document numbers a kind in a way the view cannot
  count, a `\captionof`, a `longtable`'s caption, or a float whose caption a command of the
  author's writes, that kind's pointers are not checked, and a note says so; a page
  `\includepdf` takes in, or a `\caption` in a float the reader does not know, `SCfigure` or
  a `\newfloat`, or in a command that wraps a whole float, leaves both kinds of its document
  unchecked; an `algorithm`'s caption or a minted `listing`'s numbers neither (round 3), and
  under algorithm2e's `figure` option, which numbers an algorithm as a figure, the figures
  are counted one short of what LaTeX prints (round 4). A float that holds a file input and no caption
  of its own, or a file read inside a float, numbers what the captions of the other number;
  where neither has a caption the view reads, one a command of the author's writes in the
  file, the float is counted as none, and a pointer to it may be said to point at nothing
  (round 2). A label in a file read inside a `subfigure` names nothing, so a figure cited only
  by it is said not cited (round 3). A `\ref` to a label nobody defined is the compile's to
  refuse (step 9).
- G4 reads a LaTeX figure's legend in the caption LaTeX numbers it by, in a float that holds
  a figure, the main text's and the supplement's, and counts the label LaTeX prints before it,
  "Figure 1", as two words, which a Markdown legend types: a legend written by a command of
  the author's, or in a `\captionof`, is not read, and a continued figure's caption is a
  legend of its own (step 13).
- A number typed as a LaTeX heading's or list item's numbering, `\section*{2.1 Methods}`, is
  a number like any other: LaTeX numbers them, so the rules that pass Markdown's typed
  numbering hold nowhere in a `.tex`.
- A unit after a LaTeX binding is compared only where nothing but spaces stands between them
  and inside it no command or maths: `\mg{results.dose}~$\mu$g`, `\textmu g` and siunitx's
  `\si{\micro\gram}` are not compared with the unit emitted.
- `\mg` is also siunitx's milligram, inside its commands. There it is not read as a binding,
  and `\mg{results.key}` there is refused. The values file of the second half of step 4 must
  define `\mg` so that siunitx's stays its own inside its commands.
- A `verbatim` names no language, so its numbers are said once to be unread, as an untagged
  fenced block's are, with the fenced block's hint. An `lstlisting`'s `language=` is read
  where its options stand on the `\begin` line and hold no bracket: options run over lines,
  a dialect, `language=[Sharp]C`, and `\lstset{language=R}` leave the language unread.
- A command not in the table has its arguments read, by design, so layout the table lacks,
  `\titlespacing` in the body, or a primitive with a size and no braces, `\vskip 6pt`, gives
  an unclassified number now that G2 reads LaTeX. Each found goes into the table. (A
  definition whose body follows a comment, `\renewcommand{\arraystretch}%` with `{1.5}` on
  the next line, had its body read as a group; it is the body since 2026-10-23.)
- physics' `\qty[a = b]` holds an `=`, so it is taken for siunitx's option list and blanked
  (round 2 of #400). A siunitx key with no `=`, `\qty[sticky-per]`, is taken for a value and
  read as prose words; it holds no number (round 3).
- A multi-citation's global notes, `\cites(see)(p.~5)[...]{a}{b}`, are blanked, so a number in
  one is read by no gate; its per-group notes are read (step 5). A global note is looked for
  up to 300 characters on, and not past a blank line; one longer is refused (round 2 of step
  5). A `)` in a comment inside a global note is taken for its end. A comment in the middle of
  a key, `\cite{smi%` with `th}` on the next line, leaves a space in the key, where TeX joins
  it, and `\\%` in a key list is taken for an escaped `%`.
- A citation command the reader does not know, an author's own whose name holds `cite`,
  `\mycite` or `\mycitep`, is refused where it is used, as the design asks: the reader knows
  natbib's, biblatex's, apacite's and chicago's (step 5; round 1 of #442). In the preamble
  such a command is not refused, since natbib's and biblatex's settings stand there,
  `\setcitestyle` and `\DeclareCiteCommand` among them, and nothing of it prints; biblatex's
  `\volcite` family is refused in the body (round 1 of step 5). natbib's `\citetext`,
  `\defcitealias` and biblatex's `\citereset` and `\notecite` family are read (round 2). A
  name whose `cite` is in a word that cites nothing (`_CITE_WORDS`), `\excite`, `\recite` or
  IEEE's `\IEEEcompsocitemizethanks`, is read as an unknown command, so an author's citing
  command so named, `\recite`, hides its keys from G7; so do `\citenamefont` and
  `\citeauthoryear` in a typed reference list, labels there by BibTeX's styles (2026-10-23).
  apacite's `<...>` prenote is taken after any citation command, so a `<` typed right after
  natbib's `\citep`, before its options and braces, is read as one, where LaTeX prints it
  (round 1 of #442).
- pandoc's `\citeproc{ref-smith2020}{Smith 2020, 3}`, which it writes for a citation under
  citeproc, is read as a citation is, both arguments blanked, but not recorded as one: its key
  names an entry of the typed list, `ref-` and the library's key, so G7 does not see it, and a
  locator in its text is read by no gate, where Markdown's is (2026-10-23).
- A reference list opened in one file and closed in another, `\input` between, is refused as
  left open, so what `\makeatletter` changed in its header is never carried past its
  `\end` (round 1 of #442).
- `\providecommand` of a command the reader reads is taken to define nothing, though one a
  package gives that is not loaded, `\providecommand{\url}[1]{\texttt{#1}}` with no url
  package, defines it: the reader reads it as the package's, its address blanked where LaTeX
  prints it as code. A package that a class loads is not known, so the author's `\unit` in a
  class that loads siunitx is read as the author's; the compile stops on it (2026-10-23).
- In a reference list typed in `thebibliography`, `\catcode` in a definition's body is
  accepted, though where the command runs it changes how TeX reads what follows: REVTeX's
  `\href`, where hyperref is not loaded, reads its address so, and the reader blanks that
  address as typed either way (2026-10-23).
- What follows a use of a command defined with a parameter text and no parameter is looked
  for past spaces and one line break, not past a comment, so `\eg%` with `/` on the next line
  is refused though TeX reads it. A comment between a command and its argument is passed over
  as TeX passes it, but not between `\mg` and its brace, whose binding is then malformed, nor
  between `\input` or `\import` and theirs, which are refused as naming no file (2026-10-23).
- An encoding set in a file of ASCII is held to the files of its tree, not to a file nothing
  inputs, which TeX does not read (2026-10-23).
- A citation in a hook's body, `\AtBeginDocument{\nocite{smith2019}}`, is not recorded, as one
  in a definition's body is not, and G7 warns that its key is cited nowhere (round 1 of
  step 5).
- `sync-bib` refuses a LaTeX manuscript the reader refuses anywhere, since the keys after the
  refusal are not read; `lookup` looks up the keys before it (round 1 of step 5).
- `\nocite{*}` cites what `literature/references.bib` holds, not a bibliography a class or a
  `\bibliography{}` names elsewhere (step 5).
- G4 counts an inline formula as one word and a displayed one as none; Markdown's count reads
  a formula's tokens as words. A LaTeX paper and its Markdown twin with maths in their prose
  count differently by that much (step 6).
- The heading with no title that closes an abstract is a section of its own to G4, which
  counts it as text and finds no required section in it (step 6).
- G4 counts a display item where a float's caption numbers one, and a binding where no
  caption the view reads numbers its float (see "Closed since"). A `\captionof`, a
  `longtable`'s caption, a page `\includepdf` takes in and a float numbered by a command of
  the author's count only by the bindings they place, as G2 leaves their kind uncounted. A
  table or figure in the appendix counts against the journal's limits, though G2 holds it
  as the supplement's. The submission pack's title page declares what G4 holds, the
  numbered displays (`gates.journal.measured`, 2026-10-27).
- A class's front matter command an author provides for portability, `\providecommand` or
  `\@ifundefined`, is the author's though the class keeps its own, and its argument is read
  as prose, as before the table held it. Highlights, read in the front matter, count as main
  text to G4 and are a first use to G14, as before (2026-10-23, round 2 of part 2).
- A title written in the body outside a class's front matter, as Wiley's and Springer's
  templates write it, is read as the text's, as one in the preamble is: G4 counts it as
  main text, and an abbreviation in it is used before its definition to G14. A class's
  front matter command not in `FRONT_MATTER_COMMANDS` is read as an unknown command is, its
  arguments as prose (rounds 1 of steps 6 and 7; the front matter itself since 2026-10-23).
- `\title`'s option is passed over in every class, so a word or a number that only a running
  head's short title holds is read by no gate. `\author{...}`, `\address{...}` and
  `\affiliation{...}` followed by an opening bracket, past spaces and one line break, take
  it for CAS's option list in any class: in one whose command takes none, text that opens
  with a bracket there is passed over (2026-10-23; round 1 of #443).
- A TikZ picture's text is read where the source types it, among the paper's prose, so G14
  and G9 read a node's words as a sentence there. What the picture prints otherwise is read
  by no gate, where G3 reads a picture file's text layer: pgfplots' tick labels, `nodes near
  coords` and what else it computes from the coordinates; a node's text given by a `\pic`,
  by a `\foreach` variable or by a command of the author's that writes the node; a style's
  label, `every node/.style={label=...}`, set outside the picture; and, in a picture that
  holds another in a node, what the outer prints after the inner's `\end`. A `matrix of
  nodes` is read whole, its cells' options `|[draw]|` as prose. Bind such a number with
  `\mg`, or draw the figure from a script. TikZ's inline `\tikz[...]`, PGF's `pgfpicture` and circuitikz's environment are
  read as unknown commands are, their options as prose; and a picture opened in one
  definition's body and closed in another,
  `\newenvironment{pic}{\begin{tikzpicture}}{\end{tikzpicture}}`, passes over its options
  only, and what `\begin{pic}` holds is read (2026-10-23; round 1 of #443).
- A TeX length is layout only in a definition's body: not in a hook's,
  `\AtBeginDocument{\kern2pt}`, nor in a definition's default argument,
  `\newcommand{\x}[1][2pt]{...}`, which prints where the definition is used and is read as
  prose; and only in its units' small letters without TeX's `true`: so `\vskip 6pt` in the
  body, `24 pt` with a space, `24PT` and `24truept` are numbers. A length in points a
  definition prints as text where it is used, `\newcommand{\font}{12pt}`, passes as layout
  (2026-10-23; round 1 of #443).
- Past a refusal G14 reads a LaTeX file as typed, its commands and comments as words; `check`
  fails on the refusal already (round 1 of step 7).
- `\~{}` before a number, written for "about", is taken for an accent on the word after it,
  which is then not read (round 1 of step 7).
- G6 looks for a placeholder in a LaTeX file's body as typed, as in a Markdown file:
  `\todo{...}` and a `% TODO` comment each fail as a TODO in the text does. Its preamble is
  read as the reader reads it, without a definition's body, so a package or a definition
  named for a note does not; nor do `\author`, `\date` or a comment in the preamble, which
  the reader blanks, though Markdown's front matter is read as typed. Past `\end{document}`
  nothing is read. A phrase G6 reports is not read in a comment, but past a refusal, where
  the file is read as typed (rounds 1 and 2 of step 7b).
- In a LaTeX body as typed, an optional argument that reads as a placeholder fails as one in
  a Markdown raw block does: TikZ's `\draw[fill]`, a description list's `\item[Repository]`
  (round 1 of step 7b).
- G6 reads no definition's body in a LaTeX preamble for a placeholder, used or not, so a
  placeholder a macro prints, `\newcommand{\ncohort}{[TO BE CONFIRMED]}`, is not found where
  it is used either; its phrases and residue rules still read such a body as prose; and a
  definition written in the body is read as typed (round 3 of step 7b).
- A typed reference list is judged entry by entry as a cited entry's fields are, capitals
  only: a todonotes `\todo{...}` or a lower-case `% todo` in it passes (round 3 of step 7b).
  A finding in an entry is named at its `\bibitem` line, one above a placeholder on the next
  line (round 4).
- G8 reads a LaTeX document's printed view, so a supplementary file nothing inputs reports
  nothing, where Markdown counts every supplementary file; G0 warns of the file
  (`tex-not-input`). Past a refusal G8's recomputation reads the file as typed, a comment's
  P value with it (round 1 of step 8).
- G8 keeps a line break inside a `\mg`, between the command and its brace, as a line of the
  view, beside the value it puts in: before it where nothing but spaces or a comment follows
  on its line, else after it. A binding split so and alone on its line, or two in a row, still
  leaves a line of nothing but spaces, which ends the paragraph, and a statistic before it is
  not read with a P after it (round 3 of step 8); so does an anchor split so at the end of a
  line, since it writes nothing (round 4).
- G9 reads a LaTeX claim's words as the view prints them: a command's name and braces are
  spaces, so `\emph{fixed}` says "fixed" where Markdown's `*fixed*` says "*fixed*", and a lock
  made from the Markdown of a paper reads such a claim as changed once the paper is LaTeX.
  An open paragraph is told with a space where a command's brace stood ("paper.yaml ."). The
  supplement's Methods are read in its printed document and named at its entry file (step 8).
  G9 ends a LaTeX paragraph at an empty line alone, not at `\par`: two paragraphs a `\par`
  parts on one line are read as one, the claim of the second holding the words of the
  first (round 1 of step 8). An empty line TeX never reads, inside `\iffalse` or a
  `comment` environment typed within a paragraph, ends it all the same (round 2). A typed
  table outside a float ends its paragraph, as one a `center` or a `longtable` sets apart
  does, so a `tabular` typed within a sentence parts it in two; and another environment
  that sets text apart, a list or a `quote`, ends none (round 3). A float that holds an
  anchor parts the paragraph typed round it, where TeX moves it out and the paragraph goes
  on; and an anchor typed alone after a table set apart claims nothing
  (`method-claim-empty`), as one alone after any paragraph does (round 4).
- G15 reads a LaTeX file's names of models in the words G14 reads, where a word that holds
  `\-` or an accent command is written whole from where it starts, NUL after it, which G15
  reads as spaces between it and the next word (2026-10-27). Two or more lines of comments
  between a word and the name after it are as many line breaks, so "conditional" over them
  does not make the name another model's (round 1 of G15 in step 8). A name a macro of the
  preamble prints, `\newcommand{\mainmodel}{logistic regression}`, is not read where the
  macro is used; past a refusal the headings stay as they were and the rest of the file is
  read as typed, comments too; and a float's caption is read where it is typed, not where
  LaTeX prints the float (round 2).
- G8r reads a claim to have followed a guideline within a sentence, which runs over single
  line breaks and stops at a blank line, before a Markdown line that opens with `#` or `|`,
  and at a typed table's line ends (2026-10-27). A comment line between the two lines of a
  LaTeX claim is blank in the view, and ends the sentence there; and a Markdown table whose
  rows open with no `|`, a simple or a multiline table, has its rows read as one sentence. A
  name a command parts, `RECORD\textendash{}PE`, is read as the part before it, RECORD; and
  a heading more than six levels below the shallowest, `\subparagraph` under `\part`, is
  no heading a checklist's answer can point at (round 1 of G8r in step 8). A definition's
  body is read where it is written, not where it prints: a claim a macro of a package
  prints is not read, and one an unused macro of the preamble holds is (round 2).
- The printed view types LaTeX's dashes, so a quotation G13 is given as the `.tex` has it,
  with `--`, is not found where one copied from the PDF is; and a sentence that opens with a
  typographic quotation mark is now cut from the one before in Markdown too, so a passage or
  a co-author's item recorded on the two joined is matched no more (round 2 of G7 in step
  8).
- G7 reads no quotation in a float's caption or a table's cell, which the printed view does
  not print, and a footnote's words stand at its mark, glued to the word before it, so a
  quotation or a cited sentence a footnote interrupts is read with the note's words in it
  (round 1 of G7 in step 8).
- The reader does not refuse a bare `^` or `_` outside maths, which LaTeX stops on: `check`
  reads the paper, and the build names the error at its line (step 9's agreement test passes
  such a file over).
- MiKTeX does not honour `openin_any`: under it a manuscript can `\input` a file outside the
  copy, by a path that climbs out of it, and print it. TeX Live refuses that path. A manuscript
  that names a file of its own outside its folders, `\includegraphics{../figures/x}` typed by
  hand, is refused under TeX Live, and its figures are the values file's to name (round 1 of
  step 9). So is a supplement that reads the main text by `..`, xr's
  `\externaldocument{../main}` or `\input{../preamble}`: with xr its references come out
  undefined, and fail at `--submission` (round 2).
- The build compares headings only where LaTeX numbers them, and reads them only as
  `\numberline` writes them: under `\setcounter{secnumdepth}{0}`, or in a class that writes
  its contents otherwise (amsart's `\tocsection`), it has nothing to compare, and a heading a
  macro makes is not caught. A title whose words are the `.aux`'s with some left out is the
  reader's, a title the reader reads as empty (`\section{\drug}`) among them, and the match
  looks on past the reader's headings that LaTeX does not number: so a macro's heading stands
  for a later heading of the reader's whose words it holds, or one the reader reads as empty
  (rounds 2 and 3 of step 9).
- On Windows, a program latexmk starts before latexmk is put in the build's job is outside
  the job, and is not stopped at the limit with the rest (round 2 of step 9).
- The submission folder holds every file under its own name, and only `\includegraphics` is
  written with that name. A file another command names by a path into a folder
  (`\documentclass{cls/journal}`, `\usepackage{sty/mine}`) is in the folder but not where
  the path points, so the compile alone refuses the folder and names the file. A picture found
  through `\graphicspath` is found, since graphicx looks where TeX finds files too, unless
  its name holds a folder (step 10).
- The folder writes in every file the document `\include`s, as the reader reads them all,
  so a file `\includeonly` leaves out of the PDF is in the folder's (step 10).
- A biblatex `.bbl` belongs to the biblatex version that wrote it. A journal with another
  version that compiles without running Biber gets a warning and the references of that
  `.bbl` (step 10).
- A review panel is not sent a LaTeX manuscript's preamble, nor the author's packages: a
  command an author defines there, `\drug`, reaches the reviewer as its name, and an abstract
  a class takes in the preamble (MDPI's `\abstract{}`) is not sent. A name in the body that
  authors.yaml does not give is sent; a value pdfLaTeX cannot print is sent as `??`, which
  the dry run does not count. What the blind check's patterns match is sent as `[withheld]`
  where it names no author too: a bare initial and a family name, "group A. Long-term" for
  an author A. Long, or an affiliation's three words in a sentence of the text (round 3 of
  step 12, part 2). A letter with two accents, `\~{\^e}`, or a comma below, `\textcommabelow{s}`,
  is not found as LaTeX types it (round 4). The round's copy
  keeps a picture's path and the line ends as typed, where the submission folder renames
  pictures (round 1 of step 12, part 2).
- At a revision, a LaTeX manuscript's pack has no marked-up copy: `build --marked-up` makes
  Word copies, and `submit` says so in a note (step 10).
- A LaTeX manuscript's `\title` is not compared with paper.yaml's title, where a Markdown
  file's header title is (`two-titles`), and the PDF prints the `\title` (round 1 of step
  13).
- G7's text recycling places a passage that runs on past an `\input` at its first file only,
  ending on its first line there (step 13).
- G7's text recycling does not compare a caption `\subfloat[...]` takes in its option, nor a
  `longtable`'s `\caption`, which the view blanks with the table's cells (round 2 of step 13).
- Past a refusal of the reader in a supplement's file, G16 reads that file's bindings by
  their shape, one in a comment among them; the refusal fails the file in G2 (round 2 of
  step 13). Past a refusal in any file, the compared view counts a brace in a comment the
  reader did not read as a group's, where it marks a quotation (round 3), and an option of a
  quotation's command whose braces do not close in its paragraph ends at its first `]`
  (round 4).
- `build --latex` refuses Markdown that G2's Markdown reader and pandoc read otherwise, and
  says where the digits part: measured, 38 of 180 of the suite's generated files (`texts()`),
  which hold fences closed by a line separator, `:::` divs and a YAML block left open at the
  end. It is a refusal, never a misprint (step 11).
- `build --latex` compares digits, not numbers: a raw TeX that moves a decimal point or a
  sign, `1\iffalse.\fi5` printing 15 where the gates read 1.5, passes, and a digit moved
  between a table's caption and its rows passes. Raw TeX in the text fails `tex-in-the-text`
  from `drafting` on, so this needs an earlier stage or `--skip-checks` (round 1 of step 11).
- `build --latex` reads a `[^n]:` line directly under a paragraph's line as a note's
