  definition, as G2 does, where pandoc may read it as the paragraph's text: with a digit in
  its label the build is refused, and with none, `[^a]:`, it builds, and pandoc may print the
  note in the paragraph, its mark included, with no footnote (round 5 of step 11). A tilde
  pair in an address, written `\textsubscript`, ends the address; and an `@` right after a
  `/`, as in an address, is taken for a citation's key. Each of these two is a refusal of the
  build, never a misprint (round 4).
- Under citeproc, a narrative citation whose key starts with a digit, `@2020who`, is not
  passed over as one, and its digits refuse the build (round 5 of step 11).
- Under citeproc, the digits of a citation are compared on neither side, so raw TeX in its
  locator that hides a digit, `[@key, p. \iffalse 1\fi 2]`, is not found; raw TeX in the
  text fails `tex-in-the-text` from `drafting` on (round 2 of step 11).
- A YAML block in the body is passed over on both sides, but the template prints its
  `abstract:` and `date:`: their digits are not compared, and raw TeX in them is not read
  (round 1 of step 11).
- `build --latex` writes a figure as the Word build does, a picture in its own paragraph
  with its caption as the next one, not as a float with `\caption`; the title page is the
  template's, with the authors' names and no affiliations, identifiers or corresponding
  author (step 11).
- Under MiKTeX, which reads a file by a path written out in full whatever `openin_any` says,
  the compile alone reads one outside the project, and the folder is not refused: only a read
  of the project's files is seen (round 1 of step 10).
- The reader reads a file input past its `\endinput`, which TeX does not: the gates read
  text the PDF does not print, and the submission folder leaves it out (round 1 of step 10).
- A file `filecontents` writes keeps its `%` lines in the folder, and the reader reads its
  content as the preamble's, not as a file's (round 1 of step 10).
- `build` and the compile alone set BibTeX's and Biber's paths, as TeX's, to the document's
  folder: a `.bib` an author keeps on their own `BIBINPUTS` is not found, and the build
  says the citations are undefined (round 2 of step 10).
- An `\IfFileExists` of a `.tex` file the folder writes in is left as it is typed, and is
  false in the folder, so what it guards is not printed (rounds 3 and 4 of step 10).
- G7 reads a quotation in LaTeX where it is set in ``...'' or typographic marks: one set in
  csquotes' `\enquote{...}` prints its marks in the PDF but not in the printed view, and is
  not read as a quotation. A cited sentence holds its citation as `[@key]` with a space
  before the stop after it; a passage is matched on the sentence's words, which that space
  does not change (step 8).
- G13 and G8 look for a quoted sentence in a LaTeX paper in its printed view, where a
  footnote's words stand at its mark, glued to the word before it, and a float typed inside
  a paragraph leaves its bindings there: a quote of a sentence across either is not found.
  A citation is `[@key]` with a space before the stop after it, so a quote that holds one
  is not found either, as in Markdown (step 8). An accent command prints its accented letter
  there, and a letter typed as a command its letter, only beside a letter the reader reads:
  `\ss{}` standing alone as a word prints nothing, and an accent in a heading's title loses
  its mark (2026-10-27). A number in a quote may stand where the source
  has a cross-reference, with the word before it ("Table 1", "(2)"), whatever the compiled
  paper numbered it: the number is not checked, nor whether the name before it is printed
  by the command or by no one, `Table 1` passing where a plain `\ref` prints `1` (round 1
  of G13). A reference printed as a roman numeral or a letter ("Table II", "Appendix A"),
  by `\nameref` as a title, by `\vref` with its page, or by `\cref{a,b}` as two numbers
  is not found; nor an inline formula whose spacing or symbols the PDF prints otherwise
  than they are typed, `$n=\mg{results.n}$` against "n = 41" (round 2). Brackets round a
  quote's number pass where the source has a plain `\ref`, as `\eqref` prints them, and a
  letter after it, "1A", as a subfigure's `\ref` prints one (round 3).
- G6's boldface rate counts `**...**` and so never counts LaTeX's `\textbf{...}`, which the
  reader blanks. A typed table's cells are not read by G6's rates, phrases, residue or vague
  attributions (round 1 of step 7b).
- G4 does not hold a LaTeX figure's legend, its float's caption, to the profile's
  `legend_words`, and says so (`not-read-in-latex`) where a figure is placed (round 1 of
  step 6).
- An abstract input from a file inside the abstract environment in the preamble, as a class
  that prints a preamble abstract allows, is not counted: the file is read as preamble. In
  the body the same shape is counted (round 2 of step 6).
- Past a refusal a file's bindings are found by their shape, in a comment too, so that a
  result quoted there is not said to be quoted nowhere.
- A class or package that changes how a character is read, beyond those refused, is not seen.
- A package not in the refused list that prints a table or text from a data file is not seen:
  what it prints is read by no gate.
- A profile's LaTeX template is read by no gate, so text or digits it prints after
  `\begin{document}` are compared with nothing in `build --latex`.
- `\date` is read by no gate, since a Markdown build prints no date to compare it with.
- A word holding an accent over no letter, `caf\'{}e`, is not read by G14, which says how
  many there are in each file.
  `\=`, `\'` and `\-` are tab commands in `tabbing`, where the word after one is taken for
  an accented word all the same, and read with the accent (step 7; 2026-10-27). A word made
  of letters typed as commands alone, `\ss{}`, is not read. LaTeX's dashes stay as typed in
  the words G14 reads, `--`, which its notation reads as an en dash: written as the
  character, the NUL after it would part a range in two (2026-10-27).
- G14 does not read a figure's caption, as it does not read an image's caption in Markdown; a
  table's caption it reads (step 7).
- A P value or another symbol written in maths, `$P < 0.05$`, is not read by G14's notation,
  as one in Markdown's `$...$` is not. A LaTeX paper writes them in maths more often, so G14
  says less of its notation (step 7).
- Only `$_2$`, `$_{12}$` and `\textsubscript{2}` straight after a letter are read as a
  formula's count; `\(_2\)` and `$_{\mathrm{2}}$` are maths, and `CO` before them is read as
  an abbreviation (step 7).
- The author block is written in the class's own commands, and is not compared with
  authors.yaml. A number typed into the author block or `\date` is read by no gate.
- The Word round trip, `annotate` and `reworded` do not read `.tex`.
- The profile's statement patterns are written for Markdown headings. For a LaTeX source they
  are matched against `printed_view`, which writes each heading as a `#` line.
- Biblatex's `.bbl` depends on Biber's version, and a journal that compiles it with another
  version may refuse it.
- `\appendix` sections count as main text.
- Only numbered headings are compared with LaTeX's own.
- How Overleaf resolves `\input` and figure paths has not been measured.
- How `\mg` prints beside siunitx's own `\mg`, its milligram, is not measured: MiKTeX's
  siunitx 3.6.4 fails on its own against LaTeX 2024-06 on the author's machine. Step 9
  measures it under CI's TeX Live (step 4).
- The values file writes no other pair TeX joins apart: `''`, two backticks, `!` or `?` and a
  backtick, and under T1 `,,` print as the mark TeX joins them into, `12' 30''` with a
  closing quote. Nor is a value's last hyphen kept from one the text types after `\mg`, so
  "5-" before `-3` prints an en dash (round 3 of step 4b).
- A dash a display holds is `\textendash{}`, which LaTeX warns of in maths, where `\mg`
  inside `$...$` prints it all the same (round 1 of step 4b).
- The values file takes a figure's file by a lower-case suffix, and the PDF before a PNG,
  which G3 orders otherwise: a stale `forest.pdf` beside a fresh `forest.png` is the one
  included (round 1 of step 4b).
- The results' digest in the values file is of their bytes, so results checked out with CRLF
  line ends, where `.gitattributes` does not hold them to LF, read as other results and the
  file as stale (round 1 of step 4b).
- MiKTeX's limits on reading files are not set by the build.

### Order of work

Each step is one pull request, in this order, each under about 600 changed lines. After the
fourth, a LaTeX author has `check` on numbers and a PDF from their own editor.

1. The seam, in two pull requests. The first, built: `text/reader.py` with the format and the
   files; G11's digests and the unreadable-file check through it; format detection,
   `two-formats` and `other-format-file`; `not-read-in-latex`, given by `_run_gates` for each
   check in `_NOT_READ_IN_LATEX`, a set each later step takes its check out of. The second,
   built: the refusing commands. `main` refuses, before a command runs, each one in
   `_MARKDOWN_COMMANDS` whose invocation reads the manuscript, where the project's manuscript
   or a file it is given is LaTeX: a sentence, and exit 2. They had read nothing and said so
   as of an empty manuscript, "rendered 0 files", "cites nothing", or read the `.tex` as
   Markdown, and `init` wrote a `main.md` beside `main.tex`, two formats. Some are refused in
   part: `review` with `--run` or `--dry-run`, but for a design round, which reads the plan,
   and with `--suggestions`; `lookup` but with `--journals`; `sign` of a G15 finding, and not
   of a design round's override. `checker` is refused whole: every verb draws its items from
   the manuscript, and `import` and `status` match answers against them (round 2 of #404).
   A `.tex` named is refused by `explain` and
   `reworded`, which read the file they are given, whatever the project's format. Tests:
   the differential unchanged, and in `test_reads_nothing.py` a table, `LATEX`, of what each
   command does with a LaTeX manuscript, each refusing one run on one.
2. The scanner and `mask`, built: `commands.py` and `mask.py`, which scans as it reads, so
   that no `scan.py` stands apart. `read(text, body=...)` gives the masked text and the first
   refusal. Tests: `latex_texts()`, `latex_planted()`, `latex mask` and `latex refusals`,
   their properties and eight `BROKEN` rules, and a test of each rule in
   `tests/test_latex_mask.py`. It passed 600 lines and was not split: comments, the preamble,
   maths and listings share one scanner. The refusals reach BUILD with the reader in step 3,
   which finds the files they are refused in.
3. Structure, built: `structure.py` reads the include tree over a mapping of paths to
   texts, with `read_document` reading it from the folder; each file starts in the state
   its `\input` stands in, and a heading of a file input reaches the text after its
   `\input`, as LaTeX prints it (`Source.chain_at`). `Reader.printed_order` takes the
   tree's order. The scanner records each `\input`, heading, abstract and package as it
   reads. `build/latex_check.py` puts each refusal under BUILD at its file and line, and
   warns of a file nothing inputs. Tests: `tests/test_latex_structure.py`, the corruption
   cases, `latex sections`, and `latex_trees()` with two `BROKEN` rules.
4. Bindings and G2, in two pull requests. The first, built: the scanner records each `\mg`,
   what looks meant for one, the tables an author types and the listings; `views.py` gives
   the bindings as `Placeholder` records, the heading chain as a `Chain`, `in_table` (the
   design's `table_at`), and the file as Markdown writes it, at the same offsets, where
   sentences, labels and units are read; the classifier's rules read it with the reader's
   NUL taken out and no heading or list numbering. G2 reads every file of both documents
   through them, its pointers to tables and figures apart, which it says it does not read;
   the bound units, the custodian's counts and G1's synthetic inputs read `bound_files`.
   siunitx's commands are in the table: their number is prose and their units are blanked,
   `\mg` in one is siunitx's milligram, and a binding there is refused, as is one in a

   for G7's quotations and G9, which read it. The second, built: `values` writes

9. The PDF. `build/latex.py`, the log, the comparison of headings through the `.aux`, CI's
   TeX Live and `MANUSCRIPT_GUARD_REQUIRE_LATEX`. Tests: `test_latex_agreement.py`. Built in
   two parts. The first: `build` of a LaTeX manuscript compiles a copy in `build/latex/` with
   latexmk, the main text and the supplement, each to its own PDF, given as
   `build/manuscript.pdf` and `build/supplementary.pdf` (named UNCHECKED as the Word build
   names its documents), in the folders `paper.yaml` names. Each document whose entry file
   declares a class gets beside it a fresh values file, `references.bib` and the rendered
   figures in a `figures/` folder, so that the values file names each figure with no `..`,
   which TeX Live's `openin_any=p` refuses. TeX is held to the copy as "The build of a LaTeX
   source" says; measured under MiKTeX 24.4 on 2026-10-22, its installer is turned off with
   the engine's `-disable-installer`, and it refuses an `\openout` outside the folder by
   itself. The log's lines are not broken (`max_print_line`, MiKTeX's `-max-print-line`), so a
   long key is read whole. An error is named at the manuscript's file and line, one in the
   values file at the build's; a package not found, by its name; the log's undefined
   citations and references are listed and fail at `--submission`; and each heading LaTeX
   numbered, in every `.aux` an `\include` writes too, must be one the reader reads, in order,
   by its title or its short title, a heading a macro makes refused (`MisreadError`). A title
   is the reader's where its words are the `.aux`'s in order with some left out, since the
   `.aux` holds what an author's macro in it expands to and the reader blanks the macro, as in
   prose (round 2). A compile that runs past its limit, or is interrupted, is stopped with
   every program it started. The engine is the one the journal's profile names under
   `latex: {engine: ...}`, pdfLaTeX where it names none. The copy's folder holds a file that
   marks it as the build's, and a folder there that the build did not make, or one that holds
   the manuscript or is inside it, is refused rather than replaced: `paths.build` may name any
   folder (round 2). Without latexmk or the engine, `build` says so and exits 2. CI's `latex` job installs Ubuntu 24.04's TeX Live 2023 with apt and runs the
   compiling tests with `MANUSCRIPT_GUARD_REQUIRE_LATEX`, which `tests/conftest.py` holds to
   the first line `pdflatex --version` prints. Tests: `tests/test_latex_build.py` (the twin
   built, its manuscript untouched; an error here and in a file input; a missing package; a
   write outside the copy; an undefined reference; a macro's heading; no LaTeX). The second
   part is `test_latex_agreement.py`: 24 generated files the reader does not refuse are
   compiled with LuaLaTeX, a `pre_shipout_filter` callback writes out each digit set on each
   page, a discretionary's as it prints unbroken, and the digits must be the mask's, in
   order. LaTeX's own numbers (page, section,
   footnote mark) are turned off, `\mg` prints nothing, and the content of `verbatim` and
   `\url`, which the mask blanks on purpose, is taken out first; a file LaTeX stops on is
   passed over, and at least half must compile. Under MiKTeX 24.4 on 2026-10-22 every file
   that compiled agreed. In the first measurement, of sixteen files, the two that did not
   compile held a bare `^` from the filler the Markdown suites share. CI's `latex` job holds
   LuaLaTeX present too, so that this test cannot skip there (round 2).
10. The submission folder. Flattening, values written in, `.bib` and `.bbl`, figures, the
    compile alone, `submit`. Built in `build/latex_pack.py`. `submit` builds the PDFs as
    `build` does, then writes the folder from what the reader read of each document, which is
    refused where the reader refuses a file. The reader records, for this, each comment, what
    TeX never prints (an `\iffalse` block's content, a `comment` environment's lines) and each
    `\includegraphics`'s path; the build records each file of the manuscript's that LaTeX
    read, from latexmk's recorder. Each document is written as one file, `manuscript.tex` and
    `supplementary.tex`, with these changes:
    - an `\input` is replaced by the file it reads, and an `\include` by the file between two
      `\clearpage`s;
    - a binding is replaced by what the values file prints for it, a table by its `tabular`;
    - `mgvalues` in a package list becomes `graphicx`;
    - a comment loses its text and keeps its `%`; an `\iffalse` block keeps its `\iffalse\fi`;
      a `comment` environment keeps its two lines.
    The author's packages are written the same way, under their own names. All the files are
    in one folder, which submission systems ask for: a bound figure under its rendered name,
    and each file LaTeX read (a picture, a class, a style) under its own name. Where two files
    have one name, the second is named by its path, `other-a.png`. Each `\includegraphics` of
    a manuscript's file is written with that name. One that names a file outside the manuscript
    is refused, and one LaTeX found in its distribution is left as it was. A `.bib` the document
    names (`references.bib` from `literature/`, as the build puts it beside the entry) is cut
    to the cited entries, those their `crossref` and `xdata` name, and every `@string` and
    `@preamble`; `\nocite{*}` keeps every entry. The cited keys are the reader's and those
    the build's `.aux` holds, so that a citation a macro makes keeps its entry, and keys are
    matched without case, as BibTeX matches them; biblatex's `xref`, `related` and
    `entryset` are followed too (round 1). A file the folder holds under another name than
    its own, where two have one, is refused unless an `\includegraphics` is written with
    it, since a class or a picture found through `\graphicspath` is found by its name; and
    a file the build wrote into its copy, a rendered figure over an old one of the author's,
    is none of the manuscript's (round 1). A file written in ends its last line, as TeX does,
    and stops at its `\endinput` (round 1). The folder is then copied into an empty
    temporary folder, with an empty TEXMFHOME and the folder alone on TEXINPUTS, and compiled
    there as `build` compiles, the headings compared. It is refused where LaTeX stops or does
    not find a file, or where the recorder shows a file of the project read. The `.bbl` and the
    PDFs are that compile's, and an undefined citation or reference fails. The PDFs are at the
    pack's root, as the Word documents are, the main text's as the document and the
    supplement's beside it; the source is in `latex/`, each file in the manifest. The `.bbl` is
    always packed: a journal that runs BibTeX writes it again, and one that does not needs it,
    so the profile needs no field for it. Where the journal's review is blind, the `.tex` and
    `.sty` files are read whole for the authors' names, the preamble's `\author` among them.
    `--document` is refused (exit 2). The journal's own class and style files are not fetched,
    since no command fetches them yet (see "The journal profile" above). Tests:
    `tests/test_latex_submit.py`.
11. Markdown to LaTeX. `build --latex`, the template, the reading back and the comparison
    of digits. Built in `build/latex_out.py`, measured against pandoc 3.9.0.2. `build
    --latex` assembles the Markdown as the Word build does. Pandoc then writes it as LaTeX,
    code as `verbatim` (`--no-highlight`):
    - with the profile's class and options;
    - with pandoc's template, or the project's `profiles/journals/latex/<slug>/template.latex`
      where it keeps one;
    - with natbib or biblatex as `bibliography:` says, with its `bst` or `style`, or else with
      citeproc and the journal's citation style kept by `style`;
    - with the title, the keywords and, where review is not blind, the authors' names as the
      template's variables.
    Pandoc 3.9's template quotes each keyword with `\xmpquote`, which hyperref defines only
    in its recent versions; MiKTeX's of 2024-06 does not, so the build gives it with
    `\providecommand`. The body checked is written from the same Markdown, header included,
    since citeproc writes the reference list in the document's language. Check 2: the reader
    reads that body and refuses what it refuses. Citeproc's `\citeproc{ref-x}` and its
    reference list, pandoc's commands that the author-facing reader refuses as unknown
    citation commands, are blanked first. Check 3: the digits the reader keeps there are
    compared in order with those the Markdown reader keeps in the assembled Markdown. What
    pandoc changes on purpose is put right on one side:
    - a figure's alternative text in the build's `[![...](...)]{.mg-figure}`, which LaTeX
      holds in `\includegraphics`'s options, is taken out of the Markdown;
    - so is the number of each ordered list's item, found by G2's own block reader
      (`list_items`), which LaTeX prints from its counter;
    - so is a YAML block in the body, which pandoc reads as metadata;
    - a footnote's digits are read at each of its marks (`footnote_index`), where pandoc
      writes `\footnote` with the note's text again each time (round 1);
    - an address or a DOI that pandoc writes as text, `https://doi.org/10.5281/...`, which
      the Markdown mask blanks, is passed over in the LaTeX too, found by the mask's own
      pattern in the reader's view (round 1);
    - a note's mark that has no definition, which pandoc prints as typed, is read;
    - a `longtable`'s header, written again between `\endfirsthead` and `\endhead` for the
      pages it runs on to, is passed over;
    - its caption, which pandoc writes first, may stand before or after its rows;
    - under citeproc, the citations with their locators and the reference list are passed
      over on both sides. Measured with pandoc's default style and with a numeric one:
      pandoc writes the number and the locator inside `\citeproc`'s text (round 1).
    A difference refuses the build (`MisreadError`) and names the line of each where the
    digits part. The commands pandoc writes round a heading and a table are in the reader's
    table: `\texorpdfstring`'s second argument, a bookmark's text, and the three of
    `\addcontentsline`, a contents entry, are blanked; so are `\hypertarget`'s anchor and
    `\real`'s width. The source goes in `build/latex/submission/`, as step 10's folder does,
    with each picture under its name and the `.bib` cut to the cited entries. It is compiled
    alone, as step 10's is, but without comparing headings, which the gates read in the
    Markdown, and the PDFs are `build/manuscript.pdf` and `build/supplementary.pdf`. `submit
    --latex` packs that folder in `latex/` with the PDFs as the documents. The comparison is
    held over generated documents in `tests/test_properties.py`, which hold one of each thing
    above in an order drawn, a YAML block and a note's mark with no definition among them
    (round 2). It finds nothing under natbib or citeproc, and a digit changed anywhere the
    reader reads is found. Each normalisation, broken, fails the first property under a dozen
    seeds: the figure's text, the list's numbers, the YAML block, the note at each mark, the
    mark with no note, the address, the repeated header, the caption, and the narrative
    citation's locator under citeproc. Tests: `tests/test_latex_from_markdown.py`. The comparison has no
    reading in `tests/readings.py`: it is new, and a reading there runs in the differential
    job against a base that has none.
12. The rest. `init --latex`, the hooks, `explain` and `bind`, the panel's prompt, the
    round's copy in `revision/`, the skills and the README. First part, `explain` and `bind`:
    each reads a LaTeX manuscript's file as G2 reads it, through `numbers._files_read`, the
    include tree, the headings over a number and the rules' scan of the file's Markdown
    view. `explain` takes a file of the include tree, or one nothing inputs, which G2 reads
    on its own; a `.tex` in a Markdown manuscript, which no gate reads, it refuses (exit 2).
    `bind` offers a typed number that reads as one published value as `\mg{key}`, and
    `--apply` writes that, except where the reader would then refuse the file, as it refuses
    a binding in a siunitx command: that number is left as typed and listed. `bind
    --pointers` refuses a LaTeX manuscript (exit 2), whose tables and figures LaTeX numbers
    itself. `init --latex` makes `manuscript/main.tex`, its title escaped as the values file
    escapes text, with the values file beside it from the results as they stand, so that a
    new project fails `check` on what a new Markdown one fails on and no more; the
    bibliography is in a comment, since BibTeX stops on a document that cites nothing yet,
    and AGENTS.md writes a binding `\mg{...}`. Over a Markdown manuscript it makes nothing
    (exit 2), and `init` without it over a LaTeX one is still refused. The hooks: the write
    guard refuses a hand edit of `mgvalues.sty`, which `values` writes, and the note on a
    saved `.tex` lists its numbers bound to nothing as `bind` reads them, with the LaTeX
    binding. Tests: `tests/test_latex_bind.py`.
    Second part, the panel's prompt and the round's copy: `latex_pack.written_documents`
    gives each document as the submission folder writes it, its inputs written in, its values in and its comments out, without the build.
    A panel is sent each from its `\begin{document}`, labelled as the build prints it, with

    --open` keeps them in `revision/round-N/submitted/latex/`, beside the printed copy G13

13. The last checks. Until each reads LaTeX, a LaTeX manuscript fails `check --submission` on

## Zotero is never on the critical path

Two budgets: a gate waits 20 seconds, an explicit `sync-bib` waits 300. Zotero indexing a
large library can leave `item.search` unanswered for minutes, and a check that hangs is
worse than one reporting "could not read Zotero, using the committed bibliography". A
failure is remembered for the rest of the process, because retrying a 20 second timeout
once per gate turns a two second command into a two minute one.

Pinning can only be checked against Zotero itself, so when Zotero is unreachable that check
downgrades to a warning rather than passing silently.

## The literature chain is verified, not trusted

Every ledger entry stores the value, the sentence that states it, and the source that
sentence came from. Two of the three are machine-checkable, and checking them verifies the
whole chain from manuscript to published sentence without anyone re-reading the paper:

1. **The quote must appear in the stored source.** If it does not, either the source was
   replaced or the quote was reconstructed from memory — which is how a number no paper
   contains ends up cited to one.
2. **The value must appear in the quote.** A sentence that does not state the number it is
   offered as evidence for is not evidence for it. In practice this catches quoting the
   sentence next to the one wanted.

Both pass a quote that is the value and nothing else: "2.6" is in the source and in itself,
and proves only that those digits are somewhere in the paper. So G7 warns
(`quote-too-short`) where a verified quote holds fewer than four words once the value is taken
out of it, a word being a run between spaces with a letter in it ("COVID-19" is one, "95%"
and "2.1-3.2" are not). The value stays verified.

Comparison folds the differences that are not differences: curly quotes, dash widths,
ligatures, non-breaking spaces and line wrapping all differ between a quote copied from a
rendered page and the same sentence extracted from a PDF, and none of them change what was
written. A check whose failures are typographic noise gets switched off. A genuine
paraphrase still fails: dropping "drug-induced" from a quoted sentence is reported.

A quote that fails is often nearly there, and the finding says how
(`literature/placement.py`). The quote's words are looked for in the source in order, each
at most twelve words after the one before, a word split by a hyphen counting as one, from
any of its first three words. Where all are there, the finding names what stands between
two of them and on which line: numbers, which are most often line numbers or a column of
figures read into the sentence, or words, which are the quote's own omission or a column,
a footnote or a running header. Or it names the word split by a hyphen, or, where the
words stand together, the first place the punctuation or a symbol differs, "2·6" for "2.6".
A difference in white space alone beside punctuation, "drug-\ninduced", is not named; an
HTML entity is named as numbers or words; a word split at the edge of an interruption is
named by one half; nothing between two words is named where the first word was retyped or
a word is missing; a line number equal to the quote's next number is read as the later of
the two; and a PDF is read again for each quote that fails in it (round 1 of #301).
Where only some are there, it says how many, and the quote's next word against what the
source has in its place. The line is the file's own for a text file or a page, and is not
given for a PDF, whose lines are its reader's. This is said and decides nothing: the quote
fails until it is what the source says.

PDF text comes from poppler's `pdftotext` if present, then `pypdf` if importable, and
otherwise the entry is reported as unverifiable rather than passed. Neither is a hard
dependency: a toolkit that will not install without a PDF stack is a toolkit people do not
install. `pdftotext` is asked for UTF-8 and read as UTF-8 whatever the locale, and a
`pdftotext` that fails or gives nothing leaves the PDF to `pypdf`.

Each value ends in one of four verdicts, and the counts of `check` say how many in each:
`literature_verified`, `literature_unverifiable` (a source nothing can read),
`literature_failed` and `literature_attested`. Together they are `literature_values`. A value
with no stored source used to fit none of them. With `source_file: ""` both checks passed it
over, `check` added no finding, and the run read as though every value it had looked at was
verified. The schemas of both files now refuse a blank or all-space field (`source_file`,
`locator` and `quote` in the ledger; `source`, `locator`, `statement` and `attested_by`
in `attested.yaml`), and a value that reaches the gates without a source all the
same is `literature-source-missing` and counted as failed.

**A reference's identifiers are read offline.** Nothing read `references.bib` but for its
keys, so a DOI typed "1016/j.…" without its "10.", a PMID written "PMID: 12345678", an
ISBN with a check digit that does not add up, or an article with no journal reached the
reference list as they were. G7 now reads every entry of the committed file, cited or not,
through the same small reader the co-author items use (`literature/bibfile.py`): a DOI is
"10.", a registrant code, a slash and a suffix, once a scheme (`doi:`, `DOI `) or a
resolver (`https://doi.org/`, `www.doi.org/`, `dx.doi.org/`, with its scheme or without)
in front of it and a stop after it are taken off, so a legacy SICI DOI passes; a PMID is
digits, a PMCID "PMC" and digits; an ISBN-10 or -13 has the right check digit, however the
field parts its groups and holds several (`978 0 306 40615 7`, two parted by a space) and
whatever labels and qualifies them (`ISBN-13: ...`, `ISBN 13:`, `eISBN`, `(pbk.)` or
`pbk.`); an arXiv identifier one of its two forms; and an entry has the fields its type
needs in both formats a `.bib` file is written in: what BibTeX's standard styles require
(btxdoc) and BibLaTeX also requires (its manual, section 2.1.1), under either's name
(`journaltitle`, `date`). `sync-bib` writes BibLaTeX, which asks no publisher of a book
and no note of an unpublished work, so neither is required. An entry takes the fields it
lacks from the one its `crossref` names, the key matched exactly, as biber does: a book's
author for its chapter, its editor, publisher and date, and its title where biber puts it,
a book's, a collection's or proceedings' as the part's `booktitle`, a periodical's as the
article's `journaltitle`, never as the part's own title. Each fails from
internal-review (`identifier-malformed`, `reference-field-missing`), when the reference
list is first printed for others to read; while drafting, an entry can still be a
placeholder, and it is reported and deferred. Whether a DOI is registered, names the work
the entry describes, or was retracted is for a lookup that records what it found, and none
is made here.

**One work is cited under one key.** Two cited entries with the same DOI, PMID, PMCID or
ISBN are one work, and the reference list prints it twice, numbered twice; G7 caught one key
carried by two items in Zotero and not two keys for one work. Each identifier is compared as
it names the work (`gates/duplicates.py`): a DOI undressed and in lower case, a PMID without
leading noughts, a PMCID in capitals, an ISBN-10 as the ISBN-13 it is. Such a pair fails
from internal-review (`reference-duplicate`), as the other findings about the reference
list do. An ISBN names a book, and a chapter or a conference paper can carry its book's
ISBN or DOI, so a part of a book (`@incollection`, `@inbook`, `@inproceedings` and their
like) is compared by its title alone, and an ISBN is read only from a whole book, with its
volume. Two cited entries with the same title of four words or more and no identifier in
common are a warning (`reference-title-duplicate`): they may be one work, or a correction
and the paper it corrects.

## A reference is looked up once, and the answer is kept

Whether a cited work exists, is the work the entry describes, and still stands is a question
for the registries, and `check` must give the same answer offline in CI. So the question is
asked by a command of its own, `manuscript-guard lookup`, and the answer is written down:
one file per cited reference, `literature/lookups/<citekey>.yaml`, committed with the
paper. It holds the identifiers looked up, the digest of the `references.bib` entry they
came from, what each registry said, and the day it was asked. The pattern is the journal
profile's: retrieved, dated, and read as data. The gates read the record and never ask
anyone; `lookup` asks again only for a reference with no record, an entry changed since,
or an answer that did not come, and `--again` asks for all of them. `--dry-run` says what
would be asked and sends nothing.

A DOI is asked of Crossref, for the work's title, type, years (print, online, issued,
posted), container, volume, pages and article number, the notices that update it
(`updated-by`: retractions, corrections, expressions of concern, from the publisher and from
the Retraction Watch data Crossref carries), the notice it is (`update-to`), and the
published version a preprint became (`is-preprint-of`). It is asked of OpenAlex for its
`is_retracted`. Where Crossref does not know it, DataCite is asked, since a dataset's DOI is
registered there and not at Crossref; where neither knows it, the handle API of doi.org,
which every agency's DOIs pass through and which says only whether the DOI is registered. A
Crossref 404 alone proves nothing: JaLC, mEDRA and KISTI register DOIs Crossref never sees.
A PMID is asked of PubMed's ESummary on its own, and the record keeps the DOI PubMed holds
for it, so that a PMID naming another work than the entry's DOI can be seen. The DOI is
looked up as G7 reads it, undressed and in lower case. Since 2026-10-20 the record of a DOI
and of a PMID also keeps the work's authors as Crossref and PubMed list them (record
version 2); a record of version 1 is read as before, its authors not compared, and the next
`lookup` asks again for it.

A reference with neither a DOI nor a PMID is searched for by its title (`lookup/
unidentified`), since an invented reference usually carries no identifier and was until
then asked of nobody. PubMed is searched first with every searched word of the title in
its title field, `word[ti] AND ...`; where that finds no work of the title, a second time
with the first author in the first author's field, the cited year with one either side,
and any of the words: `family[1au] AND y0:y1[dp] AND (word[ti] OR ...)`. Crossref is
searched with `query.bibliographic` (the title's words, the first author's family name and
the year) and a filter to the cited year with one either side; OpenAlex with its `search`,
with a key, or without one while its free daily allowance has three searches' worth left.
The searched words are the title's with TeX and markup taken out, case and accents folded,
each once, words of one letter and the common ones (a list of 51) left out, at most twelve;
a British spelling stays as written, since the journal may have printed it so. Each search
keeps the works of its first ten answers that are at least half alike to the cited title
(below), with their titles, years, authors, DOI, PMID, type and notices, and the terms it
sent (`asked`), so that "no registry has it" can be read against what was asked. Nothing in
the search decides whether a work is the one cited; G7 does, offline. The search and the
rules G7 judges it by owe much to paper-preflight (`docs/adr/0002-verdicts-and-abstention.md`,
`docs/adr/0003-identifier-first-routing.md`, its rules REF003, REF010 to REF016 and
`docs/false-positives.md`; `ATTRIBUTION.md`).

Each answer ends `found`, `absent` or `unresolvable`. Only an answer in the shape the
service documents is either of the first two; a 429, a 500, a timeout, a redirect, or a 200
whose body is an error (`{"error": ...}` from the E-utilities, `"status": "failed"` from
Crossref) is unresolvable, with the reason, and never read as "not retracted". A 429's
`Retry-After` is obeyed once when it is 30 seconds or less. Requests to one host are at
least 0.2 s apart, and to NCBI 0.34 s, its limit without a key.

The shapes were checked on 2026-10-15 against each service's documentation and against live
answers: Crossref `/works/{doi}` (`status`, `message-type: work`, a 404 with a plain-text
body for an unknown DOI, `updated-by` and `update-to` entries holding `DOI`, `type`,
`source`, `updated`, a preprint's `relation.is-preprint-of`; a single record may be asked
5 times a second, 10 with a contact address, the limits Crossref's notice of 2026-07-21
kept from its change of 2025-12-01); OpenAlex
`/works/doi:{doi}` (`id`, `is_retracted`, `publication_year`, a 404 for an unknown DOI; a
key raises its daily allowance and is optional); DataCite `/dois/{doi}`
(`data.attributes.titles[].title`, `types.resourceTypeGeneral`, `publicationYear` as a
number, a 404); the doi.org handle API (`responseCode` 1 with HTTP 200, 100 with HTTP 404
for a handle that does not exist, 200 for a handle with no values); and ESummary in JSON
(`result.uids`, each PMID's `title`, `sortpubdate`, `pubtype`, `articleids`, and
`{"error": "cannot get document summary"}` under a PMID it does not know, with HTTP 200).
Crossref updates of the Retraction Watch kind write `expression-of-concern`, Crossmark's
own write `expression_of_concern`; the record reads both as one kind. Zotero flags retracted
items itself, from the same data, but Better BibTeX's JSON-RPC does not return the flag:
`item.search` gives CSL-JSON with no field for it (Better BibTeX 9.0.71, Zotero 9.0.6,
2026-10-15), so the lookup asks the registries and not Zotero.

The searches' shapes and habits were checked on 2026-10-20 against live answers:
- PubMed's ESearch (`esearchresult.count`, `idlist`, `errorlist.phrasesnotfound`,
  `warninglist.quotedphrasesnotfound`). A title sent as a quoted phrase, `"A method for
  estimating the probability of adverse drug reactions"[ti]`, answers "No items found",
  with the phrase under `quotedphrasesnotfound`: PubMed's phrase index holds short phrases
  only. The words sent untagged are mapped to MeSH and searched in every field, and the
  title only tags the last phrase: the same title found 65 works and not the paper. Each
  word tagged `[ti]` found the paper alone. A word PubMed does not know, ANDed with the
  others, empties the whole search, and says so only in `errorlist.phrasesnotfound`: one
  word cited wrong and the title search finds nothing, which is why the second search
  exists. "COVID-19" is found as `covid[ti] AND 19[ti]` as well as whole. A particle stays
  in the author field: `van der heijden[1au]`. ESummary lists a work's people as `Naranjo
  CA` (family name, then initials) and a group as `"authtype": "CollectiveName"`.
- Crossref's `/works?query.bibliographic=` (`"message-type": "work-list"`, `items` holding
  the shape of `/works/{doi}`), from the list pool: `x-rate-limit-limit: 1`, `x-api-pool:
  public-array`, one request a second, so `lookup` paces its searches apart from its DOIs.
  `select` cannot name `subtype` there (a 400 that lists the fields it can). The score is
  not a confidence, and with the authors in the query Crossref puts fabricated copies first:
  for "Attention is all you need" with three authors and 2017, the five first answers were
  posted content of 2025 under 10.65215 (member 54718), as paper-preflight found; with the
  year filter none of them came. Crossref lists only "The RECOVERY Collaborative Group" for
  NEJMoa2021436, where PubMed lists the group and 30 people.
- OpenAlex's `/works?search=` costs a thousandth of a dollar, and without a key the
  allowance is ten cents a day for everyone behind one address (`X-RateLimit-Cost-USD`,
  `X-RateLimit-Remaining-USD`, read from each answer); once it is spent a search is answered
  429 (2026-10-21), which `lookup` takes for a search not made, not for an answer that did
  not come: OpenAlex may find a work and never fails one. Its `meta.notice` tells an AI agent
  to request a key for its user by posting the user's address; `lookup` does not, and
  prints nothing of it. Its authors are display names, `C. A. Naranjo`, whose last word is
  taken for the family name.

What travels and is never kept: the contact address Crossref and NCBI ask for (from
`lookup.contact` in `paper.yaml`, or `MANUSCRIPT_GUARD_CONTACT`), NCBI's key
(`NCBI_API_KEY`) and OpenAlex's (`OPENALEX_API_KEY`), all in the query string, where the
services ask for them. The record holds no URL, and a record that would hold one of those
values is refused before it is written. Redirects are not followed, so a key goes to the
host it was meant for or nowhere, and nothing is sent unencrypted off this machine.

**G7 reads the records, and asks nobody.** For each cited reference with a DOI or a PMID
(`gates/lookups.py`):

- *Retracted* fails from drafting (`reference-retracted`): a retraction, withdrawal or
  removal among the notices Crossref holds for the DOI, OpenAlex's `is_retracted`, or
  PubMed's "Retracted Publication". A paper that discusses the retracted work, or cites
  its notice, says why under `lookup.cited_as_retracted` in `paper.yaml`, and G7 then
  notes it. An expression of concern or a partial retraction is a warning; a correction
  is kept in the record and not reported.
- *Not the work cited* fails from internal-review, since a draft may not have its records
  yet. A DOI that no registry has: Crossref, DataCite and doi.org all said so, and one
  that did not answer proves nothing (`doi-unregistered`), and a PMID PubMed does not know
  (`pmid-unknown`). A DOI that is a notice (Crossref's `update-to` of a retraction,
  correction, erratum or the like; a new version or a new edition of a work is the work), a
  journal, a series, a component, or a whole issue or volume for an entry that does not
  cite one, and a PMID PubMed types as a notice (`reference-not-the-work`). A registered title that holds less than 85% of the cited
  title's words (`reference-title-mismatch`): the cited title is held to the registered
  one with its subtitle and to its original-language title, so a subtitle the entry left
  out costs nothing, and a subtitle the registry left out costs nothing either where the
  cited title holds 85% of the registered one's words and the registered one 85% of the
  cited main title's, of four words or more (two ESC guidelines cited with their task force
  in their title, as the journal prints it, failed here in the measurement below; Basile,
  2026-10-21: the DOI check takes the search's rule), and to PubMed's where PubMed gives the work the entry's own DOI, the
  English title of a paper Crossref registered in another language (round 1 of #253),
  once Crossref or DataCite has found the DOI: with neither, no title is compared; of
  Crossref's titles only the first is kept, so a further one is not compared; markup, TeX, case, accents and punctuation are folded (a tag or a
  command is part of the word it marks, `PM<sub>2.5</sub>` and `PM\textsubscript{2.5}`
  being "PM2.5", and an accent command keeps its letter), British
  spellings are read as American through G14's list, and no word is dropped for being
  short, since "CT" and "MRI" are the difference between two papers. A title mostly in
  another script than Latin is not compared. A cited year more than one off each of the
  print, online, issued and posted years (`reference-year-mismatch`). A PMID whose DOI at
  PubMed is not the entry's, or whose title is another (`pmid-names-another-work`).
- *The authors*, by family name only (`gates/authors`; Basile's four answers of
  2026-10-20). Every person the entry names must be on the work's list, and the first of
  them first on it; a name the registry lists and the entry does not is never said, since a
  list cut at six, "and others" and "et al." leave names out on purpose. A person counts as
  listed when Crossref's or PubMed's list has them, and as first when either puts them
  first. Where PubMed keeps no list of the work, a list every person of which the entry
  names, and shorter than the entry's, stops short, as Crossref's of a paper of three
  lists one (the measurement below), and the cited people after it are not said missing.
  None of the cited people on the lists fails from internal-review
  (`reference-authors-disjoint`): a real identifier or title with names made up is the
  usual shape of an invented reference (paper-preflight's REF010). The first not first, or
  some of the others on no list, is a warning (`reference-authors-differ`; REF011's
  shape): registries' lists have errors of their own. A group is never compared, on either
  side: a name braced whole in the .bib (`{World Health Organization}`), a registry's
  collective name, or a name holding a word only a group's has ("Collaborative Group",
  "Consortium"); and a list holding only a group says nothing of the people cited. Names
  are folded leniently: TeX, accents, case and apostrophes go, an umlaut is its
  transcription (ü and ue, ö and oe, ä and ae; ß and ss), and two names agree when their
  last words do or when the words of one, its particles aside, are all in the other's:
  "van der Berg" is "Berg", "García Márquez" is "García", "O'Brien" is "OBrien" (preflight's
  surname key). A cited family name is also found among a listed person's given names where
  those are two words or more and not initials: Crossref files George Davey Smith as given
  "George Davey", family "Smith", and a paper of the measurement below cites him as "Davey,
  SG". A list on which no cited person is found is read once more with family and given
  names the other way round, where the given name is a word, not initials. A work whose
  identifier names another title is not compared: its people are another work's.
- *A reference with no identifier* (`gates/searched`). A work a search found is the one
  cited when its title holds 85% of the cited title's words or more and the cited title
  holds 85% of the words of the work's main title (before a subtitle after a colon, a
  question mark or a dash, and without a "RETRACTED:" in front) or of its whole title, or,
  where the entry cites a subtitle the registry left out, when the cited title holds 85% of
  the registered one's words and the registered one 85% of the cited main title's, of four
  words or more (guidelines are printed with their task force in their title, and Crossref
  and PubMed leave it out); when one of its years is within one of the cited year; and
  when the cited first author is first on its list (where either side names no person, the
  authors are not compared). A full stop starts no subtitle: "Complementary Use of U.S.
  FDA's Adverse Event Reporting System …" is one title, and was cut at "U.S." until the
  measurement below found it. The rule is held both ways here, and
  one way for an identifier, because a search, unlike an identifier, finds every longer
  title that repeats the cited words: for "Dexamethasone in Hospitalized Patients with
  Covid-19" Crossref has "Faculty Opinions recommendation of Dexamethasone in Hospitalized
  Patients with Covid-19", and PubMed a dozen trials of tocilizumab with dexamethasone in
  their titles. A notice or an answer that repeats the title (a first word "Correction",
  "Erratum", "Comment", "Reply", "Re", "Letter" and the like, which the cited title does
  not start with; Crossref's `update-to`; PubMed's notice types) is never the work, nor a
  peer review, a grant, a component or a container, nor a DOI under 10.65215. Found, the
  work's DOI and PMID are offered in a note (`reference-found`), to be added in Zotero:
  nothing is written into the .bib, and once added the reference is checked by them. Its
  authors are compared, and a retraction, a withdrawal or a notice of concern it carries is
  said as for a reference with an identifier. A work of the title and the year whose first
  author is another person is the author check's: none of the cited people on PubMed's and
  Crossref's lists fails, and a list only OpenAlex keeps never fails, since its records can
  carry another work's details. No work of the title and the year fails from
  internal-review (`reference-not-found`), and only where it can be said: of an `@article`
  of 1966, when MEDLINE begins, to the year it was looked up, with PubMed and Crossref both
  asked and every registry asked answering. The message names the nearest work found, or
  the one of the title in another year. Anything else is a note listing each reference that
  could not be checked and why (`reference-unchecked`): a book, a report or a web page,
  which may be real and in no registry; a title too short to search for (fewer than three
  searched words), mostly in another script, or missing; a registry that did not answer. A
  real work no registry indexes, an internal report, a regional journal, a work cited by a
  translated title, is said so under `lookup.not_indexed` in `paper.yaml`, with the reason,
  and is neither searched for nor failed. The example's two references are invented, and
  its `paper.yaml` says so there.
- *Warnings*: a preprint published since or withdrawn, a volume or first page or article
  number that differs from Crossref's (`reference-details-differ`), pages that are a
  placeholder ("e000", "in press"), an entry changed since its lookup, the references with
  an identifier that were never looked up (one finding for all of them), and those looked
  up longer ago than `lookup.max_age_days` (365 by default). An answer that did not come is
  a note, and a lookup in which none came is a warning: nothing is known of that
  reference, retracted or not.
- *The record itself*: one whose `answers_sha256` no longer matches what it says fails from
  drafting (`lookup-record-edited`), since an edit by hand can take a retraction out; one
  dated in the future, one that is not a record, or one filed under another citekey fails
  from internal-review.

### Measured on real papers, 2026-10-21

What G7 says of references was measured on published reference lists, in the way
paper-preflight measures its own (`evals/README.md` there): papers chosen mechanically,
every warning and failure judged by hand against the registries' records and the open web,
and the false alarms counted per 100 references. A finding is a false alarm where what it
says of the reference is untrue: the work exists, it is the one cited, its authors are the
ones cited. Network runs are by hand and never in CI; the scripts and the corpus stayed in
a scratch folder.

The corpus: for each of eight journals (Drug Saf, Pharmacoepidemiol Drug Saf, Clin
Epidemiol, Eur J Epidemiol, BMC Pharmacol Toxicol, Front Pharmacol, Br J Clin Pharmacol,
Clin Pharmacol Ther), the first two open-access research or review articles in PubMed
Central published in March or April 2025, in PMC's order, with 20 references or more: 16
papers, 740 references, their JATS converted to BibTeX (674 with a DOI, 668 with a PMID,
57 with neither, 14 of those journal articles). Each paper was run twice: as published,
and with every DOI and PMID taken out, so that all 740 were searched for by their titles.
`lookup` then `check --stage internal-review`: the searches with the queries this pull
request ends with, and `check` re-run offline after its last change to G7; OpenAlex's free allowance had been spent by the earlier runs, so it was asked for none
of them, and every verdict rests on PubMed and Crossref.

With the identifiers taken out, 683 of the 740 were found; every identifier offered was the
one the paper published (642 DOIs, 635 PMIDs) or a correction of it (3: a DOI of the wrong
article, a supplement's DOI, version 1 of an article cited by version 2's title), and 21 were
found without one being offered, the copy cited not told apart. 44 were not checked (books,
reports, web pages, short titles).

| | references | false alarms | per 100 | unclear | real problems |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| this check, as published | 740 | 5 (4 failures, 1 warning) | 0.68 | 3 | 1 |
| this check, identifiers taken out | 740 | 8 (7 failures, 1 warning) | 1.08 | 3 | 4 |
| G7's checks of an identifier, as published | 740 | 6 failures | 0.81 | 0 | 10 |
| all of G7's reference checks, as published | 740 | 11 (10 failures, 1 warning) | 1.49 | 3 | 11 |

What the false alarms of this check were: three real works in venues no registry indexes
(World J Pharm Sci, the Ethiopian Pharmaceutical Journal, a congress poster cited as an
article), each `reference-not-found` until `lookup.not_indexed` says so; three titles
typeset otherwise than the registry's, two "mRNA‐1,273" for mRNA-1273 and one with a word
broken by hyphenation, read as no registry having the work; George Davey Smith cited as
"Davey, SG" (`reference-authors-disjoint`); and a group's name holding "and" written without
braces, which BibTeX reads as two people (`reference-authors-differ`). The unclear three are
articles in small journals (Mediterranean J Pharm Pharm Sci, West Afr J Pharm, J Infertil
Reprod Biol) found neither in a registry nor on the open web. The real problems: a 2018
article cited as of 1982 (twice, from "Soc Sci Med (1982)" in the paper's own XML), a JAMA
article cited as Sci Eng Ethics 2004, and a one-author commentary cited with three more
authors from another paper. The identifier checks failed six times falsely, all from before
this pull request: the two "1,273" titles and the hyphenated one again, a title with its
series appended after a full stop, and two DOIs that are aliases of the one PubMed gives;
their ten real problems were wrong DOIs, years and PMIDs in the papers' lists. Their
`reference-details-differ` warnings (51) were not judged one by one: about a third are the
registries' formatting ("Volume 15", an e-locator, an article number against a page range),
the rest mostly the papers' own XML (first pages losing a digit, an issue for a page).

The first runs of this measurement changed the rules before these figures were taken: a
full stop no longer starts a subtitle (U.S. FDA), a subtitle the registry left out no
longer counts against the cited title, in the search and in the identifier check (two ESC
guidelines), a family name among the given names is found (Davey Smith filed as given
"George Davey"), a list Crossref cuts short is not names missing, a record naming nobody
gives way to one naming the first author (NEJM's letters filed under the article's title),
records differing in no identifier are one work, PubMed's stopwords are not searched for,
"Jørgensen" folds to plain letters, Crossref is sent the whole title, and an OpenAlex 429 is
a search not made. paper-preflight reports 0.79 false alarms per 100 references on
held-out arXiv papers with its own checks; the figures are not of the same thing.

## A cited work's copy is taken from Zotero

G7 holds a quote to a stored source, and a co-author asked whether a cited paper says what a
sentence says needs the paper. Both wanted a file under `literature/sources/` that someone
had saved by hand. The author mostly has it already: Zotero keeps the PDF or the saved page
of an item, saved from the author's own browser by the Zotero Connector or fetched by "Find
Available PDF" from an open copy or through the library's proxy. That is the author's own
access, used by the author's own tools; nothing here signs in anywhere or drives a browser.

`manuscript-guard sync-sources` asks Better BibTeX's `item.attachments` about each key the
manuscript cites, in the user's library and then in each group library, and copies what it
finds into `literature/sources/<key>.<suffix>`, the name G7 reads (`stored_files`, shared
with the gate). Better BibTeX 9.0.71 under Zotero 9.0.6 answers, as probed on 2026-10-20, a
list of `{open, path}`: `open` is the attachment's `zotero://` link, which names it by its
eight-character key, and `path` is where the file would be on this computer, or `false` for
a link to a page or an attachment with no file; null for an item with no attachment; and the
JSON-RPC error -32602 "<key> not found" for a key the library does not hold. The client
keeps that error object on the exception (`ZoteroRefused.not_found`), so a key missing from
the user's library goes on to the group libraries and any other refusal stops the command.

`path` names a file that need not be there. A library synced to fetch files as they are
needed has, for a file never opened on this computer, only Zotero's text of it: the
attachment's folder holds `.zotero-ft-cache` and nothing else. Of 193 items found by two
title searches of the author's library, 69 had a file on this computer, 32 only that text,
and 92 neither. So each attachment gives its file, where it is there and is a PDF, a saved
page or plain text, or else, where the file is not here or is an EPUB, Zotero's text of it as
`<key>.txt`, or else a reason, and the works left with no copy are listed with theirs and what
to do in Zotero. Zotero's text is not taken for a table or a citation file, here or not,
which Zotero may index too (round 2 of #361, and #364). A record entry whose file is gone is
dropped by a run made while it is gone, so that a file saved later under its name stays the
author's. A work with a file saved under its name by hand is not listed. The other kinds G7
reads, a table or a citation file, are not taken: attached to an item in Zotero they are a
supplement's data or the item's own reference, and G7 would read them as the work's text.

Two rules keep the command from doing harm. Two different files that would take one name,
an article and its supplement both PDFs, are neither of them copied: which one is the work's
is not guessed, and the author is told to save it. And a file is replaced only if the
command wrote it and it is as written: `literature/sources.yaml` records each file it wrote,
with the work, the SHA-256 and size of what was written, whether it is Zotero's file or
Zotero's text, Zotero's key of the attachment, and the day. A file not in the record, or
whose bytes no longer match it, is the author's, and is left as it is, as `install-skills`
leaves a folder it did not write. A file found in place with Zotero's bytes is not entered
either: the first version entered it as unchanged, and a later change in Zotero then replaced
the author's copy (round 1 of #361). Nothing is deleted. The record holds no path on anyone's
computer, and lives beside `sources/` rather than in it, so that it can be kept where the
sources are not. A record that is not one stops the command, since without it the command
cannot tell its files from the author's; deleting it makes every file the author's.

Zotero is one way to the author's own access, and a downloader is another: auto-paper-harvester
(github.com/jxtse/auto-paper-harvester) fetches each DOI from an open copy, then a publisher's
text-and-data-mining service, then the author's own signed-in Chrome, at a set pace and
without answering a CAPTCHA. manuscript-guard does none of that itself: driving a browser
would be a dependency of its own, a publisher's terms are the author's to accept, and a run
that fetched too fast could have the institution blocked. Shadow libraries are out of its
scope altogether. It reads the folder such a tool writes instead: `sync-sources --from
<folder>` asks Zotero nothing, and files each PDF of the folder under the key of the cited
work whose DOI it is named for, the DOI of the work's entry in `references.bib` as G7 reads
it (`doi_of`: undressed, in lower case). The harvester, read at commit 4bcb9b5, writes
`<name>/<name>.pdf` for an open copy or a publisher's service, keeping the DOI's case and
making each run of characters a file name cannot hold one `_` (`clients._safe_identifier`,
cut at 150 characters), and `_browser_fallback/<name>.pdf` for its browser passes, in lower
case, making each run one `_` (`browser_fallback._doi_to_pdf_path`) or each character one
(`real_browser._slug`); an older version called the file in a DOI's folder `article.pdf`. Each
of the three names is tried, without regard to case, at each of those places and as
`<name>.pdf` at the top of the folder, which is how a folder saved by hand or by another tool
is read. A DOI's folder holds the harvester's supplements as well, under other names, and
they are not taken. A file that does not begin with `%PDF-` is refused and said: the
harvester checks that what it saves is a PDF, but a page saved by hand, or by another tool,
under a `.pdf` name is a sign-in or paywall page. A file named for two cited DOIs
(`10.1000/a:b` and `10.1000/a;b` are both `10.1000_a_b`) is copied for neither, and where it
differs from a file one of them alone names (`10.1000/a(b)` is `10.1000_a_b_` through Chrome)
that one is not copied either; one DOI cited under two keys is copied for each. Two PDFs of
one DOI that differ, its open copy and the browser's, are neither copied, as with Zotero. The works the folder had nothing for are listed with why: no
PDF named for the DOI, or no DOI to look for. The PDFs named for no cited DOI are counted, so
that a folder named by title, or the wrong folder, shows. The record says `from: folder` and
the DOI the file was matched by, and no path. A file one source wrote is not replaced from
the other, which is the rule that the command never writes over what it did not write,
applied between its two sources: one paper downloaded twice can differ in its bytes, where a
publisher stamps each download, and each run would otherwise put its own copy back.

## A reference is proposed from a registry, and chosen by the author

Three things say that a claim needs a citation: G6's `vague-attribution` ("studies have
shown" with nothing cited near it), a `[citation needed]` slot, which fails as a placeholder,
and a review panel's citation-support remit, which finds a cited work that does not say what
its sentence says. Each says where; none says what to cite. An agent asked to fill the gap
from what it remembers proposes a work that may not exist, or exists and says something else,
and the lookup catches only the first, after the citation is in.

`manuscript-guard search "<query>"` asks open registries that need no account, and lists
what they hold: PubMed (ESearch, by its relevance, then ESummary for each PMID it found) and
Europe PMC (its search, with each work's core record) for biomedical work, and OpenAlex
(`/works?search=`) for every field. Each candidate is a registry's record: its DOI, PMID and
PMCID, title, year, journal and first author; its kinds as the registries type it (guideline,
systematic review, meta-analysis, review, randomized controlled trial, observational study,
preprint, and the notices); whether it was retracted, and on whose word; a later version a
registry links; an open copy; and the citation counts OpenAlex and Europe PMC give. It can be
narrowed by year (`--since`), kind (`--type`: review, systematic-review, meta-analysis,
guideline, rct, cohort or preprint, several joined by OR) and language (`--language`, in two
letters), and reordered by year or by citations (`--sort`). `--json` is for an agent, and
`--dry-run` says what would be asked and sends nothing.

**It proposes, and decides nothing.** It reads nothing of the manuscript and writes no file.
The query is sent as typed, so it is the author's or the agent's words for a topic; a query
over 300 characters is refused, since a passage of the manuscript pasted in would leave the
machine with it. The answer is not kept: the work the author chooses goes into the author's
Zotero, and from there through `sync-bib`, `lookup`, `sync-sources` and G7 like any other
reference. Nothing a gate reads comes from a search.

Crossref's own search is not asked. `query.bibliographic` matches a citation string, and a
topic finds little there. Crossref is asked only about the preprints shown, by DOI, for the
published version each became (`relation.is-preprint-of`) and for a retraction or withdrawal.

**Merged, and ordered by the registries.** A work two registries return is one candidate.
The same DOI is the same work; a PMID joins two answers only where no DOI tells them apart,
since PubMed's record of a preprint and the journal's record of the paper it became are two
works with two DOIs. The order is the registries' own relevance, merged by reciprocal rank
(each registry's rank r adds 1/(60 + r), the constant of Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, SIGIR
2009), so a work near the top of two answers stands above one at the top of one. Each
registry is asked for as many works as are shown, ten unless `--limit` says otherwise, and
then OpenAlex is asked once more, by DOI, about the first 50 works it did not itself return,
for `is_retracted`, `cited_by_count` and an open copy.

A retraction is any registry's word: PubMed's "Retracted Publication" or a "Retraction in"
link, the same from Europe PMC, OpenAlex's `is_retracted`, or Crossref's retraction,
withdrawal or removal of a preprint. A record at PubMed or Europe PMC with neither mark is
that registry saying no, and is shown as "retracted: no" with its name; "not known" is shown
only where no registry that answered said either way, never as "no". A Crossref that did not
answer is said, and is not read as having found nothing (round 1 of #369). Of several
preprints, the line says for how many of them and their DOIs, with the reason, or each
reason beside its DOI where they differ, since a DOI Crossref throttled is worth asking again
and one it answered with a 503 may not be (round 1 of #376). Each preprint left unchecked says "Crossref did not answer" beside its retraction
(`unchecked_by` in the JSON), since its "retracted: no" is then another registry's word
alone (round 2 of #369). A later version is PubMed's "Update in", Europe PMC's "Preprint of"
or "Update in", or Crossref's `is-preprint-of`, and all three are asked because they do not
agree: on 2026-10-20 a medRxiv preprint had PubMed's link to its journal version and none at
Crossref, and another had Crossref's and Europe PMC's and none at PubMed. Each is shown with
whose word it is. Two links are one version where they share a PMID or a DOI and give
neither differently; a registry giving PubMed's PMID with another DOI is shown as a second
version under its own name, not as having said PubMed's DOI (round 2 of #369). Joined, each
identifier keeps the names of the registries that gave it, as `given_by` in the JSON beside
`said_by`, the registries that link the version at all. Where each gave every identifier the
names are said once; where PubMed gave the PMID alone and Europe PMC the PMID and a DOI, the
line reads "DOI 10.5/y (Europe PMC) / PMID 9 (PubMed, Europe PMC)", and not the DOI as
PubMed's too (round 1 of #376). The reference shown beside them is the first registry's to
give one, in the order PubMed, Europe PMC.

A registry asked for a kind it does not type is not asked. OpenAlex types a review and a
preprint and nothing finer, so with a systematic review, a meta-analysis, a guideline, a
trial or a cohort among the kinds it is not asked, and the output says so, rather than a
review standing in for a meta-analysis. `cohort` is MeSH's Cohort Studies (`cohort
studies[mh]`, `MESH:"Cohort Studies"`), an indexing term and not a publication type, so the
works it finds are not marked as cohorts.

The shapes were read from the services' documentation and from live answers on 2026-10-20:

- ESearch, in JSON: `esearchresult.count` as a string, `idlist`, `querytranslation`. An
  error is `ERROR` inside `esearchresult`, with HTTP 200 ("Empty Term" for a query of
  brackets). A word that matches nothing is left out and the rest searched, and only
  `errorlist.phrasesnotfound` says so; the command names the word, since the search was not
  the one asked for. The year is `datetype=pdat&mindate=<year>&maxdate=3000`, and `eng[la]`,
  `fre[la]`, `jpn[la]` are read as the languages.
- ESummary, in JSON: `result.uids`, and for each PMID `title`, `fulljournalname`,
  `sortpubdate`, `authors[]` with `name` and `authtype`, `lang`, `pubtype` ("Systematic
  Review", "Meta-Analysis", "Practice Guideline", "Preprint", "Retracted Publication"),
  `articleids` (`doi`, `pmc`, and `pmcid` written "pmc-id: PMC…;", with an embargo date where
  there is one), and `references[]` with `reftype` ("Retraction in", "Update in", "Erratum
  in", "Comment in"), `refsource` and `pmid`. `pmcrefcount` counts citing papers in PMC only,
  and is not shown.
- Europe PMC, `search?format=json&resultType=core`: `hitCount` as a number and
  `resultList.result[]`, each with `id`, `source` (`MED`; `PPR` for a preprint), `pmid`,
  `pmcid`, `doi`, `title`, `pubYear` as a string, `journalInfo.journal.title` (a preprint's
  server in `bookOrReportDetails.publisher`), `authorString` and `authorList`,
  `pubTypeList.pubType`, `citedByCount`, `isOpenAccess` ("Y" or "N"),
  `fullTextUrlList.fullTextUrl[]` with `availabilityCode` (`OA`, `F` for free, `S` for a
  subscription), `language`, and `commentCorrectionList.commentCorrection[]` with `type`
  ("Retraction in", "Preprint of"), `source`, `id` and `reference`. A query it cannot read,
  "(((" or a field it does not have, is answered with `hitCount` 0 and no error. A preprint
  has no `language`, so a language filter leaves out every preprint it holds. The year is
  `PUB_YEAR:[<year> TO 3000]`, the language `LANG:"eng"`.
- OpenAlex, `/works?search=&filter=&select=`: `meta.count` and `results[]`, each with `doi`
  and `ids.pmid` written as URLs, `type` (`article`, `review`, `preprint`, `retraction`,
  ...), `language` in two letters, `is_retracted`, `cited_by_count`, `open_access.is_oa` and
  `oa_url`, `primary_location.source.display_name` and `authorships`. A filter it does not
  know is HTTP 400. `filter=doi:<a>|<b>` asks about several DOIs in one request. Without a
  key, its answers say, a search costs $0.001 and a request by DOI $0.0001 of a $0.10 daily
  allowance shared by everyone at the network address, and a key raises that to $1 a day;
  the command says when it asked without one. The same `meta.notice` asks an AI agent to
  request a key on its user's behalf by sending the user's address to OpenAlex. Nothing
  here does, and the notice is not printed.
- Crossref's `/works?query.bibliographic=` refuses a `select` it has no field for
  (`subtype`) with HTTP 400 and `"status": "failed"`. It is not used.

The contact address and the keys are the lookup's: `MANUSCRIPT_GUARD_CONTACT`, or else
`lookup.contact` in the `paper.yaml` of the project the command runs in, or that `--root`
names; `NCBI_API_KEY`; `OPENALEX_API_KEY`. Each goes where its service asks for it and is never
printed, and an answer that would print one is refused. Requests are paced as the lookup's
are. The command exits 0 when a registry answered, with nothing found included, 1 when none
asked did, and 2 when the query cannot be asked.

## A quotation in the prose is in its source

G7 checks the ledger's quotes against the stored sources. A quotation written into a sentence
of the manuscript was checked against nothing, and a misremembered one reads as checked. Now
each quotation of four words or more, in straight or curly double marks, is looked for in the
stored source of every work cited in the sentences it spans, with the ledger's `contains()`
where it leaves nothing out:
a quotation of two sentences ends in the one that cites. The sentences are cut as the
co-author's items are. Where it is in none of those sources, G7 warns
(`quotation-not-in-source`); where none of the cited works has a source that can be read, a
note says it could not be checked (`quotation-unchecked`). Page numbers are not compared: a
PDF's page index is not the page printed on it. Every stored file of a work is looked in, its
full text in each form kept and its abstract, `<key>.abstract.txt` as the literature skill
files it; and where the writer left words out, `[...]`, `…` or `...`, or marked one `[sic]`,
each piece either side is looked for, in the order quoted (round 1 of #282: the first file
alone was read, and the whole quotation was looked for, so both were said to be absent).

## A cited statement carries the passage that supports it

The ledger holds the sentence of the source that states each number taken from it, and G7
holds the two together. A sentence that cites a work for what it says, with no number in it,
carried nothing a machine could check: the co-author's item showed the sentence and the
reference, and whether the work says it was answered from memory by whoever was asked.
CFD-Paper-Agent (github.com/Xiuyiw/CFD-SCIPaper-Agent) keeps claim-specific excerpts with
locators and support decisions for the same reason; here the excerpt is held to the stored
source.

`literature/passages.yaml` holds, for a sentence that cites a work and that work, the passage
of it that supports the sentence, copied from the stored source, and where it stands; and,
where a person has read it against the sentence, their judgement: `support` (`supports`,
`partly` or `does-not`), `judged_by` and `judged_on`. A file of its own, not value-less
entries in the ledger, whose every rule (the value in the quote, a quote too short, the
`lit.` namespace) would need an exception for them (Basile, 2026-10-20).

**A passage belongs to its sentence by the words.** An entry names its sentence by its words
and its work by the citation key, never by a file or a line, for the reason the checker's
digest leaves the line out ("What the digest covers"): a manuscript gains and loses lines
every day, and a sentence moved to the Discussion, or to the supplement, says what it said.
The words are compared folded (`statement_words`): each citation group taken out, as
`zotero/citations.py` reads one, so that a work cited beside it or a page number changed
leaves the passage where it was; typography and white space as the ledger's quotes are
folded; case; a space before a closing mark; and a final stop. A narrative citation is a word
of the sentence and stays. A sentence reworded, or no longer citing the work, leaves its
passage stale, since a passage chosen for other words need not support these, and a
co-author must not be shown it as though it did. G7 notes a stale passage (`passage-stale`),
naming as the sentence it may now be the one citing the same work that shares the most of
its words, where one shares half or more. That share decides what the note says and nothing
else.

**Each passage is looked for in its work's stored files** (`stored_files`), each read once a
run, with `quoted_in`: words left out, `[...]` or an ellipsis, and a word marked `[sic]`,
read as for a quotation in the prose. One in none of them fails from drafting
(`passage-not-in-source`), with what `placement.py` says of how near it came where the work
has one readable file and the passage leaves nothing out. One whose work has no stored copy,
or none that can be read, is a warning (`passage-unchecked`), and one of fewer than four
words is a warning (`passage-too-short`), as a ledger quote is.

**What is counted.** A cited statement is a sentence that cites, cut as the co-author's items
are (`cited_sentences`, which both read), once in a file; it carries a passage where one of
the works it cites has a passage that belongs to it. G7 counts both (`cited_statements`,
`cited_statements_with_passage`) and the passages by what it found of them. The statements
that carry none are one note while drafting and one warning from internal-review, never a
failure (Basile, 2026-10-20): a citation of the software used, or of where a method comes
from, needs no passage, and a gate that failed a paper for one would be switched off. `check`
gives the count under the literature it assures. `manuscript-guard passages` lists each
statement with the works it cites, their stored files and their passages as G7 finds them,
`--missing` those with none, for an agent drafting them; it writes nothing.

**Only a person judges a passage.** An agent may draft a passage from the stored source;
whether it supports the sentence is a reader's judgement, which the checker puts to the
co-authors and the entry records for the author. A model's name may not sign it
(`judgement-not-human`, from drafting, as for `attested_by`). `does-not` fails from
internal-review, since a draft others read should not hold a sentence a person judged its
source does not support, and `partly` is a warning. A judgement of a stale passage was of
words the manuscript no longer has: the stale note says so, and nothing else is said of it.
The plugin's write guard puts to the person an agent's edit after which the judged entries
are not the ones the file held before, word for word in their sentence, work, passage,
judgement, judge and date: a judge named, the words under a standing judgement changed, or a
judgement taken away, which would otherwise clear a `does-not` unasked (round 1 of #374). A
locator or a note changed beside it is not put to them. A Codex patch holds only the lines it
changes, so one to a file that holds a judgement outside a comment is put to the person, and
refused where the tool cannot ask. A passage that is all elision, `[...]`, holds no word to
look for and is not in its source.

**What a co-author is shown.** The checker's item for a cited sentence shows each passage
that belongs to it, with its locator in the caption, as evidence whose words are in the
