digest: a passage replaced after a co-author read it leaves their answer about one they never
saw, and the item is outstanding again. Neither what G7 found of it nor the author's
judgement is shown or digested. The first depends on the PDF reader of the machine that
built the page, which a digest must not; the second would tell a co-author the answer before
they read.

## Text from the authors' earlier papers is found before the journal finds it

A journal puts each submission through a similarity check (Crossref Similarity Check, which
iThenticate runs), and the editor reads a report of every run of words the manuscript shares
with a published paper, the authors' own papers among them. Reusing one's own words in a new
paper is text recycling, and its norms are published:

- The Text Recycling Research Project, *Text Recycling: Best Practices for Researchers*,
  version 1.1, April 2021 (textrecycling.org, CC BY 4.0). Recycling is most defensible in the
  Methods, where a standard description kept as it was lets a reader see where two studies
  differ. It is disclosed, to the editor in the covering letter and to readers in the paper. A
  synonym put in to hide it is no rewriting. The venue's policy and the publisher's contract
  decide what is allowed, and the guide sets no number of words.
- COPE's text recycling guidelines for editors, written with BioMed Central's editors.
  Overlap in the Methods may be appropriate when the earlier article is cited; undisclosed
  overlap, or overlap in the results, discussion or conclusions, is unlikely to be acceptable;
  the editor judges each case by how much is reused, where, and whether its source is
  acknowledged. Harriman and Patel give the same reasons in *BMC Medicine* 2014;12:148
  (doi:10.1186/s12916-014-0148-8).

So G7 runs that check before the journal does, on this machine and on the authors' own
copies. Basile chose its four parts on 2026-10-21.

**Which papers.** The earlier outputs `literature/related.yaml` lists, the one list G8 holds
the paper's numbers to ("An earlier output of the same data is held to this paper"), each that shares authors with this paper (`shares:
[authors]`); text recycling is the reuse of one's own words, and an output of the same data
by others is not compared here. Its citation key names the stored copy,
`literature/sources/<citekey>.*`, kept and read as a cited work's source is, out of git by
default; an earlier paper the manuscript does not cite still has a key and a copy. Basile
chose a shared list over a second one in `paper.yaml`, which this check first proposed.
Nothing is looked up. An author's ORCID iD could list their works, but this makes no registry
call, and the list is the record. A copy is read here and sent nowhere, to a model provider
least of all.

A preprint, an abstract or a protocol of this same study (`kind: preprint`, `abstract` or
`protocol`, with `study` among what it shares) is an earlier form of this paper, and the
manuscript repeats much of it. The TRRP counts reuse of one's own preprint or poster as
commonly accepted where it is disclosed, the journal's preprint policy decides, and a results
paper is expected to repeat its own protocol's methods. So it is compared like any other, and
reported once, however much the manuscript repeats: `recycled-earlier-version`, a note at the
output's line of the list, with the number of passages and words and where the first stands
(Basile, 2026-10-21; the protocol in round 1 of the review, where it warned once for each
paragraph of the Methods that did not cite it).

**How it compares.** By words. A word is a run of letters and digits in lower case. A hyphen,
an en dash or an apostrophe inside it joins its parts, and so does a hyphen at the end of a
line, so that "drug-induced" set as "drug-\ninduced" in a PDF, and "pharmaco-\nvigilance"
broken by the PDF's hyphenation, are one word each. A number is no word, and neither are the
digits at the end of a word, which is where a PDF leaves a reference's number ("risk12",
"risk²"); so a binding, a reference's number and a count the new paper updated are no
difference. A ligature is its letters. A run of eight words that the earlier paper has in the
same order marks its words shared. Shared words that stand together are one passage, and so
are two runs at most three words apart here whose places in the earlier paper are at most four
apart, so that a word changed for another does not cut the sentence in two. A passage of
twelve shared words or more is reported. "Adjusted for age and sex" is five words and never a
run; a sentence of the Discussion repeated with one word changed, eight words or more from
either end, is a passage of every other word in it. A word changed nearer an end leaves the
words beyond it in no run, so they are not counted (round 1 of the review).

A PDF is read in reading order, `pdftotext` without `-layout`, where the literature chain
reads it laid out to find a quote. Laid out, each line of a page of two columns holds a line
of each column, and every sentence of the left column is cut by the right one. pypdf is the
fallback, as it is for the chain.

**The supplement is compared as the main text is** (Basile, 2026-10-21: supplementary
material is held to the same rules). Every Markdown file under `manuscript/supplementary/`
is read with the rest, as every gate that reads the manuscript reads it; a LaTeX manuscript
is not read by this check yet, and G7 says so (`not-read-in-latex`). The supplement's
headings name its parts as the main text's do: a title that is a supplement's name for a part
and nothing else, "Supplementary discussion", "Supplemental results", JAMA's "eResults", is
that part (round 7 of the review: they named none). Only the whole title: "Online discussion
forums" or "eConsent" names no part (round 8: a prefix taken off any heading read "Online
discussion forums" under the Methods as the Discussion, which unnamed the Methods). Its Supplementary Methods are the Methods: a
description reused there with its source cited in the paragraph is a note, and one that does
not cite it warns from internal-review. A similarity check reads the supplement as it reads
the paper.

**What is not compared.** The front matter, where an abstract already fails
(`front-matter-abstract`) and the build prints nothing; the headings, which are also a bound
no passage crosses; listings, tables and comments; and the reference list, which a similarity
check is asked to leave out.

**The statements a journal asks for are compared, and noted.** Funding and the funder's role,
competing interests, acknowledgements, data and code availability, ethics and consent, patient
and public involvement, the authors' contributions (CRediT), transparency, the use of
generative AI, the abbreviations: these are the same from one paper to the next, a journal
expects them to be, and a warning of each would bury the ones that matter. A passage under a
statement's heading is `recycled-statement`, a note at every stage. A statement's heading is
known by its whole title, which names one statement or several and nothing else: "Funding",
"Data availability statement", "Ethics approval and consent to participate", "Conflicts of
interest/Competing interests", "Funding, competing interests, and data availability",
"CRediT author statement" (the heading the submission pack writes). It is a statement's
wherever it stands, at the end, under the Methods, the Discussion or the abstract, except
under the Results, whose themes may be named so ("Data sharing", "Consent") and are the
Results' own. A title that only opens with such words is the paper's own matter: "Funding
sources of the included trials", "Data sharing in pharmacovigilance".

Four rounds of the review went into this, and Basile chose the note on 2026-10-21. Read by
the part of the paper over it, "Ethics approval" under the Methods was the Methods', and its
standard words warned (round 1). The statements were then set apart, not compared, and every
heading read wrong hid recycled text: a heading of the Results read by its first words (round
2), a commentary's title (round 3), a theme of the Results named as a statement is (round 4);
and every statement title missing from the list warned (rounds 3 and 4). Compared and noted,
a heading read wrong turns a warning into a note at worst, and hides nothing. A statement's
heading is not counted as a part of the paper when a heading over several parts is taken for
a title over the paper, so that the Methods over "Statistical methods" and "Ethics approval"
stay the Methods (round 2), and the conclusions are counted with the Discussion, so that the
Discussion over "Interpretation" and "Conclusions" stays the Discussion (round 4).

Words in quotation marks, straight or curly, double or single, or in a block
quotation, are quoted and not recycled. A passage is recycled text where twelve of its words
or more stand outside quotation marks, and a quotation (`recycled-quotation`, a note) where as
many stand inside them.

**What a passage is told.** Its part of the paper is the one the outermost heading over it
names: the Introduction, the Methods, the Results, the Discussion, the conclusions or the
abstract, named as the other gates name them, the Methods being the sections
`methods_sections` takes for them. A heading over headings that name two parts or more is a
title over the paper and names none.

- In the Methods, where the passage's paragraph cites the earlier paper:
  `recycled-methods-cited`, a note at every stage, which says to mention it in the covering
  letter.
- In a statement the journal asks for: `recycled-statement`, a note at every stage.
- Anywhere else: `recycled-text`, a note while drafting and a warning from internal-review,
  never a failure. In the Methods with no citation in the paragraph, it says to cite the paper
  there or write the passage afresh; in the Results, the Discussion, the conclusions or the
  abstract, to write it afresh; in the Introduction or under no heading that names a part,
  that the journal decides.
- An earlier output with no citation key, or no copy that can be read:
  `earlier-output-not-compared`, a note at its line of the list.

Never a failure, because the journal's policy decides and neither guide forbids anything
outright. A journal profile may state that policy as `text_recycling:`, with the page's words
under `quotes.text_recycling`, which G4 holds to the stored page as it holds every rule's
quote; each `recycled-text` and `recycled-methods-cited` finding then gives those words. The
notes of a quotation, of an earlier form of the study and of an output not compared do not,
since none of them asks the author to change the text.

Each finding gives the manuscript's lines, how many words are shared, the part of the paper,
and where the earlier paper has the passage: the page of a PDF, which is the PDF's own count
and not the number printed on it, or the line of a text file or of a page saved as HTML.
`check` counts `earlier_outputs_compared` and `recycled_passages`.

## Only a person can sign an attestation

`attested.yaml` exists to record that **a named human read something the toolkit could not
retrieve, and takes responsibility for the value**. A language model cannot take
responsibility, so the gate rejects an `attested_by` naming a model — claude, gpt, gemini,
"an AI assistant" and their relatives are all refused.

This is not decoration. Without it, the one file whose entire purpose is human
accountability is the easiest file in the project for an agent to fill in on the author's
behalf, and the guarantee evaporates silently. The skill instructs the model to draft the
entry, leave `attested_by` empty, and ask. And the write hook puts an edit that names an
attester to the person before it is made (see "The plugin: skills for judgement, hooks for
the moment of the mistake").

A statement shorter than eight words also warns: "Read it." records nothing a reader in two
years could act on.

## Compliance is data, not code

Neither a journal profile nor a reporting checklist is compiled into the tool. Both are
YAML retrieved from the source that owns them and stamped with the date it was read, and
the reasoning is the same in each case.

**Journal guidelines change without announcement.** A limit hard-coded in the tool would
eventually be wrong, and wrong *silently* — the worst kind. Profiles state only what the
journal's page actually says; an absent limit is not checked, because a guessed one
produces confident failures about a rule that does not exist. A profile over a year old
warns. Switching journals after a rejection means writing a second profile and reading the
resulting failure list, which is the reformatting job itemised.

**A required statement counts where it prints as one.** A profile's statement patterns, and
a structured abstract's required headings, are searched with HTML comments and fenced code
blanked (`scannable`). A comment prints nothing, and a listing prints its lines as code, not
as a declaration. `# Funding` is a heading in Markdown and a comment in R and Python, and
inside either it met the funding statement of a paper that had none. A statement written in
a fenced block therefore does not count, and no journal takes one written as code. The
blanking is close to what pandoc prints but not the same; where they differ is under Known
gaps.

**Checklists are transcribed from their official documents, never written from memory.**
Item text that is approximately right produces confident coverage of the wrong things, and
approximately-right official wording inside a toolkit whose whole argument is that
approximately right is not good enough would undermine the thing being built.

So a checklist is a **recipe plus a document**. The recipe says where the items sit — which
table, which columns, how sub-items are written — and `manuscript-guard transcribe` turns
the guideline's own file into a profile. The transcription is a deterministic function of
the document and the recipe: re-run it and you get the same profile; run it against a
revised checklist and the diff is the revision. Every item is then verified to appear
verbatim in the document, using the same comparison the literature ledger uses for a quote.

Seventeen checklists have recipes: STROBE (34 items), RECORD (13), RECORD-PE (15), CONSORT
(41), SPIRIT 2025 (53), PRISMA 2020 (42) and its abstracts checklist (12), READUS-PV (32)
and its abstracts checklist (12), TRIPOD in its three variants (31 development, 31
validation, 37 both), TRIPOD+AI (52) and its abstracts checklist (13), STARD 2015 (34),
CHEERS 2022 (28) and ARRIVE 2.0 (21). TRIPOD+AI and CHEERS 2022 are read from tables of
their statement papers, as Europe PMC serves their full text: no checklist file of
TRIPOD+AI is better than its paper, and the file CHEERS's publisher offers did not answer
an automated download. Each recipe says which it read (`read_from`), and records a digest
of the table's rows rather than of the file. The three TRIPOD 2015
recipes record that TRIPOD+AI replaced them (`superseded_by`), and G5 warns a project that
names one. An eighteenth recipe is not a checklist: SANRA (6
items), the scale an editor or a reviewer scores a narrative review with, which exists because
no reporting guideline covers a narrative review and the first manuscript written with this
toolkit is one. A scale's profile says `kind: scale`, and the submission pack presents it as a
scale rather than as a completed reporting checklist, because those are different claims. READUS-PV is the guideline for disproportionality
analyses of spontaneous reports, and is more directly applicable to signal-detection work
than STROBE.

**The repository ships recipes, not transcribed text.** Licences were read on 2026-08-03 and
are recorded per recipe and in [ATTRIBUTION.md](ATTRIBUTION.md). The picture settles the
design: RECORD is explicitly CC BY, STROBE and ARRIVE are CC BY through their statement
papers, **READUS-PV is CC BY-NC**, and four state no reuse licence at all. A repository
shipping their text would have to satisfy the strictest of them, and one of them is
non-commercial.

**Fetching is not redistributing.** When the tool downloads from the publisher's own URL
because the user asked it to, the user obtains the document exactly as they would by
clicking the link, and the project distributes nothing. That is the structure:
`manuscript-guard fetch` retrieves, `transcribe` builds the profile locally, and both the
documents and the generated profiles are gitignored.

Three decisions follow from it:

- **Never during `pip install`.** Installs run offline in CI and sandboxes, network
  side-effects break reproducible builds, and a silent download means nobody reads the
  terms. Fetching is an explicit command.
- **The licence is printed before the download**, not filed away afterwards.
- **The document is checksummed against the recipe.** A recipe encodes which table and which
  columns hold the items, so a silently revised checklist would otherwise produce a
  plausible wrong transcription. A mismatch stops the build and names the source URL;
  `--allow-changed` overrides it deliberately.

A uniform "never redistribute" rule is kept even for the CC BY ones. Per-guideline
judgements have to be re-made whenever a guideline is revised or a new one is added, and one
command is a small price for never having to reason about it again.

A guideline named in `paper.yaml` with no retrieved checklist **fails loudly** rather than
passing quietly.

The example carries an openly invented journal and checklist, labelled as such in both
files, exactly as it carries invented literature sources.

### What the verification caught

Writing the transcriber and trusting it would have been the obvious mistake. Verification
caught two parser bugs that produced plausible, wrong output:

- **Continuation rows were read as section headings.** STROBE writes item 1 as two rows, the
  second with only the text cell filled. Treating that as a heading dropped every sub-item:
  the first run produced 22 items where the document has 34 rows, and looked right, because
  STROBE does have 22 numbered items.
- **Multi-item cells were truncated.** RECORD packs three extension items into one cell
  ("RECORD 6.1: … 6.2: … 6.3: …"). Reading only the first gave 8 items instead of 13.

A third bug was found by verification failing on correct transcriptions: `document_text`
joined Word runs with spaces, and Word splits runs mid-word, so "study's" became "study 's"
and true quotes looked false.

### Not every checklist can be verified equally

ARRIVE 2.0 publishes no Word checklist. Both its sets are printed side by side on one page
of a PDF, so there is no table to read — only a visual grid, recovered by cutting the page
at the column boundary and each column into topic, number and text sub-columns. The page is
asked for in UTF-8 and decoded strictly: one `pdftotext` cannot give in UTF-8 is refused,
not transcribed with a letter replaced.

That path cannot support the same verification. Topic words wrap into the left margin of
continuation lines and land *between* an item's own text fragments, so an item's full text
is genuinely not contiguous in the page however correct the extraction. Only each item's
**opening clause** is verified, which still catches a mis-cut column or an item attributed
to the wrong number, but not a wrongly assembled tail.

Rather than let that pass unmarked, every profile now records a `verification` field, and
ARRIVE's says `opening clause only (column-laid-out PDF)`. Two different guarantees should
not look identical in the output.

Two smaller decisions fell out of this:

- **`reporting_guideline` is no longer a closed enumeration.** Guidelines are revised,
  extensions appear, and a schema refusing CHEERS or SQUIRE would be wrong about the world
  rather than about the project.
- **"n/a" is rejected as a reason.** A checklist item excluded needs a reason a reviewer
  could read — "no interventions were assigned" — because a reviewer does read this file.

**What the Data availability statement says is the journal's rule, not the tool's.** G4 found
the statement's heading and read nothing under it. Publishers differ on what it must hold:
Springer Nature asks that data which cannot be shared openly say why, PLOS accepts "on
request" only for data that cannot be public and holds a paper until its identifiers come
(both pages read 2026-10-15), and this toolkit's own example names no identifier at all. A
universal rule would be wrong for most of them. So a profile records its journal's policy in
`data_availability`, with the page and the day it was read: the phrasings the journal does
not accept, each with what makes it acceptable (`unless`, a reason or a route), whether a
persistent identifier is required, and the journal's own forms for an article with no data.
G4 reads the statement against them and fails what the journal does not accept, from
internal review. Two warnings follow wherever a profile records a policy: storage that is
neither persistent nor archived, a shared drive or a repository on a code host linked bare
(a release, a tag or a commit is a fixed version), and a dataset DOI that the reference list
does not cite, since data a paper rests on are cited like any other source.

## Word counting is a stated rule

A limit is only checkable if both sides agree what is counted, and journals rarely say. The
rule used is written down and the count reported beside the limit: whitespace-separated
tokens after citations, tables, images, code and markup are removed; abstract and
references counted separately; headings counted, because they are printed, and their
attribute blocks (`{#sec-methods}`, `{-}`) not, because pandoc does not print them. Counting
is done on the source rather than the built document, so a binding counts as one word
whatever it resolves to and the count does not move when the analysis is re-run.

The YAML front matter that opens a file is not counted, rendered keys included. The build
strips every file's block and prints the title from `paper.yaml`, so none of it is in the document a limit is
about, and a journal counts a title and an abstract against limits of their own anyway. An
abstract counts when it is written under an Abstract heading, which is where the build
prints one. One written in the front matter is refused rather than counted as 0 words (see
the build). Until 2026-09-24 the block counted as main text: `split_sections` trimmed the
text before the first heading, the closing `---` lost the newline the front-matter pattern
needs, and the example's title line took its main text from 557 words to 573. G4 had a second
route to the same mistake. It reads the main text as one string joined from every file, so
only the first file's block was at the top, and a later file's closing `---` underlined its
last YAML line into a heading: `title: Methods of the online appendix` satisfied a required
Methods section. The title page declares the count G4 checks, from the same text.

## The AI-writing lint measures rate, not presence

The rules come from the English Wikipedia essay "Signs of AI writing", read 2026-08-03.
Much of that essay is Wikipedia-specific — wikitext, categories, edit summaries — and is
dropped. What survives is vocabulary, sentence shape, formatting and tone.

**What the gate claims is narrow: it detects habits, not authorship.** A person who writes
"it is important to note" is flagged, and a model that avoids every listed construction is
not. It is a style check against a well-catalogued target, and calling it a detector would
be a lie a user could act on.

The adaptation that makes it usable in science is measuring most rules as a **rate per 1000
words** rather than flagging each occurrence. "Robust" describes a standard error,
"significant" has a technical meaning, "key" and "highlight" are unremarkable once. Six
"crucial"s in four hundred words is a tell; one is a word. A lint that flags `dpi=300` in a
figure script gets switched off, and the same is true of one that flags robust standard
errors.

Three severities:

- **fail** — model output artefacts (`oaicite`, `[cite: 1]`, "as of my last training data",
  unfilled placeholders). No innocent reading; these must never reach a submission.
- **warn** — constructions with a defensible use but a strong association. Reported with the
  reason so an author can disagree and move on.
- **warn on rate** — ordinary words, counted.

Two refinements came from running it on this project's own example. Structured-abstract
labels are bold by journal requirement, so counting them flagged the journal's house style;
they are exempt. And technical senses are exempt by pattern, so "robust standard errors"
does not count towards the vocabulary rate.

A finding's line is counted in the file as read. The phrase and attribution rules match in a
copy with the comments, the listings and the front matter's machinery blanked, line ends
included, and an offset is the same in both. Counted in the copy, the line fell short by
every line blanked above it: a phrase under a four-line comment was reported three lines up,
on the comment. And the line is the one the matched words begin on, not the match: the rule
for a chat assistant's opening word reads from the start of a line through any blank lines,
and its finding was put on the blank line above the paragraph.

**Vague attribution gets the one check an encyclopedia cannot use.** "Studies have shown" is
reported only when no citation sits within 240 characters, because in a manuscript the fix
is a reference rather than a rewrite.

**A placeholder is a kind of slot, looked for wherever the document's text comes from.** The
rules name kinds, not spellings:
- an instruction to the writer in brackets, "[describe the cohort]", even where a hard wrap
  cuts it;
- a thing to be supplied, "[Repository]", "[DOI/accession]", "[citation needed]";
- capitals in brackets that say something is still to come, "[TO BE COMPLETED]", "[CLAIM
  NEEDS EVIDENCE]". Capitals alone say nothing of the kind: an abbreviation nested in
  parentheses, "[SJS/TEN]", is in brackets and capitals;
- filler, and instructions left for the writer: "lorem ipsum", "fill in later.", "this
  section is a template";
- the words that mark a gap: TODO, TBD, FIXME, a doubled TKTK, a run of three X or more, a
  date of Xs and a name such as INSERT_SOURCE_URL;
- a journal template's instructions to its authors, which are its own spellings (below).

"XXX" was matched only whole, so "n = XXXX patients" passed, and G2 does not see it, since
it holds no digit. What is no slot: a link's text, a bracketed span, a title translated into
English in brackets as PubMed gives it ("[Add-on therapy in epilepsy]"; outside the
manuscript "[Your ...]" is no slot either, since its quiz titles open so, "[Your
diagnosis?]"), a karyotype ("47,XXX", 45 to 49 chromosomes before the comma, so that "1,XXX
reports" is a gap), "XXX syndrome", and a single "TK", which in medicine is a kinase. What two rules find in one place is said once. The same rules
read the text of each figure G3 reads, the caption of each table in the results, and the
printed fields of each cited entry of `references.bib`: a "TBD" drawn in a figure, or a
"TODO" in a reference's note, reaches the document as surely as one in the prose. There the
words count in capitals only, since "Todo" opens many a Spanish title; in the manuscript
they count in any case, as they always did. Each is a failure from drafting, as the other
artefacts are.

**A journal template's instructions are found by the template's own words.** Papers are
printed with "In this section you can acknowledge any support given which is not covered by
the author contribution or funding sections", MDPI's text for the acknowledgements, two of
them among the 399 papers below, and no rule read it: the instructions G6 knew were this
project's own, "this section is a template", "delete this section". No kind of sentence
tells an instruction to the authors from a paper's prose, since "authors should report the
interval" is both, so the rule `placeholder-template` holds the opening words of each
instruction in the manuscript templates of MDPI, Frontiers, PLOS, BMC, Springer Nature,
Elsevier and Wiley, read on 2026-10-21, and Word's "Click or tap here to enter text." in a
field left empty. MDPI's back matter is found by what follows "in this section" ("you can
acknowledge any support", "please provide details regarding where data") and by the
statement it offers for copying after "please add", "please state" or "or state" ('Please
add: "This research received no external funding"'). The first version took any verb
after "In this section, please" and any quotation after "please state", and round 1 of its
review showed what a questionnaire reproduced in a supplement says: "In this section,
please indicate how often you took each medicine", 'If none, please state "not
applicable"'. Nor is "Click here for additional data file" a prompt, which PLOS prints
under each supporting file: "click here" stands in 105 of the 399 papers. BMC's "Text for
this section." is read with its capital and its stop, since a hard wrap puts "text" at the
start of a line in prose. It is read wherever the placeholders are: MDPI's template
captions its sample table with one.

Europe PMC shows how often they are printed. Of the open-access articles its full-text search
returned for MDPI's "This section may be divided by subheadings" (Results), for its
instructions for the Discussion, the authors' contributions and the CRediT taxonomy, and for
Frontiers' "This is a short text to acknowledge the contributions of specific colleagues",
every one sampled, five to eight of each, was printed with the instruction; some were
printed with Word's prompt. Its search drops short words, so the counts it gives for a phrase
are not repeated here.

Basile chose on 2026-10-21 that one fails from drafting, as every placeholder does, rather
than warning until submission as the words of a revision do. On the corpus of
`tools/g6_baseline.py` the rule finds the two MDPI papers (PMC7072797, PMC7504530) and
nothing else, nor anything in the 18,335 works they cite. PMC7072797 is held out, so G6
measured again would count a failure on a held-out paper, where the budget allows none. It
is a template's instruction in print, not a false alarm on prose by people;
`tools/data/g6-corpus.yaml` keeps what was measured before the rule. The rule's words share
one `\b`: with one each, it took 1.3 s on the longest paper of the corpus, and takes 0.2 s.

The phrasing rules gained what the essay, read again on 2026-10-15, lists as communication
with the user of a chat ("I hope this helps", "let me know if"), disclaimers about the
sources a model was given ("while specific details are limited", "in the provided search
results"), a hedge on a hedge ("could potentially"), the upbeat close about the future ("the
future of ... lies in"), text about the text ("In this section, we will discuss") and an
instruction to whoever fills the text in ("the user should add"). Each is a warning. Not
"not widely available" or "not widely reported", which a paper says of a drug or an adverse
event.

**Words written to the reviewers and left in the paper are the residue of a revision**
(`revision-residue`, 2026-10-20). "As requested by Reviewer 2, we added", "in the previous
version of this manuscript", "we have now clarified", "page 4, lines 120-125", "the revised
text is highlighted in yellow", "see the response letter"; and a model's words to its user,
"as you requested", "I have shortened the abstract", "Below is the revised Discussion".
They belong in the response to the reviewers, and the paper's reader never saw the review.
The idea and part of the lists are Writing Guard's `process_residue` rules
(ATTRIBUTION.md). The rules read the manuscript and its supplement only, in the prose the
phrase rules read, so a comment, a listing or a citation holds none, and one paragraph at
a time. They never read `revision/` nor the letter `respond` writes from it: that is where
these words belong, and G13 lets a reply say them.

A residue is reported wherever it stands, as an artefact is, and not counted by rate: one
is enough to be read by the journal. Basile chose on 2026-10-20 between two kinds. A rule
that answers one reviewer or the editor, or points at this manuscript, its earlier version,
its lines, its marked changes or its letter, or holds a model's words to its user, warns
while the paper is written and revised and fails at submission, as G13 and G11 do: the
residue harms nobody until the journal reads it. The rest warn at every stage: the
reviewers together or one not named ("in response to the reviewers' comments"), a
manuscript's earlier version not said to be this one's ("the revised manuscript"), tracked
changes, lines in brackets, a response letter not said to be the authors', and a change to
a text that names no part of this manuscript ("we have revised the section on renal
dosing", "This has now been clarified."). A paper about peer review writes those of the
manuscripts it studied, and a guideline's update or a label's history writes the last of
itself; neither must be stopped.

What the rules leave alone was found by running them over the 399 papers of the G6 corpus
and over the commonest ways a pharmacology or epidemiology paper writes the same words, and
each is a passing case in `tests/test_writing.py`:
- "revised" in a name, "the Revised Cardiac Risk Index", "the 1987 ACR revised criteria",
  "the Clinical Interview Schedule-Revised", "10th revision";
- the contributions, "drafted the initial manuscript", "revised the original manuscript",
  "provided final approval of this version of the manuscript", read as a verb of writing
  followed only by the words a contribution puts before the noun, so that "We revised the
  Methods because our original submission pooled the cohorts" is still read;
- the acknowledgements, "comments on an earlier version of this manuscript", "two
  anonymous reviewers for their helpful comments", "grateful to Dr. Sampaio for their
  critical review in the original manuscript", read from the thanks to the end of the
  sentence, the stop of a title or an initial ending none; "We acknowledge that" opens a
  limitation as often, and is no thanks; a thanks to one referee fails only for "this" or
  "that", "for raising this point", "for bringing this to our attention", or where the
  reviewer has a number, which a printed acknowledgement never gives, and not where it
  names what it is for, "for pointing out an error in the variance estimator";
- what a study writes of its own instrument: a Delphi panel's "our initial draft
  comprised 45 items", "the revised wording is shown in Table 3", "new sentences were
  written by two authors", "we have adapted the wording of the items";
- a label's history, "This has now been included in the SmPC", since a change that names
  no part of this manuscript warns only at the end of its clause;
- a journal's notices, "the publisher, the editors and the reviewers", "the handling
  editor declared a shared affiliation", and an invitation, "at the invitation of the
  editor";
- a systematic review's readers, "Reviewer 1 and Reviewer 2 independently extracted the
  data", "resolved by a third reviewer", "discrepancies noted by the second reviewer": a
  reviewer is one reviewer only with "the" or a number, and answered only with a request,
  a reply or a suggestion;
- and prose: "To address this concern, we used an active comparator", which 38 of the 399
  papers write in some form and Writing Guard takes; "To avoid confusion"; "the original
  submission of the dossier to the agency"; "we now report"; "(LINE 1)", a retrotransposon.

Read as at submission, the 399 papers gave no failure, and two warnings: "(LINE 1)", which
the rule for lines in brackets no longer takes, and "as suggested by one of the reviewers
of our paper", words to a reviewer that reached print. `tools/g6_baseline.py` judges as at
submission since round 1 of #377, and its measurement of the 384 papers it uses, taken
again then, records that one warning and no failure; the held-out check is unchanged, 98.9%
of the held-out papers with two warnings or fewer. Europe PMC listed 25 open-access
research articles for the phrase "as suggested by the reviewer", and the text of their XML
held it in 21: 17 only in the peer-review reports published with them, four in the article
itself, each as a reply to a reviewer ("as suggested by the reviewer earlier, triglycerides
and heart rate"). A sample chosen for the phrase says nothing of how common it is, only
that the residue reaches print.

**How often it warns on papers written by people** is measured, and the rate thresholds
come from that measurement (item 54). `tools/g6_baseline.py` drew 400 open-access research
articles under CC BY from Europe PMC, published from 2010 to October 2022, before chat
models were common, with a fixed seed: 300 to set thresholds and 100 held out. The draw
took a random day, then a random article of the up to 1000 Europe PMC listed that day, so
not every article had the same chance: one on a busy day had less, and one past the
first 1000 of its day none. What the run had to show was fixed before it: each threshold
at the 99th percentile of the first set, and, on the held-out papers, no failure and at
most two warnings on 95% of them. Each paper is read as G6 reads a manuscript's prose:
its JATS through pandoc's JATS reader, written as Markdown without the `smart` extension,
from its first heading to its reference list, its tables left out with their captions and
notes, as a manuscript's are emitted and bound. `tools/data/g6-corpus.yaml` keeps each
paper's identifiers and the digests of what was read, never its text.

- **2026-10-19.** Of the 400, 291 and 93 were used. Thirteen were shorter than 1000 words,
  one had no heading pandoc could read, and two stated no licence of their own. The
  thresholds, per 1000 words, were set by hand before this, from the project's own prose:
  "AI vocabulary" from 6 to 2.7, em dashes from 4 to 4.7, bold from 8 to 9.4, lists of
  three from 3 to 6.2, "serves as" and its kind from 2 to 0.7.
  - In a first measurement, nothing on the held-out papers failed, but only 88.2% had two
    warnings or fewer: the budget was not met. Two phrase rules warned at each occurrence,
    and each did so on about a quarter of all the papers: "not only ... but also" on
    25.8%, "plays a key role" on 25.5%.
  - Basile chose to count those two by rate, as the vocabulary is, at the same percentile:
    0.8 and 1.0 per 1000 in the last measurement. Measured again, 98.9% of the held-out
    papers had two warnings or fewer, and the budget was met. The held-out papers showed
    which two rules broke the budget, so they are no longer an independent check of that
    choice.
  - That first measurement read each paper with pandoc's `smart` extension on, which wrote
    an em dash as `---`: G6 counts the dash itself, and saw one in 18 papers of 384. It
    also counted the bold of each paper's tables. Both were put right and the corpus
    measured again (round 1 of #339). That one still counted the captions and notes of the
    tables, which JATS keeps beside the table, and where one paper had about a hundred em
    dashes: the em-dash threshold was 13.9 with them and is 4.7 without (round 2). The
    thresholds and counts here are from this last measurement, where 139 papers have an em
    dash. A licence named with its version, "Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International
    License", is read as CC BY now, and one whose further terms are spelt as CC 3.0 spells
    them, "Noncommercial" or "No Derivative Works", is not.
  - G6 counted the em dash itself, so a Markdown manuscript that typed one as `---`, which
    pandoc prints as one, showed it none. Three hyphens count as an em dash now, two do
    not, and neither does a line of dashes, a rule or a table's, inline code, nor a pipe
    table's row, since the papers' tables were left out. Measured again with that rule, the
    corpus gives the same thresholds, since it was read with the dash written out.
  - Of all 384, the other phrase rules warn on fewer: an "-ing" tail asserting significance
    on 9.4%, a hedge on a hedge on 7.6%, "it is important to note" on 5.2%, the rest on
    under 3% each. A vague attribution with no citation near it is reported on 4.2%.

What this does not measure: no text written by a model was read, so it says nothing of
what G6 catches, only how often it warns on people writing biomedical research in English.

## Abbreviations are checked against the manuscript, not against a style guide

G14 is the first check on the language itself, and it is built on one distinction. Whether
"ROR" has to be defined is a question about a journal: one house style expands "CI" and
another lets it stand. Whether "ROR" *was* defined, where, how many times, and whether
anything used it afterwards are questions about the manuscript, and they have the same
answers in any field. The gate asks only the second kind:

- `abbreviation-used-before-defined`: the short form appears above the sentence that
  defines it;
- `abbreviation-redefined`: it is defined a second time, or as two different things;
- `abbreviation-unused`: it is defined and nothing uses it afterwards;
- `abbreviation-undefined`: it is used and never defined.

**A definition is read by its shape.** A long form with the short form in brackets after
it, or the short form with the long form in brackets, where the letters of the short form
can be found in order in the long one and the first of them begins a word. That is Schwartz
and Hearst's rule (Pac Symp Biocomput 2003;8:451-62), written out here in thirty lines
because a gate that runs in CI should not take a dependency for them. The short form may
also stand in square brackets, "hazard ratio [HR]", which is how a journal writes a
definition inside a parenthesis. The short form in a definition may be anything with two
capitals, or one that is not the capital of a word (`mL`), or a capital and a digit. A
plural defines its singular: `RORs` defines `ROR`, and `mAbs` after "monoclonal antibodies"
defines `mAb`.

A bracket that gives a statistic is no definition. A short form followed by an equals sign
or a number, "(HR 1.32, 95% CI ...)" or "(MAP = 90 mmHg)", defines nothing, whatever the
words before it: "a higher risk (HR 1.32, ...)" begins with the letters of HR, and read as
a definition it was a second one after "the hazard ratio (HR)", or the only one where the
manuscript never defined HR. A short form followed by a colon is read as any other, by its
letters, exactly as before: "reporting odds ratio (ROR: 3.84)" defines, as pharmacovigilance
writes a first estimate, and so do "creatinine clearance (CrCl: 58 mL/min)", "Hamilton
Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D: 18)" and "the hazard ratio for death (HR: 1.3)", whose
letters are not one per word or whose last word does not hold the short form's last letter. Two attempts to tell a
statistic after a colon from a definition by its words, by their initials and then by the
last word, each dropped definitions like these, so a colon is left as it was and its
lookalikes are a Known gap.

And a long form takes no letter from inside a bracket it opens. In "(WSE1) and 40 (12.5%)
had a second WSE (WSE2)" the `2` of WSE2 is found only in "(12.5%)", and nothing is
defined. Where the nearest letter is inside such a bracket and another stands before it,
the bracket is passed over: the `S` of "Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (French
version) (HADS)" is the one of "Scale", and the `I` of "body mass index (in kg/m2) (BMI)"
the one of "index". A long form may close a bracket, "warning score (WSE) at 1 hour
(WSE1)", where WSE1 is the WSE at one hour, and hold a whole one none of its letters is in,
"adjusted (for age) relative risk (aRR)". Both rules come from manuscripts written in Word.

**An abbreviation nobody defined is read by its capitals.** A word met with no definition
is taken for one only when two capitals stand side by side, which keeps `McNemar`,
`DeLong` and `PhD` out of the report. Three things with two capitals together are not
abbreviations and are left alone. A numeral, `II` to `XXXIX`. A registration or accession
number, letters and then five digits or more: `NCT01234567`. And a chemical formula: a
word that reads from end to end as element symbols and their counts, with a count
somewhere. The count is what tells the two apart. `CO2`, `H2SO4` and `NaHCO3` are formulas;
`CO`, `CI` and `HCV` spell elements too and are abbreviations, and so, for the gate, are
`HCl` and `NaOH`, because nothing distinguishes them from `PCa` (prostate cancer) and `SCr`
(serum creatinine), which the first version of this rule let through as formulas. A count
is from two to twelve: nobody writes a count of one, which keeps `HSV1` in the report, and
none runs to fifty, which keeps `IC50`. A count typeset as pandoc's subscript, `CO~2~`, or
in subscript digits, is read as the count it is. A time of day is not read either:
`11:00AM` is the words `11` and `00AM`, and `10:00 PM` holds a `PM`.

**A hyphenated word is one abbreviation where it reads as one.** `SARS-CoV-2` is read
whole when it is defined or known, and so is a name that holds an ordinary word:
`RNA-seq`, `non-HDL-C`. Where nothing in it is defined or known, it is reported whole,
under the name its definition would give it: `LC-MS` and not `LC` and `MS`, `KEYNOTE-189`
and not `KEYNOTE`. An ordinary word joined on is then no part of it: `ROR-based` is `ROR`.
The defined or known name is looked for first. The second review found the order reversed:
the word was split at `seq` before `RNA-seq` was looked for, and its definition was
reported as unused. A name that opens with an ordinary word is looked for with that word's
capital lowered as well, because it takes one at the start of a sentence: `Non-HDL-C` is
`non-HDL-C`. The capitals of the name itself are never folded, so `Rna-seq` is not
`RNA-seq`.

**Three texts are read apart, because each is read apart.** The abstract is indexed and read
without the paper, so it defines what it uses. The main text does not inherit from the
abstract, and says so when that is the reason for a finding. The supplement is read after
the paper, so it inherits the main text's definitions and nothing else. Files are read in
the order the build prints them, and a file that opens without a heading continues the
section the one before it ended in.

**What is not a sentence is not read.** Listings, comments, bindings, citation keys and
link targets go with `mask`, and inline code, equations, image captions, front matter and
headings go after them: a heading in capitals is not an abbreviation. Nor is one typed as
a paragraph in bold: a manuscript converted from Word has a heading only where a heading
style was used, and "**ABSTRACT**" or "**TITLE PAGE**" is a paragraph. So in a paragraph
set entirely in bold whose letters are all capitals, and in a cell of a table's header row
whose letters are ("MODEL 1"), nothing is reported as undefined; what the manuscript
defines is still used there. A cell of a grid table's header that runs over several lines
is read whole. A table's body is not a heading, since its rows name what they count,
`COPD` and `CKD` in a baseline table, nor is a plain paragraph or a list item in capitals.
A reference list is not read at all. In a contributions, acknowledgements, funding or competing-interests
section, capitals are people and institutions, so nothing there is reported as undefined,
and a funder named once with its acronym is not reported as unused. Those sections are
found by a word anywhere in their title, since each publisher words the heading its own
way: "CRediT authorship contribution statement", "Role of the funding source".

**What may stand undefined is data.** `data/abbreviations.yaml` holds a short list of what
general English reads as a word or a name, `DNA`, `UK`, `DOI`, and a few unit symbols with
two capitals together, `MHz`, `GPa`. It is short on purpose. A long list would decide for
every field at once what its readers know, and an entry with a second meaning hides that
meaning: `AD`, `BC` and `PM` were in the first version as eras and times of day, and the
first review took them out, because in clinical prose they are Alzheimer's disease, breast
cancer and particulate matter. To it are added the names
G2 already reads as names (`terms.yaml` and the project's `terms:`), the reporting
guidelines the toolkit has a recipe for, the ones the project declares, and whatever the
project lists under `language: known_abbreviations:` in `paper.yaml`. A listed abbreviation
that the manuscript defines anyway is still held to that definition.

**A few statistical abbreviations stand undefined, unless the journal asks.**
`data/statistical_abbreviations.yaml` holds ANOVA, RMSD, RMSE and SD (Basile's decision of
2026-10-23: a short list, from what journals let stand, and nothing the evidence leaves in
doubt). Its source is the one published style manual found that says so of statistics: the
ASA, CSSA and SSSA Publications Handbook and Style Manual, whose Table 4-1 of "widely used
statistical abbreviations and symbols" "do not require definition" in those journals
(chapter 4, read 2026-10-23). Of that table, SE, SEM, CV and LSD are left out, being status
epilepticus, scanning electron microscopy, cardiovascular and the drug in clinical prose.
CI, OR, RR, HR and IQR are not on the list: JAMA's instructions ask for every abbreviation
to be expanded at first mention, and the Cochrane Style Manual's list of abbreviations that
need no definition holds none of them, so a project whose journal lets them stand lists them
itself. The journal's profile turns the list off, `abbreviations: define_statistics: true`,
or names what is to be defined, `abbreviations: define: [CI]`, which is then reported where
it is undefined whatever exempts it, `paper.yaml`'s list included. Both are rules of the
page, quoted under `quotes.abbreviations.<key>` and held to it by G4.

**A glossary defines its entries.** Under a heading titled Abbreviations, List of
abbreviations, Glossary, Acronyms or List of acronyms, in any case, each line that gives a
short form and its long form is a definition where it stands: "ROR = reporting odds ratio",
"ROR: ...", "ROR – ...", as a list item or not, and the short form and the long
form side by side in a table's row or a definition list's item (in LaTeX, a `tabular` row or
a `description` item). A use above the glossary is used before its definition, as above any.
The glossary's lines are not uses, so an entry nothing else uses is unused. Journals often
ask for the list and for the expansion at first use as well, so a definition in the text that
gives the glossary's meaning again is not reported as given twice; a second one in the text
is, and one that gives another meaning is reported as two meanings.

**A caption may restate a definition.** A legend has to be read alone. A definition in a
Markdown table's caption (`Table: ...`, or `: ...` beside a table), in a paragraph that opens
with the display it captions and a stop, a colon or a dash ("Figure 1. ...", "**Table 2.**
..."), or in a LaTeX `\caption`, is not reported as given twice where it gives the meaning
the text gave; another meaning is reported. A Markdown figure's caption, the text of its
image, is not read at all.

**A paper with no heading is read as one text.** A Markdown manuscript converted from Word
with its headings as bold lines has no section G14 can tell apart: the abstract is read with
the main text, so a definition the abstract and the Introduction both give would be reported
as given twice. Where the main text has no heading at all, G14 does not report
`abbreviation-redefined` in it, at any stage, and says so once, as a note, `no-headings`, at
the drafting stage only (Basile, 2026-10-23: "a note once, at drafting"). The headings are
added while the paper is drafted; once it is past that, the note would be said at every run
of a paper that keeps its bold lines. `check` gives G14 its stage, as it gives G3 and G12
theirs; called with none, G14 says nothing of it. A bold line is not taken for a heading.

**Every finding is a warning, at every stage.** The reading of a definition is good and not
exact, and a name in capitals is not an abbreviation. The first plan for this gate had an
undefined abbreviation fail a submission build. Run on the realistic manuscript kept in
`tests/test_language.py` it gives 22 findings, of which two are names: a trial and a
statistics package. The first review's probes in chemistry and physics added formulas
and unit symbols to what it got wrong, and the rules for those are a reading too. A check that is wrong that often may advise; it may not stop a build.

The worked example found its own slip the first time the gate ran: the Introduction writes
"(ROR ...)" and nothing defines ROR. It is left as it is, because the example's review
records are tied to the text they read, so `check` on the example prints that one warning.
`CI` is listed in the example's `paper.yaml` to show the setting.

## One term for one thing is declared, not guessed

A manuscript that says "participants" in the Methods, "subjects" in the Results and
"patients" in the Discussion leaves its reader to work out whether those are three groups
or one. Varying the word is taught as good style, and in a paper it is a fault.

Which word is right is not something a tool knows. A trial has participants and a registry
has patients, and whether "adverse event" and "adverse reaction" are one thing depends on
whether causality is claimed. So G14's second reading checks nothing it was not told. The
author declares the terms the paper keeps to, in `paper.yaml`:

```yaml
language:
  vocabulary:
    - use: "participants"
      avoid: ["subjects", "patients"]
      why: The trial's own wording, and the reporting guideline's.
```

and the gate reports each term given up that the manuscript still uses, as `term-avoided`:
once for the term, where it first appears, with how many times it is used in the whole
manuscript. One line and a count, not a line for each use: the other uses are found by
searching for the word. A check that
guessed at synonyms would be wrong about every pair of words that are two things, so there
is no shipped list and none is planned.

**A term is matched as a reader would match it.** Whole words only, so "subjective" is
not "subject". In any case, so "Subjects" opening a sentence is found, except for a word
the entry writes with two capitals together: `OR`, `WHO` and `US` are abbreviations and are
matched as written. The first version folded their case too, and an entry that preferred
"odds ratio" to `OR` reported every "or" in the paper. The rule is applied word by word:
in "phase II trial" only `II` is held to its capitals, so "Phase II trials" opening a
sentence is the term. The second version held the whole term to its capitals and found it
only as the entry wrote it. A term written in the singular is found in the plural too; one
written in the plural is found only so, which is how an author keeps "subject to bias" out
of the report: give up "subjects", not "subject". A term to avoid that is part of the term
to use is not found there: with "adverse drug reaction" kept and "drug reaction" given up,
only a "drug reaction" standing alone is reported.

**Its words stand side by side.** Between two words of a term there may be one hyphen, or
blanks, or one line break, since a sentence is wrapped where the editor wraps it; and
marks of emphasis beside any of them, which print as nothing, so `_in vitro_
fertilisation` is "in vitro fertilisation". An asterisk or an underscore inside a word is
the word, and `CYP2D6*4` and `R_0` are found as written. Nothing else: not a blank line, a
dash, the end of a list item, nor anything the reading hides. The first version allowed
any run of white space and hyphens, and found "side effect" in a heading that ended in
"side" over a paragraph that began with "Effect".

**It is read where the manuscript speaks.** Sentences and headings, in every file and in
the supplement, as one text: a heading is the paper's wording as much as a sentence is.
Not in listings, comments, bindings, citation keys, link targets, inline code, equations,
image captions or front matter, as for abbreviations; not in the reference list, whose
titles are other people's; and not in a quotation set as a block, whose words are too. A
line under `>` opens a quotation where a block can open, after a blank line, a heading, a
rule or the line of a fenced div. Inside a paragraph it does not: "ALT" ending one line
and "> 3 times the limit" opening the next are one paragraph, and are read. This is a
reading of the line above and no more: it is right for the shapes a manuscript is written
in, and Known gaps lists where it and pandoc part.

**Entries that disagree are reported and not acted on.** A term that one entry keeps and
another gives up, or that is given up for two different terms, is a `vocabulary-conflict`
at `paper.yaml`, and it is not looked for until the entries agree. Two terms are one to
this check where the reading cannot tell them apart: the same words with a hyphen or a
space between them, in the plural of a term written without one, or with another
capital in a word that has no two capitals together. So "follow up" cannot be given up
for "follow-up", and the message says the two are read as one, while `Covid-19` can be
given up for `COVID-19`, whose capitals stand together. The terms to use are compared the
same way, so an entry for "subject" and "participant" beside one for "subjects" and
"participants" is no conflict. An entry in the wrong shape is the schema's to report, a
term with no letter or digit in it included; the gate reads the entries the schema
accepts, one by one, so one mistake does not take the rest with it.

**Both codes are warnings at every stage**, for the reason abbreviations are: a list of
words cannot tell two meanings of one word apart.

The example declares one entry, "hepatic injury" for "liver injury" and "liver damage",
and keeps to it.

## One English is declared, and the list of the other is somebody else's

`paper.yaml` has always said `english_variant`, and nothing held the manuscript to it. A
paper written by several hands, or revised from a draft in the other spelling, has "colour"
on one page and "color" on the next. G14's third reading reports the words spelt the way
the paper's English does not spell them.

**The list comes from VarCon, and from the part of it that was checked.** VarCon (Kevin
Atkinson and Benjamin Titze) records, for each word English spells in more than one way,
which spelling American, British and Oxford usage prefer and which others each accepts.
`tools/derive_spelling_variants.py` cuts it down to `data/spelling_variants.tsv`: about
8,400 words, each with its kind and with what the other usage writes. The source file is
not in the repository. The script names it by its SHA-256 and refuses another, so the list
is a function of a pinned source and of a script that can be read, and it is never edited
by hand. VarCon marks the clusters it has verified against dictionaries and says the rest
held numerous errors. The first derivation took them all, and run on this repository's own
documentation it reported the "et" of "et al." as the American spelling of "aet", from a
line nobody had verified; "micelle" was the American spelling of "micellae" by the same
route. So a row comes from a verified cluster, or from another only for a correspondence
the spelling itself shows: a verb in `-ise` and its noun, and the combining forms British
spelling writes with a digraph, `haem-`, `-aemia`, `-rrhoea`. Without that second door
"haemodynamic" and "bacteraemia" would be missing, and four rows in ten come through it.
It is narrow because it let the same fault back in once. The letters of a form can be
another root's: `ped-` is the child's and also the soil's, and through `paed-` the first
review found "pedogenic", the soil's word in any English, given to American usage as a
spelling of "paedogenic"; through `amoeb-` a genus, *Entamoeba*, was respelt. For a
day both forms were taken out, and "pedodontics" and "amebiasis" passed in a British
paper. Basile chose on 2026-10-08 to keep the forms and name the words, each with its
reason in the script's table of exceptions: the seven of the soil and the six of the
two genera; then, after the review of that change, the British halves American usage
writes too, "amoebiasis" beside the "amoebic" VarCon verified for both and the
zoologist's "paedomorphosis", and a handful a line pairs wrongly. Thirty-five words
for two forms is what keeping them costs. `hem-` is also the root of "hemisphere", and
no line of VarCon makes that a spelling of anything, so it needs no entry.
ATTRIBUTION.md has VarCon's terms and how the derived file meets them.

**A variant in both usages is the spelling of neither.** VarCon gives "embedding" to
both and "imbedding" as a variant in British usage and a seldom-used one in American.
The first derivation called "imbedding" British, and a hundred words with it: "useable",
"liquify", "focussed". Where the two usages prefer the same spelling and the line tags
the word for both, it writes no row.

**A word is reported only where no line accepts it.** "meter" is the American spelling of
the unit and everybody's spelling of the instrument; "program" is British for software;
"practice" is the noun in both. Acceptance is gathered over every line a word stands on,
in every cluster, verified or not, so each of these is accepted in British usage and is
never reported there. That is the cautious side, and it costs the "meter" that should have
been a "metre".

**Science writes a few words one way everywhere, and the script says which.** VarCon
records general usage. IUPAC spells sulfur with an f in any English, British medicine
prescribes estradiol under its international name, "specialty" is its word for a branch of
practice and "rigor" its word for the sign; an American paper recruits by "flyer" and
ligates an "adaptor". The script leaves these out, each with its reason beside it, and
with them the few words a line of VarCon pairs wrongly: "pyrolyses" is the plural of
pyrolysis and no British verb. That list is meant to stay short: where a field writes a
word the list gives to the other usage, the project says so, one word to an entry, under
`language: accepted_spellings:`.

**A name keeps its spelling.** "World Health Organization" is written so in a British
paper and "Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine" in an American one. Only a word in lower
case is read, or one with a capital where a sentence, a heading, a list item or a table
cell opens. So the first word of a heading is read and the rest of one in title case is
not, and a name that opens a sentence is taken for a word. Both are in Known gaps.

**It is read where the manuscript speaks**, as the vocabulary is: the sentences and
headings of every file and of the supplement, not the reference list, not a quotation set
as a block, whose spelling is its author's, and nothing the masking hides.

**And not where the wording is somebody else's.** A contributions statement names its
roles as the CRediT taxonomy spells them, "Conceptualization" and "Visualization", and a
funding statement is the funder's sentence, "the Horizon 2020 research and innovation
programme". Read like the rest, the first gave a British paper in `-ise` a
`spelling-mixed` and the second gave an American one a finding for a word it may not
change. So the spelling is not read in the sections where G14 already reports no
undefined abbreviation: contributions, acknowledgements, funding, competing interests,
found by a word in their titles, with their subsections. The vocabulary is still read
there, since a term the author gave up is the author's wherever it stands. The price is
a slip of the author's own in an acknowledgement, which passes. This reading also
hides a little more, because markup is written in American: an HTML tag, so that
`<span style="color:red">` is no word of the paper; a block of attributes that holds a
key, `{fig-align="center"}`; and the label of a reference link. A LaTeX command is not
hidden: from `drafting` on, and where pandoc is installed, `check` fails a manuscript
that holds one, unless it is a macro's definition or a layout command, which it passes.
A word joined to a digit or to an underscore, `color2`, `tumor_size`, is a
variable's name; one that stands beside an `@`, or that a dot and a letter follow, is
part of an address or a file's name; and one that follows a backslash is a macro's name
or a folder's in a path. The second review found that last rule gone with the pattern
that hid LaTeX commands, and a macro named `center` read as a word.

**Three findings.** `spelling-variant` is one word in the other spelling: once for the
word, where it first stands, with how many times it is used and what to write. When the
other usage's spellings are five or more and are used more often than the paper's own, the
likelier mistake is the line in `paper.yaml`, and one `spelling-not-as-declared` at
`paper.yaml` takes the place of them all, with the twelve most used listed. `spelling-mixed` is for a British paper alone. British usage
takes `-ise` or `-ize`, Oxford's being `-ize`, and a paper takes one: the finding is given
once, at the first word in the ending used less, with both counts. An American paper has
no such choice, so an `-ise` there is a `spelling-variant`.

**All three are warnings at every stage.** A list cannot tell "Labor", the party, from
"labor", the word misspelt, and it is a list of general English.

A journal that insists on one English says so in its profile, and G4 already reports a
paper that declares the other. G14 holds the manuscript to what the paper declares.

**A paper may declare no English, and `init` declares none unless told** (Basile,
2026-10-23). `init` wrote `english_variant: en-GB` into every new project. Fourteen real
American papers were checked so, and seven were told they broke their declared spelling,
which nobody had declared. Now `english_variant` is optional in the schema, `init` writes it
only with `--english en-GB` or `--english en-US` (any other value is refused, and the values
it takes are read from the schema), and `Project.english_variant` is None where the line is
absent. Each reader of it has a rule for a paper that has not said:

- **G14** counts the words each English writes and the other does not, and holds the paper
  to the English of the more. Where they are level, the paper's English is that of the first
  such word met, as `spelling-mixed` keeps the ending met first when the two are level. An
  `-ize` both usages write counts for neither, and a paper with no word of either hears
  nothing. The words of the fewer are then each a `spelling-variant`, which says that
  `paper.yaml` declares no English and gives both counts; `spelling-mixed` reads the endings
  of a paper that is mostly British as it does those of a British one;
  `spelling-not-as-declared` is never given, since the other English is never the more.
- **The build** gives the document `lang: en`, English with no region. Pandoc writes `en`
  into the .docx (`w:lang` in its styles, `dc:language` in its properties). Word 16 reads it
  as English with no region (LanguageID 9) and proofs it with its American dictionary:
  checked on 2026-10-23, it marked "Colour" and not "color" in a document so built, as it
  does in one with no `lang` at all, which pandoc writes as `en-US`. In LaTeX pandoc loads
  babel's `english`. Citeproc takes CSL's `en-US` locale for `en`, and the live Zotero
  build names no locale, so `zotero_word.lua` writes `en-US`, CSL's default.
- **A dataset's date**, which the emitters print when the analysis runs, is written day,
  month, year ("1 March 2024"), as `written` writes it when given no English. That order is
  the one of the two that a reader in either English reads without stopping, and it was
  already what a paper that could not be read got. The R emitter reads the line of
  `paper.yaml` and, finding none, does the same. `dataset-date-english` holds a date to that
  order and says that `paper.yaml` declares no English.
- **The review panel** is told nothing of a variant: the line "English:" is left out.
- **G4** compares a journal's `english_variant` with the paper's only where the paper
  declares one. Where the journal's profile names an English and `paper.yaml` declares
  none, G4 says so in a note, `english-variant-undeclared`, which names the English the
  journal asks for and fails no stage (Basile, 2026-10-23). It reads no word of the
  manuscript: whether the paper is written in the journal's English is G14's count, and
  G14 holds it to the English of the more words, not to the journal's.

## One notation is the manuscript's own, and the space before a unit is the SI's

"P = 0.03" in the Methods, "p=0.04" in the Results and "*P* <0.001" under a table are one
statistic written three ways. Which way is right is a journal's to say: one house prints a
capital italic *P* and another a lower-case p, one joins the bounds of an interval with
"to" and another with an en dash. That the manuscript writes each thing one way is a fact
about the manuscript, the same in any field. It is the distinction the abbreviations
started from, and G14's fourth reading applies it to four things:

| Code | What is held to one form |
|---|---|
| `notation-p-symbol` | the symbol of a P value: "P", "p", "*P*", "*p*" |
| `notation-sign-spacing` | the spaces around the sign after `P` or `n`: "P = 0.03" or "P=0.03" |
| `notation-interval` | what joins the two bounds of an interval: "to", an en dash, a hyphen, a comma |
| `notation-percent` | "5%" or "5 %" |

**The manuscript's convention is the form it uses most.** Each other form is reported
once, where it first stands, with both counts: "the P value is written 'p' 3 times; the
manuscript writes 'P' 12 times". Where two forms are used as often, the later one is the
one shown, and the finding says they are level. A count cannot say which form the journal
prints, and the hint says so: the instructions decide, and where they are silent the
majority is as good a convention as any. A space on one side of a sign only, "P= 0.03",
is no convention anywhere and is reported whatever the rest of the manuscript does.

**A value is a value, typed or bound.** In a manuscript of this toolkit the numbers are
bindings, so "(95% CI {{results.ror.ci_low}} to {{results.ror.ci_high}})" has no digit
in it after "95". The reading takes each binding that stands in a sentence for a number,
and reads the notation around it. A binding with something hidden on both sides of it
stands in a listing, a comment or an equation, and is no number of the prose.

**Only what is typed is read.** How a bound value is printed, its decimals, its leading
zero and its thousands separator, is the emitter's doing and a journal's rule, and
consistency says little there: an odds ratio and a P value are rightly printed to
different precisions. Basile left that out of this reading on 2026-10-08.

**Only where the reading is sure.** The sign is read after `P` and after `n` and nowhere
else: "aged <65 years" is written closed in papers that space "P < 0.05", because there
the sign is a modifier and not a comparison between two things. An interval is one that
"CI", "CrI" or the words "confidence interval" introduce. Known gaps lists what that
leaves unread.

**What a house style does on purpose is not a second form.** The first review of this
reading found four things it had counted against a manuscript that was right. A house
that joins the bounds of an interval with a hyphen, as JAMA does, writes "to" where a
bound is negative, so that the dash is not read as its sign: an interval joined by "to"
with a typed negative bound says nothing of the rest and is not counted. A `P` with a
typed value above 1 is a pressure, a partition coefficient or a number of predictors,
and no P value, unless a power of ten follows its figures or it is ten itself to a
negative power, "P = 3.2 x 10-9", "P < 10^-5^". The figures are read and never made a
number:
the first fix converted them, and Python refuses more than 4,300 digits, so a line of
sevens after `P =` made the gate raise. A capital `P` that opens a sentence has its
capital from the sentence,
in "P < 0.05 was considered significant" as in "P values were two-sided"; the spacing
of its sign is still read. And a level of confidence stated after the letters, "a
confidence interval of 95%, 5% margin of error", is no bound. Nor is a first bound a
level: in "(95% CI 80%-93%; 12 studies)" the 80% was taken for one, "-93" for a bound
and the semicolon for the join, until the third review. A level has no bound in percent
after a hyphen or a minus sign against its percent sign.

**The space before a unit is not a matter of counting.** `notation-unit` reports a number
that runs into its unit, "5mg", "10mL", "37°C", wherever it stands, in a manuscript that
always writes it so too. Here a field-neutral authority speaks: the SI Brochure (9th
edition, section 5.4.3) sets a space between a numerical value and its unit symbol, with
the one exception of the degree, minute and second of plane angle. One finding carries the
count and the first few examples, since the remedy is one habit and not a list of places.
The Brochure asks for the same space before "%" (section 5.4.7), and there most medical
journals do otherwise, so "%" is held to consistency alone. Basile chose both on
2026-10-08.

**A unit is known by name, and the short names are few.** The symbols read are listed in
`gates/notation.py`. Of those of one letter only `g` and `h` are among them: "5m" is as
often five months, "1L" a first line of treatment, "30s" an age and "3A" a grade. And
those two are not read where a number and a letter are a name: in a sentence that has
named a figure, a table or a scheme before them, where "3g" is a panel; standing
against the word for a compound, a product or a derivative, alone or in a list of its
kind, "compounds 3g and 4h"; or alone between marks of emphasis, where "**3g**" is the
seventh of a series. Those words are ordinary prose too, and the second review found
"each compound was incubated for 24h" passed over, so a name has to stand against its
word. Nor is `g` read as a gram where it is a force: after a number of five figures or
more before its decimal point, or after a word of centrifuging in its sentence.
"12,000g" is printed closed, and "12,000 g" would be twelve kilograms. Four figures
was the rule for a day and took a birth weight, "2500g", for a force. Shown both,
Basile chose five on 2026-10-08: the word of centrifuging is nearly always there, and a
birth weight never has one.

**It is read where the manuscript speaks**, as the vocabulary is, the contributions and
acknowledgements included: a P value there is the author's. Not in a quotation set as a
block, the reference list, or anything the masking hides.

**Every finding is a warning**, at every stage. A `p` can be a proportion, and a majority
is not a rule.

The example joins the bounds of its five intervals with "to", sets "%" against its number
and states no P value with a sign, so it has nothing to report.

## Methods drift is a reconciliation ledger

Methods sections go stale in a specific way: the analysis changes, and nothing forces the
prose to follow. Nobody re-reads their own Methods.

No checker can read code and prose and decide whether they agree. G9 therefore records
something it *can* verify — that a person read the Methods against the analysis, and
whether anything has changed since. `methods.lock` holds a digest of every analysis file as
it stood at that moment; the gate compares and names **which files** changed, so the
re-reading is targeted rather than a vague instruction to check everything.

Digests, not timestamps: copying a tree or re-saving a file is not a change.

The claim is modest and true. It does not verify that the Methods are correct. It verifies
that somebody looked, and that nothing has moved since they did — the same bargain as the
figure review and the literature attestation. Reconciling without reading makes the file a
lie, and the skill says so in those words, because a machine-checkable lie is worse than no
check.

The lock can also carry parameters that must appear in the prose — the significance
threshold, the software version. Presence, not correctness, but those are exactly what a
reviewer queries and exactly what is left behind when an analysis is redone.

**A section that counts as present is a section that is read.** G4 counts a required
section present by finding its name in a heading, and so "2. Methods" and "Patients and
methods" answered a required Methods section. G9 found the Methods by a pattern of its own,
"Methods" or "Materials and methods" at the start of a heading, and under either of the
others it compared the lock's parameters with no text: a wrong `alpha: 0.07` was reported
under "# Methods" and passed under "# 2. Methods", with nothing said. Since 2026-10-14 one
test says which heading is the Methods, `text/section_names.py`. Its words are G4's own, a
title holding "methods", so "2. Methods", "**2. Methods**", "Materials & methods" and
"Patients and methods" are the Methods to G9 as they always were to G4. Two earlier drafts
said it by the words of a title, and each failed review: one left out headings G4 had always
counted, the other took a paper's title for its Methods. What decides between titles holding
the word is where they stand. A heading inside the abstract is the abstract's, and one under
a heading that names another part of the paper ("Limitations of existing methods" under the
Introduction) belongs to that part. One over another part is no Methods either:
"# Statistical methods for signal detection", a paper's title written as a heading over
`##` sections, is over its Results, and G9 read that whole paper as the Methods, a wrong
parameter in the Results among them. Of the headings left, one named as the Methods, by a
name of G2's, comes first, its name read here as a reader sees it though G2 reads it as
typed: "(3) Methods", "**2. Methods**" and "Materials & methods" came after "Limitations
of existing methods" standing before them (round 3 of #246). G4 uses the test for a required
section named "Methods", G9 reads the
first such section of the main text, and a project with analysis code and no such heading is
told so (`methods-not-found`, a warning). G2 and G15 read the Methods as places, where a
heading names the method without the word ("Statistical analysis", "Study design"); they
take numbered headings and
"<anything> and methods" too now, and never a heading that also names the results:
"Methods and results", a research letter's combined section, let every threshold convention
through under its results. They read fewer headings than G4 counts, and a Methods they miss
makes them report a number, not pass one.

**The supplement's Methods are read with the paper's.** Every gate read
`manuscript/supplementary/`, and G9 read the Methods of the main text alone, because G4's
required section is the main text's. A parameter of the lock that eMethods stated was
reported absent, and in a paper whose Methods are all in its supplement, as a research
