letter's often are, the lock's parameters were compared with no text: a wrong one was told
only as `methods-not-found`. Since 2026-10-21 (Basile's choice) G9 keeps one ledger. It reads
the main text's Methods as before, then, in each file of the supplement, every section that
the main text's Methods would be found as: a heading holding "methods", "Supplementary
methods", "eMethods 1. Data source", "S1 Methods" or "Appendix 1: Methods", with no Results
heading over it. Every one and not the first, since a supplement numbers its Methods and puts
its tables between them. Of each it reads its own text and that of each section under it
that names a method too ("Statistical analysis", "eMethods 2"), and not everything under it,
as it reads the main text's Methods. A supplement often has "Supplementary methods" over all
of it, as the example's has: its tables, a paragraph of results, its reporting statement. As
first written, the whole of such a file was the Methods, and a P the paragraph reported
passed G2 as a threshold chosen in advance, which main failed as unbound (round 1 of #395;
Basile then chose the narrower reading for G2, G15 and G9 alike). A parameter of the lock
is stated where either states it. The rest of the supplement is not read for one: an eTable
holds numbers of every kind, and a parameter matched in one would be no check. G4's required
Methods are still the main text's. The anchors were read in every file already, so a claim
in the supplement was held to its step, and a step pointed at from there was one some text
describes. The supplement's paragraphs that point at no step are now listed by
`methods --explain` with the main text's, where G2 reads them as the Methods.

G2 and G15 found the Methods by names of their own (`classify.METHODS_SECTIONS`), none of
them a supplement's. Under "eMethods 1" a threshold typed as a convention was a number
nothing classified, with the wrong advice, and the kind of the fitted model typed there was
never read. `classify.SUPPLEMENT_METHODS` holds the supplement's names: "Supplementary",
"Supplemental" or "Online methods", "eMethods" and "S1 Methods", each with a number or the
title of its part after it, and "Methods" under the label of an appendix or a supplement
("Appendix 1: Methods", "Appendix S1. Supplementary methods", "Supplement 1. eMethods 2").
`is_methods` takes them where one opens the run of headings, innermost outwards, that each
name a method: under "eMethods 1", or "Supplementary methods" over "Statistical analysis",
and not under "Supplementary methods" over "Table S2. The adjusted model". The main text's
names hold everything under them, as they always have. G9's paragraphs that point at no step
are found under the same headings. A name G9 reads and these do not, "Supplementary methods
and results" or "Detailed methods", is read as the main text's "Methods and results" is. No supplement's name puts a heading first
among the main text's Methods: in a main text with "Laboratory methods" and then
"Supplementary methods", the first is still the one read.

**A lock read against the main text alone stays valid, and is said of.** The lock holds no
digest of the Methods: the analysis files' digests, the parameters, and each pair's words and
its code's digest. Reading the supplement makes no lock wrong and needs no migration. But a
lock written when G9 read the main text's Methods alone may vouch for eMethods nobody read
against the code. `methods --reconcile` now writes `manuscript-guard/methods-lock/2`. A lock
of `/1`, or of no schema or an empty one, that records the files, in a project whose
supplement has Methods,
is said of once, `methods-supplement-unreconciled`, a warning at every stage that names the
supplement's files, and its files and pairs are held as before. `methods --reconcile <step>`
leaves the files and their schema as they were, since nobody read the files again. A lock of
pairs alone claims no reading of the files and is written `/2`.

The abstract is found the same way for G4's limit and its headings, G14's regions and the
word count: "Abstract" or "Structured abstract", numbered or not, or the title the
journal's profile gives it (`structure.abstract_title: Summary` for The Lancet). With a
limit on the abstract and no heading naming one, G4 says so (`abstract-not-found`, a
warning): the limit was checked against nothing and the abstract counted as main text. And
the headings inside the abstract are the abstract's. A structured abstract's "Methods" and
"Results" answered the journal's required sections in a paper whose body had neither.

## A statistic is reported with what it belongs to

A p value means nothing without the estimate it tests, a percentage without the counts it
is a share of, and an estimate without its interval. Bound one by one, each passed G2 alone:
"P = 0.012" in a sentence of its own, "52.1% were women" with no n/N, an odds ratio quoted
everywhere with its upper bound only.

So a statistic says what it belongs to when it is emitted, in both emitters: `of` names a p
value's estimate or a share's numerator, `over` a share's denominator, and `family` the tests
a p value is one of. G2 reads which bindings sit together in a sentence, and nothing of what
the sentence says: a p value quoted in a sentence that binds no estimate of it, or a share in
one that binds neither of its counts, is `quoted-alone`; an estimate emitted with an
interval and quoted in no sentence with both its bounds is `interval-not-quoted-whole`. Both
are warnings: a paper may rightly give a p value again a line after its estimate. Sentences
end where the labels of a spread read them to end (`sentence_stops`): the stop of "s.d.",
"s.e." or "s.e.m." before a number or a word in lower case ends none, so "(s.e. 0.21), P =
..." keeps its P with its estimate. A statistic whose `of` or `over` names a key no fragment
emits is told so, once per quote and whatever the sentence holds, rather than told it is
quoted alone. And the schema holds
what the emitters refuse, so that a fragment written by hand cannot step around these
checks: `over` and `family` only with `of`, and never both on one value.

Multiple comparisons are declared, never guessed. `correction("secondary", "holm")` says how
a family is corrected, and "none" is a declaration too, with its reason. G8 warns on a
family of more than one p value with no correction declared (`family-uncorrected`).

## A choice the code makes is declared, bound and read

The ledger records that someone looked. Some of what they look for needs no reading: the
alpha, the minimum number of cases, the software version. These are choices made in the
code and stated in the Methods, and typed there they pass G2 as conventions or as the name of
a thing. `explain` on the example showed `0.05 convention alpha-level` and `3 convention
disproportionality-criterion`: the gate had agreed not to look at the two numbers in the
Methods most likely to drift from the code. The example's own Methods had already drifted.
They defined a signal as at least 3 cases with a lower bound above 1, and the code computed no
signal at all.

So the analysis declares them, in both emitters: `alpha = em.parameter("alpha", 0.05)` records
`param.alpha` and hands the value back for the code to use. `em.software("statsmodels")`
records the version the run imported, and refuses a distribution the run never imported. The
Methods bind both. A version is the environment and not a result, so `verify`, re-running the
analysis on another machine, reports a version other than the one on disk as a warning
(`rerun-other-software`) and holds every other value to agreeing. Which values are versions
it reads from the re-run, so a fragment edited to call a changed result "software" is still
a difference. A fitted model's last digits are the machine's too: an iterative fit
on macOS and on Linux agree to about fifteen digits and not to the last bit. So verify holds
a float to agreeing in nine significant digits, and its display, which is what the paper
prints, to agreeing exactly. G2 fails a declared value typed instead: a Methods-only
convention whose number equals a parameter, or a software version equal to a declared one.
Only the Methods-only conventions count, because they are the thresholds an author chooses in
advance; the `2` of a `2 x 2` table names a structure whatever a parameter equals. A figure
typed against a letter, of any alphabet, is part of a name too. The convention that accepts
"I2 > 50%" covers the name of the statistic with its threshold, and read from its first digit
`I2` stated 2: an analysis that declared a parameter of 2 was told to bind the name, and one
that declared none of 2 was told `I2` was a threshold no parameter has. A name states no
number and is no threshold. The figure after it is, in an atom of its own or in the name's
(`I2>50%`).

**Declared is not used.** A parameter bound in the Methods prints the right number for a step
the code may not take, which is exactly what the example's signal criterion was. Each
emitter therefore reads the code round the call to `parameter()`, Python with its `ast` in
the file the call stands in, R with its parse data in the script the emitter was given,
and records whether the value handed back is read again (`read`). The
value thrown away, or assigned to a name nothing in its scope reads, is `false`, and G2 fails
it from the `analysis` stage. Where the value goes somewhere the reading does not follow, as
onto a class or into a list, nothing is recorded and nothing fails: a parameter kept as
`Settings.ALPHA` was once looked for as a name, found unread, and failed in use. A value
read again is not shown to change anything. It can be
read in a `print`, or in a branch that never runs, or compared with data it never decides
for. Perturbing it and re-running would not settle that either: a threshold of 3 cases with 77
cases in the data changes no result whether or not the code applies it. The record says what
was established, a read, and nothing more.

**A copy that no longer agrees is named, not failed.** The rule above finds a typed copy only
while it still equals the parameter. Once the analysis declares parameters, a Methods
threshold equal to none of them is reported as `threshold-undeclared`, a warning. It is either a
choice the code makes and does not declare, or the copy left behind by a change, and which
one is a question for the author.

A threshold is not a measurement, so a float parameter is written as typed (fifteen
significant digits, in both languages) unless `digits` or `display` says otherwise: 0.025
rounded to two places is 0.03, a different test.

**A coding dictionary is declared like a version.** "Events were coded with MedDRA version
26.1 and drugs with WHODrug Global B3 2025" passed `26.1` as a software version tied to
nothing, and failed `B3` and `2025` with no declared way to bind them. In a
pharmacovigilance paper the release of MedDRA decides which preferred terms exist. So
`em.dictionary("MedDRA", release_file=...)` records `dictionary.meddra` with the role
`dictionary`, in both emitters, and digests the file it names as an input, so that a new
release is a change G1 sees. MedDRA's ASCII release states its version in
`meddra_release.asc`, the first `$`-separated field of its first line, and the emitter reads
it from there; another dictionary's release is given, and checked against nothing, and R
refuses one that is not a single value. G2 fails a declared release typed where the
dictionary is named within a few words before it on its line (`typed-dictionary-release`),
with or without a `v` before it ("MedDRA v26.1"), and only there: "2019" is the release of
ICD-10 and the year of many other things.

## The label beside an interval or a spread is the one emitted

"(90% CI {{results.ror.ci_low}} to {{results.ror.ci_high}})" over a 95% interval, and "(SE
{{results.age.sd}})" over a standard deviation, passed every gate: a level was recorded only
on a second interval, which `level` names, and nothing said whether a dispersion is a
standard deviation or a standard error. A script now states the level of its intervals
once, on the emitter (`Emitter(__file__, ci_level="95%")`, `mg_emitter(..., ci_level =
"95%")`), and every interval without a level of its own records it on its bounds. It is said
there and not on the interval because `level` names a second interval's keys
(`ror.ci90_low`): given to the first interval, it would rename its bounds and every binding
of them. A dispersion says which it is, and of what: `em.value("age.sd", 12.3, digits=1,
spread="sd", of="age.mean")`. Both emitters write the same.

G2 reads the label nearest each such binding, in its sentence (`in_sentences`) and on its own
side of any other binding: the text from the binding before it in the sentence, or the
sentence's start, and for a spread the dozen characters after it ("12.3 (SD)"). A level is
written before the letters ("95% CI", "90% two-sided confidence interval") or after them
("CI 95%"), and the nearest one counts, so "a 90% CI elsewhere, and 95% CI ..." reads 95. It
is compared as a number, so "95.0%" is 95%. A label written otherwise than emitted is a
warning (`interval-level-differs`, `spread-label-differs`), and so is a quoted interval with
no level recorded at all, once, where it is first quoted (`interval-level-undeclared`): the
brief asked for it as a warning at first. Where no label is written beside a binding,
nothing is said.

## A P follows from its statistic

A paper's own results are bound, and their arithmetic is the analysis's. Three kinds of
number are not: a value quoted from another paper, a number typed into the prose, and two
bound values that come from different keys. "t(23) = {{results.crude.t}}, p =
{{results.adjusted.p}}" passes G2 once for each value, and says something no analysis
computed.

A t, F, chi-squared or z statistic with its degrees of freedom gives its P, and the P
printed after it in the same sentence can be held to it. G8 does this in the manuscript as
it prints, each binding replaced by its display; G7 does it in each ledger quote, where a
disagreement means the source's own numbers disagree; `audit` does it in a paper that was
never bound. The P is worked out over every value the statistic's printed digits allow:
"2.45" stands for anything from 2.445 to 2.455, and "p = .041" for anything from 0.0405 to
0.0415. The two disagree (`p-inconsistent`) when those ranges do not meet, and the
disagreement is a decision error (`p-decision-error`) when they fall on either side of the
significance level, the `param.alpha` the analysis emits or 0.05. "p < .05" stands for
anything below 0.05.

A sentence that calls its test one-sided, adjusted or corrected, Welch's,
sphericity-corrected, exact, permutation or simulated is read and not judged: the P of
such a test does not follow from the statistic by the textbook formula. All of it is a
warning, and in `audit` it is listed apart and not counted by `--strict`, because a test
can be one of those without its sentence saying so.

The package depends on nothing numerical, and the four distributions need two functions
beyond the standard library, the regularized incomplete beta and gamma functions. They are
written from their definitions in the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions,
chapter 8, whose equations `stats/special.py` names, and they are tested against values
SciPy computed once, outside the package. The two agree to a relative 1e-10.

An estimate printed with its confidence interval is held to it the same way, on the same
three surfaces (`stats/intervals.py`). An estimate outside its own interval over every value
the printed digits allow, a bound transposed past it or an estimate from another analysis,
is `interval-excludes-estimate`, whatever kind of interval it is. And two identities hold
for a Wald interval:

- **A ratio's interval is symmetric on the log scale.** The arm from the lower bound up to
  the estimate equals the arm from the estimate up to the upper bound. A bound misprinted,
  or the crude estimate printed with the adjusted interval, makes them unequal.
  `ratio-interval-asymmetric` is said where they differ by more than 30% of the
  half-width at the least, over every value the three numbers' printed digits allow.
  "ROR 2.6, 95% CI 2.1-3.2" differs by 2.8% as printed and by nothing within its rounding.
- **The interval excludes the null exactly when P is below one less its level.** The null
  is 1 for an odds, risk, hazard, rate or reporting ratio and 0 for a difference; a 90%
  interval goes with 0.10. `p-against-interval` is said where the whole rounding box of a
  bound is past the null and P is on the wrong side of the level as printed, or the reverse.

The 30% was set against the intervals that are not Wald ones and whose sentence may not say
so. A profile-likelihood interval (R's `confint()` on a logistic model) and an exact
conditional one were worked out for 2-by-2 tables, once and outside the package. Their arms
differ by 2 to 7% with tens of events in each group, 11 to 20% with three to five in the
smaller, 23 to 25% with two, and 42% with one. So 30% leaves both alone except at one or two
events, and still finds most misprinted bounds; a crude estimate beside an adjusted
interval, which differ by less, is found only when they differ by a fair share of the
half-width.

A sentence that calls its interval profile-likelihood, exact, bootstrap, permutation,
simulated, Bayesian or credible is read and judged on neither identity. One that calls its
P one-sided, or adjusted or corrected for multiplicity, is not judged on the second.
"Adjusted" alone stands nothing down: it is said of estimates far more often than of P
values, and an adjusted odds ratio's interval is as symmetric as a crude one's. A P is taken
as the estimate's own only where no other interval stands between them and nothing near it
says it is a P for interaction, trend or heterogeneity. The words between a name and its
estimate do not run across another estimate's name: "No difference in mortality, HR 0.83"
names a hazard ratio, held to 1. Bounds whose signs cannot be read
for sure are not read: "-0.9--0.1" is an en dash in Markdown or a hyphen and a minus.

An n (%) in a table of a paper given to `audit` is held to its denominator
(`stats/shares.py`): the count's own, "640/1200 (53.3)", or the "n = 1200" of its column's
header, the nearest above it in a row with no count. The count over the denominator has to
give the share printed within half a unit of its last place. The table is read as rows of
cells (`text/tables.py`): a Markdown pipe table from the masked text, so that one in a
fenced listing is not a table, and a .docx table as Word lays it out, from marks the reader
puts on the first line of each cell and takes out again, so the text the rest of the audit
reads is unchanged. A cell spanning columns counts as each.

What is read is only a column of shares. A label that names a mean, a median, an SD, an
IQR, a range or a CI, the row's or the one over its rows, or a header that does, bars it,
"%" or not: "HbA1c, %, mean (SD)" holds two numbers that are not a count and its share. So
does a row's label that ends on a unit in percent, "Oxygen saturation, %" or "LVEF (%)",
with no "n" before the "%", for a cell with no "%" of its own and a number no more than 100:
a measure, whose mean (SD) is printed as whole numbers beside the shares, and not "Male sex
(%) | 640 (58.0%)" (rounds 1 and 2 of #314). Of the rest, a cell is read where something
says it is a share: a "%" in the cell, or "n (%)", "No. (%)" or "n/N (%)" in the row's
label, in the label over its rows or in its column's header. A "%" alone in a label is a
unit and says nothing; read as "these are shares", it listed a mean saturation of 96 (3) as
8% of its column (round 1 of #314). Or a cell is read where it is one of a characteristic's
categories: the rows under a label of their own, which may have its P value beside it or a
dash, all of whose shares in its column add up to about 100 (round 2 of #314: a P beside the
label made it a header). Where the longest run of them from the top that adds up to about 100
is shorter than all of them, it is still the categories for letting a share off as a share of
their total, the row after them being the next characteristic (round 2: a row after the
subtypes joined them); but it never says a cell is a share (round 3: a whole-number mean's
running sum with the shares passed through 100, and the mean was listed).

A share is listed only where no reading of it gives the share printed: of its denominator;
of its row's total, where the row's shares add up to 100 across it; or of its categories'
total, where their shares add up to 100 down the column. The last is what the subtypes of
another row are, "Type 1" and "Type 2" as shares of those with diabetes, and what a
characteristic counted among those with data is (round 1 of #314: both were listed as
errors). A row whose label carries a footnote marker, a superscript, a footnote's reference,
a dagger, or which names an n of its own, is listed as uncertain: a note under the table may
give it the patients with data as its denominator. A share that is off says which
denominators it would fit, which is what a share of those with data looks like. Listed with
the other disagreements, and not counted by `--strict`.

A mean of whole numbers is held to its n (`stats/granularity.py`), which is the granularity
test of Brown and Heathers (*Social Psychological and Personality Science* 2017;8:363-9):
the mean of N whole numbers is a whole total over N, so 3.47 is no mean of 28 answers, whose
totals 97 and 98 give 3.46 and 3.50. A mean is possible where some whole total over N is
within half a unit of its last printed place, both ends taken, so that a mean rounded half
up and one rounded half to even are both read as printed. N is the sample size times the
number of items each person answered, where the mean is of their item means. Where N is 10
to the power of the places printed or more, the interval of totals is a unit wide or more
and holds one whatever the mean, so the mean is not assessable and said to be so, not
passed. So it is for a few N just under, whose totals and the ties between them, each read
both ways, print every mean: 8 at one place, 80 and 96 at two, 800, 960 and 992 at three
(round 1 of #331, where the generated tables found 96). Each mean of one unit is tried for
N from half the power up; under half, each total prints at most two means, so some mean is
none. Trailing noughts are places: 2.50 is printed to two.

Nothing reads a mean as one of whole numbers on its own. A paper does not say so, and a
guess from a label, "number of" or "score", would read a mean of rates or of a continuous
scale as a misprint. So the author says it. In the literature ledger an entry takes
`mean_of_whole_numbers: {n, items}`, and G7 holds the value, as its quote prints it, to
them: `quote-mean-not-possible` (a warning) where no total gives it,
`quote-mean-not-assessable` (a note) where N is too large or the value is not a decimal. In
`audit`,
`--whole-numbers` names the rows of a table that hold such means, by words of their labels,
matched at word edges in any case. Each cell of such a row shaped as a mean, alone, "3.47
(1.20)", "3.47 [1.20]" or "3.47 ± 1.20", a minus sign read as one, is held to its column's n,
read from the header cells as the shares read theirs. A mean that does not fit is listed
with the disagreements, with the totals either side and the nearest sample sizes it fits,
below and above, since a mean of those with data has a smaller n than its column; one not
assessable is listed apart, and a label under which no mean was read is said. A row whose
label carries a footnote marker or names an n of its own is uncertain. Every cell that is
not a mean is read for the n it names, in a named row too: a header whose first cell is the
scale's name, "Pain score | Treated (n = 28)", is still a header (round 1 of #331, where
it was read as a row of means and nothing under it was read). The row's own n is not
taken for its means: with two columns it would name one of them. The rows are held over
generated tables (`mean_tables` in `tests/generated.py`), with a row of every kind in each
and a pair of means half a unit from a total.

## A model is read from its fit, and each variable says what it is

A parameter is one number. A model is a set of decisions: which outcome, which kind of
model for it, which variables, each entered how, against which reference, on which rows. A
Methods section states them in a sentence, and the sentence is written once and never read
against the fit again.

So the analysis records the model as the fit describes itself. `em.model("adjusted", fit,
name=..., description=...)` reads a statsmodels fit made through the formula API, and
`em$model()` an R `lm` or `glm`. Each records the engine (language, class, family, link), the
formula, every term with how each variable entered it (as a number, or as categories with
their levels and reference), the rows used and dropped, the events of a binary outcome by
level of each categorical term, and convergence. A fit the emitter cannot read is refused,
not described: a model typed by hand is the thing this replaces.

**The variables of a term are the data's columns.** `splines::ns(age, knots = knots)` reads
`age`; `knots` is an object of the script, and a variable nobody could declare. Python has
the frame the fit kept. In R a `glm` keeps its data and an `lm` only its call, whose `data`
is read again where the formula was made.

**A comparison is a term of its own.** `I(stage == 'IV')` is true or false of each row. It is
not `stage`: its levels are not the four stages and its reference is no stage, and Python
enters it as categories where R enters it as a number. Each emitter knows it by its syntax
(`==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `in` or `%in%`, at the top of the expression, bare or
inside `I()`, and the negation of one) and marks the term, or the outcome, `comparison`. G15
asks that the variable it reads be declared and holds the comparison to none of that
variable's kind, levels and reference. The mark is the one fact added to the fragment for
it: the gate could not tell a comparison from the expression without reading two languages.

**Grouped data are events among trials.** A binomial model of a table, one row a group, is
fitted to the proportion of each row, and the sum of those proportions is no number of
events. For `successes + failures ~ ...` in statsmodels, and in R for
`cbind(successes, failures) ~ ...` or a proportion with the trials as `weights`, the card
holds `events`, the successes summed over the rows, and `trials`. A card without `trials`
is one observation a row, as every card was. The columns of a grouped outcome are counts,
or their proportion, and are declared so: the binary outcome is each trial's.

The data cannot say what a variable is meant to be. 1 to 4 is a grade, a code or a count,
and an identifier looks like an integer. `em.variable("age_group", "categorical", label=...,
levels=..., reference=..., values=...)` says it, beside the code that derives the variable,
and records what the data held: the levels, the distinct values, the missing ones.

**Facts in the fragment, names derived once.** The emitters write facts and nothing else.
What a model is called (`logistic regression`), the sentence that describes it and the
table that prints it are derived when the results are read, from `data/models.yaml`, in
Python, for both languages. Two emitters naming models would be two lists to keep equal.
The model has two names and two descriptions. Its name (`Adjusted model`) and its
description (what it is for) are the author's, since no fit knows them. Its kind and the
generated sentence come from the fit, and that is what G15 checks the author's words
against. `{{results.model.<key>.kind}}` binds the kind, and `{{table.model_<key>}}` places the
table: the outcome and each variable with the kind it was declared, how it entered, and its
levels with the reference marked. A table the toolkit made from facts is not held to the
rule for typed cells, and is placed or reported like any emitted table.

**What G15 settles.** The comparisons a reader would make if they had the card in front of
them: the outcome is a kind the model is for (a binary outcome under a linear model fails);
each variable entered as the kind it was declared (a nominal code entered as one slope
fails, an ordinal one entered as a trend is a warning); the reference and levels the fit
used are the declared ones; every variable a model reads was declared; the fit converged
and no level of a categorical term is without events; rows dropped for missing values are
stated in the manuscript. Few events for each coefficient is a warning, at ten, Peduzzi's
rule, which the literature has argued over since. The kind of a model the analysis fitted, typed in
the Methods, fails as a typed parameter does, since it is the copy left behind when the model
changes; a kind it did not fit is a warning. Both are read in the prose G14 reads, in any
case, across a hyphen or a line break, and in the plural, and not in a heading, which names
the analysis it heads.

**A longer name is another model.** "Conditional logistic regression" holds the words
"logistic regression" and is not one: no `glm` fits it. Read as the fitted kind it failed,
and the hint offered a binding that misnamed the model. `data/models.yaml` therefore lists
the words that, directly before a name, make it the name of another model (conditional,
multinomial, ordinal, mixed-effects, penalised, Bayesian, zero-inflated, generalised and
their kin), and after one the name is not read at all, as the fitted kind or as a model
that was not fitted. The words that leave the fit what it is are kept off the list on
purpose: "multivariable", "adjusted", "crude", "weighted", and "modified" and "robust"
too, since a Poisson regression with a robust variance is the same fit and "modified
{{results.model.<key>.kind}}" is what to write. A list was chosen over a rule because no
rule knows which adjective changes a model; it is a judgement, and it is kept in the data
file where it can be corrected.

**What it leaves to people.** Whether the adjustment set is the right one, whether an
assumption holds, whether the model answers the question. `manuscript-guard models` prints
each card for that reading: the author's name and description beside the kind and the
generated sentence, and the table of variables. Once a co-author page can carry items, the
card is the item, and its digest covers both descriptions.

**The unit of analysis is declared, and counted from the fit.** A model fitted on several
rows per patient, a visit each, with ordinary standard errors is one of the commonest
statistical errors in clinical papers: every interval is too narrow, and nothing in the
numbers shows it. `em.model(..., unit="patient_id")` names the column of the data whose
values the rows belong to, in both emitters, and the card records how many units the rows
used hold, beside the fit's covariance type: statsmodels' `cov_type`, and "model-based" for
an R `lm` or `glm`, whose fit keeps no sandwich estimate. G15 warns
(`unit-rows-independent`) where there are more rows than units and the fit is neither
cluster-robust (`cluster`, or a HAC by group or panel) nor a mixed model or estimating
equations. The R emitter finds the data in the fit (`glm`) or where the call names it
(`lm`), and leaves out the rows the fit dropped.

**Two models compared are fitted on the same rows.** A crude and an adjusted estimate are
set side by side to say what the adjustment did, and a covariate's missing values drop rows
from the adjusted model only: the change between the two is then partly the rows'. Equal
counts can hide different rows, so each card records a digest of the labels of the rows
its fit used (`rows_sha256`: pandas' index, R's row names). G15 warns
(`models-on-different-rows`) where two models of one outcome, one's terms a strict subset
of the other's, were fitted on different rows. One outcome is the same variables written
the same way, spaces aside: `I(score > 5)` and `I(score > 10)` are two. The same terms on
different rows are a subgroup, by design, and are left alone.

**A Poisson regression of a binary outcome has a robust variance.** Poisson regression of a
binary outcome estimates a risk ratio, and its model-based variance overstates the error;
a sandwich variance corrects it (Zou, Am J Epidemiol 2004;159:702-6). G15 warns
(`poisson-binary-variance`) on a Poisson model of an outcome declared binary, or of a
comparison written in the formula, whose card records model-based standard errors. A fit
with an offset or an exposure is left alone: events over person-time estimate a rate ratio,
and that model's own variance is the right one. Each emitter records the offset on the card,
in the formula or given beside it, where it differs between rows: a constant one, nought or
the log of one person-time for all, is the intercept's and makes no rate.

## A step of the code and the text that points at it

The ledger of G9 records that a person read the Methods against the analysis, file by file.
A file is a coarse thing to have read. A comment edited in it asks for the whole Methods to be
read again, and the report cannot say which paragraph describes the code that changed.

So the reading can be kept pair by pair. The analysis marks a step of its code, in either
language:

```python
with em.step("ci"):                          # R: em$step("ci", { ... })
    se = math.sqrt(1 / a + 1 / b + 1 / c + 1 / d)
    low = math.exp(math.log(ror) - z * se)
```

The Methods end the text that describes it with `{{method.ci}}`, an anchor that prints nothing,
in the document or the annotated copy, from `render`, or to a review panel. Its line stays,
so a line that holds nothing but anchors and spaces prints as an empty line, and an empty line
ends a paragraph. Inside a paragraph, with one sentence to a line and an anchor on the line
under its sentence, the document then breaks the paragraph in two where the source has one.
`check` warns of each such line (`method-anchor-line`): one with a line of the paragraph above
it and, below it, a line that is neither blank nor another such line. Lines of anchors one
under the other are one run, warned of once at its first line, where the paragraph ends; so
anchors one to a line at the end of a paragraph, above a blank line, are not warned of. As
first written the rule looked only at the line directly below, and warned of `{{method.a}}`
over `{{method.b}}` at the end of a paragraph, which ends nothing. The line was printed as no line for a while, and that turned a list
or a table written directly under the anchors into running text, with nothing reported. What
stands under the line cannot say whether the author meant a new block or the same paragraph,
so the printing is left as it was and the author is told. A property holds that the lines
warned of are exactly those after which pandoc reads a new paragraph that the source does not
have.

**What an anchor claims.** The text before it, back to the anchor before it or the start of
its paragraph. A blank line or a heading starts a paragraph, and a comment on a line of its own
does not. Anchors side by side claim the same text, for a sentence that describes two steps.
An anchor on a heading's own line is in no paragraph, so it claims nothing and nothing judges
it (Known gaps).
The extent is where the author put the anchors. A rule that found the sentence an anchor ends
would have to know where sentences end, after "e.g." and "et al." and a number, and a pandoc
span around the claim would make every Methods paragraph harder to read in the source. An
anchor that opens its paragraph claims nothing and fails.

**What a step records.** The lines of its block and a digest of its code read as code: the
Python AST without positions, docstrings or the type of each string, and R's `deparse`, so a
comment, a blank line or a re-wrapped call changes nothing. Functions the step calls that the
analysis defined itself are followed, through the functions they call, and are part of the
digest; a package's function is not. A step that never runs, in a branch the run did not take,
is not recorded. The Python digest is not `ast.dump`, which writes the same tree differently
from one Python to the next.

**What the lock records.** Each step and the claim pointing at it, as a pair: the step's name,
the claim as written with its spaces read as one, the digest of the code, and the day it was
read. `methods --reconcile` records every pair and every file; `methods --reconcile ci` only
the pairs of `ci`, leaving the files and the other pairs as they were, since nobody read those.

Either may come first. A lock that records a pair is a lock for the pairs, whether or not it
records a file, wherever the analysis folder holds a file G9 reads: after
`methods --reconcile ci` in a project nobody has reconciled, the pair of `ci` is held to its
code and its text, every other pair is one never read, and `methods-never-reconciled` goes
on saying, once, that the files were never read against the Methods. Where the analysis
folder holds none, as with steps marked in scripts outside `analysis/`, `check` holds no
pair to the lock and says nothing of a step that changed, while `methods --explain` reports
each pair as it stands whenever the lock records one. A lock of pairs alone written now has
no `reconciled_on`, which is the day the files were read; each pair has its own `read_on`.
One written by 0.2.436 keeps the day it recorded, and a later `methods --reconcile <step>`
keeps it too. No gate reads that day. As first released, a lock counted only once it
recorded the files, so the step read first could change with nothing reported but that
warning.

**What is checked.**

- An anchor in a paragraph that names no step the run recorded fails, at every stage. A
  sensitivity analysis described in the Methods and left in a branch no run takes is found
  this way.
- From `internal-review`, a pair fails when its step's code changed since it was read, when its
  text changed (the finding says what it was), or when it was never read. A second text
  pointing at a step is a pair never read, not the first one changed.
- A step no text points at is a warning.
- A line of nothing but anchors inside a paragraph is a warning at every stage,
  `method-anchor-line`: the document ends the paragraph there.
- A Methods paragraph that points at no step, in the main text's Methods or the
  supplement's, is counted, and listed by `manuscript-guard methods --explain`, not reported
  as a finding. A paragraph on ethics
  approval or on the data source has no step to point at, and a warning nobody can clear is
  one that gets ignored.

`methods --explain` prints every claim with the lines of the step that backs it and how the
pair stands, then the open paragraphs, then the steps nothing describes. That is what a person
reads to check the Methods against the code. Whether the text describes the code correctly is
still theirs to say: an anchor shows that someone pointed a sentence at some code. `checker
build` puts the same claims and open paragraphs to the co-authors, each beside its code
("The Methods against the code").

**In Word.** An anchor prints nothing, so a co-author never sees it. The round trip does not
place it by Word's words. Anchors that end their paragraph are set aside before the paragraph
is aligned and put back after it, so a rewording in Word comes back with them. An edit to a
paragraph with an anchor anywhere else is refused, with the reason, since Word's text cannot
say where the anchor goes in the new wording.

**In the example**, reading each pair turned up the ambiguity a review round had already named:
the signal criterion spoke of "a lower bound of the confidence interval" where the analysis
computes two intervals and uses the 95% one. The text now says which.

## A rewording is held to the words

A language pass is trusted with the words: a co-author tidying a paragraph, an editing
service, a model asked to make the English read well. `check` cannot say whether it kept to
them, because `check` reads the manuscript as it is. An edit that writes
`{{results.ror.ci_low}}` where `{{results.ror.ci_high}}` stood leaves two bindings that
resolve. One that drops a citation leaves a sentence. One that retypes "90% CI" as "95% CI"
leaves a number the conventions know. Every gate passes all three.

`manuscript-guard reworded` compares the text with what it was and holds three things to
their places: every binding, every citation key and every typed number. It is a command and
no gate, because a gate has one text and this needs two. Basile chose its four terms on
2026-10-08.

**The text before is a commit's, or a copy.** By default each manuscript file is compared
with itself at the last commit, which is where an edit not yet committed is seen; `--since`
names another revision, and `--before` a copy of one file, for a text that is not in git. A
file that is new or gone since the commit is reported with the count of the facts that came
or went with it.

**Gone, new or changed fails; another order warns.** A fact that stood and does not, or
stands and did not, is either more than a rewording or a slip, and whoever reads the edit
should know which. The same facts in another order are a clause moved to the front of its
sentence, which is harmless, or two values that changed places, which is not. Nothing here
can tell those apart, so each place is shown and the command passes. G2 reports two bounds
that changed places where they were emitted as one interval; two counts in a sentence it
cannot know apart.

**A number is compared as typed.** "3" spelt out as "three", "1,200" closed up to "1200"
and "0.50" cut to "0.5" are each reported. The first two may be style and the third is not,
and a rule that guessed would have to read "one" as a number or as a pronoun. What an edit
does to the notation around a number is free: the space before a unit or a per cent sign,
the spaces around a sign of comparison, a hyphen made a true minus sign. So the edits that
tidy a manuscript's notation pass.

**A minus sign fails where it is sure, and is shown where it is not.** "-0.3" made "0.3" is
a number changed, and "1.2-3.4" made "1.2 to 3.4" is a range retyped. Which of the two a
dash is, is known by what stands before it, and only sometimes. After a space, an opening
bracket, a comma or a sign of comparison nothing stands that it could join: it is the
number's sign, and one that is gone or new fails. After a letter, a figure, a closing
bracket, a per cent sign or a bound value it joins, and is no sign. After a mark that can
open or close, an asterisk, an underscore, a dollar, a caret, a tilde, a quotation mark, it
is a sign where the mark opens and may be the dash of a range where it closes: "*-0.3*"
and "*n*-1", "10^-5^" and "10^3^-10^5^". And a mark that looks as if it closes may be a
product or a power, "x*-1".

Two reviews read that last case by rule and found the rule wrong each time. The first rule
took every such mark to open, and refused a range made "to" after one. The second took a
mark after a letter or a figure to close, and let the sign of "10**-6" go with nothing
said. It also read the sign of an exponent after "e", and so refused "Figures 1E-1G" made
"1E to 1G". Shown this, Basile chose on 2026-10-08 what the order already does: where it
is sure it fails, and where it is not the place is shown and the command passes. A mark
that can only open leaves the sign sure: one whose run stands at the start or after
something that does not join, or the first caret of its word. After any other, after a
figure and "e", and after a figure and one space or a line end, a dash that came or went
is a warning. A dash that stands as it stood and is read as a sure sign in one text and
as perhaps one in the other, "x*-1" made "x * -1", is no change.

The third review found what was concluded from this wrong where a number stands in
several places. All of it is from counts, and three things had to be counted apart. A
dash that may be a sign and stood before the edit is itself: counted among the dashes
now, the `*n*-1` of a later paragraph answered for a slope of -1 made 1, which only
warned. Only a dash that may be a sign and is new can be the sure one in another place.
The places count too: "fell by -0.3 and rose by 0.3" made "fell by 0.3 and rose by
-0.3" has the same figures and as many dashes, and with the sign no part of what is
compared nothing was said of it. Two signs that changed places and two clauses that did
look the same, so it is the order's case and a warning, `sign-moved`. And a number is
named with its sign only where the other text holds none of it.

The fourth review found the counts wrong the other way. Two edits of notation on the
same figures, `x*-1` spaced out to `x * -1` and "n-1" made `*n*-1`, each pass by
themselves, and together have the counts of a sign that came: one sure sign more, and
no fewer dashes that may be one. So where a number stands as often as it did, a sign
fails only if the counts say so and one of the number's places, taken in order, went
from a sure sign to no dash or from no dash to a sure sign. Beside the slope one does;
here none does, and the warning has it.

Two or three hyphens before a number are the dash pandoc prints for them, and are read
as one dash by what stands before the first: "1--3" is a range, and "-5 to -3" made
"-5--3" has lost the sign of the 3. A plus sign is part of the figures where a minus
would be a sure sign, and is not read elsewhere: "0.5, +0.3" made "0.5 +0.3" is told
as one number gone and one new.

A number with no nought keeps its point, ".05", and raised and lowered figures are
figures: the first review found "-.30" read as "30", and ten to the minus eight typed with
the characters made ten to the minus six with nothing said.

**A sign of comparison belongs to its number.** Until 2026-10-14 only the spaces around
one were spoken of, and the sign itself was free with them: "The association was
significant (P < 0.05)" made "(P > 0.05)" was reported as nothing to report, and the sign
says the opposite. Now `<`, `>`, `≤`, `≥` and `≠` before a number or a binding are read
with it, so "P < 0.05" is the fact `<0.05`, and a sign that is gone, new or turned round is
a fact gone and a fact new, which fails, as a changed number does. An `=` is read as what a
number standing alone says: "(OR = 1.52)" made "(OR 1.52)" is a copy-edit and passes, and
"P = 0.04" made "P < 0.04" fails. The spaces around the sign are still free, a space of any
width and one line break, and so is how it is typed:
"<=", "≤" and "⩽" are one sign, and so are the full-width forms and the escape `\<`
that Word's round trip writes. A ">" is no sign where it is the head of an arrow, "5 ->
10", escaped as pandoc writes one, `5 -\> 10`, or in full width; where it ends an HTML tag,
"<sup>2"; or where it marks a block quotation: at the start of its line, after a blank
line, a quoted line or nothing. A ">" that starts a line in the middle of a paragraph is the sign of a sentence
wrapped there, since pandoc opens no quotation without a blank line before it. The sign
before a binding is held as well, because "P < {{results.p}}" made "P > {{results.p}}"
turns the result round as surely as a typed one. "≈" and "~" are not signs of a
comparison and are left as they were.

**It is read once, with a count.** Whether a fact is gone or new is known from how often it
stands in each text. Where the order changed is known from a count of what one text has had
that the other has not: each stretch ends where the count is settled, so two clauses moved
in two sentences are two warnings. Lining the texts up fact by fact, as `difflib` does,
takes the square of a manuscript's length on a text where one number stands on every line.

The readings of a binding and of a citation are the gates' own: `placeholders.PLACEHOLDER`
with what pandoc drops blanked, and `find_citations`. A test holds the bindings to the ones
`placeholders.parse` calls well formed, which this does not call. When this was written
`parse` counted each binding's line from the top of the file, and a comparison of two long
texts showed it; #213 has since put that right.

## A rewording keeps what a sentence claims

Holding an edit to its facts leaves the words free, and some words carry the claim. "Use was
associated with a higher risk" made "use increased the risk" keeps every binding and
citation and claims an effect where the analysis showed an association. A "may" dropped
makes a possibility a finding, and a "did not" dropped turns the result round. A language
pass by a model does each of these as it smooths a sentence, and an AI reviewer's suggested
edit (#367) can do it too.

So `reworded` compares each sentence the edit changed with what it was, for the words that
set how strongly it claims, and warns where they moved. The words are in
`src/manuscript_guard/data/claim_strength.yaml`. The idea and the ladder are adapted from
the Claim-Strength Contract of Yila-AI/awesome-research-skills (Apache-2.0, credited in
ATTRIBUTION.md), which asks that a draft never move a claim silently in either direction.
There are four kinds of word:

- a **hedge**, "may", "might", "appears": one gone makes the claim stronger, one new
  weaker;
- a **limit**, "only", "in this sample", "under these conditions": the same;
- a **negation**, "not", "no", "never", "non-significant": one gone or new turns the claim
  round, whatever else moved, and is told as that;
- a word of the **ladder**, whose rungs run from consistency ("consistent with",
  "suggests") through association, prediction, contribution and effect ("increased",
  "led to") to causation ("caused", "demonstrated that"). A word moved up makes the claim
  stronger, down weaker, and within a rung it is free: "associated" made "linked to".

Basile chose the four terms on 2026-10-20.

**A move is a warning, and the command passes.** A list of words cannot know whether the
author meant the move, and a reviewer who asked for "associated" where the text said
"caused" meant it. A warning needs no acknowledging: the author reads it, and the next
commit makes the edit the text before. The codes are `claim-stronger`, `claim-weaker`,
`claim-moved` (moves both ways, or ladder words changed with no direction to tell) and
`claim-negation`, collected as `reworded.CLAIM_CODES`.

**Only the sentences the edit changed are read.** A causal verb that stood before the edit
passes, in an observational paper as anywhere. Reading the whole text against the design
`study_type` declares would be another gate, with more false alarms, and is not built.

**The words are a list, in English.** Each is read as a whole word, in the forms listed and
no others, in lower case or with a capital where it opens its sentence; "may" in lower case
only, since "May" is a month. A word joined by a hyphen to the one before or after is part
of a compound and is not read, "drug-induced", "cause-specific"; nor is a form in "-ed" after
"a", "an" or "the", "an increased risk", which is an adjective. What `mask` blanks is not read,
and inline code is blanked too.

**A suggested edit that moves a claim is written, and says so.** A review panel's suggested
edit (#367) is dropped where `reworded` finds anything to say of it. Basile chose on
2026-10-20 that a claim's warning be the one exception: the edit is written as a tracked
change, and its comment in Word carries the warning, so that the author sees the move where
they decide it. `CLAIM_CODES` is how the edits tell the two kinds of finding apart.

**Hedges, limits and negations are counted; the ladder by its rungs.** "May" made "might"
is the same count of hedges and no change. Where ladder words left some rungs and came to
others, the move is up when every rung that came is above every rung that left, and down the
other way, and otherwise it cannot be told. Where words only left or only came, the
sentence is read by its lowest rung, which is its claim where one word of the ladder holds
another: "associated with increased mortality" claims an association, and made "increased
mortality" it claims an effect. A sentence with no word of the ladder states, and a word of
consistency makes it claim less than that.

**The sentences are lined up as patience diff does.** Each text is cut into sentences at a
stop and a space before anything but a lower-case letter, at a blank line, at a line that
opens a block, and at each line of the front matter. A sentence's key is its words with
every run of spaces and blanked text made one, so rewrapping changes nothing. Those that
stand once in each text are lined up first, the longest run of them in order, in n log n:
the time stays linear in the manuscript, as the facts' comparison does. Between two of them
lies what the edit changed, its ends that stand in both taken off. Where a stretch has as
many sentences before as after, they are compared one by one; where it has not, a sentence
was split or joined and the stretch is compared whole. Where it has none on one side, a
sentence was added or deleted whole, and nothing is compared: that is no rewording of a
sentence, and its facts are held by the facts' comparison. A finding is placed on the
sentence that holds a word that came, or on the stretch's first sentence where words only
left.

## Review panels: the record is the contract

Every other gate checks a property of the text. G11 checks that somebody competent
disagreed with it, or failed to, on the record.

The unit is a **review record**, not an agent. A model can produce one in minutes, a
co-author can write one by hand, and the gate treats them identically — which is what keeps
the toolkit usable by someone who has never run an agent. Agents are one way to fill the
records, not the mechanism.

Two choices carry most of the value:

**The panel is written down, with reasons.** A panel's composition decides what it can see;
three methodologists will not notice that the clinical framing is wrong. Recording who was
asked and why makes the gaps visible while there is still time to fill them. Composition is
derived per paper from the design, the reporting guideline and the target journal.

**The second panel is blinded by default.** A second round that reads the first round's
findings inherits its sense of what matters, and the errors worth catching in round two are
exactly the ones round one was not looking for. An unblinded later round warns.

**Severity depends on what is being built.** An author mid-draft must be able to produce a
document to read, so ordinary builds warn. `--submission` raises every review warning to a
failure: the version that goes to a journal should not carry unanswered major findings.
That flag is the only place in the toolkit where a gate's severity is contextual, and it
exists because the alternative — blocking every build on a complete two-round review — would
make the gate something to switch off.

**An override is a legitimate answer.** A major finding needs a resolution saying what was
done, or an `overridden` saying why it was not. Recording the reason turns it from an
oversight into a decision, and it is the thing you want when a real reviewer asks the same
question. Silence is the only unacceptable answer.

**What a reader wrote is sealed.** Answering a finding is the author's edit; what the reader
wrote is not. Until 2026-10-14 nothing held that line: the header of a filed reading said
"Nothing else here is yours to edit", and turning a `major` into `minor`, rewording a finding
or deleting it made it stop binding, with nothing in `check` to say so. A reading now carries
`reading_sha256`, a digest over the verdict, the summary, the rejection tests and each
finding's `id`, `severity`, `where` and `finding`, and its `ask` where it has one,
serialised as a co-author item is. The
answers (`resolution`, `resolved_on`, `overridden`) are not in it, and neither is
`file_sha256`, which the review-panel skill tells a reader to trim to the files they read.
G11 computes it again and reports `reading-altered` where it differs, as it reports the rest
of a round: a warning while drafting, a failure at submission. `review --run` seals each
reading it files. A record started by `review --record` has no findings yet when it is
written, so `review --seal <reviewer> --round <n>` seals it once they are typed in: it adds
the one line at the end and changes nothing else in the file, and it will not seal a reading
twice. A reading with a major finding and no seal, and any reading `review --run` filed
without one, is `reading-unsealed`, a warning and never more, because every record written
before 2026-10-14 is unsealed. The author chose the sealing step over writing the hand-filed
case down as a gap. The example's thirteen records were sealed with the command when it was
added.

Editing the manuscript marks the reviews stale, which is correct: a review of the old
Results is not a review of the new ones. **What it marks stale is scoped to what each
reviewer read.** The first version hashed every byte of every manuscript file together, so
fixing a typo in the Discussion voided both completed rounds, including the
biostatistician's read of the Methods — and since `review-stale` is a hard failure at
submission, the harshest check in the toolkit fired at the moment an author is copy-editing.
A record may now carry `file_sha256`, the files it actually read, from `manuscript-guard
review --files`; it goes stale when one of those moves, and the finding names the file. A
record without the key means the whole manuscript, so older records keep the behaviour their
writer intended.

That scoping is only honest because of its companion, `review-uncovered`: a round is
incomplete while some manuscript file is on nobody's list. Without it, trimming the map
would have been a way to review the Methods and pass — the same fix-opens-the-next-hole
pattern that three review rounds kept finding, so the two landed together.

**A revision is answered by a further round, which supersedes the rounds before it.**
`review --record` will not re-stamp a record, because the digest is the only thing
separating "somebody read this version" from "somebody read a version", and it tells the
author to record the new reading as a further round instead. Until 2026-09-24 that advice
led nowhere: the earlier records stayed `review-stale`, and a file added in revision left
every earlier round `review-uncovered`, so `check --submission` could pass only after
somebody hand-edited a digest or deleted a round. Now, once a later round is complete and
current, each earlier round that is stale or uncovered is reported as `review-superseded`,
an INFO naming the round that superseded it. It still counts towards `rounds_required`,
because it was a complete reading of the paper it read, and its unanswered major findings
still fail the submission: history is not absolution. A round that never finished is not
rescued, since a missing record is a remit nobody answered, whenever that was. The author
chose this over the alternatives: re-reading every round after every change (the strongest
guarantee, and the one most likely to be switched off), superseding only across a journal's
revision round (which left copy-edits before the first submission at the same dead end), and
no change.

**A remit can be read by several readers.** One reviewer had one record a round, so a remit
could be read once. A panel read by models from several providers has several readings of
each remit, and a co-author may read a remit a model also read. Each reading is a record of
its own, `review/round-N/<reviewer>.<reader>.yaml`, beside the plain `<reviewer>.yaml`; a
reviewer's id cannot hold a dot, so the first dot ends it. The record says the same `reader`
inside. Nothing is merged into one file, because a record several writers append to is a
record that can be re-stamped.

**The panel says who reads, and is held to it.** A reviewer's entry lists the `readers`
asked to read the remit, and G11 wants a reading from every one of them: `reading-missing`
leaves the round unfinished. With every model reading every remit, one provider failing
must not leave a round that looks complete, and this is what lets the readings that did
arrive be filed: the round is visibly incomplete until the missing reader reports or is
taken out of the panel, which is a decision somebody made and the file records. The author
chose this over two alternatives. Counting a remit as read once anybody had read it passes
a round two of three models answered. Filing nothing unless every call succeeded throws
away replies already paid for. A panel that names no readers needs one reading, the
reviewer's plain record, which is how every round written before this is read; the
example's two rounds give the same findings as they did, which is none. What is new for
them is a count of readings in the report and the list of who read what in
`manuscript-guard review`.

**And only the readers the panel names are read.** A file `<reviewer>.<reader>.yaml` is a
reading if the panel lists that reader for that reviewer, and nothing else beside a record
is one. `review --record <reviewer> --reading <reader>` lists the reader when it files the
reading, the way `--record` puts a reviewer on the panel. The first two versions of this
decided from a file's contents whether it was a reading, and two review rounds each found
one that dropped out of a round without a failure. A reading whose author answered a
finding with `resolution: Fixed: it now says reporting`, which is not YAML, was taken for a
note: a warning, and its other major finding stopped binding. With that fixed by looking
for a `reader:` line, one saved again in UTF-16 was taken for a note, and so was one with
the key quoted. In the other direction, a note in another code page that the gate had no
business opening took it down. The author chose to stop guessing over two alternatives:
patching each shape as it was found, and treating every such file as a reading, which
would have failed a submission over a copy kept in the round. So:

- A file under a name the panel asks for is that reader's reading, whatever it holds. It
  must parse (`reading-unreadable` if not, a failure at every stage like any malformed
  record), fit the schema, and say inside the reader, the reviewer and the round its place
  says (`reading-misfiled`). Until it does, the round is unfinished.
- Any other file beside a record is not opened. It is reported as `reading-unnamed`, a
  warning at every stage, with how to make it count. `biostatistician.old.yaml`, a note in
  UTF-16, a folder: none can fail a submission or take the gate down, as none could before
  readings had names.
- The reviewer's plain record is the reading nobody named, and answers for no named reader
  whatever it says inside.

The cost is the one case the warning is for: a reading put beside a record by hand, with
its reader not in the panel, is not counted until somebody adds the reader.

**A reader is known by the name that names its file.** A reader's name becomes part of a
file name with its letters, digits and the marks that belong to them kept, in any script,
lower-cased and composed, and every run of anything else as one hyphen. That form is how
the gate recognises a reader, so the panel's `Dr. Tanaka` and a reading filed as
`Dr Tanaka` are one reader; matched letter for letter, the gate asked for a file that
existed and `review --record` refused to write it. The marks are kept because in scripts
that write a vowel as a mark on its consonant two names can differ in nothing else, and
with them dropped Reena and Raina were one file. The name is composed because some file
systems store an accented letter as the letter and its mark, and the same reader has to be
the same file wherever the project is checked out. Two readers of one remit whose names
still make one file name are `duplicate-reader`: one file cannot hold two readings. A name
with no letter or digit names no file, and is refused where it is typed and reported where
a panel holds one.

**Any reader can raise a finding, and nobody's reading answers another's.** Every reading
is judged as a record always was: stale when a file it read changes, counted for coverage,
and each unanswered major finding blocks a submission, with the reader who raised it named.
The gate does not match similar findings across readers. Two models saying the same thing
in different words are two findings to answer, and deciding they are one is a judgement the
author makes in the resolution.

**The strictest verdict is reported and decides nothing.** `manuscript-guard review` lists
who read each remit, what each concluded and the round's strictest verdict. G11 has never
decided anything on a verdict, and still does not: a record cannot be re-stamped, so a
verdict could be cleared only by a further round, and what an author can act on is a
finding.

**What a model's reading may keep.** A record may carry `provenance`: the provider, the
model as asked for and as the provider named it, the host, the SHA-256 of the request body,
the provider's response identifier, how the reply ended, the token counts and the version
of this tool. The schema refuses any other field there, so nothing has a place to put a
key, a header or the prompt's text. What goes into the fields the provider words (its name
for the model, its response identifier, its reason for stopping) is for whatever writes the
record to clean. `rejection_tests` records what the reader decided would have to be true
to reject, and what the manuscript showed. The gate reads neither.

The worked example carries a real two-round panel. Round one found that the paper had no
case definition, no mention of duplicate records, and no contingency table for a result that
was a single ratio; all three were fixed, and the manuscript is better for it. Round two,
blinded and differently composed, found the remaining soft spots. Two findings are recorded
as deliberate overrides rather than fixed, because the honest answer was that the synthetic
data do not support what the reviewer wanted.

## What a panel did not see, and what it asks for

Three things about a reading were known to the tool and said by nothing. A round read only
by one provider's models has one family's blind spots, which `panel/__init__.py` names as the
reason for several providers: G11 warns (`round-one-provider`) where every reading of a round
came from one provider, and says nothing where a person read any of it. A model is never sent
the figures, so a model that passed a remit covering them passed what it did not see: G11
warns (`figures-not-seen`) where a model's reading passed a remit whose words name figures,
plots, graphs or charts. Both are warnings at every stage, as a new rule starts.

And a finding may say what it asks of the authors (`ask`): a disclosure of what they have, a
computation of a new number, or new data. A computation is a new emitted result and a new
reconciliation of the Methods with the code, so the prompt asks a reader to say why the
numbers and tables already reported cannot answer it, and an open major finding that asks
for one says so. The ask is the reader's, and sealed with the reading where it is given:
only there, so that every record sealed before findings could ask keeps its seal.

## A reading may suggest the wording, and the author decides it in Word

Basile asked on 2026-10-20 whether the panel's readers could make their changes the way a
co-author does, as Word tracked changes the author accepts or refuses. They can, for prose,
and only where the change is placed exactly. Four terms were his, chosen that day from the
recommendations put to him: the edit is found by its words and not by a paragraph's
identifier, every model reading is offered edits, the command is `review --suggestions`, and
a refused edit is answered only by a reply in Word.

**An edit belongs to a finding, and is the reader's.** A finding may carry `edits`, each the
manuscript's words as they stand (`old`) and the words to put in their place (`new`), and
ten at most are written from a reading. The reply schema takes them, null and an empty list
read as left out, as null is for `where` and `ask`. They are optional, so a reply is not
refused for one that cannot be placed: one that is empty, or past the ten, is dropped when
the document is made, and said to be (round 1 of #367 found the empty list, which the prompt
invites, refusing the whole paid reading). A design round's reader is not offered them,
and a design reply that carries some is refused, since what it read was the plan. They are
sealed with the reading where a finding has them (`SEALED_WHERE_GIVEN`), so every record
sealed before edits existed keeps its seal, and an edit changed after filing is
`reading-altered`: Word shows it under the reader's name. A reading written by hand or by an
agent in the session carries them the same way, before `review --seal`.

**The words say where, and only once.** A model is sent the manuscript as the build prints
it, with no identifiers, so an edit cannot name a paragraph; it names its words. They have
to be found exactly once in the manuscript's prose, front matter and comments left out,
inside one paragraph that carries an identifier, and exactly once in that paragraph as the
build printed it. Pandoc's typesetting is read as what it is, a straight quote finding a
curly one and `--` an en dash, and a space a line break or a no-break space; the words are
whole words, so "the" is not found in "other". Words found twice are not placed by choosing
one: the reader is told to quote more of them. A generated property holds the finding to
every run of words, typed and printed (`test_an_edit_s_words_are_found_where_they_stand_typed_or_printed_and_nowhere_else`).

**Prose only, by the rule `reworded` applies.** An edit holds no character Markdown reads as
markup, so it can open no binding, citation, emphasis or link; its words lie inside no
binding, citation, code, link, footnote or other inline construct; and the paragraph before
and after it gives `reworded.compare` nothing to say of a binding, a citation or a typed
number. An edit that changes "2 x 2" to "3 x 2" is a finding, not a tracked change.

**What is accepted is written where its words were, or is not offered.** `import` merges a
rewording from Word by rebuilding each edited stretch between two values or citations from
Word's text, which holds no markup: emphasis, code or a link in that stretch is flattened,
or the paragraph refused. An accepted suggestion is not merged so. Its words are known, from
the sealed record, and so is where they were found, so `import` writes the new words there
and touches nothing else (`suggestions.write_in`); see "An accepted suggestion is written,
then the rest is merged" below. `review --suggestions` offers an edit only where that write
holds: written into the source, the paragraph reads as Word shows it with the edit accepted
(`roundtrip._reads_as`, the reading the merge holds its own result to), and the file still
marks it as a paragraph of its own under its identifier (`_stays_marked`, by `tag`'s own
reading of blocks). Two edits of the same words are both dropped; one that would not hold
with the edits before it in its paragraph written too is dropped. Each dropped edit is listed
with its reason and stays a finding.

**The document is the build, with the changes in it.** `review --suggestions --round N` builds
the document offline, as `build --offline` does, into `build/suggestions/round-N.docx` (and
`round-N-supplementary.docx` where an edit is in the supplement). Not into `build/` itself:
`check` holds every document there to the source, and this one is stale the moment an
accepted edit is imported. The build's own record of what it printed is written as every
build's is, and the document names it, so `import` reads it as exactly as the document a
co-author is sent. `tracked.write` then makes each edit in the runs pandoc wrote: the old words
moved into `w:del`, the new ones in a `w:ins` with the first old run's formatting, both under
the reader's name, a comment over them holding the finding, and a bookmark `mg-s-<n>` around
them. Only runs that hold nothing but text are edited: never inside a field, a link or a
symbol, nor across a bookmark the build placed. The file is kept only if, read with every
change rejected, it is the build character for character, and read with every change
accepted, it is the build with each edit made.

What the document records of its suggestions is in its properties, split as the paragraph
record is: each suggestion's number, round, reviewer, reader, finding and author, and
digests of its old words, its new words and its comment. Never the words: a document's
properties stay with it through everything an author deletes before sending it on.

**Word 16, as seen over COM on 2026-10-20.** Each change appears as a revision by the reader's
name, accepted or rejected one at a time or with Accept All and Reject All. The bookmark and
the comment stay through either, around what is left: the new words once accepted, the old
once rejected. Accepting the deletion and rejecting the insertion leaves nothing inside the
bookmark, and Word removes the bookmark, the comment and its mark. A reply is a comment of
its own over the same words, which `word/commentsExtended.xml` ties to the comment it
answers (`w15:paraIdParent`), under the name Word has for the person replying. Word merges
runs and renumbers comments when it saves; nothing here reads either.

**`import` refuses an undecided suggestion, and answers what was decided.** It reads every
tracked change as accepted, and read so, a suggestion nobody looked at would merge. So a
document that records suggestions is refused, with nothing written, while it holds a change
under one of their authors. Changes by anybody else are read as they always were. Once all
are decided, the text inside each bookmark is the new words (accepted), the old (refused),
other words (typed in after deciding), or the bookmark is gone. The panel's own comments are
its findings, already in the records, and are not listed as a co-author's; nor are the
replies to them, which are said with the suggestions. With `--apply`, each finding is
answered in its record (`record.answer_finding`, which adds the lines after the finding's
last and changes nothing else in the file):

- an accepted edit is the finding's `resolution`, dated, naming the words, once `import` has
  merged its paragraph with the new words in it; refused beside it in the same finding, the
  other edits are named as refused;
- a finding whose edits were all refused is `overridden` by the author's reply in Word,
  `overridden_by` the reply's author, and with no reply it stays open: turning down a
  wording does not answer what the finding says, and G11 asks for a reason;
- a finding with an edit changed in Word or gone, one answered already, or one whose record
  no longer holds the edit the document was made from or no longer reads as sealed, is left
  to the author, with the reason.

The answers are outside the seal, so the reading stays sealed.

## An accepted suggestion is written, then the rest is merged

The first version offered an edit only where `import`'s merge would bring it back exactly,
and that merge rebuilds an edited stretch from Word's text. So an edit in a stretch that
also held emphasis, code or a link was dropped: in a Results paragraph with an italic *P*,
or an Introduction paragraph with no value in it and *E. coli* anywhere, that was every
edit. Basile chose on 2026-10-20, from the options put to him, how an accepted suggestion
and the author's own edits in the same paragraph come back together, and that an edit
inside emphasis is offered.

**The suggestion first, exactly.** For each paragraph holding a suggestion the author
accepted (its bookmark `mg-s-<n>` holds the new words, `tracked.decided`), `import` takes the
words from the sealed record, held to the document's digests of the new words and the
comment, as the answer to the finding is. It finds the old words once in the paragraph's
source and once in what the build printed, and the printed ones are the ones the document
recorded a digest of. They lie outside every binding, citation and inline construct, and
across no hard line break, which writing them would delete. The new words go into the
source there, and into the printed text, and each value's place in that is moved along by
the difference. Written, the paragraph has to be a change of words to `reworded` and read as
Word shows it. Emphasis beside the words stays as the source has it, and emphasis around
them goes round the new words: Word gives an insertion the formatting of the run it
replaces, so the author saw them so when accepting.

**Then the rest, by the usual rules.** Whatever else the author changed in that paragraph is
merged by `roundtrip.align` against the source and the printed text with the suggestions
already in them (`merge.plan_import`, `accepted`). A stretch the author left alone is kept
from that source, markup and all, as for any rewording; a stretch the author edited is
rebuilt from Word's text, as for any rewording. So the suggestion never costs markup, and the
author's own edits cost what they cost on main. Where the author changed nothing else, the
merge gives back the written source exactly. Every check `import` makes of a merge is made of
this one too, the identifier test of `_identified` among them.

**Where the words cannot be written, the paragraph is refused.** Old words no longer found
once (the source changed since the document was made, imported with `--force`), printed
words that are not the document's (the record's old words changed and sealed again), a
record that is gone, values and citations with no place (the marked build could not be
read), or a write that would not read as Word shows it: the whole paragraph is
refused, with the reason, and the finding stays open. Merging it from Word's text instead
would be the merge this design exists to avoid, and could flatten the markup the edit was
offered beside. A suggestion refused in Word, or whose bookmark holds other words, writes
nothing: Word's text there is merged as the author's own, and the finding is left to them as
before.

Considered and not built: refusing any paragraph that holds an accepted suggestion and
anything else changed, so that nothing is ever composed. It costs the author's other edits
in that paragraph, which would have to be made again in the .md, and it protects nothing the
composed merge does not: what the author's edit flattens there, it flattens on main.

## A panel read by several providers

The panel existed only as a skill for one agent. A scientist without that agent could not
run it, and a panel drawn from one model shares that model's blind spots. So the reviewers'
remits can be read by models from several providers, listed once in `paper.yaml`:

```yaml
review:
  models: [openai/<model>, mistral/<model>, moonshot/<model>]
```

**This is a layer beside the gates, not a gate.** `src/manuscript_guard/panel/` holds every
provider call, and nothing under `gates/` imports it; a test reads the imports. The gates
still run in CI with no network and no model. A model files a review record, and G11 reads
records as it always has. A model does not decide whether the manuscript is clean.
