**One client, no new dependency.** OpenAI, Mistral, Moonshot (Kimi), DeepSeek, OpenRouter,
Google's Gemini endpoint and a local Ollama all speak the chat API OpenAI defined, and
Anthropic speaks its own. Two request shapes on `urllib` cover all of them, so a preset is
four facts: the base URL, the name of the variable holding the key, the shape, and how the
vendor spells an output cap. Each was read from the vendor's documentation on 2026-10-02 and
a test holds the table. No preset names a model: model names change faster than a release,
and the author supplies them. A provider that is not built in is added under
`review.providers` by its URL. A built-in name cannot be pointed elsewhere, and a provider
that is not built in cannot name a built-in provider's key variable as its own: either
would let a `paper.yaml` somebody else wrote send the reader's key to a host of its
choosing. The address must be one host, a port if it needs one, and a path, in plain
characters; `http://[::1].evil.example` and `http://@localhost` are refused, since what
decides whether a call stays on this machine is the host. The host itself is letters,
digits, dots and hyphens, or a bracketed address, with nothing encoded: urllib decodes a
percent-encoded host before it connects, so `api.openai.com%2e%65%76%69%6c.example` was
shown to the author as written and reached `api.openai.com.evil.example`. The host the
statement names has to be the host that is connected to, and that is now checked as such:
the host shown is compared with the host urllib derives from the address, and no `%` is
taken in it. Listing the shapes that mislead missed one twice; the second was a `%` after
an address in brackets, which reads as a zone id. A host that ends in a number is an
address and must be four numbers with dots, since `2130706433` and `0x7f.1` are each read
by the resolver as an address the text does not show.

**Keys.** A key is read from its environment variable when a call is made and goes into one
request header. It is not in the request body, so the body can be printed and digested. It
is not written to a file, a record or a message: `review --providers` says only whether each
variable is set, and a rejected key gets a message of our own. Anything printed that
somebody else wrote, a provider's error or an exception's text, has every run of four or
more of the key's characters taken out first, because a provider's message for a bad key
can quote its first and last few; the review of the first version found the whole key
printed when it held a line break, inside the message `http.client` gives for a header it
will not send. A key holding a space, a line break or a character outside ASCII is now
refused by its variable's name before it reaches a header, and what an exception says
about a request it would not build is never repeated. `key_env` must look like a
variable's name, upper case, so that a key pasted there is refused rather than committed.
Keys go over https, or to this machine. A redirect is not followed: it would carry the key
and the manuscript to a host nobody agreed to. A request to this machine does not go
through the proxy the environment names, which urllib would otherwise have handed it to.

**The manuscript is unpublished, and sending it to a third party is the author's
decision.** The toolkit cannot know what a provider keeps, for how long, or whether it
trains on it; that is in each provider's terms, and they differ and change. What it can do
is say what would leave the machine before anything does. `review --run --dry-run` builds
every request exactly as a run would, prints which files go to which host and how many
calls that is, writes the bodies under `build/` with a readable copy of their text, and
opens no connection. A model that Ollama runs on this machine is the option that sends
nothing anywhere. The statement used to say "this machine; nothing leaves it" of any
address on this machine, and Ollama's server there also serves Ollama's cloud models, whose
requests it sends to Ollama's servers. A model named as Ollama names those, `-cloud` or
`:cloud`, is now said to leave the machine, and any other model on this machine is said to
stay there unless the server there passes it on, which the address cannot show.

**What a reviewer is sent is a fixed list**: the paper's title, keywords, journal and
guideline from `paper.yaml`; the journal profile and the reporting checklist where the
project has them; every manuscript file; and that reviewer's own role, remit and reason.
Nothing else is sent. That list is how the second panel stays blinded when models run it.
The earlier rounds' records, the other panels and the response to a journal's reviewers are
not on it, so no request can carry them, and a test plants a marker in each and looks. For
the same reason `authors.yaml`, `results/` and the literature sources stay where they are.
`results/` and the ledger are read, for the values the bindings print, and only those
printed values reach a request.

Three entries of that list are named in `paper.yaml`, and the first version joined each
name into a path without looking at where it led. `reporting_guideline:
[../../review/round-1/biostatistician]` put round one's record in every round-two request,
`target_journal: ../../authors` sent `authors.yaml` as the journal profile, and
`paths: {manuscript: .}` made the notes beside the review and the response to the reviewers
into manuscript files. A journal or guideline now has to be a name, and the file it
resolves to, with links followed, has to sit in the project's `profiles/` or the shipped
ones and not under `review/` or `revision/`, which a `profiles/` directory that is itself
a link could otherwise lead to. The manuscript directory may not take in `review/` or
`revision/`, nor sit inside
them, and a manuscript file that is a link to somewhere outside it is refused. A
`paper.yaml` its schema refuses is not planned from at all.

The manuscript is sent as the build prints it. Each binding is replaced by its value and
each table rendered, because a reviewer shown `{{results.ror.point}}` cannot check a
number. Each file's YAML header and every HTML comment are left out, as the build leaves
them out: a comment is where authors are told to keep their notes, and "the round-one
statistician asked for this" is not something to hand a blinded reviewer. The files go in
the order the build prints them, `main.md` first and the supplement last.

**Agreeableness is the failure to design against.** A panel of personas that all approve
has told the author nothing. Each reviewer is told to decide first what would have to be
true, within its remit, for it to recommend rejection, and to check each against the text;
the reply must carry those tests, so a reading that attacked nothing shows.

**A reply is untrusted input.** It is accepted when it is one JSON object that fits the
reply schema, bare or in a single code fence, and refused otherwise. Nothing is repaired:
prose around the object is not trimmed, a truncated object is not closed, a verdict outside
the vocabulary is not mapped to the nearest one. A reply cut short by a token limit is
refused even if it parses, and so is one the provider marks as a refusal. The reply schema
holds only what a reader can know. Who read, when, and which version are filled in by the
tool, and a finding's `resolution` is the author's to write, so a reply carrying one is
refused: it would file a major finding already answered. One thing is read as what it
plainly says: a finding's `where` may be left out, a model that leaves a key out often
writes `null` for it, and null there is taken as absent. No other key may be null, prose
made only of white space is not prose, and a character that could not be written to a
record (a NUL, half of a surrogate pair) refuses the reply while it can still be refused.

**Nothing is asked twice without a reason.** A rate limit or an overloaded server is
retried twice, because no reply was produced. A timeout is not: the provider may have run
the request and billed for it.

**By default every model reads every remit**, because the point of several models is that
one's blind spot is another's finding; `--one-each` deals one model to each reviewer in
turn, for a third of the cost with three models. With no panel file, rounds one and two
have a starter panel that assumes no field, so a first run needs only the list of models.
It is shown before anything is sent and left in the panel file to be edited. A second
starter panel shares nobody with the first.

**Sending needs a yes, and the yes is asked after the statement.** `review --run` prints
what the dry run prints, then asks, and takes only the word `yes`. Where nobody is there to
ask, in a script or under an agent, it sends nothing unless `--yes` was given. Everything
that can be known beforehand is checked before the question: a key that is not set, or is
set to something that is not a key, stops the run with nothing sent to any provider, because
half a panel sent for a reason that could have been said in advance is a manuscript already
disclosed and a round to finish. So does a record that could not be filed whatever the
reply: a record lists the files that were read, its schema takes no `..` in a file's name,
and with a manuscript file called `appendix..v2.md` every call was made and every reply
refused. The tool's own part of each record is now tried against the schema first. When
every reading of the round is on file there is nothing to send, and no yes is needed to
send nothing. Ctrl+C at the question is a no.

**A run can be stopped.** Ctrl+C after the yes stops the sending: no call is begun after
it. A call already made cannot be recalled, so it is waited for and its reply filed, and
the command says how many calls were not sent. The first version handed each provider
its calls as one task and waited for all of them, so an author who changed their mind
could only kill the process.

**The panel is written before the first call.** It names every reader that is about to be
asked, so a run that is interrupted, or in which a provider fails, leaves a round G11 sees
as incomplete: each reading that did not arrive is a `reading-missing`. A round with no
panel gets the starter panel the author was shown; a panel that exists keeps every word of
its own and gains the readers. Running the command again asks only for the readings that
are missing, and the ones on file are not asked for, paid for or replaced a second time.
If the panel no longer names a reviewer the statement named, because it was edited while
the question waited, nothing is sent.

**The command does not call a round read while its panel waits for a reader.** A run asks
the models listed now. The panel may name others: a model taken out of `review.models`
after a provider failed, or one that `--one-each` dealt to another reviewer this time.
The first version said every reading of the round was on file, or that two of two were
filed, and exited 0, with G11 still reporting `reading-missing`. It now lists the readers
the panel is waiting for, says how each is released, and exits 1.

**A reading is filed whole or not at all.** A reply becomes a record only after it came
back finished, parsed, fitted the reply schema, and the record built from it fitted the
review schema and read back from YAML as it was written. That last check is made by
making the trip: YAML writes U+0085 as it is and reads it back as a line break, so a
finding reached its record with a word boundary the model did not write, and a reply
that does not survive is refused rather than filed changed. The record is written under
a temporary name and linked into place. A link
refuses a name that is taken, where a move replaces what is there: somebody can file a
record by hand between the look for one and the move, and a record is not re-stamped, by a
run any more than by `review --record`. Every word of the review in the record is the
model's. The tool adds who read, when, the digests of what was sent, and the numbering of
the findings; it writes no `resolution`.

**What the record says of the call** is under `provenance`: the provider, the model asked
for, the host, the SHA-256 of the request body, the token counts, and the version of this
tool. The request body never holds the key, so its digest can be compared with the dry
run's. Two more fields are the provider's own words, the response id and the name it gives
the model it served, and they go into a file that is committed. Each is filed only when it
is one printable line of at most 200 characters with no four characters of a key in a row;
otherwise the record does without it. A review that holds twelve characters of a key in a
row, or the whole of a key of eight to twelve, is not filed at all. A model is never sent the key and cannot repeat it, but a gateway
between could put it in a reply, and the rule is that no key reaches a file.

**A reply that is refused is kept to read and counted nowhere.** It goes to
`review/round-N/refused/` as text, with a line saying why and that it is not a review
record. No gate looks there. The author paid for the reply and may want to see what the
model said; it cannot become a record, and it goes when that reading is filed. The key, or
any four characters of it in a row, is taken out first.

**One provider failing does not undo the others.** Providers are asked side by side, each
one call at a time. The readings that arrive are filed, the command exits 1, and it says
how many of how many were filed and that the round is incomplete.

**Two writers of one panel take turns.** A run writes the panel, and so does every
`review --record --reading`, which an agent may call for six readers at once. Each read the
panel, added its reader and wrote it back, and six at once left a panel naming two, three
or five of the six, with the other readings unread by the gate and only a warning to say
so. A panel is now held, through a lock file beside it made by exclusive create, while it
is read and written. A writer waits up to thirty seconds for it and then refuses in words
that name the file; a lock older than two minutes is taken for one its writer left behind.
A folder that cannot be written to makes no lock and leaves none to wait for: that is
refused after two seconds, where the first version tried again without a pause and
without an end. `review --record` reads its own round's panel only while it holds that
panel's lock. One version asked whether a reviewer was on the panel before asking for
the lock, so that a refusal would leave no folder behind; a writer rewriting the panel
empties the file first, and a reading for a reviewer who was on it was refused, about
three times in a thousand calls made at once. That question is now asked early only
where there was no `review/` when it looked. A writer can still make `review/` and a
panel between that look and the read. A refusal from it is then the one the call would
have had if it had come first, so it is never a wrong one; a panel that names the
reviewer lets the call go on to the lock.
The record itself is written by exclusive create, so two calls for one reader cannot both
succeed.

## What the panel finds of the defects we know

A measurement with its date (item 53), of a real model on the example's manuscript, which is
synthetic: no real paper was read. `tools/panel_measure.py` puts the example's round-1
panel, its three reviewers and their remits, to four copies of the example, each three
times, through the requests `review --run --dry-run` writes. The copies are the version that
panel read, which had the four defects its records name, twice over; the fixed version; that
first version cut to its title and abstract; and the fixed version with two minor defects
planted, an undefined "ICSR" and a Table 1 caption that no longer says its values are n (%).
Each reader of the cut copy, the "blank reader", is sent what every reviewer is sent besides
the manuscript: the paper's facts from `paper.yaml` (its title, its keywords), the journal's
profile and the reporting checklist, DEMO-OBS, whose item 3 asks how records were selected.
Each finding is settled by the words of `tools/data/panel-rubric.yaml`, written before any
reply was read, where a major or minor finding uses one defect's words; the rest, comments
among them, are adjudicated blind, with nothing that says where they came from, and may
raise several defects. The rubric counts the planted defects in the replies of all three
reviewers, as written in advance, though no remit is about presentation: the
biostatistician's, whether a reader can reconstruct the estimate from what is reported,
comes nearest a table's caption, and none reaches an abbreviation, while the panel's
instructions keep a reviewer to the remit. The report gives each reviewer's count beside the
total. The script writes the report; nothing in it is by hand.

- **2026-10-19, Claude Opus 5.5, through Claude Code (`--safe-mode`, the panel's system
  text as the whole system prompt, no tools), 45 readings, $4.10 at API prices, run under
  a subscription.** No reading was refused unread. The blind findings, 313 with the
  controls, were adjudicated by the same model, which put all six controls of known grade
  right; no person checked it. Each count is of the three readings by the reviewer whose
  remit the defect is in. The script's counts for the first two copies were then checked in
  both directions by the agent session that ran the measurement, not by a person: every
  finding a count rests on was read, and so was every reading by the reviewer whose remit
  holds the defect where a count, or a rating as major, is absent. Where the reading
  differs, it is given beside the script's.

  | Known defect | Raised, two sets of three | Rated major | Raised by the blank reader |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | No case definition | 3, 3 | 3, 3 | 3 of 3, all major |
  | The 2 x 2 table's counts not given | 2 (the script: 3), 2 | 0, 0 | 3 of 3, all major |
  | Duplicate reports not mentioned | 3, 3 | 3, 2 | 3 of 3, 2 major |
  | Record selection not described | 3, 3 | 3, 3 | 3 of 3, all major |

  - A finding raised is not evidence that the manuscript was read. The reader given the
    title and abstract raised every one of the four, nearly always as major, with 5.9
    major findings a reading against 1.8 and 1.7 from the readers of the whole. The case
    definition is the panel's own instructions' example of a finding, and record selection
    is asked for by item 3 of the checklist that reader was sent.
  - Read, every reading counted as raising one of the four on the version the panel read
    has a finding that says it is missing, but one reading, whose only finding counted for
    the 2 x 2 table is on the unit of analysis, which the table's words settle. Every
    reading counted as rating a defect major has such a finding rated major. No reading
    where a count or a major rating is absent raises the defect, or rates it major, in
    other words; where the 2 x 2 table is not counted, the reading praises the counts given
    or says nothing of them. Some readings have other findings counted in a defect's words
    that are about something else, the age bands of Table 1 under item 3 for one, which
    change no count. Each of the six checklist-auditor readings has a major finding that
    item 3's record selection is not described, five of them adjudicated blind. Beyond the
    2 x 2 table, what differs between readings is severity. The 2 x 2 table, major in the
    round-1 record, was rated major by no reader of the whole and by every blank reader.
    Duplicates were rated major in three readings of three, then in two, for the same
    request: a difference of one reading in three is noise.
  - A first adjudication, made before round 1 of #334, gave each finding one defect at
    most, and counted duplicates in two readings and then none. The pharmacoepidemiologist
    raises duplicates inside a finding about record selection, and that adjudicator had to
    choose. The second differs in more than that rule: it is another run of the model, on
    a file that no longer gives each finding's `where`.
  - On the fixed version the readings gave 0.2 major findings each. Defects the fixed
    version does not have were still counted, as minor findings: the 2 x 2 table and record
    selection in three readings of three, the caption in three of nine. They are other
    findings in the same words: the unit of analysis, put through the table's words; under
    item 3, how a report was put in the drug's group, which the fix left unsaid; and a row
    of Table 1 without percentages under a caption that says n (%), which is so in the
    example. Words settle a finding by its vocabulary, not by what it says is missing, and
    a finding they settle is given that one defect, not another it raises in other words.
  - The planted minor defects were not found. The undefined acronym was raised in none of
    nine readings. The caption was counted once, by the biostatistician, and that finding
    is about the row without percentages. Neither was rated major. No remit is about
    presentation and the instructions keep a reviewer to the remit, so this panel, as
    built, does not look for such defects; it is no measure of over-escalation either.
  - The record's digest (`bcb8549c...`) is of a later version than the one the round-1
    panel read: the records came with the fixes, and were stamped again with each change
    after. The version read is the example's first, `e6a8cca6`. A first run on the later
    version found none of the four, since they are fixed there, and is not reported. The
    record's resolution of record selection says the Methods now describe inclusion
    without restriction on age or sex; that sentence was in the first version already.

## A document reviewed blind names none of its authors

A journal whose review is double-blind asks for a manuscript that does not say who wrote it,
and the profile said so only in its free-text notes. The profile now says it (`blinding:
double`, or `triple`), and the build looks for the authors in the document it made: their
names, ORCID iDs and e-mail addresses from `authors.yaml`, and the institutions of their
affiliations. It reads the text, the notes, the comments, the headers and the footers, the
text a tracked change deleted, the text of the figures, Word's author fields and its company
field, the author of each tracked change and comment, the list of people Word keeps, the
address behind a link and the code of a field that holds one (`HYPERLINK`,
`INCLUDEPICTURE`, `INCLUDETEXT`, and `LINK` or `DDE` for a table pasted as a link to its
file), a `mailto:` or an ORCID iD behind words (round 1 of
#273). Not a citation's field code, which holds the cited work's data: a self-citation
of a thesis names the author's school there (round 1 of #349). A name found is a
`BUILD` failure (`blind-document-names-author`): `build` writes the document, says so and
exits 1, and `submit` does not assemble the pack. `submit --document` reads the copy it is
given, which is the one that comes back from a co-author with Word's fields filled in.

A name is looked for as one is written: the given and the family name, the initial with its
stop before the family name ("A. Example"), and after it behind a comma ("Example, A."), any
space between the words and either apostrophe, since pandoc prints a typed one curly. A bare
initial is not read: "A Cross-sectional study" does not name Anna Cross, nor "Ward A" Alice
Ward. The family name alone is not, because many are ordinary words; an institution is the
part of an affiliation between its commas that has three words or more, in any case, because
a city or a country names many other things. So an institution of two words ("Example
Institute") is not looked for, and an initial with its stop before a word that is a family
name reads as that author, "Panel A. Example" as Ada Example
(`test_what_the_blind_check_reads_wrongly_is_pinned`). The reference list, a paragraph
whose style is named "Bibliography", is not read, nor the addresses it links to, wherever
else they are linked, by a link or a field (so a link Word adds in the body to one of them
is not read either; the list prints that address anyway): the journals that review blind
mostly ask for the authors' own work to be cited in the third person, not taken out, and a
self-citation prints their names there.

## The submission pack writes nothing twice

Everything a journal asks for except the covering letter is already recorded in the project.
`authors.yaml` becomes the title page, the CRediT statement and the declarations; the
reporting completion file is copied as it stands; the build produces the document. Nothing
is transcribed, so the title page cannot list an author who left two revisions ago and the
funding statement cannot contradict the acknowledgements.

Two places where the generator says something rather than papering over it. An author with
no CRediT roles produces a statement saying so, because most journals now require them. An
author whose `competing_interests` field is empty is listed as having made **no
declaration** — an empty field is not a declaration of none, and journals ask per author.

The manifest records every file with its sha256, because six months later "which version
did the journal actually get" has no reliable answer otherwise. It also says what made the
pack: the version of manuscript-guard that checked it (`checked_with`), so that a later fix
can say which packs to check again; the project's commit, and whether anything in the
project's folder outside `build/` differed from it (`tree`, each file of a folder git
has not been given counted, round 1 of #250); the day the journal's profile
and each reporting checklist were read from their sources; and every review finding a
person chose to leave as it was, with the reason and who decided (`overrides`, from
`overridden` and `overridden_by` in the review records). Where a record names nobody,
the manifest says "not recorded". `git` is asked twice, the commit and the state of the
folder, and given 30 seconds each time, with its file system monitor off; a project
outside git says so.

The abstract goes in as `abstract.txt` as well, for the box every submission system has for
it: the section headed "Abstract" with every binding filled in by the value the build
prints, as pandoc writes plain text, up to its keywords. Pasted from the .docx, it carried
whatever Word and the clipboard made of its emphasis and its line breaks; this is the
checked numbers and nothing else. An abstract that pandoc reads as holding a citation, a
footnote, an image, a table or a figure gets no `abstract.txt`, and `submit` says so: the
build formats a citation in the journal's style, or as a live Zotero field, and plain text
written another way would not be what the document says. The main text is read whole
through pandoc's own tree, so that a footnote defined at its end is a footnote, and the
abstract is written only where everything in it is words, their emphasis, quotation marks,
a link that shows its own address, and sub- and superscripts plain text can carry: digits
and signs are kept as Unicode scripts, a subscript label ("C~max~") and an ordinal's
superscript ("2^nd^") are written as their letters, and any other (`2^k^`, `e^x^`) leaves
the abstract out, since written flat it would be another number; anything else, and a
keywords label inside a paragraph, leaves it out with the reason. Two drafts that read the
source by pattern each missed a form of citation or footnote, or cut a sentence that
mentioned keywords, and a draft that read the abstract alone missed a footnote defined
below it.

The pack refuses to assemble while `check --submission` fails. That is what the check is
for.

The covering letter is deliberately not generated. It is the one part addressed to a
particular editor about a particular paper at a particular moment, and a generated one reads
exactly like a generated one.

## A number a summary gives is one the paper reports

An abstract summarises the paper, and a conclusion what it found: neither introduces data.
Nothing held that. G2 holds a binding to the analysis wherever it stands, so a key bound in
the Abstract and nowhere else passed, and G8 compared the results only with themselves. G8
now warns (`summary-not-reported`) of a results key the Abstract or a conclusion binds that
the paper reports nowhere: not bound in the Methods or the Results, not declared the same
quantity as a key that is (`same_as`, either way), not bound in the supplement, and not
printed in a table or drawn in a figure the manuscript places.

The Methods count as reporting because an abstract's own Methods restate them: the example
gives its study period there, and the Methods are where it is reported. The Discussion and
the Introduction do not. A section is found by the one reading of headings the gates share
(`text/section_names.py`): the Methods as G4, G9 and G14 find them, the abstract by its
heading or the title the journal's profile gives it, the Results by a title that opens with
"Results" or "Findings", numbered or marked, and a conclusion by "Conclusion", "Concluding
remarks" or a title that is "Summary" alone. The outermost heading that names a part decides,
so the abstract's own "Results" summarise and a "Summary" under the Results is theirs. A
heading over the Introduction or the Methods is the paper's title written as a heading, and
names no part. The headings are carried from one file of the paper into the next, as G14
carries them.

It is a warning: a new rule starts as one, until what it says of real papers is known.

A box the journal's profile asks for (`boxes:`, highlights or key points, below) summarises as
the abstract does, and G8 reads it so: its heading is a summary's, and in LaTeX so is its
environment, whose numbers the printed view keeps under whatever heading stands over it.

## The boxes a journal prints beside the abstract

Journals print short texts beside the abstract: Elsevier's highlights, JAMA's key points, the
Lancet's research in context, a plain-language summary. Each comes with rules a desk editor
holds a submission to (three to five items, 85 characters each, the headings Question,
Findings and Meaning) and nothing held them. The profile now records each box the page asks
for under `boxes:`, as data like the rest: its id, the heading it goes under (a regular
expression, searched in the title as printed), the LaTeX environment that writes it, whether
it is required, its item and word limits, the headings it carries, and whether the journal
takes it as a file of its own. Each box is one rule of the page, quoted under `boxes.<id>`.
Each number of a box above 1, and each of a graphical abstract's lines, is held to its quote as
a limit's is (`journal-limit-not-in-quote`, naming the box's field): an `item_max_chars` typed
58 for the page's 85 otherwise passed, since the quote was on the page. A graphical abstract's
number that is not whole (`max_file_mb: 2.5`) is held to its digits, "2.5", "2.50" or "2,5",
whatever its size, since a page cannot write it as "a" or "no", though not to a comma before
three digits ("2,500"), which separates thousands; its `aspect_ratio` to both its parts in
their order, with a colon, a multiplication sign, an x, a slash or "by" between them, and not
inside a longer ratio or a date, so that "5:2" and "1:16:9" do not state 16:9 (rounds 1 and 2
of #464). A block's own `retrieved_on` is held to its age as the instructions' is
(`journal-profile-stale`, naming the block and, where it gives no address, its page). A
reread refuses only a block that may name a page of its own and that the schema refuses
(`boxes: 3`); the rest of a profile the schema refuses is read again as before (round 2 of
#464: round 1 refused the whole profile). Two blocks that
name one page with two digests have the one that is not the page's said. A `quotes` key for a
block the profile does not have is held to the instructions page, as before blocks named
pages of their own.

A box, the graphical abstract and the sharing policy may each name a page of their own
(`page_file`, with its `page_sha256`), where the journal gives them apart from its
instructions: an artwork guide, a self-archiving policy. Their quotes are then held to that
page and no other, and `journal --reread <file> --page <page_file>` reads that page again on
its own. Kept in the instructions page's file, a policy's text read as removed each time the
instructions page was read again (Basile, 2026-10-28).

G4 reads the boxes of the main text (`text/boxes.py`) and holds each to its rules
(`gates/journal_boxes.py`): `box-missing`, `box-items`, `box-item-long`, `box-over-limit` and
`box-headings-missing`. In Markdown a box is the section under its heading; in LaTeX its
environment, or a section under its heading, a chapter's or a part's among them, which runs
to the next heading of its level or above or to an abstract, whatever the box's level (round 1
of #464: a LaTeX abstract after a box was read as its last items). An item is a line of the
box's list, run on over the lines after it, or, where the box has no list, a paragraph: what
prints as one. A list nested in an item is that item's text: in Markdown an item whose mark
is indented as far as the open item's text, as CommonMark and pandoc place it, whatever the
list's own indentation; in LaTeX an `\item` inside a list environment nested in the box's
list (round 1 of #464: "- A" over "  - a1" counted two items). After a blank line a line is
the open item's only where it is indented to the item's text, else a paragraph after the
list, and a thematic break (`- - -`, `***`) is no item. In LaTeX an itemize's or an
enumerate's label (`\item[--]`) is the item's mark and not its text, a description's term
is, and a list's options (`\begin{itemize}[noitemsep]`) print nothing, read so in the box's
reader and not in the mask the other gates share (round 2 of #464). A heading the box must carry
is found as words of its own: "meaningful" does not carry "Meaning". It is
measured as printed, a binding as its value's display, a comment and a listing passed over,
Markdown's marks and LaTeX's commands off. Each finding warns until submission and fails there
where the box is required, as the author decided (2026-10-28): a box is written last, and a
draft without one is the ordinary state. A box written only in the supplement is not the box,
and `box-missing` says where it is. A heading that is no regular expression fails from
internal review (`box-heading-invalid`), as the profile's other errors do.

The profile also records two blocks no gate reads yet, so that the profile is filled once from
the page: `graphical_abstract` (required or asked for, its size, aspect, formats and limits,
each line a rule quoted under `graphical_abstract.<name>`) and `sharing` (for each version of
the paper, where it may be shared, after how long, under which licence and with which
statement, quoted under `sharing.<version>`). A required graphical abstract is only noted
(`graphical-abstract-missing`) while `communication/graphical-abstract/` does not exist: the
`communicate` commands make it there and hold it to these rules. Without a `sharing:` block
nothing is refused here; the author decided (2026-10-28) that those commands will then share
a link to the DOI and upload nothing. The policy is the journal's own page, never Sherpa
Romeo, which needs a key, and nothing in the toolkit is paid or keyed.

## An earlier output of the same data is held to this paper

Several papers come out of one database extraction or one cohort: a conference abstract, a
preprint, a protocol paper, the article, a second article on another outcome. A cohort of
1,204 in the abstract and 1,187 in the article, with nothing said, is a number nobody can
account for, and an article that does not say the abstract exists is an undeclared
overlapping publication, which ICMJE asks authors to declare and journals treat as
misconduct. Nothing compared this paper with anything outside it.

`literature/related.yaml` names each earlier output, what it is, and what this paper shares
with it (`data`, `study`, `authors`), as the author says it (Basile, 2026-10-21, the seven
answers below all his). G8 reads it; without it G8 says nothing new, and no count is added,
so a project that keeps none reads as before.

**The earlier work's own files, where an author of this paper made it.** A comparison read
from a PDF is a comparison of what was printed, rounded, with the reader's eye between. Where
an author of this paper is an author of the earlier output, the skill asks for that work's
files: its manuscript-guard project, at the revision the output was made from, or, with no
project, its analysis outputs copied in. The path is the author's answer and is never
looked for. `manuscript-guard related --take <id>` copies the project's results fragments,
its frozen plan, its plan and its data dictionary, as git holds them at that revision (or as
they stand, with HEAD recorded and whether they differ from it), into
`literature/related/<id>/`, with a record of each file's digest. `check` reads the copy and
never the project, so CI and a co-author's machine, where the earlier project is not, give
the author's answer: the lookup's pattern of asking once and keeping what came back. A
copied file whose digest changed, or a file added beside them, fails from drafting
(`related-snapshot-edited`), as an edited lookup record does: a result edited in the copy
compares an invented number. Each digest is taken as an analysis's input's is
(`input_digest`), its line endings folded for `.json`, `.yaml` and `.md`: a plan saved with
CRLF and committed under the `eol=lf` that `init` writes is checked out with LF everywhere
else, and was read as an edit on every machine but the author's (round 1 of #391). A file
whose name begins with a dot, the `.DS_Store` a system leaves, is neither copied nor counted,
and the fragments' `.sha256` beside them are not copied, since nothing reads them there.
`--take` writes over nothing it did not write. Until one of
the three is there, or `files_unavailable` says why they cannot be had, an output that
shares the data or the study with authors warns (`related-files-missing`); one of the same
authors on other data (`shares: [authors]`) is listed for what other checks read of it and
has nothing to compare (round 1 of #391). A project named and never copied warns, and
fails at submission (`related-not-taken`): nothing was compared. A copy of another project or revision
than the entry now names warns, and fails at submission (`related-taken-elsewhere`): it
compared another output than the one named.

**Numbers: every key both emit, and the pairs the author declares.** Through a copy, each
results key that both projects emit and both papers print (`quoted`) is compared. A key
renamed since is paired (`earlier: n_cases`, `here: cohort.n`); keys that share a name and
not a meaning are set apart by pattern with a reason (`not_compared: ror.*`). Comparing only
declared pairs would be quieter, and would never show the difference the author did not
think of. Two values are the same where they print alike, or where both are numbers equal to
nine significant digits, as `verify` holds a re-run: "2.3" and "2.31" of one estimate are
one value printed to other places. A pair naming a key one side does not emit compares
nothing, and warns and fails at submission (`related-pair-unmatched`).

From a published text, or from outputs copied in, the author records each value as the
ledger does: as the earlier output prints it, with the sentence that states it and the
stored copy under `literature/` it is quoted from. The sentence is held to the copy and the
value to the sentence by the ledger's own functions (`related-quote-not-in-source`,
`related-value-not-in-quote`, `related-source-missing`, failing from drafting as the
ledger's do). The printed value is compared with this paper's as a number, to within half a
unit of the coarser of the two printings, where both read as one (grouped by commas or
spaces, a middle dot for the point, a sign, a percent sign, and no zero before the point
in a style that drops it, ".45"), and as text otherwise. A value YAML would read as a number,
`1.50` or `0.00005`, is read as typed, and so is a revision that is a short commit of
digits: read as numbers, `1.50` was `1.5`, which its quote's "1.50" does not state (round 1).

**A difference is explained when the manuscript says why.** The pair or the value records
the reason (`because`) and the manuscript's sentence that tells the reader
(`manuscript_says`), and the sentence is looked for as G13 looks for a quoted change: in
the manuscript with its bindings filled in, without comments, emphasis or line breaks, and
with a binding in the sentence filled in too. A reason the reader is never given explains
nothing to the reader. Explained, it is a note (`related-number-explained`); with a reason
and no sentence found, `related-reason-not-in-text`; with neither, `related-number-differs`.
Both warn and fail at submission. No new reading of text is made: the rule is G13's
`as_quoted` and `rendered_manuscript`, held by the generated inputs already ("as quoted").

**A choice of the analysis that changed is a change of method.** A value the analysis
declared as a parameter or a coding dictionary's release, or a label (a period, a verdict
in words), that differs is `related-method-differs`: a warning at every stage, a note with
a reason (`related-method-explained`), and never a failure, since a method may rightly
change between two papers and the review panel, not a gate, weighs whether it was said and
justified. A software version is not compared: every later paper runs later software.

The same holds of what both projects record of their methods as data (Basile's answer 5).
A model both fitted under one key is compared by its card: its family and link, its outcome
as the formula writes it, and every way it enters each variable, its expression, as what and
its reference ("its family is Poisson/Log there and Binomial/Logit here; it enters sex here
and not there"; `age` and `np.log(age)` differ though both are numerical, and so do `age`
alone and `age` with `I(age**2)`: round 1 of #402). And each section both plans have under
one heading is compared word by word: the earlier plan as it stood when its first results
were written (the copy's `plan.frozen.yaml`, or its `plan.md` where it kept none), this
paper's plan as it stands, each read as G12 reads a plan (its line endings made `\n`, a
byte-order mark left out, and one not in UTF-8 read with what cannot be decoded replaced,
not refused). The sections are read as G12 reads a plan's, and a heading is matched by its own words,
without its number ("2.", "2.1" or "2", not "2019"), emphasis or case. A heading that stands
twice in either plan, a `### Definition` under the Exposure and another under the Outcome, is
not compared, since which answers which would be a guess, and a note says so
(`related-section-ambiguous`): matching by the headings above needed the plan's title told
from its first section, and two rules for that each broke an ordinary plan (rounds 2 and 3 of
#402); words without comments, emphasis or line breaks and in either case,
as G13 reads a quotation (`as_quoted`); and the plans' Deviations and Planned results, which
are each paper's own, are not compared, nor anything under them. A section that reads
otherwise is said with a few words of each side from where they part. Each is
`related-method-differs`, a note with a reason under `methods:` (`model:` or
`plan_section:`, a heading both plans have once, and `because:`), and never a failure. A reason that names no model both fitted, or no section both plans have, explains
nothing and is said (`related-pair-unmatched`). What the words mean is
not compared: two sections that say one thing in other words differ, and the panel's
earlier-outputs remit reads them.

**The data dictionaries, variable by variable.** Answer 5 named the data dictionary as well,
which was on no branch then; #382 brought it. Where both projects keep one (the copy holds
the earlier project's `design/data_dictionary.yaml`, and this paper's is read by the loader
G12 reads it with), each variable both have under one name, its case included, is compared
part by part:

- its definition, word by word, in either case and with line breaks aside. A dictionary is
  YAML, not Markdown, so a `*` or a backtick in it is read as written, which G13's reading
  of a quotation would drop: "ALT above 3*ULN" is not "ALT above 3ULN";
- its type;
- its codes, as the values they give, written out or named by their list alike: a code one
  side has and the other lacks, a code labelled otherwise (in either case), and an ordinal
  scale's codes in another order;
- its unit, as written, its case included, since mg and Mg are two units;
- its range, a bound read as a number where it is one, so that 110 and 110.0 are one bound,
  and as a date or a time where it is one, as the loader reads it: YAML gives an unquoted
  timestamp in ISO form and keeps a quoted one as typed, and `2015-01-01 10:00:00Z` and
  `2015-01-01T10:00:00+00:00` are one instant (round 1 of #415). That reading is the
  type's, so it is used where both sides give the variable one type; a variable whose
  type changed has its bounds compared as written, and a date there and a datetime here
  of one written range is said to differ in its type alone (round 2);
- its standard: another system, or one side with none, is one difference; within one
  system, its release, its level, its term and its code each (the level and the term in
  either case);
- what it is derived from, in any order, and its derivation, word by word as a definition.

The study period, the dictionary's own, is compared as well, and one given on one side only
differs. Each variable that differs is one `related-method-differs` that says every part
that does ("variable hepatic: its MedDRA version is 26.0 there and 27.1 here"), and the study
period one of its own; each is a note with a reason under `methods:` (`variable:`, the name
both dictionaries write, or `dictionary: study_period`) and never a failure. A reason that
names a variable not in both, or a study period neither gives, explains nothing and is said
(`related-pair-unmatched`). A dictionary on one side only is compared with nothing, and
nothing is said. One that does not read, on either side, is said in a note
(`related-dictionary-unreadable`), and nothing of either is compared: this paper's own is
failed by G12 as `dictionary-invalid` already, and the copy's is what the earlier project
held at that revision, which only another revision can change.

**An overlap of data or study with authors is disclosed.** It is disclosed where the
manuscript cites the earlier output (its citekey, in a citation a reader sees, comments left
out), or where `disclosed_by` gives the manuscript's sentence that says so, found as above,
for an abstract a journal does not want cited. Undisclosed, it warns and fails at submission
(`related-undisclosed`). No file holds the covering letter, so `submit` lists the outputs to
declare there.

**The supplement is held as the main text is** (Basile, 2026-10-21): cohort counts and
definitions often stand in an eTable or the eMethods. On this paper's side, values are
compared by results key wherever they are printed, so a count bound only in
`manuscript/supplementary/` is compared like any other, and a sentence that explains a
difference or discloses the overlap, or a citation of the earlier output, counts in the
supplement as in the main text: G8 reads the manuscript's files as every gate that reads prose
does. On the earlier output's side, a copy holds every result its project emitted, those its
supplement printed among them, and a value read from its text may be quoted from its
supplement stored beside it (`sources/<citekey>-supplement.pdf`).

`manuscript-guard related` prints every value compared, both printings and what came of it,
and `--json` the same with the findings: what the author and a panel read, beside what
`check` decides.

## The design gate warns and never blocks

Writing down what you intended before you did it is the strongest single thing available for
the credibility of a result — not because deviating is wrong, but because a deviation that
was declared is a decision, and one nobody recorded is indistinguishable from having tried
several things and reported the best.

Blocking would be the stronger discipline and would be unworkable. Exploratory work is real
work, and a gate that prevents you writing code until a plan is agreed is a gate that gets
bypassed on the first afternoon it costs something. So G12 warns: when analysis code exists
with no plan behind it, and when a plan's section is a heading with nothing under it. A
"Deviations from the plan" heading followed by nothing is the common case, and naming it is
most of the value.

**A plan is written knowing what the data hold.** A plan can set out an analysis of data
nobody has counted: an adjustment for a covariate missing in half the rows, a subgroup of
twelve patients. The author's own script counts them, never the tool, and publishes the
counts like any result under `feasibility.`: the cohort at each selection step, the
outcome's events, the missing values of each planned variable, the date range, the
duplicates. At the `design` stage, G12 warns (`feasibility-not-run`) where the plan's
analysis section says something and no result is emitted under `feasibility.`. It is a
warning, as the rest of this gate is: an author may know the data from a registry's own
report. It is asked at the `design` stage only: from the `analysis` stage on, the results
say what the data hold, and it is not asked, whether anything was emitted under
`feasibility.` or not.

**A panel reads the plan before there are results.** A review panel reads the manuscript,
which exists once the analysis has run; by then the design is spent, and a reviewer who says
the comparison cannot answer the question says it too late. A design round is a panel that
reads `design/plan.md` and the feasibility results at the `design` stage. It is kept apart
from the manuscript's rounds, in `review/design/` (`panel-<n>.yaml`, and
`round-<n>/<reviewer>.yaml` for a reading), so it never counts toward `rounds_required`
and no manuscript round answers it. `manuscript-guard review --record <reviewer> --design
--round <n> --verdict <verdict>` files a reading with the digest of what it read: the
plan's bytes and each `feasibility.*` result's value and display. G12 then says a reading of
a plan that has changed since, or of data counted again, is stale (`design-review-stale`),
until the same reviewer reads the plan as it stands in a later round, which supersedes it
(`design-review-superseded`, information; its open majors still bind);
a reviewer on the panel who has not read (`design-review-missing`); and a major finding not
answered by a resolution or an override with its reason (`design-major-open`). The last is
a warning, and a failure at submission only, as the author decided: what an unanswered
design objection means is the author's to weigh while there is still an analysis to change.
A reading is sealed as a manuscript reading is (`review --seal <reviewer> --design`), and
one changed after its seal is said (`design-reading-altered`), failing at submission. A
project with no design round reads as it did before, counts included.

A design round is read by the models as a manuscript round is: `review --design --run`
plans it from `review/design/`, says what would be sent where, asks, and files each reply
as a design reading, `round-<n>/<reviewer>.<model>.yaml`, sealed and carrying the digest of
the plan it read (`plan_sha256`). What is sent is a list of its own (`prompt.gather_design`):
the paper's facts from `paper.yaml`, `design/plan.md` without its front matter and comments
and with its feasibility results printed into it, and the feasibility results and the counts
of the data checks (`quality.*`, "The data are held to the dictionary"), each under its key.
Not the manuscript, and no result but those: a binding in the plan to any other result, a
value or a table, is sent as written, since a design round reads the plan
before there are results (round 1 of #316: a table the plan bound was printed whole).
Where `paper.yaml` declares a study design (`study_type`), what a plan for that design has
to settle is sent too, under "What this study design needs": each section
`data/study_types.yaml` gives the design, what it says and the guideline item it comes from,
for the reviewer to ask of the plan as far as their remit goes. So a cohort's plan is asked
about its time zero and follow-up, its confounding and its missing data, and a trial's
about its estimand, its randomisation and its interim analyses: the risks of the study type
item 46 asks the remits to name, from one table that G12 and G5 read too. Each
reviewer is told it reads a plan before its analysis is run, and that a major finding is one
the design cannot meet: the instructions are the manuscript round's, rewritten in ten places
and naming no manuscript, so the reply asked for is the same. A
first design round with no panel gets a starter one, a methodologist whose remit names the
study type's risks and a statistician who reads the plan against the feasibility results;
a later design round needs its panel written. The guard hook puts `review --design --run
--yes` to the author as it puts `review --run --yes`, saying that the plan is what goes.

A design remit read more than once, by several models or by a model and a person, is filed
as a manuscript round's is: each reader the panel lists for the reviewer under `readers` has
a reading of its own, `round-<n>/<reviewer>.<reader>.yaml`, written by `review --record
<reviewer> --design --reading <reader>`, which also lists the reader in the panel. Each is
read and judged on its own: stale, superseded by a later reading of the same remit by the
same reader, sealed, its majors open or answered, and an override of one signed by the
statistician under a key that names the reader. A reader the panel names who has not read is
`design-review-missing`; a named reading that says another reader inside is
`design-reading-misfiled` and not counted; and a file beside the record whose reader the
panel does not name is said (`design-reading-unnamed`) and not read. Until this, a design
panel's named readers were not read at all, and a remit read by two models counted one
reading. As in G11, a reviewer the panel lists twice is said (`design-duplicate-reviewer`)
and read once, with the readers every one of its entries names and its plain record where
one names none, so that one record does not
answer two remits nor its overrides go to the statistician twice; a reading that gives one id to two findings is said
(`design-finding-id-repeated`), since an answer and a sign-off are held to a finding by its
id; and two readers whose names would be filed as one, or a name with no letter or digit,
are `design-reader-unnamed`. All three fail at submission, as G11's do (rounds 1 of #308,
#313 and #315).

An override of a design-round major, a reason given for leaving the objection standing, is
the statistician's to accept, not the author's alone (`sign_offs`): G12 warns
(`design-override-unsigned`) until the statistician `authors.yaml` names signs it, with
`manuscript-guard sign --as <them> --finding G12/design-override/<round>/<reviewer>/<id>`.
The sign-off is bound to the objection's words and the reason, so a reason rewritten after
it wants it again. A finding with a resolution needs none: the plan changed to meet it.

**The results the plan promised are reported.** G2 says when the analysis emits a value
that nothing quotes (`unquoted-result`); nothing said when the plan promised a result the
analysis never emitted. A plan may now hold a section headed "Planned results", not one of
the seven, whose list items each open with the key of a result the paper will report, in
backticks: `ror.point`, or `results.ror.point` as the manuscript binds it, or a group,
`ror.*`. The first code span of each item is its key, read up to the next item or the
item's first blank line, and a span with no dot is code, not a key; a key with no dot of its
own is written bound, `results.dose`. Once the stage is past
`design`, G12 warns where a key listed there names no value, table or model the analysis
emitted (`planned-result-missing`; `table.*` and `model.*` name the tables and the models),
or names only values emitted with `quoted=False`
(`planned-result-unquoted`), unless the Deviations section names the key: dropping a
promised result is a deviation, and saying so is the remedy. A section that names no key at
all is a warning of its own (`planned-results-unkeyed`). A plan without the section says
nothing to hold the results to and gets no finding. A heading that is also the Deviations
section's heads the Deviations where the words of a change come first, "Changes to the
planned results", and the list where the planned results do, "Planned results and
amendments".

**The plan is frozen when the first results are written.** A plan rewritten after the
results are known is the pattern of a hypothesis fitted to its results, and it can be told
mechanically. The first time either emitter writes results, it keeps the plan as it stood:
`design/plan.frozen.yaml` holds its text, its digest, the day and the script, and nothing
writes it again; the write hook refuses an edit of it. In a file of its own, beside the plan,
because the results folder is cleared and written again on every run, and a copy kept there
would be frozen again on the changed plan. Written as JSON, which is YAML too, so that R needs
no package to write it. G12 warns (`plan-changed-after-results`) when the plan's words differ
from the copy's and its Deviations section says what it said then: changed with nothing said.
A plan re-wrapped without a word changed is unchanged, and so is one saved with or without a
byte order mark: both emitters keep the plan without the mark, and G12 compares it without
one. Results with no copy, written before
the emitters kept one, are a note. The worked example commits its copy beside its plan, as it
commits its results. Until it did, every run of its analysis left the copy in a file git
neither tracked nor ignored, which the next `git add -A` would have committed; a test now
runs the example's analysis and `check` in a copy of its tracked files (skipped outside a git checkout) and fails on any such file. The
test fixture deletes the copy along with the results, so that its run is a first run.

**A plan says what its design needs.** The seven sections are the same for every plan, so a
disproportionality analysis with no case definition or comparator, or a trial with no
estimand, passed. A project names its design in `paper.yaml` (`study_type`: cohort,
case-control, self-controlled, disproportionality, trial, systematic-review,
prediction-model), and G12 then asks the plan for the sections that design needs as well:
the estimand of a trial (ICH E9(R1)), the time zero and the confounders of a cohort
(STROBE, TARGET), the risk windows of a self-controlled design, the deduplication, case
definition, comparator and measure of a disproportionality analysis (READUS-PV). Each
section in `data/study_types.yaml` names the guideline item it comes from and the date that
item was read, and the finding's hint carries it. The same table gives the guidelines the
paper follows, so G5 says (`reporting-guideline-for-design`) when the design is named and
none of them is declared; the reporting-checklist skill shows the table, and a test holds
the two to one another. A project that names no design is asked for the seven, as before.
What the sections say is the author's and the panel's to judge, never a gate's.

## A registration is looked up once, and the paper is held to it

A registration is the plan made public before the study: what it will measure, in whom, and
how. Outcome switching is the paper then reporting something else, with nothing said: a
registered primary outcome dropped or reported as secondary, a secondary one promoted, an
outcome nobody registered reported as though it had been. COMPare followed the 67 trials
five general medical journals published over six weeks of 2015, and found outcomes other
than those prespecified, with nothing said, in 58 of them (Goldacre and colleagues,
Trials, 2019). Observational studies registered in the EU PAS register, on
ClinicalTrials.gov or on OSF are open to it in the same way. A registration made
after the study started, or after its first results, registered nothing in advance. Until
this, a registration number was a structural token to G2 (`data/structural.yaml`) and
nothing more.

**The registry is asked once, and the answer kept.** The pattern is the lookup's. `paper.yaml`
lists the registrations under `registration`, each by its identifier, and `manuscript-guard
lookup --registrations` asks each one's registry and writes what it said to
`design/registrations/<id>.yaml`: the registered date, the study's actual start and the start
of its analysis where the registry gives them, its type and design, each field of the record
under the registry's own label (outcomes among them, with their role where the registry keeps
primary and secondary apart), the day it was asked, and an `answers_sha256` that catches an
edit by hand (`registration-record-edited`, failing from drafting). Asked again are a
registration with no record, one whose answer did not come, and one whose record was edited;
`--again` asks for all, and `--dry-run` sends nothing. Nothing of the manuscript is sent: the
identifier is the whole of each request. G12 reads the records, and asks nobody.

Which registries, as Basile chose on 2026-10-21, and the shapes they answered in that day:

- **ClinicalTrials.gov**, API v2 (2.0.5), `/studies/{nctId}?fields=protocolSection&
  markupFormat=legacy`, which gives the descriptions as plain text where the default is
  Markdown with its characters escaped, and a 120 kB answer where the whole record with its
  results is 2 MB. The registered date is `statusModule.studyFirstSubmitDate`; the start is
  `startDateStruct.date` where its `type` is `ACTUAL`, a day or a month; the outcomes are
  `outcomesModule.primaryOutcomes`, `secondaryOutcomes` and `otherOutcomes`, each with a
  `measure`, a `description` and a `timeFrame`. Its OpenAPI document gives the identifier as
  `^[Nn][Cc][Tt]0*[1-9]\d{0,7}$`, so `NCT123` is answered as NCT00000123: only NCT and eight
  digits is taken as an identifier, and an answer for another study than the one asked is
  no answer. An unknown study is a 404 with "NCT number … not found" as plain text; an alias
  is a 301 to the study it stands for, and is said, not followed. The API serves no earlier
  version of a record: the history the site shows is behind `/api/int/`, which answered 403.
- **OSF Registries**, API v2, `/registrations/{guid}/`, JSON:API: `date_registered`, the
  answers in `registration_responses` keyed by the template's question ids, which
  `/schemas/registrations/{id}/schema_blocks/` names (each `question-label` block's text
  labels the inputs after it), and `original_response` and `latest_response`, which differ
  where the registration was updated; `/schema_responses/{id}/` gives what each version said,
  and the later one's `revision_justification`. A 404 or a 410 is a registration OSF does
  not hold, a 401 or 403 one it does not show. A question whose label names an outcome, an
  endpoint or a dependent variable is kept as the registration's outcomes. 44 templates were
  listed that day, one of them the joint ISPE and ISPOR "Real World Evidence Recommended
  Minimum Study Registration Template".
- **ISRCTN**, its query API, `/api/query/format/default?q=<id>`, in XML
  (`http://www.67bricks.com/isrctn`): `allTrials@totalCount`, each `fullTrial/trial` with its
  `isrctn@dateAssigned`, `primaryOutcome`, `secondaryOutcome`, `recruitmentStart` and
  `primaryStudyDesign`. The trial is the one whose number is the one asked, among those the
  query answers. Its single-trial path, `/api/trial/<id>/format/default`, answers an unknown
  number with HTTP 500 and a web page, and is not used. Parsed by `safexml`, which refuses a
  document type declaration.
- **The EU PAS register**, now the HMA-EMA Catalogue of real-world data studies, has no API:
  it is a Drupal 11 site, a `?_format=json` is redirected back to the page, and its export of
  search results is a server-side batch that needs a session. So its pages are read, by the
  labels and classes they carried that day, which the module's docstring lists. `/study/<n>`
  answers 302 to `/node/<k>/administrative-details` for the study whose Study ID is `<n>`,
  and 404 for one it does not have. A number of the catalogue's own scheme, begun in 2024
  (EUPAS1000000417), is its Study ID; an older one is not (EUPAS11379 is Study ID 23396), and
  is found by the catalogue's search, whose results link `/study/<n>`. The page a number is
  read from has to give that number, or it is another study's. The registered date is the
  page's "First published"; the starts are the actual start of data collection and of data
  analysis, each a `<time datetime>`; the outcomes are the methodological page's "Outcomes"
  field, which holds primary and secondary as one text. A page without its title, its date or
  its number is not of the shape read, and the answer is `unresolvable`, never read as the
  study having none. The site is asked at most once a second, and its `robots.txt` was read:
  it closes `/search/`, with the slash, and not the study pages.
- **Not asked.** PROSPERO's record page is a script that reads an internal API
  (`/PROSPERO/api/record/view/?code=`), which answers "header value undefined" without a
  `prospero-auth-token` header that the page makes from the clock; that header is the
  registry's choice of who reads its API, and it is not made here. The WHO ICTRP's web
  service is for partners under an agreement, with its costs recovered. A registration with
  either, or with ANZCTR, DRKS, jRCT and the rest, has a record copied by hand
  (`source: by-hand`, `copied_by`, `copied_on`, no digest): G12 holds it as it holds any other
  and notes once that what it says is that person's word (`registration-by-hand`). `lookup`
  never writes over a record copied by hand, nor over one it cannot read.

**What G12 holds a paper to** (`gates/registration.py`), each registration in turn:

- *That there is one to hold it to.* A study `paper.yaml` names a trial with no registration
  fails from internal-review (`registration-missing`). Where none is listed and the
  manuscript gives an NCT, ISRCTN, EU PAS or PROSPERO number, that is a warning
  (`registration-undeclared`): it may be this study's or another's, and only the author can
  say. Where one is listed, the other identifiers the manuscript gives are taken to be other
  studies', as they are in a review.
- *That it is the registration the paper says.* An identifier whose shape names no registry
  and that names none under `registry` (`registration-id-malformed`), one the manuscript
  does not give (`registration-not-in-manuscript`), one with no record
  (`registration-not-looked-up`), and one the registry does not know (`registration-unknown`)
  fail from internal-review, as a cited work the registries do not know does. A record that
  is not one, that is another registration's or that is dated in the future fails from
  internal-review too. An answer that did not come is a warning, and nothing else is said of
  that registration: nothing is known of it.
- *That it was made in advance.* The registered date is held to the study's actual start and
  the actual start of its data analysis, as the registry gives them, and to the day the first
  results were written, which is `frozen_at` of `design/plan.frozen.yaml`. First results
  written from synthetic inputs only, a dry run on simulated data, date nothing of the study:
  both emitters mark such a copy `synthetic: true`, and a registration after it is a note
  (`registration-after-dry-run`), as Basile chose in round 1 of #390. Two dates are
  compared as far as the less precise goes, so a study registered on 27 April that started in
  April may have started after it and is not said to have; a start dated after the day the
  registry was asked is a plan, and is not compared. A registration after any of them
  (`registration-late`) warns, and fails at submission unless `paper.yaml` gives the reason
  under `retrospective` and the manuscript says the study was registered retrospectively
  ("retrospectively registered", "registered retrospectively", "retrospective
  registration", "registration was retrospective", a line break between the words allowed,
  and never "registry": "a retrospective registry-based cohort" says nothing of the
  registration, round 1 of #390); then it is a note. With the reason and not the words, it is
  `registration-retrospective-unsaid`.
- *That it is the study.* A registry's interventional study for a paper whose `study_type` is
  observational, or the other way round, is `registration-design-differs`; a withdrawn
  registration is `registration-withdrawn`.
- *That the outcomes are the registered ones.* Under each registration the author quotes each
  outcome the registry holds, `registered`, in its words, with the `role` it has there and the
  planned result that reports it, `reported_as`, written as the plan's Planned results write a
  key. A quote is held word for word to the record: to a field of its role where the registry
  keeps them apart, to the fields of outcomes where it has them and to any field where it has
  none, and to the first version of an OSF registration updated since. Case, spacing, line
  breaks, compatibility forms, dashes and quotation marks are folded and nothing else. Not
  found, it is `registration-outcome-not-registered`, or `registration-outcome-added-later`
  where only the later version has it; found in the other role, `registration-outcome-role-
  changed` (a registered secondary reported as primary, or a registered primary as
  secondary; ClinicalTrials.gov's other pre-specified outcomes count as secondary ones); with no `reported_as`, the outcome is not reported, and the plan's Deviations
  section has to quote the same words (`registration-outcome-dropped`); with a key the plan
  does not list, `registration-outcome-unplanned`; with one that emits nothing quoted,
  `registration-outcome-unreported`. A change the Deviations section names by the result's
  key, as it names a planned result it drops, stands each of these down. No quote at all is
  `registration-outcomes-undeclared`.
- *That nothing registered is left out.* Where the registry lists its outcomes apart, each
  primary one has to be quoted (`registration-primary-unquoted`), and the others not quoted
  are one warning (`registration-secondary-unquoted`): a trial may register thirty, and
  report some elsewhere. A quote stands for one registered outcome only, assigned so that as
  many are covered as can be: one vague quote found in five primary outcomes covers one. Where
  the registry gives its outcomes as one text, as the EU PAS register and OSF do, neither the
  role of a quote nor whether every outcome is quoted can be read, and G12 says so once
  (`registration-roles-unchecked`).

Each finding of the last four kinds warns while the paper is drafted and fails at submission,
as Basile decided: a draft can still change, and a paper sent with a switched outcome not said
is the failure this is for. Three are less: `registration-secondary-unquoted` is a warning at
every stage, and `registration-roles-unchecked` and `registration-after-dry-run` are notes.

**What it does not decide.** That the words quoted mean the outcome the paper measures, that
the population, the exposure and the analysis are the registered ones, and that a reason given
for a change is a good one: these are the co-authors' and the panel's, read against the record
kept. A remit for the panel and the co-author checker's items that put the record beside the
Methods are the next step, not yet built.
## The data dictionary is one contract with three readers

A plan that sets out an analysis of data that do not exist yet (a survey, a chart review, a
cohort, a trial, an extraction form) has a second thing to settle before the data do:
exactly what will be collected. `design/data_dictionary.yaml` says it, one entry for each
variable: its name as the data will hold it, its label, a definition precise enough that
two people recording it from the same source record the same value, its type, its unit, its
codes or its range, the codes that mean missing, whether it is required and where it
applies, the form and the visit it belongs to, who records it and from what, the variables
it is derived from and how, the validated instrument and item it records, the standard
definition it follows (MedDRA, CTCAE, ICD-10), the reporting-checklist items that need it,
and, where nothing in the plan needs it, the reason it is collected. The same file describes
data that already exist: a dataset in several tables names them (`datasets`), and a name may
hold capitals or dots, since an existing dataset's columns do.

Three readers take it as it is written. G12 holds it to the plan. The data-quality checks
hold the collected data to it: its `study_period`, `pattern`, `within_study_period` and
`rules` (an order between dates, a set of variables unique per row, or a rule the author's
script tests) are for them, and were agreed with that work so that the schema changes once.
And the export gives it to whoever builds the form. One loader serves all three,
`contracts/dictionary.py`, and what it accepts is what all three trust.

**A dictionary that does not read fails, at every stage.** G12 warns and never blocks, but
a malformed contract is not a plan with a gap in it: a data check that read a variable's
codes from the wrong list, or an export that wrote them, would be worse than none. The
schema says the shape; the loader says what a schema cannot, each as `dictionary-invalid`
at its line: a name or an id given twice, a reference to a form, a list of codes, an
instrument, a dataset or a variable that is not there, codes on a type that has none, a
binary variable without two, a code given twice or as both a value and a missing code, a
range on a type that has none or a bound its type cannot read, a pattern that does not
compile, a condition on a variable with no codes. It is said once, by G12; the other readers
are handed nothing and say nothing of the file's shape. A gap in the plan is not a fault of
the file: a categorical variable whose codes are not decided yet, or a derived variable whose
inputs are not in the dictionary, reads, and is G12's to warn of. A project with no
dictionary is not asked for one.

**A value is compared as text, so YAML may not read it first.** `1` and `"1"` are one code.
PyYAML reads some plain values as something else before any check sees them: `010` as the
number 8, `8:30` as 510, `1_000` as 1000, an unquoted `No` or `off` as false. A code `010`
read as 8 would never match the data's "010", and `label: No` would fail the schema with
"False is not of type 'string'". Each is refused at its line with the words to write
instead, in quotes, and the schema's own finding on that line is left out as the same
fault said less usefully. Where the value is a yes or a no, `required: yes`, the word means
what it says and is read (round 1 of #382). A code written `1.0` or `+1` is refused too:
JSON Schema takes the first for an integer, and as text the two are "1.0" and "1". A number
written as it reads, `200.0` or `-0.5`, is left alone. And a key given twice in one mapping
is refused at the second: YAML keeps the last without a word, so a code list given twice
under one name handed its second codes to every variable that named it (round 1 of #382).
A variable that gives both `values` and a `code_list` is refused for the same reason.

**The dictionary is held to the plan, both ways.** Every variable the analysis uses is to be
collected, with its definition, and nothing collected that nothing needs (Basile,
2026-10-20). So G12 reads the plan for the variables it names, and the plan names one by
writing it in backticks exactly as the dictionary names it, `age`, anywhere outside its
Deviations section and the sections under it (Basile chose this of three ways, 2026-10-21:
names read from the Planned results alone would have left a covariate named only in the
Analysis unchecked, and a list of uses kept in each entry would have been the same fact in
two files). A code span that is a dictionary name is a use of it, a dotted one included. A
span that reads as a variable's name, letters, digits and underscores from a letter, and
that the dictionary lacks is `plan-variable-undefined`, at its first mention; where the
dictionary has the name in another case, the hint says so. Code is written so that it does
not read as a name, `glm()` or `stats::glm`; a result's key has a dot; nine values, `NA`, `NULL`,
`TRUE`, `FALSE`, `None`, `True`, `False`, `NaN` and `Inf`, are not read; nor is what
masking hides, a fence or a comment. A heading that names both the planned results and a
change is the Deviations where the change comes first, as the list is read. The plan's
title is not its Deviations: "Statistical analysis plan (amendment 2)" heads the plan
(round 1). The title is a first heading at level 1 with a deeper one after it, whatever
follows, so an appendix at its level leaves it a title; a first heading at level 2 is a
section, so a plan with no title that opens with "## Amendment history" is not read there
(round 2; Basile chose the level, 2026-10-21). In the other direction, an entry is needed
where the plan names it, where
a variable the plan needs is derived from it or asked under it (`applies_if`), again and
again, where it names a reporting-checklist item, or where it gives a reason, and so are the
inputs and the condition of an entry kept for an item or a reason (round 1); any other is
`dictionary-entry-unused`. A reporting item is looked for in the guideline's checklist where
the project holds one (`dictionary-reporting-item-unknown`), and is a note where it does
not. Whatever the plan, an entry that leaves its codes undecided, a derivation without its
inputs or inputs without it, an input the dictionary lacks, or a derivation that ends in
itself, is said. All of these warn at every stage, as the rest of G12 does (Basile,
2026-10-21); without a plan only the last group is asked. The `data-dictionary` skill
drafts the dictionary with the author from the plan, and names a validated instrument and
its licence rather than writing its items. The reading is held over generated plans
(`plan variables` in `tests/readings.py`), one section of every kind in each.

**The dictionary is written out for whoever builds the form, and is not changed by it.**
`manuscript-guard dictionary` writes three copies of it, each a function of the file alone
and written again whenever it changes (Basile asked for the export with the rest,
2026-10-21). `--redcap` is REDCap's data dictionary, the CSV its Online Designer imports:
the eighteen columns of its template in its order (as REDCap writes them in a dictionary it
