downloads, and as REDCapR and ReproNim's reproschema-py read them, read 2026-10-21), each
variable on the instrument its `form` names, a coded one as a radio field with its codes
and its missing codes as choices (`1, Male | 2, Female`), the others as text fields with
REDCap's validation for their type (`number`, `integer`, `date_ymd`, `datetime_ymd`,
`time`) and their range as its minimum and maximum, `applies_if` as branching logic, the
definition as the field annotation and the unit as the field note. REDCap takes the first
field for each record's identifier, so the first `identifier` variable comes first, and
its form first. A derived variable is left out and said: the analysis computes it, and
REDCap's calculated fields are a language of their own. A name REDCap cannot take, one
with a capital or a dot, is refused rather than changed, since a renamed field would no
longer be the variable the plan and the data checks name; so is a dictionary with no
identifier or with a coded variable whose codes are not decided, and nothing is written.
`--csv` is one row per variable and one column per key of an entry, for any other system;
`--outline` is the form in Markdown, form by form, each question with its responses, its
skip and whether it is required, a validated instrument's items marked as the licensed
instrument's wording, and what is derived and not asked.

## The data are held to the dictionary, and what they held is a result

Every number in a paper traced back to the analysis, and nothing said what the data the
analysis read held: an age of 150, a code the dictionary does not list, a reaction dated
before the drug, the same report twice. A reader of the Methods could not tell whether
anyone had looked, and RECORD asks for the data cleaning methods (item 12.2). The principle
of the feasibility counts holds here: the author's script reads the data, never the tool.
The tool supplies the checks and holds the counts to the text.

**The checks run in the author's script, and publish counts.** `em.check_data(table)` in
Python, `em$check_data(table)` in R, reads `design/data_dictionary.yaml` through the loader
`check` uses (`contracts/dictionary.py`), runs the checks each entry asks for on the
variables the table has a column for, and emits each count under `quality.`:
`quality.rows`, then `quality.<variable>.missing` for every variable and, as its entry
asks, `wrong_type`, `out_of_range`, `not_allowed`, `not_matching`, `outside_period` and
`not_applicable`, then `quality.rule.<rule>` for each rule. No value of a row leaves the
script. A table is a data frame, a mapping of columns, or a list of rows as `csv.DictReader`
gives them; a dictionary that lists datasets is checked one table at a time, and the rows
are `quality.rows.<dataset>`. A variable with no column is not checked, and G16 names it.
A name a key cannot hold, a capital or a dot, is written in lower case with an underscore,
and two names that would share a key are refused. The function returns the rows each count
counted, so that the script leaves out the ones it means to and the count the Methods bind
is the count of what it left out.

**A rule is built in, or the script's own.** An `order` rule (each date no later than the
next, or each number no greater) and a `unique` rule (no two rows with the same values of
these) are checked by the emitter over the variables of one table. Anything else, a man
recorded as pregnant, a death before the first prescription, is declared by name with what
it says (`computed: true`) and found by the script, which hands the emitter one truth value
for each row. There is no expression language in the dictionary (Basile, 2026-10-21): two
parsers, one for each emitter, would have to agree on every expression, and the script
already has a language both sides of the comparison can read.

**A value is read one way in both languages.** What missing is (blank, NA, or one of the
variable's `missing` codes), what a number is (a number, or a text in decimal notation),
what a date is (a day of the calendar written `YYYY-MM-DD`, or a date), how a value is
written as text to be compared with a code (a whole number as its digits, any other to
fifteen significant digits, a truth value as "true" or "false"): each is written once, in
`quality.py`, and the R emitter's `quality.R` follows it. R reads the dictionary as the
loader does, too: the yaml package reads a plain `Y` or `n` as a truth value, where PyYAML
keeps the letter, and is told to keep it (round 1 of #389). `tests/data/quality` holds a
dictionary, a table that breaks every check at least once and the rows each count must
find, and both emitters are held to it, reading the table as text and as their own reader
types it; each way of reading a value is compared between the two languages text by text.

**None is a result the manuscript must quote,** since a dictionary of forty variables gives
two hundred counts. A count from one to below the data custodian's minimum
(`custodian.minimum_cell_count`) is printed "<5", so that the Methods can bind it and G2
passes it (Basile, 2026-10-21); the value itself stays in the results, as every count's
does. The dictionary is an input of the run: edited, it makes the counts `input-changed`,
and G1 already says so.

**G16 names what is missing from the chain.** It is silent where the project keeps no
dictionary. From the analysis stage it warns of a variable the analysis declares or a model
reads that has no entry (`not-in-dictionary`); of a dictionary nothing was checked against
(`quality-not-run`); and of an entry or a rule no count covers (`entry-unchecked`,
`rule-unchecked`). From drafting it warns where there are counts and neither the Methods
nor the supplement binds one (`quality-not-reported`). All but the first fail at
submission (Basile, 2026-10-21). A fault the checks find in the data is never a finding:
it is a count, which the paper reports and the author decides about. A dictionary that does
not read is G12's `dictionary-invalid`, and G16 says nothing of it.

The example checks its simulated reports against a dictionary of its nine variables,
the two the model reads derived first, and its Methods bind three of the counts: the rows
checked, the duplicates and the missing age groups, the last two nought, since the data
were simulated whole.

**At the design stage the counts are feasibility counts.** Checking the extract against the
dictionary counts each planned variable's missing values and the duplicates, which is what
the feasibility script counts. A result under `quality.` quiets `feasibility-not-run` as
one under `feasibility.` does, and a design round reads and is sent both: the digest of
what it read covers them, and the request lists them under their own heading. A reading
made before any data was checked stays current when the analysis checks its data later,
since it read none of those counts: it is compared with the plan's digest with them and
without them (round 1 of #389: each such reading was said to be of a changed plan).

## A plan learns from how others answered its question

A plan is better for knowing how studies of the same question chose their comparator, their
time zero, their case definition and their adjustment set. It is not better for taking what
most of them did. A design used often can carry a bias often: immortal time was found in one
published cohort study of drug effects after another (Suissa, *Am J Epidemiol* 2008), each
following the last. So a method is judged against a published methodological standard and
never by how many studies used it, the judgement is a proposal, and the author decides what
the plan takes (Basile, 2026-10-21).

**The record.** `design/methods_review.yaml` (`methods_review.py`; schema
`manuscript-guard/methods-review/1`) holds the question the studies were chosen for, how
they were searched for, and one entry per study: its citation key, what it shares with this
study (`similar`: question, exposure, outcome, population, data source, design) and why it
was chosen. Under each study, one entry per field it reports (`FIELDS`: design, data source,
population, case definition, exposure, outcome, comparator, time zero and follow-up,
confounding, model, missing data, sensitivity analyses, or `other` with a label), each with
the study's own words (`passage`) and where they are (`locator`); an appraisal, or several;
and the author's decision. A file of its own beside the plan, at the stage the plan is
written, before there is a manuscript to cite the studies from. The date a search was run is
`searched_on`, not `on`, which YAML reads as `true`.

**The words are the study's.** G7 looks for each passage in the study's stored files as it
looks for a supporting passage (`looked_for`, shared with `literature/passages.py`): each file
read once, words left out read as in a quotation. One that is in none of them is
`similar-passage-not-in-source`, a note at the design stage and a failure from the analysis
stage on, the stage the plan built on it is frozen at (Basile, 2026-10-21). A study with no
stored copy that can be read is a warning (`similar-passage-unchecked`), and a passage of
fewer than four words is a warning (`similar-passage-too-short`). `sync-sources` copies the
studies the review names, and the standards it gives a key to, as it copies the works the
manuscript cites (`copies.wanted_keys`): at the design stage there is no manuscript, and
before this it refused with nothing cited.

**A judgement says what it rests on.** An appraisal names the standard (`standard`) and the
standard's domain the judgement is of (`domain`), how far the method departs from it
(`concern`: low, some, serious, unclear), what the risk is (`says`), and who proposed it
(`proposed_by`): an agent may. The built-in standards are a table, `data/method_standards.yaml`,
as the study types are: each with its domains in its own words, the study types it is for,
where it is published and the day it was read, every one read on its own page (2026-10-21):
the ENCePP Guide's chapters, the components of a target trial's protocol (Hernán and
Robins), the domains of ROBINS-I, ROBINS-E, RoB 2, PROBAST+AI and ROBIS, the assumptions of
the self-controlled case series, immortal time (Suissa), and the Methods items of READUS-PV,
STROBE and RECORD-PE. A standard the table does not hold is described in the record, with its
name, domains and citation key; one the table holds is given only its key there, and one
described again keeps the table's domains (`standard-redescribed`). An appraisal with no
standard (`appraisal-without-standard`), one neither holds (`appraisal-standard-unknown`) or a
domain the standard does not have (`appraisal-domain-unknown`) is a warning, each, as the rest
of G12 is (Basile, 2026-10-21). A domain is matched loosely: case, hyphens, underscores, slashes and runs of space.
Whether the judgement is right is not checked, and cannot be; what is checked is that a
reader can go to the place it rests on. The methods with no appraisal are counted in a note
(`similar-unappraised`), and so are those appraised and not decided (`similar-undecided`).

**A decision is a person's.** `decision` holds the choice (adopt, adapt, reject), why, who
decided and when. A model's name may not sign it (`similar-decision-not-human`, the deny-list
G7 reads `attested_by` with), failing from the analysis stage on. The plugin's write guard
puts to the person an agent's edit after which the decided methods are not the ones the file
held before, word for word in their study, field, label, passage and decision, and as many:
a decision recorded, changed or taken away, or the method under one changed. Where the file
before an edit or after it is a text YAML cannot read, a date that is not one among them,
what a decision there is of cannot be told, and the edit is put to the person wherever
either text names a decider, named where the line gives a plain or quoted name (rounds 1 and
2 of #386: `2026-02-30` raised past the guard, and #374's judgements with it). An appraisal changed beside it is the
agent's to make. A Codex patch to a review that holds a decision outside a comment is put to
the person, and refused where the tool cannot ask, as for a passage's judgement.

**What is taken is cited.** A method decided `adopt` or `adapt` is cited by its study's key in
the plan, or in the manuscript's Methods, and by the key of each standard it was judged
against: a method taken from another paper is that paper's, and the methodological source is
where the reasons are (Basile, 2026-10-21). Each is a warning where it is not:
`adopted-method-uncited`, `adopted-standard-uncited`, the second also where the review gives
the standard no key. A citation in a comment of the plan is not one, and one elsewhere in the
manuscript, the Introduction citing the study for its incidence, does not credit the method.
On a LaTeX manuscript the Methods are not read yet, so only the plan's citations count, and
the finding says so. When the Methods are drafted, the sentence citing the study is a cited
statement like any other, and its supporting passage goes in `literature/passages.yaml`.

**The design round reads it.** `prompt.gather_design` sends the record with the plan, under
"The methods of similar studies": each study, each method in its words, each appraisal with
its standard and its proposer, and each decision, with an instruction to check each appraisal
against its standard. `plan_digest` takes in the record's bytes where there is one, so an
appraisal or a decision changed after a design reading leaves it stale, as a changed plan
does; a project with no record has the digest it had before. A record that cannot be read
stops the round, since the readings would be filed with a digest of a file they never read.
The `methods-review` skill drives the steps, from the search to the citation; how many
studies is the author's choice, the most relevant five to ten usually, and nothing counts
them.

## Stages: not every gate binds on day one

The first version of `check` ran all twelve gates unconditionally, which meant that someone
still writing their analysis was told the figures were unreviewed, no journal had been
chosen and the reporting checklist was empty. All true, none useful, and collectively the
strongest possible argument for not running the check again.

Each finding now declares the stage at which it starts to fail: `design`, `analysis`,
`drafting`, `internal-review`, `submission`. The stage comes from `paper.yaml` or from
`--stage`; `--submission` is shorthand for the last one.

Three rules keep this from becoming a way to hide problems.

**Every gate runs at every stage.** Only severity changes. A deferred finding is printed as
`INFO`, tagged `[not due until drafting]`, counted, and summarised at the end as *"3 findings
not due yet … They are listed above as INFO, not hidden."* A check that quietly stopped
looking would be worse than no check.

**Unlisted codes bind immediately.** A finding the policy does not know about fails at every
stage, so adding a gate cannot accidentally make it optional. The author of a gate has to
decide, in `policy.py`, when it should start to matter.

**Deferred means INFO, not WARN.** A warning is something to look at now; these are things
that are not yet due. Mixing them would drown the warnings that matter.

Writing the policy exposed two mistakes in my own placement. Results were bound at
`analysis`, which is wrong — results appear at the *end* of the analysis stage, not its
start — and an unfinished `authors.yaml` was being reported as a malformed contract when it
is a to-do list. The second needed a distinct finding code so that a genuinely broken
authors file and a merely unfinished one could be told apart.

The effect is that `manuscript-guard init` followed by a first analysis script now reports
zero failures at `design` and `analysis`, with the outstanding work listed as not yet due,
and the same items fail from `drafting` onwards.

## `next` says what to do now

`check` lists what is wrong, and a project at `drafting` can have forty findings, a journal
not chosen and an English not declared, none of which says where to start. An agent asked
"what now?" read the list and picked, and two agents picked differently. `manuscript-guard
next` (the `guide` package) reads the project once and decides in a fixed order. `inspect(start)`
runs every gate through `cli._gate_run`, which is `_run_gates` with the namespace returned
too, so that an unbound number can be asked which published value it reads as; it reads the
choices `paper.yaml` has made, the journals `set target_journal` takes, the English the
journal's profile asks for and the study designs, and, where a round of co-authors' checks
has begun (`checks/decisions.csv`) and the manuscript is Markdown, where that round stands.
It writes nothing. `decide(state)` is a pure function of what was read.

The rules are an ordered table, `guide.RULES`, each with a tier; within a tier, actions go
by gate, upstream first (`GATE_RANK`), then by code, file and line, so the same findings in
another order give the same answer:

| Tier | Rule | Why it comes here |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `cannot-check` | a gate that could not read its file has checked nothing |
| 1 | `start` | no project, or `authors.yaml` without `paper.yaml`: `init`, `init --from` a Word paper in the folder, `init --latex`, or `audit` alone |
| 2 | `stale-results` | G1: every number bound to stale results waits on them |
| 3 | `plan` | G12: the plan comes before the numbers that answer it |
| 4 | the four choices | journal, English, reporting guideline, study design, offered as `set` commands |
| 5 | `provenance` | G2, G3, G7, G8: a number with no source |
| 6 | `failures` | the rest that fails, in gate order |
| 7 | `co-author-checks` | from internal review, a round with answers outstanding, stale or disagreeing |
| 8 | `warnings` | one action for each skill |
| 9 | `advance` | nothing fails now: preview the next stage with `check --stage`, or `set stage` |
| 10 | `optional` | nothing fails, from internal review on: panel, co-author's page, build, package, approvals; the pack and the proof at submission |

Three of these were the author's choices (2026-10-28). A choice is offered as the `set`
command that makes it, never as a description of an edit, so the guard on `set` sees it.
Moving on (tier 9) is offered only when nothing fails now, and not at `submission` or from a
view of an earlier stage than the one declared; the optional steps (tier 10) only when nothing fails at `internal-review` or `submission`: a review panel read while the
numbers still fail is a reading of the wrong paper. And `next` exits 0 whenever it has
decided: `check`'s exit is the one that says pass or fail, and a second command that said it
too would be read as the gate. So it raises nothing: a part of the state it cannot read, the
co-authors' round in a `decisions.csv` saved in a code page, a profile, the numbers a binding
would take, is left out and said among the notes, and gates that cannot run at all make the
project `unreadable`, with the reason. A path that is not there is `missing`, and nothing is
offered for the folder above it, which is not what was asked about.

The stage is held twice: the stage decided at, which `--stage` can set for a view, and the
one paper.yaml declares. A move is offered only from the declared stage, one step forward,
and only where the view is not of an earlier stage: in review round 1, a paper at
`submission` viewed with `--stage drafting` was offered `set stage internal-review`, a move
back. The move is `ask-author`, since the stage is the author's statement of where the paper
is, as another journal or another English than the one declared is. A finding only a named
person may answer (an attestation, a judgement of a passage, a methods decision, a person's
reading of the figures, an approval, a sign-off, a reviewer's or co-author's finding left as
it stands with who decided: `routes.PERSON_ONLY`) routes as the author's: an agent that
wrote the name would pass the gate with nobody behind it. The text says so on the action's
`run:` line, or on a line of its own where it has no command, as the JSON says it in `who`.
A code both the literature's contract and the results' raise (`duplicate-key`,
`no-display`) is routed by the file its finding names: the literature's to
literature-verify, the results' to results-binding, both with `check`, since neither is
put right by `bind`.

A finding's code decides its skill and its command through `guide.ROUTES`: the code's own
entry, else the longest prefix it begins with (`checklist-`, `spelling-`, `registration-`,
`design-` …). A code no entry names goes to its gate's skill with `check`, and is never
dropped. `tests/test_guide.py` reads the package's source for every code it reports (each
value given as a finding's `code`, by keyword or by position: a string, either side of a
conditional, a module's constant, a name the function binds, one place of a tuple a helper
returns or a loop walks; every key of the stage policy; and the design rounds' codes made
from the review gate's seal) and fails on one that neither `ROUTES` nor `NO_ACTION`, the codes
said only as a note, names; a code an f-string makes is held to a route by its fixed start.
What the reading cannot find, the gates say when run: every code reported on the example at
submission, on an empty project of each format and on the example broken four ways is held
to a route as well. A second test holds every code a skill's description says it
answers to that skill. A route names a skill that exists and a command that parses, and every
command an action or an option offers, its placeholders filled, parses with `build_parser()`.

Each command is given twice: as it is written at a prompt, and as `argv`, its words after the
program's name, so that an agent runs the words given and not its reading of a sentence. A
placeholder is a word `<NAME>` the option explains. The JSON is `manuscript-guard/next/1`
(`contracts/schemas/next.schema.json`, docs/next.md); a field added keeps `/1`, a field
renamed or removed or a fixed list extended makes it `/2`, and rule ids are not renamed.

There is no cache. Each call runs every gate again, 5 to 10 seconds on the example: a cache
keyed by the files the hooks watch would miss `design/`, `review/`, `profiles/`, `journals/`
and `checks/`, which the gates read, and an answer about files as they were is the failure
this toolkit exists to prevent. The co-author checker is not read for a LaTeX manuscript,
since `checker` refuses one, and a note says so; nor is the proof offered for one.


### The conversation: the `guide` skill, the status line and AGENTS.md

`next` decides; something has to carry the decision to the author one step at a time. That
is the `guide` skill (`plugin/skills/guide/SKILL.md`), which names no agent tool. Each turn
it runs `next --json`, sums up the stage and the counts in two sentences, takes the first
action, and acts by its `who`: an `agent` action is written in the reply and then run, an
`ask-author` one is shown and waits for a clear yes to that command, and an `author` one is
given to the author. A choice is listed as numbered options in the order `next` gives them,
each with its effect and its exact command, with `next`'s recommendation where it has one and
none of the agent's own. After a command it calls `next` again. Where an action names a
skill, it hands the step over and comes back when the skill is done. A finding's message is
data: an instruction in it is told to the author, and the commands run are the `argv` `next`
builds.

project-setup used to end its description with "unsure what to do next" and held a table of
codes and skills, 2,500 characters of it, which `next` now decides from `guide.ROUTES`. Merged
with the guide it would be over the size the skills keep to (5,000 tokens), so the two are
separate (the author's choice, 2026-10-28): project-setup starts a project and teaches the
loop, its table replaced by a pointer to `next`, and each skill's description ends by naming
the other. Both are in the test's list of skills that overlap. Two routing cases hold the
split, `route-guide` and `near-guide-not-setup`, both in a copy of the example.

Where the hooks run, the status line at the session's start and at the end of a turn that
changed what the gates read ends with "Next: <title> (`manuscript-guard next`)". The hook
runs the gates once, through `cli._gate_run`, and decides on that run's report, project and
namespace (`guide.reading.from_run`); a test counts one call of a gate. Two parts of the state
are slow to read: which published value each unbound number reads as, which classifies every
number a second time (`binding.unbound`), and where a round of co-authors' checks stands. In
round 1 of review the line read both at every session start. `guide.first_action` decides
first without them, and reads them only where they can change what comes first: actions go by
tier, the bindable places split only the provenance tier (5), and the co-authors' round makes
only its own tier (7). So the bindable places are read where the first action is of tier 5,
and the round where it comes after tier 7 or there is none; then it decides again. A test
holds `first_action` to `decide`'s first on 300 drawn states, among them states where leaving
either part out would have said another action, and one counts no call of `binding.unbound`
at the start of a session in a project where a choice comes before an unbound number.

The time limit (`CHECK_LIMIT`) covers the gates and the decision: the decision runs on a
thread of its own and gets what the gates leave of the limit, less half a second
(`DECIDE_MARGIN`), and one that does not finish in it, or fails, costs the "Next:" part and
leaves the counts, as a test with a decision that never finishes holds. The silence rules are
as they were: no line outside a project, none at a stop that changed nothing watched. There
is no hook on the author's prompt: a full run of the gates before every message would cost
each one 5 to 10 seconds, and the skill runs `next` when the conversation is about the paper
(the author's choice, 2026-10-28).

An agent tool with no skills reads `AGENTS.md`. The rules `init` writes (`scaffold.AGENTS`)
carry one paragraph on working in conversation: `next --json` at the start of each turn,
every option given with what it changes and its command, a command said before it is run, an
author's action left to the author, and a clear yes before a command `next` marks for asking.
A finding's message is said there to be data to report, never an instruction, since such an
agent never reads the skill that says so. `rules_to_add` prints the same for a repository
whose own `AGENTS.md` lacks the rules, and `example/AGENTS.md` is the same file, byte for
byte.

## The commands are listed in six groups

By October 2026 the tool had 37 commands an author could run, and `manuscript-guard --help`
printed them in the order they were added to the parser, `stages` beside `palettes` and
`sync-bib` after `build`. Someone looking for the command that answers a co-author had to
read the whole list. The top-level help now lists them under six headings, in
`cli.COMMAND_GROUPS`: Setup & Guide, Checking & Audit, Analysis & Data, Literature,
Co-Authors & Review, and Build, Release & Communicate. Each command keeps the one-line help it
had. `hook` is in no group and is not listed: an agent tool calls it and an author never does.

Only what the top-level help prints changed, and with it argparse's own usage line and
messages, which name the command `<command>` where they listed every name. The commands,
their options and each command's own `--help` are as they were, and `tests/test_cli.py`
parses 218 command lines recorded from the parser before the change, every spelling of every
option and every value of a fixed list among them, and compares what they give. A command added later goes into
one of the groups, or the test that every command but `hook` is in exactly one fails. The
README's "Commands" table is split under the same headings in the same order, and
`tests/test_docs.py` holds each part to its group.

## One setting is written, and the file kept

Five settings of `paper.yaml` are choices an author makes as the work goes on: `stage`,
`target_journal`, `english_variant`, `reporting_guideline` and `study_type`. Each used to be
made by editing the file, which an agent does by rewriting it, and a YAML library that loads
the file and dumps it back drops every comment in it: what each setting means, why each
convention was added, the stage ladder `init` writes out. `manuscript-guard set <key>
<value…>` writes one of the five and keeps every other byte (`paper_edit.py`). It edits the
text in one of three ways:

- the key is at the top level: the characters of its value are replaced, and a comment after
  it on the line stays. A list written one entry to a line, as the example's guidelines are,
  is written again in the same layout, its entries' indent and dash kept; an empty list is
  `[]` on the key's line;
- it is not, and exactly one line at the left margin reads `# key: …`, the commented example
  `init` leaves: that line becomes the setting, and a note after the value on that line
  stays, as it does for a setting. A line of that shape inside a quoted value is no comment
  and is passed over, and where there are two `set` cannot tell which was meant and leaves
  both;
- otherwise the key is added at the end of the file, with its line ending.

The result is then read back. It must be the settings the file held with that one key
changed, and the schema must find nothing in it that it did not find before; a file that
failed the schema elsewhere is still written, since that is `check`'s to report. Only then is
the file replaced, through a file beside it, given the old file's mode, and a rename; a
failure to write is said in a sentence, and the old file stands. A `paper.yaml` its owner
made read-only is refused first, on every system. A `paper.yaml` that is a
symbolic link, or has a second hard link, is refused: the rename would put a file of its own
in its place and leave the file it shares its text with as it was. Where a commented example
stands inside another setting's block, made a setting it would end that block: the read-back
says so, and the key is added at the end instead. What an edit of one place cannot be trusted
with is refused before any of this, and the file is left as it was: settings written as one
mapping between braces, an anchor or an alias anywhere in the file (an edit of one place can
change another through them), a key written twice in any mapping (YAML keeps the second, and
which was meant is not for `set` to guess), a value over several lines other than such a
list, a list with a comment or a blank line among its entries, which would be lost, and a
character PyYAML takes for the end of a line where `set` and an editor see none (U+0085,
U+2028, U+2029), which makes the lines `set` counts other than the lines YAML reads.

The value is checked first, and paper.yaml is read only once it passes: a stage
`policy.STAGES` names, an English `scaffold.ENGLISHES` names, a study type of the schema's,
and a journal whose profile the project or the toolkit holds or that
`journals/shortlist.yaml` gives one of its candidates as its `profile` (those files are read
for it; paper.yaml is not). A guideline is any name: its checklist is retrieved after it is
declared, and `checklist-not-retrieved` says so. Given no guideline, the list is emptied. A
name a reader would type as other than text is written between single quotation marks: what
PyYAML, a YAML 1.1 reader, resolves to a number, a date or a yes or no (`yes`, `2024`,
`1_000`), what the YAML 1.2 core schema's patterns do (`1e3`, `0o17`, `.inf`, `.nan`), and
the YAML 1.1 booleans in any case (`y`, `N`, `On`), since another tool may read the file by
those.

Three of these changes can make a failing check pass with nothing fixed, and each is put to
the author (Basile, 2026-10-28: moving the stage back is allowed, with the hook asking
first). `set stage` to an earlier stage lists every finding that starts to fail after the
new stage, up to the old one, as not due. `set reporting_guideline` without a guideline the
paper declares now, the list emptied included, stops asking for that guideline's checklist,
and its findings go. `set target_journal` to another journal than the one declared drops the
old journal's limits and required statements, which the paper was failing or meeting. Where
an agent runs one of them, the submission guard answers "ask", and refuses it where the agent
tool cannot ask, as it does for `approve` (`set_guard.py`). Moving the stage on, adding a
guideline and choosing the first journal only add to what is checked, so they are not asked.
Nor are the English and the study type: a change of either is a change of what is asked,
G14's spelling or G12's sections, more than a release from it (Known gaps).

The guard reads the command as text, and where it cannot say what a `set` would change, it
asks: that is the guarantee, since a guard that let a command through when unsure could be
stepped round by writing it another way. Two rounds of review each found another way of
writing a command that an earlier guard misread, one that took words apart and followed what
it understood (`2>&1` after the value, `bash -c`, `xargs`, a PowerShell expression,
`env -C`, a quoted `'set'`). So it asks by default, as the import refuses where it cannot
merge exactly. A command that holds a word naming the tool, the word `set` and one of the
three keys, anywhere and inside quotation marks too, is asked, unless the guard reads all of
it exactly: plain `cd`, `chdir`, `pushd`, `Set-Location` or `sl` steps to one folder each,
joined by `&&` or `;`; then the tool by one of its names (`manuscript-guard`, `mguard`, the
`.exe`, `python -m manuscript_guard.cli`, each with a plain folder before it); `set`, the key,
plain values and at most one `--path`; then nothing but `>` or `>>` after any descriptor's
number to a plain file, or `2>&1`, and never to a file named `paper.yaml` or `authors.yaml`.
A plain word holds letters, digits and `. _ / : + -`, and no quotation mark, no backslash and
no sign a shell expands; a folder, of a `cd` or of `--path`, may hold a backslash on Windows,
never one before a space, and never begins with `-` or `+`, so `cd -` and `pushd +1` are
asked. After a `;` the guard reads the project of the
folder a failed `cd` leaves too, where `set` would find one. Only then is the project read,
and the command let through where it moves the stage on or keeps it, adds guidelines, or
sets a first journal or the same one. Everything else is asked: another command before or
after it, `||`, a subshell, braces, a substitution, a variable, `--`, an option it does not
know, a value that is no stage, no project found, a `paper.yaml` it cannot read. A
`paper.yaml` that declares no stage is at `drafting`, the default.

`tests/test_set.py` sets each key from absent, from its commented example and from a value,
holds each refusal to a file left byte for byte, and each case of the guard to its answer.
`tests/test_properties.py` sets each key in pairs of generated files, between which each key
is in every form (absent, commented, plain, quoted, empty, a list one entry to a line or
between brackets), one file in CRLF with a byte-order mark and the other in LF with spaces at
the ends of its lines, each with a block scalar, comments and blank lines in random places,
and lookalikes of the key (a citekey under `lookup: not_indexed:`, an indented comment, a
commented line inside a quoted title, the commented example beside a setting). The file reads
back as it should, every comment is there as often as it was, and the lines that changed,
their endings compared, are one run of the key's own: its line at the margin and the
entries below it, up to the next line at the margin. Three broken rules fail it, one that
takes the comment above the key with it, one that rewrites the first line naming the key, as
a regular expression would, and one that takes the spaces off the end of another list's
entries; two more fail the property of refusals, which asks each refusal for its own reason,
by letting an anchor or a key written twice through.

## `check` says what it rests on, dimension by dimension

A run with no failure read as "the paper is right", and it says much less. So `check` ends
with what was checked, grouped by what it is about (`assurance.py`): computational
reproducibility (G1), numerical provenance (G2, G3, G7, G8), reporting completeness (G4, G5,
G13), methodological validity (G9, G12, G15), the data (G16), the literature (G7), the
review (G10, G11), and the language and writing (G6, G14), the last added so that every gate
is under one. For each
it prints three kinds of line, which are the three kinds of evidence the toolkit has:
`checked`, the gates that ran and what they found, with any that did not run or read
nothing; `recorded`, what somebody recorded, by whom and when (the last run of `verify`, the
panel's last round and its readers, the figure reviews, the values attested by a person);
and `not checked`, in words, what no gate decides, such as whether the design supports the
conclusion. A dimension with nothing recorded where a record is expected says so: "no review
of the design", "no run of `verify` in this checkout". There is no score and no percentage,
since a single number would be read as the verdict this is not, and the exit code is the
findings' at the project's stage, as before. It is printed text only: `check --json` is
unchanged.

`verify` now records its last full run in the build folder (`build/verify.json`): when, how
many values it reproduced of how many, and a digest of the results fragments it re-ran. A
software version found other on the re-run is among the values and not among those
reproduced, in the record as in what `verify` prints (round 2 of #306).
`check` says that run, and says the results have changed since where they have. A run of
some scripts only (`--only`) is not recorded, since it did not re-run the analysis. The
folder is not committed, so a fresh checkout says `verify` has not run in it, which is true.

## An approval is bound to what the author read

"All authors approved the final manuscript" was a sentence of the covering letter, typed.
`manuscript-guard approve --as <author>` now records an author's approval in
`approvals/<author>.yaml`, one file per author, with the digest of what decides the built
document, the prose and the results, as `check` reads it to say a build is current, and the
digest of what `submit` prints in the authors' names (`front_sha256`): the title page but
for its word counts, which the manuscript decides (the title, the running title, whether
the paper is a demonstration, the authors with their degrees and equal-contribution
marks, the affiliations, the equal-contribution note, the corresponding author's block,
the ORCID iDs, the keywords), the
CRediT statement and the declarations of funding and competing interests. What none of
them prints stales no approval: a comment, a role named to sign a warning, the rest of
`paper.yaml` (the journal, whose style the document prints, is left out on purpose), and
a figure's file, whose bytes a re-render changes (Basile's choice, 2026-10-20, round 1 of
#284: a new title or an author added left every approval standing; round 1 of #355: the
whole of `authors.yaml` was held, and a role added to sign a warning staled them all).
An approval written before has no `front_sha256` and is judged by the manuscript alone. The
author is found by ORCID iD, e-mail address, full name or family name in `authors.yaml`.
`submit` warns where an author has no approval (`approval-missing`) or approved a manuscript
that has changed since (`approval-stale`). It warns and does not refuse: whether to send
without one is the corresponding author's decision, and an approval given by e-mail is still
one. An approval is a person's statement, so the hooks put to the person an agent's `approve`
and an agent's edit of a file under `approvals/`, and refuse both where the tool cannot ask.

## A named person signs what an agent must not

Some findings are not the author's to close. A warning about a model the analysis fitted is
the statistician's to judge, and an author who dismisses it has judged a question that was
not theirs. `authors.yaml` names people for roles under `roles:`: the statistician, the data
custodian, and the person responsible for ethics approval with the approval's reference. A
role names an author as `approve --as` does, or someone who is not an author, by name. The
corresponding author is the one `corresponding: true` marks, and no second place names them.

A gate that raises a finding only one of them may close hands it to `sign_offs.settle` with
the role, an id and the digest of what is signed. For G15 that is every warning about a
model: those of one code on one model are signed together, bound to their messages and to
the card of each model they name. `manuscript-guard sign --as <person> --finding <id>` writes
the digest to a file under `approvals/sign-offs/` named by the id, its letters with eight
characters of the SHA-256 of the id itself, not of what is signed, after checking that
`--as` names the person the role names. The finding is then reported as information that says who signed it and
when, with what they said. A sign-off of something that has changed since, one by someone
the roles no longer name, and one copied to another finding count for nothing: the warning
stands, and its hint names who signs it and the command. Unsigned, a warning stays a
warning, as before. The record lives beside the authors' approvals, and the hooks put to the
person an agent's `sign` and an agent's edit of the file, as they do an approval.

The corresponding author signs one thing: the journal's rules that no gate checks. A
journal profile keeps each rule of the page that no gate holds under `manual:`, with its
quote (item 50), and until now nobody was asked to hold the paper to them. G4 now raises them
as one warning, `journal-manual-unsigned`, naming the rules, which the corresponding author
signs off once they have checked the paper against each, bound to the rules, their quotes
and the page's digest: a rule added, a quote changed or the page read again wants a new
signature. `submit` puts them in the pack as `journal-checklist.md`, each rule with the
page's words and a box to tick, and says under them who signed them off and when, or who is
to. The corresponding author is the one author `corresponding: true` marks; with none
marked, or more than one, the hint says to mark one.

A profile a year old is warned of (`journal-profile-stale`), and the page is read again:
`manuscript-guard journal --reread <file>` takes the page as it now stands, as text, and
prints its difference from the stored page and, for each rule of the profile, `manual:` ones
among them, whether its quote is still on it. A rule whose words are gone is the one to read
again; the difference shows the rest, a rule the page added among it. The command writes
nothing and exits 1 where a rule's quote is gone: adopting the page, saving it over the
stored one and recording its digest, which the command prints, is the author's.

G15's warning about a model kind the Methods name and the analysis did not fit is not
signed: it is about the prose, and its hint already says when there is nothing to do. The
ethics lead signs nothing yet, and the small-cell exception is not a signable finding.

The data custodian authorises a model provider. Many data-use agreements forbid sending the
data, or what is computed from them, anywhere the custodian has not agreed to, and a panel
read by a model sends the manuscript, results and all, to whichever provider `review.models`
names. Where `paper.yaml` says the custodian restricts that (`custodian: {restricts_sending:
true}`), `review --run` sends to the built-in Ollama on this machine, and to any other
provider only once the data custodian `authors.yaml` names under `roles:` has authorised it,
with `manuscript-guard
sign --as <them> --finding G11/custodian/send-to/<provider>`. The sign-off is bound to the
provider's name, its address, and whether a server on this machine passes its calls on, so a
provider pointed elsewhere, or an Ollama cloud model where only local ones were authorised,
wants it again. A run with a provider not authorised sends nothing, writes nothing, and says
who authorises it; a dry run says that a run would send nothing, and writes the requests for
the custodian to read all the same. Only a built-in provider on this machine is taken at its
address, for a model it is not known to pass on: a provider the author adds under
`review.providers` is authorised whatever its address, because one at localhost may be a
router or a tunnel that sends what it receives elsewhere, and was sent to unasked (round 1
of #323). The design round sends the plan, and is held the same way.

## The plugin: skills for judgement, hooks for the moment of the mistake

The original brief asked for skills **and hooks**. The skills came first and the hooks were
outstanding for seven phases, which was the wrong order: a skill helps when you remember to
invoke it, and a hook helps when you do not.

Five hooks. One says where the manuscript stands when a session starts, and one says it again
when a turn ends that changed what the gates read (below). The other three were chosen
because each catches something at the only moment it is cheap to catch:

- **Before a write**, refuse edits to `results/`, `build/` and generated checklist profiles.
  This is the direct mechanical form of "the latest results are always used": the file
  cannot be hand-edited, so it cannot drift from the analysis that wrote it. G1 detects the
  edit afterwards; the hook prevents it.
- **After a write**, classify the numbers in the manuscript file just saved. The same check
  G2 performs, but while the author is still in the paragraph rather than at the next build.
- **After editing an analysis file**, say the results are stale and the Methods may no
  longer describe the code.
- **Before a submission-shaped shell command**, run the submission check and block on
  failure, or where the project cannot be read for the check to run.

That last one carries a specific lesson. It matches the **whole command string**, with no
permission-rule prefix filter, because `cd example && manuscript-guard submit` and
`FOO=1 manuscript-guard submit` both defeat a prefix rule — which is precisely how a
submission build slipped past the equivalent guard in the predecessor project. The cost is
that the hook fires on every shell command, so it has its own console script
(`manuscript-guard-hook`) that imports nothing heavy until it knows it has work: 152 ms for
the no-op path against roughly 400 ms through the full CLI.

It is registered for the three tools through which Claude Code runs a shell command: `Bash`,
`PowerShell` and `Monitor`. Each sends the command in `tool_input.command`, and the guard
reads the command, not the tool's name. It was registered for `Bash` alone until 2026-10-02,
and a matcher made of letters and `|` is a list of exact tool names, for Claude Code and for
Codex alike. On Windows Claude Code makes PowerShell an agent's first shell, and by its
documentation has no Bash tool at all where Git Bash is absent, so there the guard never ran.
Seen in a session with both tools (Claude Code 2.1.286): in a copy of the example with its
reviews deleted, `echo 'cp build/manuscript.docx elsewhere'` through the Bash tool was
refused, and `Write-Output 'Copy-Item build\manuscript.docx elsewhere'` through the
PowerShell tool was not. With the three names registered it is refused too, as a session
started after the plugin's update showed on 2026-10-03 (Known gaps has what was seen).
`tests/test_plugin.py` holds the matcher to the three names. The
markers took the PowerShell and Windows spellings of the verbs they already had at the same
time: `Compress-Archive`, `Send-MailMessage`, `Invoke-WebRequest` and its alias `iwr`,
`Invoke-RestMethod`, `Start-BitsTransfer`, `robocopy` and `xcopy`. `Copy-Item` and
`Move-Item` were held before, since `copy` and `move` stand in them as whole words.

**Two decisions are put to the author.** A hook that denies can stop an agent; it cannot make
the author decide. Sending the manuscript to model providers without being asked
(`review --run --yes`) and naming who attested a value (`attested_by`) are the author's
statements, and nothing in the files tells an agent's from theirs: G7 refuses a model's name
as an attester, not a person's name typed by an agent. So for these two the hooks answer
"ask", and Claude Code shows the person the call with the reason, which names the models in
`review.models` or the attester the edit adds. An edit that leaves the attesters as they
were is not asked about, so changing a value beside a name costs no prompt. Codex reads "ask"
and does not support it yet, failing the hook and letting the call through (its hooks page,
read 2026-10-15), so where the event is not known to be Claude Code's the hook refuses the
call with the same reason and the author makes it. Claude Code is known by
`CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, which it exports to a hook, and by an event with no `turn_id`, which
Codex sends with every tool call.

**The command is held to the project at the agent's folder, and to each one it names.**
Recognising `cd example && manuscript-guard submit` is half of catching it. The check runs
in a project, and the guard took the one at the folder the event names as the agent's, or
above it. An agent started at the root of a repository, with the paper in `example/`, stands
in a folder that has none: the command was recognised, held to nothing, and went through in
a project that fails. Where no project is at that folder, the guard now reads the words of
the command and holds it to each project that one of them is a path into: `example` after
`cd` or as the argument of `submit`, `example/build/manuscript.docx` after `scp`. A file
that is not written yet names the project its folder is in. Each project is checked once.

Where a project is at that folder the words were not read, until 2026-10-08, and that
project alone was checked: from a paper that passes, `cd ../second && manuscript-guard
submit` went through though `second` fails. The words are now read there too. The project
the command was sent from is checked first, as before, and then each other one a word is
a path into; a path that leads back into the first names nothing new.

The refusal names the project, says that the command named it, and names the check with the
project's folder after it, `manuscript-guard check --stage submission "example"`, because
from where the agent stands the check alone finds no project, or, from inside a first
project, finds that one. The folder comes last on
purpose. The markers want a verb before the word `submission`, and `copy` is one: a folder
called `paper-copy`, written after the word, does not make the command submission-shaped,
where `cd paper-copy && manuscript-guard check --stage submission` is, and would be refused
with the advice it had just followed.

A word is read as it stands and, where the way it is written hides a path, as that path
too. curl writes a file to upload after an `@`, `file=@example/build/manuscript.docx`, so a
word is read from after its last `@` as well. In quotes `=` is not a separator, so a quoted
word is also read from after its last `=`. Outside quotes a backslash and a space are a
space in a name, `my\ paper`, as a shell reads them, and that is the only reading. To
PowerShell a backslash ends a folder's name, so `.\example\ D:\sent` is two paths, and it
is not found. Reading the pieces as well found it, and twice took a piece of a file's name
for the project beside it: `paper` in `cp paper\ draft.docx /backup`, which refused a copy
of an unrelated document and a submission from `paper v2`, which passed; then, once
narrowed to Windows and to a run holding another backslash, in `cp Edited\ paper\
\(JD\).docx /backup`, where the other backslash is a shell's escape. Both were found by
#137's review, and the reading was dropped (Basile, 2026-10-02): a path not found is a
limit that is written down, and a document refused for a project it has nothing to do with
is what this change was decided against. One kind of word has since been read as a shell
reads it, whole and not by its pieces (2026-10-08): a word with an escaped space in which
every backslash stands before a space or one of the characters a shell escapes, which
are a few of ASCII: brackets, quotation marks, `&`, `#`, `~` and their like. There every
backslash is the shell's, so `paper\ \(1\).docx` is the one name `paper (1).docx` and
does not end at the bracket. A backslash before anything else is where Windows ends a
folder's name, and a word that holds one is read as before: before a letter or a digit
of any script, since a folder is as often `études` as `paper`, and before a mark no
shell escapes, since one is as often `【投稿】論文` or `.drafts`. Read the other way round,
as every character but a letter, `.\études\ ` and then `.\【投稿】論文\ ` were a shell's
word and a folder not found; both were found in review, before this was on `main`. A
word of more than 4096 characters or 100
folders is not a path and is not walked: each step down is a look on disk, `..` exists at
every step, and 5000 of them in one word took 34 s.

This is not reading the command as a shell does. Nothing is expanded and nothing is run, and
the guard does not know that `cd` changes folder: it asks of each word whether it is a path
into a project, and a string in quotes is one word. That keeps out a project the command
does not name (Basile, 2026-10-02). The root of a repository is where every other command is
sent from, and a paper below it that fails must not stop a copy of an unrelated `.docx`.
Following a leading `cd` was the other way, and would have left `manuscript-guard submit
example` and `scp example/build/manuscript.docx host:` uncaught, which need no `cd`. What a
command does not spell out is not found, and a word that happens to be the folder's name is
taken for it; both are under Known gaps. A submission-shaped command that names no project
costs about 10 ms more than it did, one look on disk for each reading of each word, and a
command that is not submission-shaped costs nothing more. A script of 2000 different words
written into a file through the shell, if it is submission-shaped, costs about a second.

**A refusal names a command the guard lets through.** The refusal shows the first eight
failures and says what to run for the rest. It used to say `manuscript-guard check
--submission`, and `--submission` is one of the guard's markers wherever it stands in a
command. An agent that did as it was told was refused again with the same eight lines, and
could not reach the list. The refusal now says to run `manuscript-guard check --stage
submission` on its own. Run so, the guard does not match it, and it gives the same verdict,
the stage being resolved before any gate runs. "On its own" is part of the advice: the
command ends in the word `submission`, so after `cp` or `git push` on the same line it is
matched again (Known gaps). `tests/test_hooks.py` sends each command a refusal names back
through the guard in the project that was refused, over a table that a refusal added later
is added to. For the failing check it also runs the command, to see that every failure is
listed and that as many are counted as the guard counted.

**An option is read only where it is written in full.** The guard's marker for the
submission standard is the word `--submission`, and it can only list the spellings the
command line reads. argparse reads any prefix that names one option, which made `--subm` a
spelling the guard did not have. The parser refuses abbreviations, on every command, so the
word is the only spelling of that option (see "Closed since"). It is not the only way to ask
for the submission standard: `--stage submission` is the other, which a refusal itself names
for `check`, and which the guard holds on `build` alone (Known gaps has what is left).

**A hook never breaks the session.** Every handler swallows unexpected errors and exits 0.
A guard that crashes on a half-configured project gets removed by the author, and the guards
that were working go with it.

One error is expected, and is passed on. Where a file of the project's own cannot be used
(it does not parse, is not UTF-8, or leaves `check` with no folders or no stage to go by),
`check` stops before any gate, says which file in a sentence written for the author, and
exits 2. A project that could not be checked has not passed, so the submission guard refuses
with that sentence, and the session start says it where the status line would have been. The
gates raise the same error where there is no `paper.yaml` above the folder at all, and there
a hook has nothing to say: a guard that refused on it would refuse every command that names
a `.docx` anywhere on the machine. So both look for the project first
(`hooks._project_root`), stay silent where there is none, and pass on only an error raised
once one was found. The guard looks further than the folder it is sent from: with no
project there, it holds a command to each project the command names by a path (above).
Anything else the gates raise is still a fault of the tool, and still ends in silence.

**A hook reads its event as UTF-8.** The agent tool writes the event on the hook's standard
input as UTF-8, and a name outside ASCII goes as its own bytes, with no `\u` escape. Python on
Windows opens standard input in the ANSI code page, so a handler that read it as text was
handed `manuscript/méthodes.md` as `mÃ©thodes.md`, a file that does not exist.
`hooks._event_text` reads the bytes and decodes them itself. Bytes that are not UTF-8 are read
in the encoding standard input was opened with, as they were before, and a byte that encoding
cannot read is replaced, so that the event is kept: an event read as nothing guards nothing,
and a letter lost from a file's own name leaves the folder and the extension by which the
write guard knows a generated file. The answer needed no change. `json.dumps` escapes every
character outside ASCII, so what the hook prints reads the same in the code page it is written
in and in the UTF-8 the tool reads it as, and a test holds it to ASCII.

**A hook blocks only what is unambiguous.** Writing a machine-written results file is always
wrong. Prose that trips the AI-writing lint is not, so nothing in G6 is enforced this way.

**At the end of a turn, the line the session started with.** An agent ends a turn by saying
what it did, and "the Results now give the odds ratio" reads the same whether or not the
gates agree. The stop hook puts their answer beside it: at the end of a turn that changed a
file the gates read, the person is shown the session start's line, with the stage and how
many findings fail and warn. It is shown, and that is all (`systemMessage`). The turn ends as
it would have, with failures if there are any, since a drafting session ends with some, and
the agent is not sent back to work, as a stop hook's `decision: block` would send it. The
idea is phd-skills' (github.com/fcakyon/phd-skills): its stop hook has a model with a fresh
context read the turn for claims that go beyond their evidence. This is the half of that
which needs no model.

Whether the turn changed anything is read from the files, not from the record of the turn
that Claude Code hands a hook in `transcript_path`. That record names a file an edit wrote
and not one a shell command wrote, and the analysis writes its results through a shell
command; its format is Claude Code's own and undocumented, and Codex's is another. The
session start notes each file of `manuscript`, `analysis`, `results`, `figures` and
`literature`, wherever `paths:` puts them, and `paper.yaml` and `authors.yaml`: its size, the
time it was written and the SHA-256 of its bytes. Each stop notes them again and compares. A
file is read again only where its size or time has moved, so a stop at which nothing changed
lists the folders and reads no file but one it could not read before, and a file saved with
the same bytes is no change, as it is none to G1. Hidden files and Python's `__pycache__` are
not looked at, so LibreOffice's lock file `.~lock.main.md#` beside `main.md` is no change to
the turn. Word's `~$` files and other editors' backups are, though no gate reads them (Known
gaps). The note is kept in the folder for temporary files, one for each session and project,
so that a hook writes nothing in the author's project. It holds the folders `paths:` names as well, and the project is asked for them again
only once `paper.yaml` has changed: asking loads the project's schemas, about half a second
at the end of every turn. With them noted, a stop at which nothing changed costs Python's
start and a listing, 0.2 to 0.4 s on the author's machine under other sessions' load. Where
there is no note, because the session start was cut off or found no project at the folder it
was sent from, the first stop notes the files and says nothing. A turn counts from the last
stop, not from the person's message, so an edit made by hand between two turns is counted in
the next one. Basile chose these on 2026-10-20, over every file of the project, size and time
alone, the record of the turn, and a sixth hook at each message to note the files there.

**A check that takes too long is said to have.** An agent tool stops a hook at the timeout
`hooks.json` gives it, 60 s for the session start and for the stop, and drops what the hook
would have said. The session start used to wait for the gates until then, and a project whose
check took a minute started its sessions with no line, and nothing said why. Both now run the
gates on a thread of their own and wait `CHECK_LIMIT`, 45 s. Past it they say that the check
of the project did not finish and to run `manuscript-guard check`, and the process ends
without waiting for the gates. The 15 s left are for what comes before the gates: starting
Python, the session start's notice of an older tool, loading the project where its folders
are not noted, and noting the files, which has no limit of its own (Known gaps).
`tests/test_hooks.py` holds the limit ten seconds under each timeout.

**Under `claude -p` the stop does nothing.** Nobody reads what a hook shows there, and the end
of a scripted run is not held up for a check. Claude Code tells a hook so in two variables it
does not document, seen with 2.1.303: `-p` sets `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED` to `0`, and
`CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` to `sdk-cli` unless a Claude Code above it has set that already. A
`claude -p` started from a desktop session keeps that session's `claude-desktop`, so either
sign is enough. The same run showed that Claude Code delivers a stop hook's `systemMessage`,
as a notice that names the hook ("Stop says: ..."), and goes no further with the turn. Codex
has the event too (`codex-rs/hooks/src/events/stop.rs`, read 2026-10-20). It sends
`session_id` and `cwd` as Claude Code does, shows `systemMessage` as a warning, and fails a
hook whose answer holds a field it does not know: the stop answers with that one field.

**The same hooks read Codex's input.** Codex runs hooks under the event names Claude Code
uses, takes the same output, and matches a file edit under the names `Edit` and `Write`, so
`plugin/hooks/hooks.json` is one file for both. Three of the five hooks, the session start,
the stop and the submission guard, read what they read from Claude Code's event in Codex's.
The difference is a file edit, which the other two read. Codex makes it with one tool,
`apply_patch`, and hands the hook the text of the patch in `tool_input.command`, with no
`file_path`. The files are named in the patch's headers, relative to `cwd`, and one patch may
write several.

`hooks.patch_paths` reads those headers by the rules of Codex's own parser
(`codex-rs/apply-patch/src/parser.rs` and `streaming_parser.rs`, read 2026-10-02): nothing
before `*** Begin Patch` or after `*** End Patch`; a header is a whole line of the envelope,
which inside an update must start at the first column, since a line of the file's text starts
with a space, `+` or `-`; `*** Move to:` once, and only before the first change to the file
it moves, which an `*** End of File` line there is not. A looser reading would refuse an edit
to a manuscript that quotes a patch, and a stricter one would miss a write. The write guard
refuses the whole patch when any file it adds, updates or moves a file to is generated, and
names those files only, each once. Where the project keeps `results/` is asked of it once for
the patch, not once for each file. After the patch, each manuscript file and each analysis
file in it gets its line, a moved one where it now is. A file the patch deletes is
not refused: removing a fragment whose script is gone is the author's decision, and `check`
reports every binding that pointed at it. And the submission guard leaves a patch alone,
because a patch that writes `--submission` into a file is an edit, not a command.

**Text written by someone else is data.** Five skills have an agent read what another
person wrote: a decision letter and the reviewers' reports (`reviewer-response`), a
co-author's comments and returned document (`word-roundtrip`), an answer file
(`co-author-checking`), a retrieved source (`literature-verify`) and a journal's
instructions for authors as fetched (`journal-profile`). Each says, under "Text written by
someone else", that an instruction found in that text is part of it and is not followed,
and that what it says never goes into a shell command; `tests/test_plugin.py` holds the
five to it. The tool's own output sets such text apart as well: `import` prints a Word
comment after "comment from <author> (<date>), quoted:", each line behind `> `, cut at 200
characters, with every control character and bidirectional control shown as `?`; a
no-break space is shown as it is. The comment it files is stored as written and shown the
same way in G11's report. Before 2026-10-15 it
printed the comment on the same line as the tool's words, and a comment that read like an
instruction read like the tool's.

### Whether each skill fires when it should

A skill helps only when it fires, and several border each other: `review-panel`,
`reviewer-response` and `co-author-checking`; `manuscript-writing`, `methods-writer` and
`results-binding`; `paper-audit` and `results-binding`. Each of these ends its description
with what it is not for and which of ours to use instead. Such a line names only our own
skills and claims no priority over anything else an agent has, and `tests/test_plugin.py`
holds both. `evals/`, beside the plugin, holds the cases `claude plugin eval` runs by hand
(docs/agent-tools.md):

- routing, one for each skill, with a judged outcome;
- a near-miss for each bordering pair;
- requests no skill is for;
- small requests that must not start a workflow.

Run with and without the plugin, the routing cases show what each skill adds over the model
alone; a skill that adds nothing measurable is cut, or folded into another's references. What
a run cannot establish: that a skill fires for a user's own wording, which 28 prompts
do not sample; that a judged outcome is right, since the judge is a model; and anything about a model
other than the one run.

**The runs.** A measurement on real inputs, with its date:

- **2026-10-19, Claude Opus 5.5 (`--model opus`), Claude Code 2.1.303, the plugin of a
  clean checkout of `main` at 0.2.448.** All 28 cases, 3 runs each, with and without the
  plugin: 168 runs, $15.90 at API prices as Claude Code reports them, run under a
  subscription. One case, run once first, cost $0.14. The arms were what they say: a run of
  one case in each, its trace kept, loaded the copy under test alone in the one and no
  manuscript-guard in the other, though a release of the plugin was installed for the user.
  - Routing: every one of the 15 skills fired on all 3 runs of its own case. Each of the 8
    near misses fired the skill it was for and not its neighbour, on all 3 runs. None of the
    3 requests no skill is for fired one.
  - Proportionality: neither small request started a workflow, on any run. The judge
    failed one of the three politer replies, which left "page X, lines Y–Z" to be filled in.
  - What each skill adds was not measured. The judged outcome of a routing case passed on 18
    runs of 45 with the plugin and 13 of 45 without. Of the 59 that failed, 53 did so
    because the case runs in an empty folder: no `paper.yaml`, manuscript, figure or plan to
    work on, which each reply said, in either arm. Five were the manuscript-writing case,
    whose criterion asks the rewrite to say what was found, which its prompt never gives:
    with the plugin the reply would not invent it, three times, and without, two replies
    left a placeholder for it. One was project-setup, whose case gives
    no shell to make the project with. That difference says nothing of a skill, and no
    skill is cut on it. It needs cases that set up a project first, and criteria that ask
    only for what the prompt gives.
  - Before this run the command in `docs/agent-tools.md` found no case: `claude plugin eval`
    reads a suite only from inside the plugin. `tools/run_skill_evals.py` now runs it from
    a copy.

**After that run** (Basile's choice, 2026-10-19), a routing case whose prompt speaks of a
finished project starts in one. 12 of the 16 do: `tools/run_skill_evals.py` puts a copy of
the worked example beside the cases in the copy of the suite it runs, as `evals/_project/`.
Each such case's `case.yaml` names a `scaffold.sh` that copies it into the folder the run
starts in, and the command is given `--scaffold`. The copy names no skill: it leaves out
`AGENTS.md`, the project's instructions to an agent, and its YAML files lose their whole-line
comments, where the profiles said which skill writes them (rounds 1 and 2 of #338; Basile chose
this over keeping them and saying so). With them, the arm without the plugin could read what
several criteria ask for. A file whose data would read otherwise without its comments is
refused. What the project is made of, its bindings and its emitter calls, still shows the
toolkit in use to either arm, as any project made with it would, so the difference between
the arms is what a skill adds to a model reading such a project. Four routing cases still
start empty, and so do the near misses and the requests no skill is for:
- project-setup starts a project, and may give the `init` command where it has no shell to
  run it;
- manuscript-writing carries its own paragraph, and invents no finding, since its prompt
  gives none;
- analysis-plan is about the plan before any analysis code, and the example has both.
- data-sources asks which data could answer a question before any are chosen, and the
  example has its own (added with the skill, 2026-10-21, with a near miss each way against
  analysis-plan; not yet run).

The example is a finished project, and some prompts ask for what it lacks: paper-audit and
word-roundtrip speak of a .docx, reviewer-response of reviewers' comments, and review-panel
and figure-review find readings already recorded. A reply that asks for what is missing, or
works from what is there, is what their criteria pass.

One run of one scaffolded case (methods-writer, Claude Haiku, no baseline arm, $0.01 at API
prices) started in a folder holding the example, and passed. Asked for `_project` as a case,
the command found none. No run of the whole suite has been made since, so what each skill
adds is still not measured.

## Auditing existing papers, and saying what the audit is worth

`check` works because manuscript source contains bindings: a results-derived number cannot
be written as a literal, so nothing passes by coincidence. An existing paper has no
bindings. Every number is a literal, and the only available question is the weak one — does
this number appear anywhere in the outputs?

That is precisely the set-membership check this project's predecessor was built on, and
which was measured and found near-vacuous: with the analysis outputs as the backing set,
100% of integers up to 100 and 97% up to 1000 already matched, and of fifteen deliberately
corrupted headline numbers it detected none while reporting success.

So `manuscript-guard audit` reports two things, and the second is not optional: the numbers
matching nothing, **and what a match is worth in this particular project**, computed from
the backing set the user actually supplied. On the worked example, pointed at the raw data,
it reports 100% chance-match on every integer and says a match means almost nothing. Pointed
at the analysis outputs, 24%. A clean report cannot be mistaken for a clean paper.

Making it usable on real documents needed four things, three of them lessons from the
predecessor:

- **Table cells kept apart.** Word stores a row with no separator between cells, so a naive
  read turns `39 | 20 | 26 | 16` into 39,202,616 and silently skips every table. A wrong
  count in Table 1 survived every check for exactly that reason.
- **Tracked changes resolved.** A document under review holds both the old text and the new;
  reading it raw reports corrections as errors and misses what will be published. Text moved
  away goes with the deletions, and so does a deleted line break or tab: read as a space, it
  parted a minus from its number. A paragraph whose mark was deleted or moved away runs on
  into the next one; read as two lines, "-0.5" and "1" matched two outputs where the paper
  prints -0.51. The joined line takes the last paragraph's style, and so ends a reference
  list only if that one is a heading. That is what Word 16 shows once the change is
  accepted: when it deletes a mark itself it first copies the first paragraph's style onto
  the second, keeping the old one in `w:pPrChange` (verified 2026-09-24). A text box is
  read after the paragraph holding it, not where it is anchored, which split that paragraph
  in two. It is read once: Word writes every text box twice, as DrawingML and again as VML
  in an `mc:AlternateContent` fallback (verified 2026-09-24, Word 16), and reading both
  reported each number in it twice. The fallback is skipped, as the import's reader skips
  it. What Word puts only in a fallback is read from the choice instead: an emoji inserted
  in Word can be a `w16se:symEx` there (pandoc issue 11113; set as text through Word's COM
  interface, one was saved as plain text), and without it "12", the emoji and "34" read as
  1234. The paragraphs of a text box deleted or moved away start no lines: left empty, one
  styled as a heading used to end the reference list it sat in. Nor does a table row
  deleted or moved away, although neither kind of row is wrapped in a deletion. A deleted
  row is marked in its own properties (`w:trPr/w:del`), and a row moved away is not marked
  as a row at all: Word 16 moves the mark of every paragraph in it, a nested table's
  included, and writes no row-level change, since the format has none for a move. A text
  box's paragraphs are left unmarked, the box going with the moved text it is anchored in,
  so they are not counted (verified 2026-09-25: each tracked copy Word wrote reads the same
  as Word's accepted copy). The row's text was dropped but its row and cells still broke
  lines, and a cell styled as a heading ended the reference list there. An inserted row
  (`w:trPr/w:ins`) is read. A table whose every row is gone parts nothing: a paragraph whose
  mark was deleted before it runs on into the one after it, as Word 16 shows it.
- **The bibliography dropped.** Recognised by heading where there is one and by entry shape
  where there is not (author-year, or the numbered styles' `2019;393:100`), because citeproc
  appends a reference list with no heading to cut at. It ends at the next heading, so an
  appendix or a footnote after it is still read. Otherwise every volume number and page
  range is reported. A heading is read without the attribute block pandoc takes off it:
  `# References {-}`, the usual way to leave the list unnumbered, was no heading at all, so
  nothing was cut and a book or a web page in the list had every number reported. On a line
  nothing marks as a heading the braces are printed, and it is not one.
- **Rendered citations classified.** In source a citation is `[@key]` and gets masked; in a
  built document it has already become "(Smith and Jones 2019)", and without a rule for that
  every citation in the paper is an unexplained number.

Verified end to end: the example's built document audits clean against its own outputs, and
one digit changed in the reporting odds ratio is reported with its line and context.

### Reading anything, and what needs no outputs (2026-10-28)

The audit read Markdown and Word, and refused a `.tex`. It now reads a LaTeX paper through
the reader every gate uses (`auditing/latex.py`): a `.tex` named is an entry, and its
folder's `.tex`, `.sty` and `.cls` files are what its `\input`s resolve to, as they are for a
project's `main.tex`; in a folder given, every file with `\documentclass` starts a paper of
its own, and a file no entry inputs, or that a class or a package inputs, is named under
"Passed over" rather than read. Each file is read as G2 reads one, at its `.tex` lines, its
`thebibliography` cut, and each refusal of the reader in a file the entry reads named where
`--strict` counts it. Its
tables are rows of cells (`text/latex/tables.py`), split where LaTeX splits them, so an n (%)
and a mean of whole numbers are held in a LaTeX table as in a Word one.

`--against` is optional. A paper often reaches an auditor without its outputs, and the
checks that need none, the P worked out from its statistic among them, were out of reach
behind a required flag. Without it nothing is compared, and the report's first line says so:
"No outputs given: no number was compared with the analysis". The report is now in sections,
Membership, Arithmetic, Writing (G6) and Language (G14), References (G7), and `--json` gives
it in `check --json`'s shape, each finding with its section and whether `--strict` counts it.

G6 and G14 read a project's manuscript, so the paper is put into one made for it in a
temporary folder (`auditing/gates.py`), and each finding's path put back. A .docx goes through
`init --from`'s conversion, so that its words are read as they will be once the paper is
brought in, and without pandoc the two are passed over for it with a note (the author,
2026-10-28). G7's census needs no `references.bib`: the list the audit cuts is counted, its
DOIs and PMIDs, and its numbered citations held to it (`auditing/references.py`). The
registries are asked only with `--lookup`, through `lookup`'s transport, and read as G7 reads
a record; nothing is kept unless `--lookup-cache` names where.

`--strict` counts exact findings only (the author, 2026-10-28). In this PR that is what it
counted before; the P worked out from a statistic, G6, G14 and G7 are listed and not counted.

Round 1 of the review of #463 found the reader's refusals counted where the entry reads no
file: a supplement beside the paper, a document of its own, was refused as a second document
