inside it, and a file passed over had its refusals counted under `--strict`. Only a refusal in
a file the entry reads is counted now. A `\bibitem` is reported in the file that holds it. A
.docx's list is numbered by place only where one Word numbering counts every entry 1, 2, 3
from the list (`text/word_numbering.py`, read from ECMA-376 part 1, 17.9): a bracketed number
in an author-year paper's text, `range [0, 100]`, had made every entry "cited nowhere", and an
empty list under a final heading had raised. A Markdown list is numbered as pandoc prints it,
from its first number up, and a number pandoc escaped, `1\.`, as typed. A DOI ends before
`](` and before a stop or a closing bracket it did not open; one no registry has, and a PMID
PubMed does not, is reported, and "no registry said a work was retracted" says how many
entries were asked and how many a registry knew. A table's rules and colours, `\midrule[1pt]`
and `\rowcolor{gray!20}`, print nothing (`text/latex/commands.py`), where their arguments had
been read as the cell's text and as the paper's numbers. Under `--json` an audit that did not
happen, exit 2, prints `{"ok": false, "error": ...}`: `check --json` prints nothing to stdout
for its errors, so this is the audit's own.

Round 2 found the table's rules and colours the mask now knows refused where an author
defines them, `\let\toprule\hline` among them, and the rest of the file read as typed by
every gate: they are a package's commands now, an author's own where booktabs or colortbl
is not loaded, and an author may define them again where it is. A SICI DOI keeps its
`<...>`, and an emphasis or a code mark after a DOI is no part of it. A Word level is read
as counting 1, 2, 3 only where it is resolved for sure, its own level's number alone in its
text, and an empty paragraph of a numbered list takes its number, as Word 16 prints it
(checked over COM). Word 16 also showed a numbering with a `startOverride` starting again at
1 after another of the same abstract numbering, and a third with none counting on from the
first, which is how `word_numbering.py` keys a count. What is compared above the list is the
count alone: a paragraph with words outside a table, numbered in the list's count, makes
the list not numbered by place; one in another count, an empty one, or one in a table's cell
is not looked at.

### A table's totals, and a count held back that they give away (2026-10-28)

A total printed beside its counts is arithmetic a reader can do, and nothing did it.
`stats/margins.py` reads a table, a paper's in `audit` or an emitted one in `check`, as
lines: a total and the two or more counts it totals. A row labelled Total, All or Overall,
anchored at both ends, any case, nothing after the word but an n, an "n (%)", footnote marks
and punctuation, totals the rows above it back to the last row with no count in it or the
last total row; a column so headed totals the columns before it back to the last total
column or the labels. A count is a whole number or the n of an n (%) that `stats/shares.py`
reads as one; a count held back, "<5" or "≤4", is the interval from 0 to the largest its
bound allows (`gates.custodian.held_largest`, which `_small` uses too). A line with a cell
that is no count is not read, nor a row or a column that names another statistic, a P or a
ratio. One routine, `feasible`, serves both checks: each member's range given the total is
the total less the others' highs up to the total less their lows, within its own, and no
range at all is a total the printed counts cannot make, `sum-off`. A range of one value is
a count held back that the line gives away. Categories whose shares add up to 100
(`shares._summed`) and whose counts add up to more than their column's header n are the one
contradiction read of a header n (`over-header-n`); fewer is missing data.

In `check`, G2's `count-recoverable` (from internal review, as `count-below-minimum`) reads
each emitted table the manuscript or the supplement binds, each declared sum, and each step
and the arms of each flow whose keys are all bound; a step whose reasons overlap is no
partition and is not read. It fails where a printed total gives the count away, and warns
where only a column's header n does, since the n is the categories' total only where none of
the column lacks the characteristic (the author, 2026-10-28). Nought is no small cell, so a
count given away as 0 is not said. `deposit`'s preflight asks the same of every table of the
results files it carries, through `recoverable_cells`. In `audit` the Arithmetic section
lists the totals off and the categories over their n, and "Small cells recoverable by
subtraction" each count given away with its value, at `--minimum-cell-count` or, without
one, from 1; `--strict` counts `sum-off`, `over-header-n` and a count a printed total gives
away, and not one only the header n gives (the author's rule of 2026-10-28: exact findings
only). Two lines are never put together: see Known gaps.

## A paper written in Word is brought in through pandoc's tree

The route the skills gave for moving a Word paper into a project was `pandoc paper.docx -t
markdown`. Tried on fifteen openly licensed Word papers (2026-10-23), it wrote tables of
seven as multiline tables, whose lines of dashes `check` refuses at every stage
(`rule-opens-a-block`), so those seven failed whole, and those of four more as grid tables; and each title page landed in the
text, names, affiliations and all. `init --from paper.docx` (Basile's choice, 2026-10-23)
has pandoc read the document into its JSON tree, with tracked changes accepted, changes
three things in the tree (`from_word.py`), and has pandoc write the rest as it would.

**Tables.** A table whose cells hold only paragraphs, line blocks, headings or quotations of
those is rewritten so that pandoc writes it as a pipe table: each cell's paragraphs and line
breaks joined with spaces, inside emphasis too but not inside a note; every column's width
left to its cells; a merged cell's text in its first row and column, the cells it covered
left empty; a second header row and the footer's rows made rows of the body. No text is
added or left out. Simple and multiline tables are switched off in the writer, so that a
table of one-line cells is a pipe table and any other a grid table, and the line is made
long enough that a table of more than nine columns is not written as raw HTML, which
pandoc's default of 72 columns did. A table with anything else in a cell, a list, a table
or code, is left a grid table and named in what `init` prints. `check` reads a grid table's
rows as a table's (a line that starts with a pipe), and the audit does not read its cells.
The tree, not a Lua filter: the change is a function of pandoc's tree and is tested on trees
built by hand, without pandoc.

**Pictures** go to `manuscript/media/`, and each image points there from the project's root,
where the build runs pandoc. A picture pandoc saves elsewhere than its `media/` folder keeps
the rest of its path under `manuscript/media/`, so that no image points into the temporary
folder pandoc saved it in, which is deleted once the paper is read; an image pointing at a web
address is left as it is. Not `figures/`: every file there is taken for a figure an
analysis rendered, and a picture from Word would be reported as one with no text layer and
no review.

**The title page.** pandoc reads Word's Title, Subtitle, Author, Date and Abstract styles as
the document's metadata, and nothing else is taken as a title or a name: no line is judged
by its capitals or its place. The title goes to `paper.yaml` (where `--title` gives none),
as plain text. A Title paragraph that holds what plain text loses, a note, a superscript, a
link or a picture, goes into the comment as well, as it does when `--title` gives the title:
a note on the title is where a paper often names its funder or its corresponding author, and
taken as plain text it was written nowhere. A superscript at the title's end made of digits
or the usual signs (`*`, `†`, `‡`, `§`, `¶`, `‖`, `#`), several with commas between, is the mark of such a
note and is left out of the plain title, which kept its text and read "a fall1"; it stays in
the comment with the title, and `init` names it. A superscript inside the title, or of
anything else, "CD4^+^ T cells" or "Na^+^", is the title's. A unit's power at the end, "per
m^2^", is taken for a mark too, and named, for the author to put back. Each Author paragraph that is one name goes to `authors.yaml`, in a comment
over an entry whose given and family names are left empty, since which part is the family
name cannot be read from the name; one holding a comma, a semicolon, "and", a digit, a
superscript or a link is several names or carries a mark, and goes to the comment. The
abstract becomes `# Abstract`. pandoc puts the Abstract style in the metadata only when it
follows the Title, Author and Date paragraphs, and its own writer puts an "Abstract" title
paragraph in between, so an abstract is often read as text instead. What stands before the
first heading, with the metadata no file takes, is set aside in one HTML comment at the top
of `main.md`, where no gate reads it and the build prints nothing of it; a `-->` in it, which
pandoc leaves in code, is written `--&gt;`.

Before the first heading is not always a title page. Of the fifteen papers, six had no
paragraph in a heading style, one's first heading was an entry of its reference list, after
10,106 words, one's was an empty paragraph near the end, and one's an APA paper's "Method"
after its introduction (2,064 words). Set aside, each of those would have hidden the paper
from every gate. So the run is set aside only up to 600 words, which a title, a long author
list and a 300-word abstract stay under; the two title pages among the fifteen held 18 and
375 words. A longer run stays in the text, as does everything in a paper with no heading.

**Over nothing.** `init` keeps a file that is already there, and so would have kept a
`paper.yaml` or an `authors.yaml` while saying it wrote the Word paper's title and names into
them. `init --from` refuses before reading the paper where a manuscript is there. Once it has
read the paper, it refuses where `paper.yaml` is there and the Word title would go into it
(no `--title` given), and where `authors.yaml` is there and the paper's Author paragraphs
name someone; where nothing from the paper would go into the file, it keeps the file, as
plain `init` does. It refuses as well where a picture cannot be written: something already
at its path, a file where the project or one of its folders goes, or two pictures whose
paths differ only by case, which Windows and macOS take for one file. The pictures are
written after the rest of the project, and an error then left half a project. Each refusal
makes nothing.

Measured on the fifteen: the seven that failed now pass `check` at the stage `init` sets,
with 39 tables written as pipe tables and 2 left as grid tables (a numbered list in a cell,
and a layout table holding two others); five titles came from a Title paragraph, one of
them the journal's name; no
paper's Author style was used, three having put their authors in the Subtitle style; two
title pages were set aside, and three runs before the first heading were left in the text.
The three `.doc` papers are refused, with "save it as .docx".

## What an adversarial review found, 2026-08-03

Four reviews were run against the finished toolkit — security, Python correctness,
architecture, and an adversarial one that built a project and attacked it 56 ways. Every
claim below was reproduced against the code before anything was changed; several other
claims were rejected on the same test. The defects clustered, and the cluster is worth
naming, because it is the shape of mistake this kind of tool makes.

**Nine of the eleven fixed defects were a rule matching a shape instead of a value.**
`conventions.yaml` says in its own header that a pattern must be pinned to specific
conventional values, "because a rule matching `p < <any number>` would wave through every
reported p-value." Five rules broke their own file's rule:

| rule | matched | so this passed |
|---|---|---|
| `rate-denominator` | `per \d[\d\s,]*` | `12 per 83,214 patients treated` |
| `age-band` | `\d+\+\s*(?:years?)?` — unit optional | `enrolled 500+ patients` |
| `categorical-label` | `arm\|cohort\|grade… \d+` | `in the exposed arm 47 hepatic events` |
| `time-label` | `years?… \d+` | `over the study years 1204 reports` |
| `author-year-citation` | a whole parenthetical containing a year | `(Smith 2019, n = 412)` |

Each is now bounded to the magnitudes a label can actually have, and the last is marked
`audit_only`: it exists to read a document citeproc has already rendered, and in manuscript
source — where citations are `[@key]` and masked — it bought nothing and cost the gate.

**Three defects made the tool report less than it checked, or check less than it claimed.**

- `find_atoms` split on `\S+`, but `mask()` writes NUL to preserve offsets, and NUL is not
  whitespace. So `3.84[@smith2020]` was one run, the run contained NUL, and the whole run
  was discarded — the visible 3.84 with it. Any value written hard against a citation, a
  footnote, inline code or a pandoc attribute was invisible to G2. Two reviewers found this
  independently.
- The twelve gates sat behind `if contract_report.ok and load_report.ok`. A project with no
  results yet — the ordinary state at `design` and `analysis` — failed that condition, so
  none of them ran, and the run printed `0 failing, 0 warnings`. The stage-policy test
  asserting that an early project is not buried in failures passed *because nothing was
  checked*. It now has a companion that asserts G2 and G6 actually ran.
- YAML front matter was masked whole. Pandoc renders `title` and `abstract` from it, so the
  most-read part of the paper was outside every check. Rendered keys are now read; `lang`,
  `zotero` and the rest of the machinery stay masked. (Later: a `---` followed by a blank
  line was taken for the opening of front matter too. Pandoc prints it as a horizontal rule,
  with the prose after it, which went unread up to the next `---`. The build found the end
  of the front matter with a pattern of its own, and the two had to be made one: fixed in
  the gates alone, G2 read a `## Methods` heading that the build still stripped, and
  `p < 0.001` under it passed as the alpha chosen in advance. There is one pattern now, and
  `test_pandoc_agreement.py` holds it to pandoc's reading. Every reader also applies it to
  the text as written: the heading scan blanked HTML comments first, so a comment on the
  YAML's first line read as a blank one and the front matter went unrecognised. And nothing
  opened in the front matter closes in the body, as pandoc reads it: a `<!--` in a title ran
  on to the next `-->` in the body, and a fence opener in an abstract paired with a fence
  below, hiding everything between from G2 and the audit, and the bindings between from
  G2's binding checks. The masking, `explain`, G2's fence and binding readers and the
  heading scan all stop at `front_matter_end`; all but the binding reader also look for
  fences on each side of it. What is still open is under Known gaps.
  Later still: the one pattern counts a block only where pandoc keeps it as metadata, so a
  header opening on an HTML comment is not front matter at all, and pandoc refuses it; see
  "Front matter closed by `...` took the body with it" under Known gaps.)

**Two were the same value compared the wrong way.**

- `contains(quote, display)` is a substring test, so a ledger value of `3.4` was accepted
  against a verbatim quote reading `13.42`. The manuscript could then attribute an ROR of
  3.4 to a paper reporting 13.42 — a misquotation of a real source, which is worse than an
  unsourced number because it carries a citation and looks checked. G7 now requires the
  value as a whole numeric token.
- `_judge_string_number` matched a figure script's numeric literal to candidate atoms by
  digit string rather than by position, so `ax.annotate("OR 3", …)  # cf. Table 3` cleared
  the hardcoded annotation using the comment's structural `Table 3`.

**And three were about the tool's own claims rather than its logic.**

- `--submission` and `--stage submission` gave different verdicts, because G11's severity
  came from the raw flag while everything else came from the resolved stage. A project
  declaring `stage: submission` in `paper.yaml` — the natural thing to write when
  submitting — never had the review gate enforced by `check` at all.
- `no-digest` was a warning. A fragment with no sidecar is one no emitter wrote, and while
  this warned, a hand-written `results/national.json` with a fabricated estimate and
  interval passed `check --submission` cleanly. It is a failure from `analysis` on.
- `pip install manuscript-guard` shipped no recipes. They lived at the repository root and
  were resolved as `parents[2]`, which from `site-packages/manuscript_guard/` is
  `<venv>/Lib`. `manuscript-guard fetch STROBE`, the second command in the README's own
  walkthrough, answered `no recipe for 'STROBE'` for everyone who installed as documented.
  Recipes now live inside the package; downloads and generated profiles go to the project,
  never into `site-packages`.

The R emitter also wrote CRLF on Windows — `writeLines(x, path)` opens a text connection and
`useBytes = TRUE` does not change that — so an R analysis produced a byte-different fragment
per platform, and the digest that guarantees the fragment reported `results-edited` on a file
nobody had touched.

Every one of these has a regression test naming the escape it closes.

## Round two, 2026-08-03

A second adversarial pass, run against the machinery the first round produced. Three
reviewers again; every claim reproduced before anything changed. The pattern this time was
narrower and more uncomfortable than the first: **most of what broke was a consequence of a
fix, not of the original code.**

- Fenced code stopped being masked, because it renders. `#` is a comment character. So an
  ordinary `# Methods` comment in a Python listing became a level-1 heading, popped the real
  `## Methods`, and made everything after it — including the Results — read as Methods. A
  fabricated `p < 0.001` in the Results was then accepted as the pre-specified alpha. An
  HTML comment did the same thing while being invisible in the rendered document. Heading
  detection now runs over text with fences and comments blanked. (Later: it still took any
  `#` line for a heading, and pandoc does not let a heading interrupt a paragraph. `## Methods`
  directly under a line of Results prose is printed as part of that prose, and the
  `p < 0.001` below it passed as the alpha chosen in advance. A setext title was the same,
  `numbered-heading` filed "## 3.84 times higher" in such a line as heading numbering, and
  `\s+` let a lone `#`, an empty heading, take the next line for its title. A blank line is
  not the rule either: a heading directly under a table, a fence, a div or another heading
  needs none. `text/blocks.py` now walks the document a line at a time, knowing what the
  line above left open, and `test_pandoc_agreement.py` holds it to pandoc construct by
  construct. The round trip no longer tags a setext heading. The audit no longer starts a
  reference list at a heading line pandoc prints as prose, and still ends one at any line
  shaped like a heading. The walk reads a construct it does not model as a paragraph, which
  swallowed a real `# Results` under a table of dashes and ran the Methods on over it, so
  for G2 a line shaped like a heading ends the section it stands in whether or not the walk
  places it. One the walk does not place can say Results and never Methods, and a number is
  in the Methods only if the printed headings alone say so too, so such a line can take
  Methods away and never grant them. A title is read as Results through the marks it may
  keep: pandoc prints `# Results` over a rule as a heading reading "# Results", and taken
  literally it matched no Results pattern and re-admitted the Methods rules under it.)
- `p < 0.05` became Methods-only, and the heading test ended in `\b` — a prefix match. So
  a Results subsection called "Protocol deviations" or "Design of the sub-study" re-admitted
  every threshold rule beneath it. Anchored at both ends now. (Later: anchored, a title that
  kept its pandoc attribute block was another word. `# Results {#sec-results}` was not
  Results, so a "Sensitivity analyses" subsection under it made a reported `p < 0.001` the
  alpha chosen in advance. A title is now read without its attribute block, backslash
  escapes in its values included. Other markup stays: `# **Results**` is not Results.)
- Table cells were classified with no section at all, which meant every `methods_only` rule
  applied — in the one place a *reported* p-value is most likely to be typed.
- `display=` was checked against its value, so the same fabrication moved one line across
  and went out as a **string value**: `em.value("ror.headline", "12.34 (95% CI 8.00 to
  19.00)")` published an estimate and an interval through an ordinary binding, with every
  gate green. String values now have to be labels or be traceable.
- The display check itself computed its tolerance from the mantissa and ignored the
  exponent, so for any small magnitude it was a no-op: a value of 1.2e-6 accepted a display
  of "1e-2".

Two more were original, and both are the same shape as the citation bug the first round
missed:

- **Numbers in a citation suffix rendered but were masked.** The mask covered the whole
  bracket, so `[@smith2019, which reported an ROR of 9.99 (95% CI 7.10 to 14.02)]` printed
  every number and no gate read any of them. This is ordinary pandoc usage, and it is the
  worst case in the whole design — a fabricated value carrying a citation. The mask now
  covers the citation *key*; a `citation-locator` rule handles the `p. 33` that legitimately
  lives in a bracket. An atom ends at the `]` that closes a bracket opened before it, so
  punctuation written hard against a citation does not join its locator: `[p. 3]/` was the
  unbound atom `3]/`, and `import` writes that when a co-author deletes the words between a
  citation and a value. The bracket's contents are still read: masking a narrative
  citation's bracket would hide a value in its suffix, `@key [reported 9.99]`, as masking a
  bracketed citation whole once hid the one in `[@key, which reported 9.99]`. The audit's
  own rule for a printed marker such as `[12]` no longer takes a `]` before it: with one,
  `3.40][12]` was a single match, and a bound closed by a bracket and written hard against
  the marker went unaudited. A value glued to the marker, and a bracketed whole-number
  interval after its value, are audited too now; see Known gaps.
- **Table captions and column headers were checked by nothing** — not by the emitter, not by
  `verify`. Both render with the table.

And `verify` had three of its own, of which one was serious enough to invalidate the
command: see its module docstring for what it now does and does not prove, and the Known
gaps below for what remains.

## A unit after a binding is the unit emitted

The analysis records a value's unit, and only G8 read it, to keep a count of 56 apart from a
share of 56.0%. "{{results.dose}} mg" printed "250 mg" of a dose emitted in micrograms, and
nothing said so. G2 now reads the symbol written right after each binding, from the list of
symbols G14 knows a number is not to run into, and `%` and `‰`, with a power after it or a
slash and what it divides by, and warns (`unit-differs-from-emitted`) where it is not the unit
emitted. Spellings of one unit are one: µg, μg and mcg; mL and ml; °C and ℃; a litre after
a slash, mmol/l and mmol/L (round 1 of #279). A value emitted with no unit, or with one that
is no symbol ("years"), has nothing to compare it with. The gap between the binding and its
unit may be spaces of any width, pandoc's escaped space (`\ `), the entity of a no-break
space in any of its spellings, an HTML comment, which is not printed and ends at its own
`-->`, and one line break, which pandoc prints as a space; a blank line, or a word between,
ends the unit's claim to the binding, also between two comments (round 1 of #341).

## A rule names values, not shapes

The classifier's allowlists are the one place where being generous is the same as being
wrong, and the same mistake has now been made eight times: a rule written to match a
*shape* rather than to name specific *values*, which then swallows a real measurement.
`rate-denominator` took any digit run after "per". `age-band` made the unit optional.
`categorical-label` and `time-label` took any number after a keyword. `author-year-citation`
spanned a whole parenthetical. `software-version` was narrowed from `\d+\.\d+` — which had
classified an odds ratio of 3.84 — to "three or more components", and promptly absorbed
`2.10-7.02`, which is how a confidence interval is written in this field.

Every one of those was caught by a person reading the regex, never by a test, because each
rule only ever had positive cases. `tests/data/rule_cases.yaml` now carries `accepts` and
`rejects` for every shipped rule, and `tests/test_rules.py` fails the build if any rule
lacks a negative case — so a rule cannot be added without someone writing down what it must
not do. Negative cases are checked against the *whole* rule set rather than their own rule,
because `2.10-7.02` was absorbed by `software-version`, which nobody would have thought to
test.

There is one exception to "name the values", and it is worth being precise about why.
`alphanumeric-identifier` matches a general shape — one to three letters followed by digits
— and is safe not by enumeration but by construction: **nothing that begins with a letter is
a quantity.** It covers ICD-10 `K71.0`, ATC `L01XC`, trial registrations `NCT01234567`, and
the named disproportionality statistics `IC025` and `EB05`, and it cannot absorb a
measurement because a measurement is not written that way. Rules that match digits get no
such licence.

A realistic pharmacovigilance Methods section produced 27 findings, 25 of them false: coding
systems, the null value of a ratio and the published signal criteria all read as unexplained
numbers. That is the failure mode that gets a gate switched off, and it mattered more than
any individual rule. What fixed it was four rules — the identifier rule above,
`coding-system-code`, `ratio-null-value` and `disproportionality-criterion` — each written
so that the numbers a paper is actually claiming stay unbound. `IC025 > 0` is a criterion;
`IC025 was 1.42` is a finding. The Methods section now classifies completely and the
Results section is untouched.

Two of them needed care about *span* rather than value. A rule matching from "ROR" through
"excluded 1" would also cover the interval in between — `the ROR (1.02 to 3.84) excluded 1`
— and file both bounds, the actual result, as conventional. `ratio-null-value` therefore
anchors on the comparison word and stops at the end of the clause, which is also what
separates "the interval excluded 1" from "the cohort excluded 1 patient": a null value ends
its clause, a count is followed by what it counts. `coding-system-code` has to reach, since
real prose writes "coded with MedDRA version 26.1; the preferred term 10019663" — so the
bridge between the system name and the code is a whitelist of punctuation, version numbers
and function words. Nothing a measurement can be written as is allowed to sit in it.

Dates needed no rule at all. A date already binds as one unit, which is what a study period
should do: `em.value("period.start", "2015-01-01", display="1 January 2015")` and
`{{results.period.start}}`. The reported study period ought to be the data's actual range,
so making it traceable is the point rather than the friction — but the finding's hint now
says that, instead of telling an author to bind a year to a result.

## The table rule lives in the fragment, not in the emitter

"Tables are emitted, not written" was, for a while, a check inside the Python emitter and
nowhere else. That is a guarantee with a hole the size of a language: a rule enforced in one
emitter is a rule an author steps around by switching to another, and the results fragment
is supposed to be the contract. It was also unverifiable after the fact — edit a fragment,
re-sign it, and the cell was never looked at again.

The rule now lives in `tables.py` and runs twice. At emit time it raises, naming the call
just made, because a message about the line you are writing is worth more than a finding two
commands later. In G2 it reports findings about whatever is on disk, whoever wrote it. One
implementation, so the two cannot drift.

That required the fragment to say which cells the emitter produced, because a composed cell
and a typed one are the same characters by the time anyone reads the file. The `composed`
block records the cell, the literal part of its template, and the displays derived for it.
Plain numeric cells are recorded the same way: only the emitter knew it had formatted them,
and the tempting shortcut — let the gate accept any cell that is a single number — waves
through a 9999 typed straight into the file.

The block is a record, not a licence. Its literal text is still checked, so adding a
`composed` entry beside a typed cell does not launder it; three corruption tests do exactly
that and are caught.

With the rule off the emitter, the R package could grow `table()`, `cell()` and
`code_list()` without weakening anything, and a test asserts that the same table written in
both languages produces the same `tables` and `code_lists` blocks. It found a divergence on
its first run: R had no branch for comparator displays, so `<0.001` — a p-value too small to
state — was legal in Python and an error in R. The R function carrying a docstring promising
to mirror the Python one had been wrong for as long as it had existed, which is what such a
promise is worth without a test that exercises both on the same input.

## Round four, 2026-08-04

Four reviewers, three of which ran their own reproductions. The domain reviewer had no
shell, so every one of its fourteen claims was executed here before being acted on; all
fourteen held. The pattern of this round is worth naming: **most of what it found was in
code written the same day**, by the fixes for round three.

**The composed-cell exemption verified nothing.** It checked the *declared* literal instead
of the cell, so an entry declaring an empty literal exempted whatever the cell actually
said — and `Verbatim`, whose own docstring claimed a script could not build one, was an
ordinary importable dataclass. `check` passed on a table cell reading "True mortality
4281003.55% (fabricated)". Separately, `parts` were folded into one project-wide allowlist,
so a phantom entry in a table with no rows whitelisted its strings in another fragment.
DESIGN had already called this "verified rather than trusted". It was not. It is now: the
fragment records the template, the gate rebuilds the cell from template and parts and
requires the result to equal the text on the page, and a code-list cell — which holds no
number the emitter derived — is checked against the code list published beside it.

**A regression from this same day's performance work.** `$` in `ratio-null-value` had meant
end-of-string inside a 160-character window; under the `re.MULTILINE` the document-wide scan
needs, it came to mean end-of-line. Every manuscript here is hard-wrapped, so "...that
excluded 1\npatient with missing data..." read as the null value of a ratio because of where
an editor wrapped. A value passing by coincidence, in the file whose header says that cannot
happen. `\Z` now.

**Five rule leaks, four of them the shape-not-value mistake yet again**, and one worse:
`is_methods` matched *any* heading in the chain, so a Results subsection called "Sensitivity
analyses" — which most pharmacoepidemiology papers have — re-admitted every `methods_only`
rule, and a reported `p < 0.001` classified as the pre-specified threshold. That is precisely
the failure `methods_only` was built to close, reintroduced through the chain rather than
through the heading text. A Methods-like heading now counts only while no ancestor is a
section that reports what happened.

**A footnote is read where it stands and where it is referenced.** Pandoc prints a footnote
at its reference, and G2 read its text under the section its definition line sits in only,
so a finding referenced from Results and defined under Methods, `p < 0.001`, passed as the
alpha chosen in advance, while the document printed it as a footnote to a Results sentence
(found reviewing #65). `sections.footnote_index` finds each definition's text and its
references, and a number in it must pass under the section where it stands and under the
section of every reference in the same file (`chains_at`, `Classifier.classify_under`; see
Known gaps for another file): a note referenced
from Results fails there, and one referenced from Methods and from Results must pass in
both. `explain`, `bind` and the annotated copy read it the same way. A number is judged in
no fewer places than before, so nothing that failed passes. The first version judged it at
the references alone, and review of #77 found five ways the gates took text for a note's
that pandoc prints where it stands: a `[^n]:` line pandoc reads as the paragraph above's,
paragraphs a list item or a comment holds, a line of no-break spaces taken for blank, a
note nested in another's, and a note referenced from another file. Each let a Results
claim pass at a Methods reference. Judged where it stands as well, each fails as it did.
The note's text is the definition's line, the lines under it up to a blank one or one that
may start a block, then each block after blank lines indented four spaces or a tab; where
that misreads pandoc, it only adds a section to pass in. Each note's reference chains are
found once, one in Methods and one elsewhere at most, since a verdict reads nothing else
of a section: judged under every section referencing it, a note of a thousand numbers
referenced from a thousand sections took two minutes (the fix-only review of #77).

**And the worked example named the wrong guideline.** It claimed STROBE and RECORD-PE;
RECORD-PE is for routinely collected health data and the example is a spontaneous-report
disproportionality study, so the guideline that applies is READUS-PV. It declared neither in
`reporting_guideline:`, used `p < 0.05` as a decision rule, and never demonstrated
`code_list()`. Every new user copies that file. The deeper fault was that **no gate read the
sentence**: an adherence claim is a claim about the paper's own conduct, which makes it worse
than an unbound number, and nothing reconciled it with the checklist actually completed. G5
does now, sentence by sentence, over masked text — so a guideline named in a comment is a
note rather than a claim.

## The annotated copy: four colours, and yellow is not green

`check` produces a verdict. It does not let a co-author, a supervisor or a reviewer *see*
why any individual number is trusted, and "the tool says it is fine" is not a thing a
careful reader should have to accept. `build --annotated` writes
`manuscript.annotated.docx`: every number highlighted by what backs it, carrying a link.
Hover it in Word and the provenance appears; click it and you land on its row in the
provenance appendix. Figures get a contact sheet in the same file — the picture, the values
declared presentational and why, and the record of the person who reviewed it.

**Four tiers, because a binary scheme would lie in the one place that matters.** Traced
means an artefact and a digest over it. Attested means a named person's written word, which
is traceable to a name and a date but not to a document. Exempt means a convention or a
structural reference: **the gate agreed not to look at this number.** Defect means unbound.
Colouring a convention like a traced value would make the annotated copy actively
misleading, in the document whose whole purpose is to be trusted at a glance — and an author
who sees how much of their Methods is amber has learned something the pass/fail line cannot
tell them.

Two implementation notes, both about not repeating this repository's recurring mistake.

The annotation is emitted **during substitution**, where the pipeline already knows exactly
which key it is replacing, and from the same classifier the gate uses. Re-reading the built
document and inferring what each number was would be a second implementation of "what is
this number", which is precisely the drift several rounds of review have been spent
correcting elsewhere.

The first version of this shipped two defects that a passing test suite could not have
caught, both found by opening the file. **The highlight never reached the page**: it was a
custom character style wrapping a link, OOXML allows one `w:rStyle` per run, pandoc's Link
writer puts `Hyperlink` there, and the custom style was silently discarded — styles defined,
document valid, every number unmarked. And **the annotated copy had no tables and no
figures**, because it annotated the source and substituted only *value* bindings, so
`{{table.baseline}}` printed literally. An audit document missing the artefacts a stale
number is likeliest to survive in is worse than none. The colour is direct run formatting
now, ordered after `w:rStyle` because Word drops run properties it finds out of place, and
the tests assert on the bytes rather than on the style definitions — reading the XML for a
style definition is exactly what missed it.

**Two numbers that read the same never share a provenance.** Marks are built from offsets —
a binding's span from the placeholder parser, a literal's from the tokenizer — and never by
matching text, so two keys that happen to render `1` are two marks with two anchors and two
tooltips. In a paper full of 1s and 2s that is the common case rather than an edge one. The
same reasoning runs the other way: a literal that happens to equal a published value is
still coloured red, because in source a results-derived number may not be a literal at all.

And the tooltips are injected into the `.docx` afterwards, because **pandoc drops a link
title** on the way to Word — verified before the design depended on it, not assumed. They
are keyed on a per-occurrence anchor rather than on the visible text, because two numbers
that read the same must not share a provenance, and in a paper full of 1s and 2s that
happens immediately. The highlight itself is a character style injected into pandoc's own
reference document, generated at build time rather than committed: a reference `.docx` is a
binary, and this repository ignores `*.docx` precisely so a build product cannot be mistaken
for a source.

**A mark never changes how the text reads.** The number finder reads raw text, and takes
markup in with a number: `HbA~1c` out of `HbA~1c~`, `CO~2` out of `CO~2~`, `span>7</span`
out of `<span>7</span>`. A mark around what it found left the closing `~` outside, so
pandoc read no subscript, and a number in a code span, `` `x2` ``, got its mark written
inside the span, where the link printed as text. So the annotator places each mark first:
- **Code, equations, a link's text and the front matter take no mark.** Code spans are
  paired a run of backticks with the next run of the same length in its paragraph, which
  is pandoc's rule but for two edges (see Known gaps). Equations are pandoc's dollars,
  looked for outside code: a `$` in `` `df$age` `` opened one that ran to the next code
  span's (review of #76). A dollar sign before a number is a currency's, not markup, and
  `US$5` is marked whole; one after a number stays outside the mark, where `5$ … 10$`
  faced each other across the marks between, and a backslash before a number goes
  inside it, where it escaped the mark's own bracket (the fix-only review of #76). An
  escaped dollar is text: `\$10-\$50` is marked whole, and `5\$` leaves its `\$` outside.
  So is a backslash before anything but a space, a bracket or a backslash, in a number
  read across several runs: pandoc makes text of a symbol after one, and keeps it before
  a letter or a digit, as text or a TeX command, the same inside a mark as outside, so
  `5\%-10\%`, `\~5-\~7`, `5\°-10\°`, `1.2\pm0.3` and `data\2021\05` are marked whole (the
  rounds after the extra one, and the follow-ups). A link's text, the target a URL or an
  anchor, can't hold a mark, which is itself a link. A bracket is a link's text when a
  target follows it; when a second bracket follows, by that one's label, or, the second
  empty or holding a citation or a footnote's marker, by its own text, which pandoc falls
  back to; and alone, by its own text. A label is a link's definition, where pandoc reads
  one, or a heading's title: pandoc reads `[95% CI 1.2-3.4][@smith2021]`, `[…][^2]` and
  `[12][13]` as text, and their numbers are marked (the extra round of #76, and the
  follow-ups). A number in a link's definition takes no mark, and a binding in a link's
  text is put in as its value, unmarked.
- **Inside other markup, the mark goes around the digits.** The mark goes around the one
  run free of markup that holds a digit, inside the subscript or the span, where pandoc
  reads a mark as well as anywhere: around `1c`, inside `HbA~1c~`. When several runs hold
  digits, `10^-3^`, it goes around the whole of what was found, if every sub- and
  superscript in it opens and closes there; brackets in it are escaped in the mark and
  read as text, `12][13`, and a `@` makes a citation, so none goes there. No mark opens
  straight after a `]`, where pandoc read two brackets as a reference, nor after a TeX
  command, which took it for its argument. An ordered list's own numbers take none: marked, the list was a paragraph.
  Otherwise the number is left unmarked.

That rule is a model of pandoc's inline reader, and models of pandoc's readers have been
found wrong round after round in this repository. So the build then asks pandoc: each file
is read with its marks and without, the marks unwrapped and each block compared, and every
mark in a block that reads differently is taken out. Which mark did it is not worked out,
so a paragraph can lose all its marks for one; a number in an HTML tag's attribute,
`width="300"`, is the example the tests hold. What still reads differently after that loses
every mark in the file, so the annotated copy never reads otherwise than the manuscript,
marks aside. Two things are left out of the comparison. A pipe table's column widths: a
longer row, marks in it, makes pandoc give the table widths, which changes the layout of
the annotated copy's tables and not their words. And a citation as written, which pandoc
keeps and citeproc replaces: with a mark on its locator, `p. 33`, it differed, and the
paragraph lost every mark (review of #76). A number left unmarked is
still listed in the appendix, with the reason, and the build says how many there are. It
costs two runs of pandoc's reader a file, and a third where a mark is taken out.

The annotated copy is deliberately **not stamped**. The source stamp is what G1 reads to
decide whether the document a co-author opens is current, and there must be exactly one such
document. This one is named so it cannot be mailed to a journal by accident, for the same
reason `manuscript.UNCHECKED.docx` is.

## What a data custodian forbids is declared

Many custodians of health data, pharmacovigilance and claims databases among them, forbid
publishing a count below a minimum, since a cell of two patients in a rare category can name
them, and forbid the data leaving their hands. Neither was written anywhere a gate could
read. `paper.yaml` now says the custodian's minimum (`custodian: {minimum_cell_count: 5}`),
and G2 fails each count the manuscript or the supplement binds that is at least one and
below it (`count-below-minimum`), naming the key, from the `internal-review` stage: a team
reads its own small counts while it drafts, and a panel sent to a model provider is already
outside it. A count is a whole number the analysis emitted with no unit, that is neither a
parameter, a software version nor a label; "3 years" is emitted with its unit and is no
count of people, and nought is no small cell. A display that holds the count back behind a
bound, "<5" or "≤4", its bound a whole number or a decimal, alone or followed by a word,
"<5 patients", passes only where the bound allows every count the custodian forbids: "<2"
or "≤3" under a minimum of five still say the count is one, or at most three, and fail
(round 3 of #275, round 1 of #341). A count the analysis emits as a decimal, 3.0, or with a
unit naming people, "patients", is not taken for one (pinned by
`test_what_the_count_reading_gets_wrong_is_pinned`).

An input is declared restricted where the analysis declares it, in either emitter
(`em.add_input(path, restricted=True)`, `em$add_input(path, restricted = TRUE)`), and the
results record it. G1 fails while git tracks such a file (`restricted-input-tracked`), from
the first stage: a pushed repository is a copy outside the custodian's hands. Git is asked
with a time limit, in English, whose words are read, for the path as written, not as a
pattern ("data[1].csv" is not "data1.csv"), and whatever its case where git ignores case; a
path outside the repository's work tree is not tracked by it (round 1 of #275). git's answer
is read as UTF-8, so a restricted file whose name is in another script or carries an accent
is found, where the system's code page could not read it (round 1 of #341). Where git
cannot be asked, the finding is a warning.

An input is declared synthetic the same way (`em.add_input(path, synthetic=True)`,
`em$add_input(path, synthetic = TRUE)`): simulated data, a dummy extract, a test fixture, on
which an analysis is often written while access to the real data is waited for. A binding
proves where a number came from, not that the data it came from were real, and a number from
such a run passed every gate. G1 now names, for each run that read a synthetic input, the
results of it the manuscript binds (`synthetic-input-quoted`): a warning while the paper is
written, a failure at submission, so that `submit` refuses. A run whose results nothing binds
puts no number into the paper, and is not said. A paper that is a demonstration, a worked
example or a teaching paper, says so in `paper.yaml` (`demonstration: true`): the finding is
then information, and the submission pack's title page says that the data are synthetic. The
example declares its simulated reports and is a demonstration. Nothing guesses that an input
is synthetic from its name or its contents: a declaration is the author's, and a heuristic
would be wrong both ways.

## An input can stay out of the repository

A custodian who forbids the data leaving their hands leaves a project two ways to keep them
beside the code without committing them: Git LFS and git-annex (which DataLad uses). Both
commit a pointer that names the content, and in a clone where the data are not fetched,
which is what CI and a co-author have, the pointer is what sits at the input's path. G1
hashed it, and said `input-changed` of an input nobody had touched, or `input-missing` of an
annexed one, whose link points at nothing: a project on restricted data failed G1 in CI
from the analysis stage. Neither the design nor the docs said so.

Both emitters now record each input's SHA-256 over its bytes as they are (`raw_sha256`),
beside the digest that ignores line endings, since that is what a pointer names the content
by. G1 reads a pointer at an input's path before it hashes anything (`pointers.py`):

* a Git LFS pointer, as the tool's specification writes it: `version
  https://git-lfs.github.com/spec/v1`, then `oid sha256:<hex>` and `size <bytes>`, under 1024
  bytes;
* a git-annex key, `<BACKEND>-s<bytes>[-<field>...]--<name>`: the target of a link that
  points at nothing, or a small file holding `/annex/objects/<key>` (an unlocked file) or the
  link's target (a link checked out where links are not made). SHA256E, git-annex's default,
  names the content by its SHA-256 and its extension, SHA256 by the SHA-256 alone; DataLad's
  default is MD5E (`datalad.repo.backend`, read in DataLad's source).

A pointer whose SHA-256 and size are those the emitter recorded is the input as it was, and
G1 says so in a note (`input-by-pointer`) without the data. One that names another size or
another SHA-256 is `input-changed`, now truthfully. One that cannot be compared, by MD5, an
LFS pointer with an extension (whose oid is of the content after it), or results written
before `raw_sha256`, is a warning that the input is not fetched (`input-not-fetched`), where
`input-missing` had failed. A file over 1024 bytes, or one that reads as neither, is the
data, hashed as before.

## A package to deposit, with what the custodian keeps left out

A journal asks for the code and the results to be deposited where a DOI names them, and the
Data availability statement to cite it. Everything a deposit needs was already recorded: the
scripts, the fragments and their digests, the inputs each read, the language and the version
each was written with, the lockfiles, the plan. Nothing put it together, so an author zipped
a folder by hand, and the folder held what was in it: the stored PDFs of cited papers, a
restricted extract that git ignored but the disk did not, and the review records with the
co-authors' names. `manuscript-guard package` writes `build/package/<name>/` and the .zip of
it. Basile settled four questions on 2026-10-21; each is below.

**What goes in is a list, and an input goes only by the author's word.** The package is made
from what may go, not from the project less what may not, so a folder the list does not name
is never looked in (`deposit/plan.py`): `analysis/` and `figures/` file by file, the
fragments with their digests, the plan, its frozen copy, the data dictionary and the record
of the data sources by name, the literature ledger and `references.bib` (never
`passages.yaml`, which holds the manuscript's own sentences and the names of those who judged
them), the lockfiles, and
the licence. In a repository, a file git does not track is withheld and said, since it may be
data kept out of git on purpose, and so is a link. A folder `paths:` sets to the project
itself is refused, since it would take every file of the project (round 1 of #388), and so is
a file collected at a name the package writes of its own, `paper.yaml` or `README.md`. A
declared input is held out of the folders by its name and by the file it is: another name for
the same file, a hard link, or its name in another case where the system ignores case, is the
input all the same (round 1). One of those records declared as an input, the data
dictionary the data checks read, goes as the record it is, unless it is declared
restricted. Declared paths are compared in one spelling, so that
`./data/raw.csv` declared restricted by one script and `data/raw.csv` declared shared by
another are one input, and restricted (round 2); a path that steps up, "data/../x.csv", is
held to be outside the project as written. An input that goes is held to the files of those
that do not, so that another name for a withheld file stays out with it (the fix round). A
folder `paths:` names that leads out of the project by a link is refused. A project git takes
for part of a repository and cannot list, or one git cannot be asked about with a `.git` at
its root or above it, is refused, since what git would have kept out could not be (round 2);
one git says is no repository, beyond a mount or a ceiling, is none (the fix round). An input
that is itself a results file of the project, one script reading what another wrote, goes in
as results unless it is declared restricted, and then its digest stays out with it and its
counts are not asked to be signed off. An input goes in only when the analysis
declared it synthetic or `paper.yaml` lists it in `package.share`; one declared restricted
never goes, and listing it is refused. Every other input is withheld and listed in INPUTS.md,
with its size, the SHA-256 of its bytes and how to obtain it (`package.request`, required
when anything is withheld), so a copy obtained from the custodian can be checked against the
one the results were computed from. A stored copy of a cited work never goes, and neither do
the review records, `authors.yaml`, the approvals and sign-offs, or the build.

**A fragment is deposited whole, so the custodian's minimum is read across all of it.** G2
reads the counts the manuscript prints, and "<5" in the paper holds nothing back when the
file beside it says 3. Where `custodian.minimum_cell_count` is declared, the package refuses
while a fragment holds a count from one to below it: a value that is a count as G2 reads one,
whatever its display; a table cell past the first column that states one count alone, over a
denominator, with a share in round or square brackets, or both, the share with a point, a
middle dot or a decimal comma, "3/412 (0.7%)" (`count_in_cell`, round 1 of #388), and a
footnote marks after the count or the share or none, "3 (0.7%)*", "3ᵃ (0.7%)", "3^a,b^"
(round 2 and the fix round). A share behind a bound is a share with its percent sign or
without, "3 (<1%)" or "2 (<0.1)" in a column of n (%); a P behind a bound, "1 (<0.001)", reads
the same, and is signed off: requiring the sign let the small count through (the fix round).
A model card's rows
read, used and dropped, its events and its events at each level, and a variable card's rows
missing are counts too (`deposit/counts.py`). The data custodian `authors.yaml` names may sign the list off
(`PACKAGE/custodian/small-counts`), and a list that changes is another statement. Where the
custodian restricts sending, the package is written only once they have signed off its files
and their digests as they stand (`PACKAGE/custodian/deposit`, and `-with-manuscript` for the
package that carries it); a changed script is a package they have not seen.

**The prose stays out.** Whether a manuscript may be deposited before it is published is the
journal's and the author's to say, so BOUND.md lists instead each value, table and figure the
manuscript binds, what it prints and the file and section that print it; `--with-manuscript`
adds the source.

**The supplement is packaged as the main text is** (Basile, 2026-10-21: supplementary material
is held to the same rules). Its tables and figures come from the same folders, so their
scripts, their results and their renders go in with the paper's, are run again by `verify`
in the same way, and their counts are held to the custodian's minimum. BOUND.md lists what
`manuscript/supplementary/` prints beside what the main text prints, each row with its file,
and `--with-manuscript` takes the supplement's source with the paper's. No built document
goes, `supplementary.docx` no more than `manuscript.docx`. The one reading that stays with
the main text is the Data availability statement's: a journal asks for it in the paper, and
`package-doi-not-named` looks for the DOI there (`tests/test_package.py`,
`test_the_supplement_is_packaged_as_the_main_text_is`).

**The tool uploads nothing.** It prints the steps: reserve the DOI where the repository
allows it, write it as `package.doi`, package again so that README.md and CITATION.cff carry
it, upload. Once `package.doi` is declared, G4 warns while neither the Data availability
statement nor a Code (or Software) availability statement names it, and fails at submission
(`package-doi-not-named`). The statements are read in the main text as one, across its files,
as G4 reads it (round 1 of #388). A DOI is named when a statement writes it, bare or in a
link, in any case, in emphasis, a code span or quotation marks, or cites by key an entry that
has it, and not when it writes a longer one that begins the same way.

The package refuses while G1 fails, as `submit` does while the submission check fails, and
`--skip-checks` writes it with MANIFEST.yaml saying so. No file it writes holds a date or a
clock, and the .zip gives every entry the same date and holds them in order, so two packages
of an unchanged project are the same bytes and a custodian's sign-off of one holds for the
other. The commit, the tree's state and the version of the tool that packaged it are in
MANIFEST.yaml, which nobody signs. Each file copied is hashed again in the package and held to
the plan's digest; one that changed in between stops the package.

**A crate states what the files show, and RELATIONS.md the rest** (Task 4, the design
Basile accepted on 2026-10-28). Each option is the author's to ask for, and the package
without them is the bytes it was. `--citation` adds `.zenodo.json` (`deposit/metadata.py`):
the authors as "Family, Given" with their ORCID iDs and affiliations, the keywords, the
licence, and as related works only the DOIs of the data sources
`design/data_sources.yaml` chose, under a fixed sentence about the package, since what the
paper found is the paper's to say; never `package.doi`, the package's own (see Known gaps),
and it is refused where `authors.yaml` names no author, or one with no name
(`package-no-creators`), rather than naming a creator nobody listed. `--ro-crate` adds `ro-crate-metadata.json`, an RO-Crate
1.1 and a Process Run Crate (`deposit/crate.py`), with `RELATIONS.md` and, where models were
fitted, `MODELS.md`, the G15 cards as `models` prints them (one function writes both,
`cards.py`), of the models of the fragments the package holds only: a card of a withheld
fragment would publish its rows and events, which the custodian's minimum was never read
against, so MODELS.md says how many it leaves out and why. What G15 says of the Methods'
wording and of a variable's data is left out of it, since held to the held models alone it
would say a model the Methods name was fitted by none: `check` says it. A card's trials
are counts the minimum reads too, since they are printed (round 1 of #454): the list of
small counts is then another list for a fragment whose card has trials, so a package the
custodian signed off before is to be signed off again (`PACKAGE/custodian/small-counts`),
and a default package with a card of fewer trials than the minimum is refused until it
is. Every entity is made from a record: the authors with no address, each file of
the package with its digest and size, each run of a script from its fragment, each drawing
of a figure from its `*.render.json`, each withheld input by its recorded digest with
`package.request` as its conditions of access, and the paper as a contextual article based
on the package, its source a part of it only with `--with-manuscript`. Each action names its
script as its instrument, which the profile requires: the file in the package, or a
contextual entity with the recorded path and digest where the package lacks it; whether it
is the script whose `generated_by_sha256` (or `rendered_by_sha256`) the record holds is
said in RELATIONS.md where it is not. Every other relationship is in `@graph` only where it
holds now: an input has the digest the run recorded, a fragment the digest of its
`.sha256`, a file a figure's script drew the digest its `*.render.json` recorded. A crate that states a link the record names and the files do not
bear out describes a package nobody ran; so each such link, and each no record makes, is a
row of RELATIONS.md, under "not as recorded" or "not recorded". `datePublished` is
`package.date`, a new optional field, or the day the latest results were written; no file
reads the clock, and a crate with neither is refused (`package-crate-undated`), RO-Crate 1.1
requiring the date. JSON is written with its keys sorted, the entities in order and `\n` line
ends, so that two packages of an unchanged project, made in two folders, are one set of
bytes. `--root-citation` writes `CITATION.cff` and `.zenodo.json` at the project's root
only where none is (decision 7(a)): one there is the author's, is never written over, and
the fields where it differs are named. The crate and the citation files are files of the
package, so where the custodian restricts sending a package with them is another package to
sign off (`PACKAGE/custodian/deposit-citation`, `-ro-crate`). The tests are in
`tests/test_ro_crate.py`, and the corruption cases, a script edited after its run, an input
changed and a figure redrawn, each listed in RELATIONS.md and only the last two left out of
`@graph`, and a model of a withheld fragment kept out of MODELS.md, in
`tests/test_corruption.py`.

**The companion page is a reading of the records, and says nothing of its own** (Task 4,
part B, the design Basile accepted on 2026-10-28). `package --companion` (decision 3(a): a
flag, not a command) adds `ro-crate-preview.html`, the name RO-Crate 1.1 gives a crate's
page for people, and the same bytes as `index.html` for a site. It implies `--ro-crate`,
whose crate the page's JSON-LD names as what it is based on; the crate does not list the
page, which is its preview and none of its data. The page is one file
(`deposit/companion.py`, `companion_evidence.py`, `companion_parts.py`): its style inline,
each picture a data URI, and no script but its Schema.org `ScholarlyArticle` (headline,
authors by ORCID iD with their affiliations, keywords, licence, `isBasedOn` the package's
DOI, the crate and the chosen data sources' DOIs, `identifier` the recorded DOI, `version`
one more than the revision rounds), every `<`, `>` and `&` in it written as an escape. Its
six sections are each made from a record. The overview: the abstract, a citation of the
package, the dated events the records hold (the plan kept with the first results, each
results file written, each revision round received, `package.date`), a digest of every
results file by name and bytes, the set `fragments_digest` reads for `check` and `verify`
(the withheld ones too: their digest, not what they hold), taken in the order of the names'
POSIX spelling so that it is one on every system (`fragments_digest` orders by path, which
on Windows ignores case), and a digest of SHA256SUMS's lines for every file but the page, its
copy, the crate, RELATIONS.md, MANIFEST.yaml and SHA256SUMS. The key findings are the
abstract's own sentences that print a value, word for word with the values in (decision
1(a)); the evidence map is BOUND.md's rows from the same `bound_rows`, with each results
file's digest, its script and the script's recorded digest; a sentence that cites a work is
shown with its G7 passage only where the passage is in the stored copy and a person judged
that it supports the sentence as it reads, and then by its locator, never its words
(decision 4(a)). The figures: a picture, the SVG, only where the file in the package is
the one its `*.render.json` records, the script beside it the one that drew it, and no
record ties it to a file the package withholds: an input its `*.render.json` lists, which
no writer of the tool records yet (only a record edited by hand holds one), or one a run of
its script declared it read, compared in the case the system compares names in. Which
results a figure was drawn from is otherwise recorded nowhere, so a figure drawn from a
withheld file that no record names is shown, the usual case. The
caption, a
Markdown legend after the binding or the one caption of a LaTeX float that holds the figure
alone; the alternative text; where G10 says the review stands, and when, but not by whom.
The bound tables from their fragments, and the G15 cards of the held models by
`model_cards` with `cards_only`, as MODELS.md has them, so that a kind only a withheld
results file fitted is not said to be unfitted; the lines it writes for G15's findings are
left out and the findings under a card listed by their code and place. The methods: each
script and how to run it, what each run recorded of its language and platform, the lockfiles with whether the runs recorded the same
digest, the inputs, each Methods claim with its step and where it stands against
`methods.lock`, and the last run of `verify` with the date it recorded. The limitations: each
section of the manuscript or the supplement titled for them, the plan's Deviations as
written, G12's findings by their code and place, and each dimension's `unchecked` from
`assurance.py`. The co-authors: `checker`'s decisions counted by author, anyone else counted together and not
named, and each author's approval, current or given to an earlier manuscript.

Prose goes to pandoc in one document, each piece after a mark, and comes back cut at the
marks: two runs for the whole page (`deposit/prose.py`). Pandoc's reader has every extension
that passes HTML or TeX through or sets an attribute turned off; a picture becomes its
description, a link not to the web or an address its words, a footnote its text in
brackets; pandoc's user data directory is not read. Without pandoc `--companion` is refused
and the rest of `package` is not, nor is a sign-off of a package without the page: a record
the page cannot read stops the page with what stopped it, and `sign` leaves out only the
page's variant, and says so. The page's own parts name nobody from a record but the authors
`authors.yaml` lists, in the byline and beside their approvals: a reviewer, a figure's
reviewer, a passage's judge, a checker or a role's holder is said by the role, counted or
dated, and a gate's finding (G12's, G15's; G10's as a fixed phrase for each code) by its code
and place, never its words, since a message may name whoever a record names. Its place is
printed only where it is a file the package ships, the manuscript, the plan or paper.yaml; a
record under `review/` is placed by the folder of its round, since a named reading's file is
called after its reader; any other by no place. A finding is given as `check` gives it at
the project's stage (`policy.apply_stage`), the design rounds read as `check` reads them at
submission. No record's text can address a piece of the prose: the mark that holds a
piece's place is a character `esc` takes out of every record's text. Nothing is taken
out of the page once it is written: a round of review found a scrub of names from the written
page both missed names and changed words and authors' names, so the page prints no such text
instead. The manuscript's prose and the plan's Deviations are the authors' text, published
with the paper and the package, and are printed as written, with the plan's comments blanked
as the manuscript's are; the design's "no reviewer or checker names" is about what the page
itself lists. Of a results file the package withholds nothing is shown, its values printed
as "[withheld]" in the prose too, and what the page shows is held to the plan's own list of
the results files it withholds (`shows_nothing_withheld`): one held by mistake stops the
page. So a count below the custodian's minimum the page shows is one of the package's own,
which its small-count check refuses until the custodian signs it off. The bytes are a
function of the records and of pandoc: no clock, no path of the computer (a finding's place
is from the project's root), no version of the tool (MANIFEST.yaml names it, and pandoc's as
`companion_written_with`), records sorted, and `\n` line ends. A package with the page is
another package for the custodian to sign (`PACKAGE/custodian/deposit-companion`), and it
holds more than the files of the package: every approval, every checker's decision, every
run of `verify`, a figure review and a G12 finding changes the page, and so stales the
custodian's sign-off of the package with the page, which is signed again. The tests
are in `tests/test_companion.py`: each section from the example and from records a test
adds, a LaTeX manuscript and a supplement, the page twice and from another folder the same
bytes, the fragments and every mapping of the results in any order the same bytes, a date
only where a record has it, no name but the authors', no passage's words, a G12 message
by its code, no word changed for a name, and one script, whose JSON-LD parses. In
`tests/test_corruption.py`, the values of a results file the package withholds are never in
the page, one held by mistake stops it, and a small count the page would show stops it.

**A deposit is staged where it can be read, and the custodian is asked first** (Task 4,
part C and its third pull request, the design Basile accepted on 2026-10-28). `deposit
--target <target> --bundle <bundle>` (`deposit/command.py`) writes
`build/deposit/<target>-<bundle>/` and its archive, and sends nothing: the clients that
upload to Zenodo and OSF are the next pull request's. A pair that makes no sense, arXiv with
a plan or a site with a preprint, is refused with the reason (`bundles.PAIRS`). The order is
the point. First the data custodian's checks (`deposit/preflight.py`): the small counts of
the results files the bundle carries, through `package`'s own reading of them and its
sign-off (`PACKAGE/custodian/small-counts`); for a preprint G2's `count-below-minimum` over
the manuscript, since a preprint prints it; `check_restricted_inputs`; and Task 3's check of
a masked cell recovered by subtraction from a table the bundle carries,
`gates.custodian.recoverable_cells` (`count-recoverable`). A release is
taken to carry the results files the package holds, and so is the site, whose page shows
them; a plan and a preprint carry none. Anything these find stops the deposit before
anything is built. Then a release, the site that is its page, and a preprint are held to
`check --stage submission`, as `submit` is: a public preprint is held to the submission's
standard (Basile, 2026-10-28). Then the bundle is planned in memory, a list of `plan.Entry` with their digests, and
refused where a file of it is an input declared restricted, by its name, by the file it is,
or by its bytes, those a run recorded or the input holds now, since `pack_latex` copies each
file the LaTeX build read into the arXiv folder under a name of its own
(`deposit-restricted-input`), where two of its files share a name in the case a system that
ignores case reads (`deposit-name-taken`), and, where the custodian restricts sending, until
they have signed off its list of files and digests as it stands,
`DEPOSIT/custodian/<target>/<bundle>`, through `sign_offs.settle` as every sign-off is. Each
target is another place, so `zenodo-sandbox` is signed off apart from `zenodo`. A release's
MANIFEST.yaml is left out of that list, as `package` leaves it out of its own: it names the
commit and whether the tree is clean, which writing the sign-off changes, and every file it
lists is in the list by its own digest (round 1 of #460). What is signed is the bytes that
go out, so a document `deposit` builds is built to the same bytes every time: the medRxiv
`.docx` is built with `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` set to 1980-01-01, the date the archives' members
carry, by which pandoc dates the .docx's members and its core properties, and the build's
stamp dates its own part as pandoc dated the rest (`preprint.fixed_date`,
`roundtrip.stamp_into`). Not the last commit's date, which committing the sign-off would
move. A LaTeX manuscript's PDF is compiled by the author's TeX, which may write the clock
into it and which the tool never runs in a test, so it is signed by what it is compiled
from: every file of the folder and their digests, with the tool's version and the LaTeX
engine the journal's profile names (`preprint.built_from`, Known gaps). The stamp's own
part is a Unix member, as the archives' are, so that the system a `.docx` is signed on is
not written into it (round 2 of #460); its bytes still depend on pandoc's version and on the
zlib that compresses it, so a custodian who signs on one machine may have to sign again on
another (Known gaps). A restricted input is looked for by both digests a run
records, the one blind to line endings and `raw_sha256`, so that a verbatim copy of a CRLF
input is found with its original gone. The
package's findings that the deposit asks itself, its small counts and its own sign-off, are
left out of a release's report, so that the custodian signs one list. Only then is anything
written (`deposit/archive.py`): the folder, its SHA256SUMS, and the .zip `package` writes or,
for arXiv, a .tar.gz of the source with its members in order, each dated 0, owned by user and
group 0 with no names and mode 644, in the POSIX format, and the gzip stream dated 0 with no
name in it, so that the same files are the same bytes from any folder on any day. A plan is
no pre-registration once `design/plan.frozen.yaml` records the first results: the bundle is
then refused unless `--retrospective "<why>"` is given, and it is labelled "Analysis plan,
deposited after results were first written on" the day the record gives, with the reason and
the frozen copy (`bundles.preregistration`); the custodian signs a plan deposited that way
with the same reason (`sign --retrospective`), since its README holds it. `--retrospective`
with a release or a preprint, which hold no plan to label, is refused (exit 2) by `deposit`
and by `sign`, and is never written into a command the refusal suggests; `sign` refuses it
with any finding that is not a deposit's too. The release is the
package with its crate and companion page, its MANIFEST.yaml, the dictionary's exports, each
reporting checklist as `submit`'s table, and VERIFICATION.md and .json
(`deposit/verification.py`, decision 5(a)): `check --stage submission` by gate, counted and
named by code; each dimension's machine line and what no gate decides, from `assurance.py`, without
the lines that name a panel's readers, a figure's reviewer or a passage's judge, by decision
4(a); the last `verify` run as `build/verify.json` records it; `checker`'s counts by author;
each author's approval; and the document, front and results digests the approvals and
`check` hold to. The arXiv bundle is `pack_latex`'s folder, or for a Markdown manuscript
`build --latex`'s, both needing TeX, the main document's files only, with
`arxiv_submission_sheet.md`; the medRxiv bundle is the `.docx` built offline, or a LaTeX
manuscript's PDF, the supplement, the figures, the checklists, the declarations and the
CRediT statement, with `medrxiv_submission_sheet.md` mapping each question of the form to
what the project records or "not recorded" (`deposit/preprint.py`, `deposit/sheets.py`). A
figure is one of the formats `submit` packs; a picture in another (`.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.svg`)
and a link are each named as left out, a link as `package` withholds one. The sheet names
each author as `authors.yaml` spells them, with "ORCID not recorded" where it gives none,
every affiliation, and an affiliation id that `affiliations` does not list as not recorded,
which no gate reports; two authors marked corresponding are said to be two. The Data
availability statement is printed as the document prints it: its bindings are their
displays, as the abstract's are, a LaTeX formula is read as maths as the abstract's is, and
pandoc writes it as plain text by the abstract's rule, its paragraphs and no-break spaces
kept (`submission.plain_passage`); it is read as written (`sheets.statement_source`), its
listings not blanked as G4 blanks them. Where anything is left that plain text cannot show,
a citation, a footnote, maths, a subheading, a listing, a bracket or a binding left
unfilled, the sheet says to copy it from the document and prints none of it (round 2 of
#460). What
a sheet says of a server's rules is the rule as the sheet names it: the abstract's length
against 1,920 characters and the archive's size are the tool's counts, the limits arXiv's.
The site is `index.html` and `.nojekyll`, and the git commands to publish them are printed,
never run; they take the `gh-pages` branch where it is, here or on the remote, and make it
where it is not, one command a line with no `||`, which Windows PowerShell 5.1 does not
parse, and say to use the worktree where the branch is checked out already. The tests are in `tests/test_deposit.py`: every bad pair, each bundle's files, the
retrospective label, each check of the custodian's stopping it with nothing written, the
sign-off and its staling, a release refused while the submission check fails, the archives
twice and from another folder the same bytes, both sheets, the site, and no connection
opened; the preprint bundles with LaTeX and Word stood in for, so that no test compiles. In
`tests/test_corruption.py`, a count planted in a table stops a release and the site before
anything is built, a restricted input a plan would carry stops it, one copied into a LaTeX
folder under another name is found by its bytes, and a release's sign-off does not change
with its MANIFEST.yaml. A verbatim copy of a CRLF restricted input is found by its raw
digest, a PDF compiled with another engine is signed off again, a stray `--retrospective`
leaves the small counts unsigned, and a statement with a LaTeX formula, a subheading or a
listing is not printed in the medRxiv sheet.

What this rests on: deterministic tests in CI (`tests/test_package.py`): the example packaged,
unzipped and run again by `verify` from the unpacked folder with every value reproduced; an R
analysis the same way where R is installed; a restricted input, an input nobody declared
shareable, a pointer in place of an input, a file git does not track and a cited work's stored
copy each left out of the folder written; each kind of small count refusing it; the
custodian's two sign-offs; every digest of the manifest; and the generated reading of a cell
and of a DOI (`tests/test_properties.py`). It has not been used on a real deposit.
## The data a paper analysed are named by the analysis

"Data were extracted from VigiBase on 1 March 2024, covering reports to 31 December 2023" is
a claim like any number. A date typed in the Methods already failed G2, each of its digits
unbound, and the way out G2's hint gave was a string emitted with its display,
`em.value("period.start", "2015-01-01", display="1 January 2015")`. That route had two
holes. Nothing compared a string value with its display, so the display could be another
year; and the call raised, the digits of an ISO date being taken for a measurement. Neither
tied the date to the data: the extract could be replaced and the analysis run again, and the
old date went out with every gate green.

Many databases have one version, or none a user can name (Basile, 2026-10-21), so a version
cannot be what identifies the data. The date of the extraction can, with the file. The
analysis declares both where it reads the file, in either emitter:

    em.dataset("vigibase", "data/vigibase.csv", extracted="2024-03-01",
               covers=("1968", "2023-12-31"), version=None,
               fingerprint="3f9a1c2b7e4d5a60", dates=frame["received"])

It declares the files as inputs and emits `dataset.<name>.extracted`, `.covers_from`,
`.covers_to`, and `.version` only where the source has one, each with the role `dataset`.
The fragment carries a `datasets` record: the files, the pin, the dates and what the data's
own dates were found to span. Dates are ISO 8601 to a year, a month or a day, and each is a
span of days: data covering "2023" end on 31 December 2023. They are printed in the English
`paper.yaml` declares, "1 March 2024" or "March 1, 2024", a month as "March 2024" in both.
