  is ended, and the test with it, without the input being cut down: a hang would be
  waited for again at every smaller input, and the smallest would be named as the cause.
  `pytest.fail` does not do that, since Hypothesis takes it for a failing input.
- **A base that cannot be asked.** A reader says at its start which readings its source
  does not have and which it has and cannot make, and the two are not treated alike. A
  reading the base does not have is passed over: it is newer than the base. That is a
  skip, and it is also written on the job's page, since a skip is one line among
  hundreds. A reading that needs a program this machine lacks, pandoc for the round trip,
  is skipped on either side, and only skipped: CI has the program. A reading the base has
  and cannot make is a comparison that was not made: a helper it goes through takes other
  arguments now, or the base needs a dependency that is not installed for the working
  tree. It fails, unless the pull request says in `differential_expected.yaml` that it
  changed what the reading goes through, and then it passes with that said. Both used to
  be passed over, which left a job green that had compared nothing; and a base that can
  be asked for none of the readings is refused outright. A command line that refuses a
  reading's arguments, in a base older than an option the reading passes, is an answer
  like any other and is compared: it used to end the process that was answering.
- **The comparison is held to being one.** Two processes on this source under two hash
  seeds must answer alike on every reading, which also catches a reading that walks a
  set. And twelve lines are changed in a copy of the source, one at a time, and the reading
  that goes through each must differ: among them the mutant the review of #181 found
  alive, the offset of a quotation's lines losing a character at each line break, an
  import that writes no rewording, a finding that points at another file with its line
  kept, which the readings did not compare at first, and a sign of comparison that is no
  part of its number.

Run against main as it was before #181 and #183, it reports the vocabulary reading
changed, on a vocabulary of one entry, and `check` changed; passes over the spelling
reading and the paper's own words, which that base did not have; and finds the other ten
readings the same, the round trip and the abbreviations among them, the second of which
#181's description said and its reviewer ran 1,500 projects to see.

### What the first runs found

Nothing in the gates. The invariants over 6,000 inputs each with the first generator, and
every property at ten times its examples with the second, held on main at 0.2.430.
What turned up is three ways the sentence of a vocabulary conflict is worded by the order
of the entries, which is under Known gaps and held by a test.

## The check a gate cannot make, and who can make it

Every gate here asks a question a machine can settle: is this number the number the analysis
wrote, is this quote in the stored source, is this value in that quote. The question none of them
asks is the one a reader of the source asks — **does the sentence say what the document says**.

That is not a gap in the implementation. It is the boundary of the whole approach. A value can be
right, its quote can be right, the quote can be in the source, and the sentence can still name
the wrong denominator, the wrong subgroup or the wrong year. On the first manuscript written with
this toolkit, that is precisely what happened: a share whose value and quote were both correct,
in a sentence that agreed with the ledger about the wrong denominator, three machine passes clean.
A co-author reading one item against one quote found it.

So the question goes to people. The design problem is that the people who can answer it are
clinicians and pharmacologists, not programmers, and every step between them and the question
loses most of them.

### One file, and nothing else

**Chosen:** `checker build --for "<name>"` writes one self-contained page. Every item, every
sentence, and every piece of evidence is inside that file — images as data URIs, tables and text
excerpts as data. It opens by double-clicking, offline, in any current browser. Nothing is
installed, no
account is made, no network is touched, and the page sends nothing anywhere. A button writes the
answers file; the person sends it back however they already send files.

**Rejected: a page on the project's own site, with a token for each co-author.** It was the first
thing asked for, and it is worse on every axis that matters here.

- A manuscript's unpublished numbers would sit on a public host. A token in a URL is not access
  control: it travels in mail, in browser history and in referrers, and one forward makes the
  numbers public before the paper is.
- Collecting answers needs something that accepts writes. A static page cannot, so it means a
  service, which means an account, a secret and an operator — in a toolkit whose dependencies
  are PyYAML and jsonschema.
- It fails exactly where it is needed: offline, on a hospital network that blocks the host, in a
  mail client that rewrites links.
- The author would maintain it, and an author writing a paper is not an operator of web
  services.

What the page gives up is a return path that needs no action from the person: they must send one
file back. That is a real cost, paid once per person per round, and it buys a round that works on
any machine with a browser.

### The items are found, not written

A project should not have to describe its own paper to get a round started. `checking/produce.py`
reads the files the project already keeps and offers five kinds: values quoted from the
literature, each with the passage it came from; sentences that cite something; the Methods
beside the code their anchors name ("The Methods against the code"); references as
`references.bib` holds them; and the authors. Nothing of this is particular to one paper.

What it cannot offer is a number transcribed from a table in a source document, because only the
project knows that this value came from row 14 of that workbook — that is what its own tracing
records. A project writes those into `checks/items.json`, and they are asked **first**, because a
project that went to the trouble knows what it wants asked first. Page images live there too: a
PDF renderer is a dependency this toolkit does not have and will not take for this, and what a
checker reads is the quote, which is text the ledger already holds.

**A group the project fills is the project's, whole.** Not item by item: the two producers key
their ids on different inputs, so the same value gets two ids, nothing deduplicates it, and a
co-author is asked about it twice. The paper this was first run against fills the four groups
it then had itself, with each value traced to a row of a source document the toolkit cannot see;
asking its own version of each beside them would have added a few hundred duplicate questions to
someone's afternoon. So one contributed item in a group takes that whole group, and
`build` prints how many of its own it left out — a thing to notice, rather than to discover from
a co-author. Not `methods`: its items carry G9's code digest, which a project's own could not,
and its answers include `code`, so `checker build` refuses a project's file that declares a
group of that id.

### What the digest covers

Every answer carries the digest of the item as its maker saw it. An answer whose digest no longer
matches is not counted as agreement: the sentence moved after they looked, so their yes is about
text nobody has now, and the item is outstanding again. It is written down all the same, with
the digest they saw, and so is an answer about an item the project no longer has: both count
for nothing, and the note in each is kept, because "the source says 17.4" is worth having
whatever happened to the sentence since (decision 3 of Task 1, 2026-10-28). They were refused
at import before.

The digest therefore covers the words — the title, the facts, each sentence's text and
section, **and the words of each piece of evidence**: a quote's text, a table's cells, an
excerpt's lines, a facts table's rows, and the caption and note that frame them. The evidence
was left out of the first version, on the argument that a page re-rendered larger is the same
page — true of an image and false of words, and applied to both. For the literature group the
evidence *is* the question, "Does the quoted passage say this number?", so a quote replaced
between build and import left a co-author's yes recorded against a sentence they never read.

Deliberately not in it:

- **how a piece of evidence was drawn, or where to look in it.** An image's file, a table's
  outlined cell, an excerpt's line numbers, the substrings highlighted. A page re-rendered
  larger is the same page.
- **where the sentence sits.** The line is how to find it, not what it says, and a manuscript
  gains and loses lines every working day. With the line in the digest, adding one paragraph to
  the Introduction would refuse every answer about every sentence below it, none of which
  changed. That was in the first implementation, and it survived there twice: out of the digest
  in the first fix, and left in a claim item's **identifier**, where it did the same thing by
  another route until a review found it.
- **the question the group asks.** Rewording "Does the quoted passage say this number?" would
  otherwise discard every answer in that group, and the questions are prose about what a group
  is rather than about any one item. The cost is that a group asked a materially different
  question keeps its old answers, and nothing notices.

### Append-only, and a person's name on it

`checks/decisions.csv` is appended to, never rewritten. The question it answers — was this
checked, by whom, and when — is asked months later by whoever is writing to a reviewer, and a
file that gets rewritten cannot answer it. The latest decision by one person for one item counts;
the superseded ones stay and say what changed. Where two people answered the same item
differently, `status` reports it, because a disagreement between two readers of the same source
is itself a finding.

Which decision counts is the latest about the item **as it is now**, where the person gave one,
and otherwise the latest of all (`store._latest`). With stale answers written down, an earlier
round's file imported after this round's would otherwise have taken the place of every current
answer it named, and put those items back in the queue. A "wrong", an "unsure" or a note about
an earlier version, given after the person's answer about this one, counts for nothing and is
listed by `status` as a flag on an earlier version, so that its note is not lost to sight.

An answer the record already holds is not written again (`store._already`): one with the
status, note and digest of the person's latest decision on the item, or, where the page stamped
it with the time it was given, one with the status, note, digest and time of any earlier
decision of theirs on it. The page it came from is not compared: a page rebuilt for the same
person brings back from the browser the answers they gave on the last one, under its own
identifier. So importing a file twice adds nothing, and nor does importing it again after a
later one from the same person, which made its old answer the latest once more (round 1 of
#455). A person who changes their mind back answers at another time, and that is recorded.

### A page for each author, and whose word an answer is

`checker build --all` writes `checks/check-<name>.html` for every author `authors.yaml` lists,
the corresponding author among them (`--except` leaves one out, `-o` names the folder);
`--for` still writes one page, for an author or for anyone else, and says when the name is no
author's; a family name two authors share names neither, and is refused.

A page's file name is the same in every run. Two names that fold to one, "José García" and
"Jose Garcia", each add six characters of the SHA-256 of the name as written in Unicode's
composed form, `check-jose-garcia-<six hex>.html`: numbered by their order instead, "Jose Garcia"
built alone took the file "José García" had been given in the run before (round 2 of #455).
Whether a name takes the suffix depends on the authors `authors.yaml` lists (and on whom the run
builds for): adding a second author whose name folds to the same file name gives the first
author's next page a new file name. Their answers still match, by the page's identifier; the
old file stays where it is. A file the register says was last built for someone else is not
replaced, compared as the file system compares names (on Windows without case), and `--all`
holds every file it would write to the register before it writes any, so a page found to be
another person's refuses the run before any page is written, and names the file. A page is
written under a temporary name, recorded in the register, and only then given its own, so a register
that cannot be written (open in a spreadsheet) leaves no page to be sent unrecorded; the
temporary file is removed on any failure, and one a failed run left is removed first.

Answers go back to the corresponding author unless `--to` names someone. Each page carries
`person` (name and ORCID iD), a random 128-bit token (`secrets.token_hex(16)`), and the digest
of the items it asks; its header says "Made for NAME. Your answers will carry this
name." The page's identifier digests its items, its person and its token, so no two builds
share one; the browser keeps unsent answers under the first two only, so a page rebuilt with
nothing changed for that person keeps their progress.

Every page built is a row of `checks/bundles.csv`, append-only like the decisions and kept from
an agent's editor by the hooks: when, for whom, the identifier, the token's SHA-256 (never the
token), the digest of the items, how many, and the file, relative to the project where it is
inside it and by its whole path where it is not. The page writes `checking-answers/2`, which
adds the token, the ORCID iD and that digest to what `/1` wrote; both are read.

`checker import --answers a.json b.json ...` takes any number of files and needs no `--for`:
each says whose it is, and is held to the register (Basile's decision 4 (a)):

- a file naming a registered page must carry that page's token, name and ORCID iD. Otherwise it
  is refused with the reason, exit 2, and since every file is read before any is recorded,
  nothing from that import is recorded;
- a `/1` file naming a registered page is refused: no registered page writes one;
- a file naming no registered page, a `/1` file, one built on another clone or one with an
  identifier made up, is recorded under whatever name it gives, and its decisions are
  **claimed**: `import` says so of the file, `status` of each decision, and a later reader can
  tell them from the rest by their page's absence from the register. Nothing holds the name in
  such a file to anything.

Every file is checked whole before any is recorded: a field of the wrong type, an `answers` that
is not a list or an answer that names no item refuses the import (round 1 of #455).

The name is looked up in `authors.yaml` (`checking.people`): by ORCID iD, full name, e-mail
address or family name, compared in Unicode's composed form and without case, so "Example" and
"Ada Example" are one person and a name typed with a combining accent is the name spelt with a
precomposed one. It is recorded as `authors.yaml` writes it, as before this register.

**Two authors whose full names are one name are refused by checker.** Decisions are kept by
person and item, so the two would share every decision: both were recorded as "Wei Zhang", and
one's "wrong" was replaced by the other's "ok" (round 1 of #455). Telling them apart by a key
made of what `authors.yaml` says of them, "Wei Zhang <ORCID iD>" or "Wei Zhang (2)", was tried
and dropped (round 2): an iD corrected, or an author added above them, changes the key, and
would move their decisions in a record that is never rewritten. So `checker build` says "two
authors are named Wei Zhang; checker cannot keep their answers apart; write one of the names in
a form of its own in authors.yaml (a middle initial, say)": `--for` either of them is refused,
`--all` builds for every other author and lists the two as left out, and refuses only where
everyone is a namesake. Whatever names one of them, the full name, one's ORCID iD, one's e-mail
address or the family name, is refused the same way, in `--for` and in an answers file: one's
address resolved to the shared name and merged their decisions (round 3). Decisions recorded
under a name before a second author with that name was added are marked by `status` as
"recorded before this name became shared": whose they are is no longer known. Two authors
given one ORCID iD are a mistake in `authors.yaml`, and `checker build` and `checker import`
refuse to start until it is put right, naming the iD.

A name that is no author's is recorded as given and marked as such. A name that is an author's
given with an ORCID iD that is not theirs, or an author's iD given with another's name, is a
mismatch. In a file from a registered page it is refused, since `authors.yaml` has changed since
the page was built (an iD corrected, say), and the message says to rebuild the page. In any
other file it is recorded as "Name <iD>", apart from the author, claimed, and marked "ORCID
differs".

**What this proves.** The token shows which page a file came from, not who answered. Whoever
holds a page holds its token: a page forwarded is answered by whoever it was forwarded to, and
the corresponding author, who sent every page, holds every token. What it stops is a file that
names a registered page being edited to read as another co-author's, and one page's answers
passed off as another page's or another round's. It does not stop a file that names no
registered page from reading as anyone's: that file is recorded as claimed, under the name it
gives. The name on a decision is a claim, and the register says whether the page it names was
built for that name. Nothing is signed.

An agent's `checker import` is put to the person by the hooks, as an `approve` is (decision
5 (a)): it puts a co-author's name to the answers in a file, and which file is taken as whose
word is the author's call.

**The hook asks unless the command plainly runs no import.** Each round of review of #455 found
another shell form that hid one from a reader of commands: an operator inside quotes, `$(...)`,
`bash -c`, `eval`, a here-string piped to `iex`. So a command that holds a word naming the tool
(`manuscript-guard`, `mguard`, `manuscript_guard`) and the words `checker` and `import`,
anywhere and inside quotes too, is asked, and refused in Codex. The one exception is a command
read cleanly as a POSIX shell reads it and as Windows does (quotes first, then the `;`, `&`, `|`
and line ends outside them; no command substitution, no unclosed quote), in which every word
that says `import` stands in an invocation that is plainly `checker build`, `checker status` or
`checker recap`, the tool its first word, with `import` only as an option's value: `--title "Drug import and
safety"`, `--for import`. Main's pattern asked wherever `checker` and then `import` followed the
tool's name, so this keeps what it asked and asks more.

### The Methods against the code

G9 records that someone read a claim of the Methods against the step it points at; whether the
text describes the code is still a person's to say, and a co-author who wrote or reviewed the
analysis can say it where the author cannot see their own slip. So the toolkit's fifth group,
`methods` (`checking/methods.py`), asks "Does this Methods text describe what this code
does?" (Task 1, PR 2, 2026-10-28).

**What an item is.** Exactly a claim of `gates/methods.anchored`, one item each: anchors side by
side claim one text, and that text is one item showing every step it points at. A claim naming
a step the run never recorded is not sent, nor one that claims no text, and `build` prints a
line for each. Under decision 2 (a), each **open** paragraph is an item too, saying "no code is
linked to this text": a paragraph G9 itself reads as the Methods' and that holds no anchor,
which is G9's own list of them (`anchored`'s second half, what `methods --explain` lists as
`open`). That is a paragraph under a heading `classify.is_methods` reads as the Methods, in
the main text or the supplement, other than a table, a figure placed by its binding, a fenced
listing or a fenced div. A paragraph with no anchor outside the Methods is no item.

**What it shows.** The claim, its values filled in and marked, its section the file's path
under `manuscript/`, so a supplement's Methods say they are the supplement's. The facts: the
steps, each step's script and code digest, and each `results.` value the claim binds with its
value as printed. The evidence: a new kind, `code`, numbered lines with no highlighting,
read from the script on disk: the step's body, and for a Python script each function the run
followed into, as its own block, found with `ast`; R gives the body only. Where the script's
digest is not the one its fragment recorded, each block and `build` say the code shown may not
be what ran, and a fragment that records no digest of its script is said by both to leave it
unknown, and one whose script is not there is said by `build`. The Methods are read strictly,
as G9 reads them, with the results they bind: a manuscript file that is not UTF-8, or a results
file that does not parse, leaves the group out of the round, and every verb names the file,
while the other groups, which read neither so, are sent; `import` refuses the group's answers
with that reason. **Not shown**: how the pair stands in `methods.lock`, which would answer for the
co-author before they read anything.

**The identifier and the digest.** The identifier is the file under `manuscript/`, the steps
joined by `+`, and the claim's place among the claims of the same steps in that file, an open
paragraph's among the open paragraphs (its steps none): not the words. The items stand in the
order the documents print the files, the main text's then the supplement's, and in each file
by line, claims and open paragraphs alike. An edited claim then
stales its answers, which keep their notes and are asked again, rather than orphaning them.
Under decision 1 (a) the digest holds the code as G9's digest of it read as code, among the
facts; a `code` block's lines, its note and its line numbers are outside it
(`items._words_of`), so a comment edited, a call re-wrapped or a line added above the step,
with the run made again, keeps every answer. Only the methods group's: a project's own `code`
block carries no code digest, and its lines are in its digest as an excerpt's are.
`Step.where`'s lines are for that reason not
among the facts: the page shows them from the block. The values are in it twice, in the
sentence and in the facts, so a value printed otherwise stales the claims that bind it.

**The answers.** A group may list its own (`answers` in the schema, each a status and its
button's words); the methods group lists "Text matches the code" (`ok`), "Text needs
changing" (`wrong`), "Code needs changing" (`code`) and "Not sure" (`unsure`). The page draws
its bar from the item's group, Y, N, C and U, and a key answers only with a status the group
lists. `code` is refused at import outside a group that lists it, with the reason; an answer
about an item the project no longer has is written down with `ok`, `wrong` or `unsure`, as
before, and refused with `code`, since its group cannot be known. Every answer but `ok` asks
for a note, on the page and at import, which refuses one without, naming the item. A group may
not list a status twice. `checker build` refuses a project's items file that declares a group
`methods`, which would send the project's items under the toolkit's question and none of the
toolkit's; `import` and `status` read it as before (Known gaps says how to move). `decisions.csv` keeps its nine columns: `code` is a status like
the rest. `status` lists a `code` with the `wrong` and the `unsure`.

**Tests.** `tests/test_properties.py` holds over generated Methods (`method_claims`, reading
`checker methods`) that each claim is one item with its text, that a value printed otherwise
changes the digests of exactly the items binding it, and that an edit to one item's words keeps
every identifier and changes that item's digest alone; an identifier keyed on the text, and a
digest without the bound values, each fail it.

### The recap, and what its chain can show

`checker recap` writes `checks/recap.md` (decision 8 (a) of Task 1) from the record, the
register and the items as the project has them now (`checking/recap.py`, Task 1, PR 3). It is
the page to read after a round, and the one a journal's question "did the co-authors check
this" is answered from:

- **the changes asked for in the manuscript**: each current `wrong`, with the item, the
  co-author, when, their note, and each sentence the item stands in, by file and line;
- **the changes asked for in the code**: each current `code`, with the steps, where the text
  stands, the co-author, when and the note; and below, the steps of the analysis no Methods
  text points at, as G9's `method-step-undescribed` finds them;
- **what is still open**: each current `unsure`, and each item two people answered otherwise;
- **what was said of a version of an item that is gone**: the answers recorded with the digest
  their maker saw, about an item that has changed since or that the project no longer has, and
  the flags given after an answer about this version. They count for nothing, and their notes
  are here (decision 3 (a));
- **what each co-author checked**: a row for each author, in the order `authors.yaml` gives,
  then each other name the record holds, as it writes it (two spellings of one name are two
  rows, as `checker status` counts them), with their current answers by status, their answers
  about an earlier version, and how many current answers are **claimed**, from no page built
  for them;
- **the verification, item by item**: a row for each literature value, cited sentence and
  Methods item, and for each item of a group a project contributes: its digest, who verified it
  (a current `ok`, marked "claimed" where its page is not in the register), who flagged it,
  who answered an earlier version only, and for a Methods item how its pairs stand in
  `methods.lock` ("on 2026-10-22", "code changed since ...", "text changed since ...",
  "never", or "no code is linked" for an open paragraph). The references and the authors are a
  line each of counts (decision 6 (a)): verified, flagged, not answered.

Its last section holds the document digest of the manuscript (`gates.review.document_digest`:
the prose, the results, the ledger and the references, as `approve` and `build` take it), the
number of rows of `checks/decisions.csv` and the head of a chain over them, the earlier recap's
row count and head, with whether the record's first rows still give it, and a **root digest**:
the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the two tables, the counts, the manuscript's digest and the
chain head. Nothing in it says when it was written, so a recap made again of the same record and
the same manuscript is the same bytes.

**The chain.** h0 is the SHA-256 of `manuscript-guard/decisions-chain/1`. Each next head is the
SHA-256 of the head before it, in hex, followed by the canonical JSON of one row: the row as the
CSV reader gives it, every cell under its column, the columns as the header line writes them and
a cell past the last column under `+`, the keys sorted, UTF-8, no spaces. Every row is in it,
one with no id among them, which `read_decisions` passes over. The chain is computed whenever it
is wanted and stored nowhere but in a recap: `decisions.csv` keeps its nine columns.

**The earlier recap.** A recap names the one it replaces: the row count and head that
`checks/recap.md` recorded, and whether the first that many rows of the record still give that
head. Made again of a record that has not changed, it names the one that recap named, so that
running it twice changes nothing. A record whose first rows no longer give the earlier head is
said by `checker recap` and written into the recap, and not refused: the recap is the record of
it, and `--check` against a copy kept elsewhere is what fails.

**`checker recap --check [file]`** reads a recap (`checks/recap.md` unless a file is named: the
pack's copy, or one kept in git; a relative file is read under the project, whatever folder
the command runs in, where `--items` is read from the working folder as before; a folder is
refused with a message, since the project is named before `--check`), makes it again from the record and the manuscript as they are,
naming the earlier recap the file names, and compares the two byte for byte. The same: exit 0,
with the row count, the head and the root digest. Otherwise exit 1, naming the first line that
differs, as the file has it and as it is made now, and what the file's footer says of the
difference: the manuscript has changed since; rows were added to the record since and its first
are the ones the recap was made from, so the recap is to be made again; or the first rows of the
record do not give the head the recap records, so a row among them was edited, deleted or moved.
A file that is not there, or cannot be read, is exit 2. `--check` writes nothing. Either way it
says that the line naming the earlier recap was read from the file and not verified: it is
taken as the file gives it (round 1 of #465), since nothing outside the file holds it.

**What this shows, and what it does not.** The recap is tamper-evident by a hash chain, unsigned,
and it says so in those words. Held to a head recorded elsewhere, an earlier recap kept in git,
the copy in a submission pack or a digest quoted in a message, it shows a hand edit of any
line of the recap but the one naming the earlier recap, and a row of the record edited,
deleted or moved. It does not show a rewrite: someone who
can write to the record and to every copy of the head can make them agree, since nothing in the
chain is secret. Nothing in it is signed, and it is never called certified. A name on a decision
is the answers file's claim, as before: a page's token shows which page answers came from, not
who answered. `checks/recap.md` is kept from an agent's editor by the hooks, as the record and
the register are, so that an agent cannot write one by hand; `checker recap` is among the verbs
the hook reads as plainly no import.

**At submission** (decision 7 (a)): `submit` writes `coauthor-verification.md` into the pack
where the project has a `checks/decisions.csv`: the publisher's copy of the recap, titled
"Co-author verification", with the statement above, the two tables and the counts, and the same
last section, and without the co-authors' notes, which are the authors' working and not the
journal's. It names the earlier recap `checks/recap.md` names, so `checker recap --check
build/submission/coauthor-verification.md` holds the pack's copy to the record. And it warns,
`coauthor-flag-open`, of each current `wrong` or `code` that is still the latest answer of the
person who gave it, with the note: any later answer of theirs about the item as it is now
takes its place and closes it, an `ok`, or an `unsure`, which leaves the item under "Still
open" in the recap; and so does an edit to the item, which makes the flag about an earlier
version. It does not
refuse: whether to send with a co-author's flag open is the corresponding author's call, as an
approval missing is. The warnings need the record and the items only, so they are said where
the copy cannot be made, a register a spreadsheet re-saved, say, beside the note saying why. No gate of `check` changes. A LaTeX manuscript, which `checker` refuses, is
packed without the file, and `submit` says so.

**Tests.** `tests/test_checking.py` holds that a recap made twice is the same bytes, that
`--check` names the first line where a row of the record was edited or deleted or two were
swapped, says rows were added where they were and that the earlier recap's line is
unverified, refuses a folder and reads a relative file under the project, that the earlier recap is named and held, that
stale answers' notes reach it, that a claimed answer is marked, and its wording.
`tests/test_corruption.py` holds a recap edited by hand and `submit` with a flag open.
`tests/test_properties.py` holds over generated records (`decision_records`) that each row reads
back as it was written and that a row edited, deleted or swapped anywhere gives another head; a
chain that passes over a row with no id fails it.

### Nothing in it belongs to a vendor

The file is a page, the answers are JSON, the record is a CSV. No model, no provider and no agent
tool appears anywhere in the path, and none is needed to run a round. That is deliberate: a
co-author's reading is the one part of this toolkit that must not depend on anyone's subscription.

## The publisher's proof is held to what was sent

Every guarantee here stops at the document the author sends. The journal then has it typeset,
by people and programs that can change a digit, set a decimal comma, drop a minus, swap two
cells, renumber a reference or lose an affiliation, and sends back a proof that the author
reads by eye, usually within two days. `manuscript-guard proof <proof> [path]` reads the
proof's text and holds it to the document sent, and lists what the author has to ask the
production office to correct. It sends nothing. Basile chose each of the four points below on
2026-10-21, of the options put to him.

**What it is compared with.** The paper in the submission pack, `build/submission/`, or the
document named with `--against` (`proof.sent`). The pack's copy is what the journal was sent,
and its manifest says so: the report says whether the manifest lists the file with these
bytes, for which round; whether every author's approval is of the build it came from, by the
stamp the document carries; and whether the source has changed since, in which case a
correction may already be in the source. What changed after the pack is not compared, so a
revision's accepted changes are kept out the same way: rebuild and pack the version the journal
accepted, and the proof is held to that. `--supplementary` compares a supplement typeset as a
document of its own with the pack's supplement.

The document is read as the build reads it when it writes its record of what each block
printed (`docxtext.blocks`, "The build records what each paragraph printed"), from the
document itself rather than from the record. The record is that reading, made on the machine
that built the document; the document is what was sent, and reading it gives the same blocks
anywhere. Each block is a part. A table is its cells, each a part with its row's label and its
column's header, read as `audit` reads a table (`text.docx.read_docx_text`). A figure's picture
and a displayed equation are not compared, and the report says so.

**Reading the proof** (`proof.reading`). A PDF is read by `pdftotext` where it is installed, in
two orders: the order of the page's layout, which poppler and Xpdf each work out their own way,
and the order the PDF draws its text in (`-raw`). Neither is right for every proof. On a proof
written by `tests/proof_pdf.py`, Xpdf 4.00's layout order read two columns with a narrow gutter
a line of each in turn, and poppler 24.04's gave the margin's line numbers as a column of their
own and joined a compound broken at its own hyphen ("example-" and "drug" became
"exampledrug"); the drawing order of both, and pypdf's, kept the columns. So both orders are
read, and the comparison keeps the one that lines up most of what was sent, less what it adds
that was not sent: a reading with the line numbers among the words finds every word and adds a
number between each line. Without `pdftotext`, pypdf reads the drawing order. A proof sent as
JATS XML or HTML is read by pattern, one line to a paragraph, cell or heading, and not parsed,
so an entity it declares is not expanded and nothing it names is fetched; an author's JATS
name, in `<contrib>`, is turned given name first, as a title page prints it, and a
reference's is left as its style prints it, "Smith A". A proof saved as text is read with its pages parted by
form feeds, as `pdftotext` writes them. A proof with no text, a scan, is refused (exit 2).

What every page repeats is taken out first, from the top and the bottom of each page (its first
and last four lines, a fifth of a short page and two lines at least): a line that, its digits
aside, stands once on half the pages or more, on the same side of each, the top for a head and
the bottom for a foot, its numbers alike on every page but for one, the page's own (a running
head or foot: a table's rows share a shape and stand many to a page, and differ in many
numbers); and a number alone on its line that counts up with the pages on most of them (the
page number). Read anywhere on the page, a line of a generated proof's text that happened to
stand on half the pages, "reports records.", was taken for a running head, and the end of
each paragraph it closed was reported as words the proof left out; read on either side, a line
two paragraphs shared stood at the top of one page and the foot of the next, and was taken out
of both. A proof's line numbers are judged over the whole proof: they
count up by one, five or ten nearly always, stand on enough of its lines, and start each page
at one or on from the page before, so a column of years is none and a first page of four
lines is no exception. They are kept where they stand at the start of a line, so that a
correction names its line, and dropped where a reader gives them as a column.

**Comparing** (`proof.tokens`, `proof.align`, `proof.compare`). Both texts are read in Unicode's
compatibility form, so that a ligature is its letters and a thin space a space, and cut into
numbers, words and marks. A number is read with its sign where a sign can stand, as `audit`
reads one, and with its decimal mark. They are lined up with every number standing for any
number, so that a number changed in place lines up with the number it was. difflib's matcher is
exact and quadratic: an article of eleven thousand tokens took eleven seconds, three times that
took ninety. So runs of keys found once on each side are anchors, the longest chain of them in
order on both sides is kept, and only the gaps between, once small, go to difflib, as a
patience diff does. Where no run stands once on each side, a table of numbers alone or a
passage the paper repeats, runs that stand as often on each side, up to eight times, are paired
first with first. Two readings that line up as many tokens are not alike to the author, so two
rules choose between them. A stretch printed and not sent, or sent and not printed, is slid
along the tokens alike on both sides of it to start where a part starts, where it can: a
paragraph left out of the proof would otherwise take the full stop of the one before it. And a
part left out next to a part the proof changed is left out whole, where that lines up as many
(`align.whole_parts`): the words two paragraphs end with were lined up with the second's end,
and the paragraph left out read as part of a copy-edit of the first, which is a correction
not counted. A run the chain leaves out and the proof prints elsewhere, a table set where the
page had room or a statement the journal's template moves, is found there and compared there.

Each difference is then one of these:

- **A correction** (exit 1, and the list `--out` writes): a number's digits, sign or decimal
  mark changed, or a number gone or come within a part; a unit, a percent or degree sign or a
  comparator changed beside a number, or after a number and a hyphen, "5-mg" (a unit's case is
  kept, so "mM" is not "mm"; the two spellings of a litre and of a microgram are one); a
  unit of time spelt out and printed as another there, "12 weeks" as "12 months" or
  "12-week" as "12-month" ("12 wk" and "12 week" are copy-edits); any change inside a citation
  (brackets, parentheses that hold a year, a short number set against a word as a superscript
  is) or an entry of the reference list; a part the proof does not print at all, or a
  paragraph, a caption or a reference of six tokens or more none of which it prints in place,
  whatever stands there instead; on the title page, an author's name (with its affiliation
  marks set against it, "Example1,2", it is the name), the authors' order, an affiliation, an
  ORCID iD or the corresponding author's e-mail address. A correction of a number names the binding that printed it and the line of
  the source, or says it was typed (`proof.origin`); a cell names its table's binding. Two
  corrections that trade what they print are said to be swapped.
- **Typography**, shown and not counted: the same number set otherwise, grouped ("19 950"), a
  true minus or a minus set as a hyphen or a dash, a leading zero dropped (".001"), a middle
  dot for the point; a name printed with its initials.
- **A copy-edit**, shown for the author to accept or query: any other change of words.
- **Moved**, shown: a paragraph or heading set elsewhere. A table's cells and a caption move
  as floats do, and are not shown.
- **Added**, shown: text the proof prints between parts that was not sent. The title page's
  lines, once found to be the title page, are not.

The title page is not in the document sent: the pack writes it from `authors.yaml`. So it is
held to `authors.yaml` (`proof.front`), anywhere in the proof's text: each name letter for
letter, accents kept, case and the shape of quotation marks aside; each affiliation; each ORCID
iD, where the proof prints any; and the corresponding author's address.

**The report** is on the screen, in the proof's order: the corrections with the page and the
line number the proof prints, the copy-edits, then what was shown and what was not compared.
`--out <file>` writes the corrections as a numbered list to paste into the reply to the
production office, and `--json` writes everything. Nothing is written without `--out`, and
nothing is sent. A proof that reads as less than 30% of the document is not compared (exit 2):
it is another paper's, or its text could not be read in order, and a report of every part
missing would say nothing.

`tests/test_proof.py` plants each kind of change in a proof of a few parts, and runs the
command on proofs of the example's own pack typeset as two-column PDFs with running heads.
The PDFs are written by `tests/proof_pdf.py`, in Helvetica with a map from each code to its
character as a typesetter's fonts carry one, and read by pypdf, pinned in the development
dependencies, and by each `pdftotext` on the machine. `tests/test_properties.py` holds the
comparison over proofs `tests/generated.py` draws (`proofs`): the parts' words, their order,
the width the proof wraps to, the length of its pages and whether it numbers its lines, with a
long word and a compound broken at a line's end. A proof of the parts as sent reads as them;
one with one of every change of `PROOF_CORRECTIONS`, every setting of `PROOF_TYPOGRAPHY`, a
word copy-edited, a unit of time abbreviated and a part left out, each in a part of its own,
reports each once, in its part, on its page and its line. Eleven rules broken in place each
fail one of the two, under a dozen seeds. The two rules above that choose between
readings were found by them.

## Known gaps

Recorded because a gate whose limits are undocumented gets trusted beyond them.

- **A co-author round records answers, and nothing more.** `checker status` says who answered
  what; it cannot say who read anything. Nothing proves the file was opened, that the evidence was
  looked at, or that a `ok` was not a row of clicks. The record is a person's word written down
  accurately, with the text they were shown pinned to it, and that is the whole of the claim.
- **An answers file is not signed, and its name is a claim.** `by` is the name the build put in
  it, and whoever holds the file can edit any part of it before sending it back. A registered
  page's token stops the file being made to read as another co-author's, but whoever holds the
  page holds the token: a forwarded page is answered by whoever has it, and the corresponding
  author, who built and sent every page, holds every token. Within a group of co-authors that is
  the same trust as mail, which is how the file travels; it is not evidence against a person who
  wants to misreport, and it is not meant to be. The attestation of a source, where that bar does
  apply, stays in `literature/attested.yaml` and is signed by one person.
- **A page built on another clone reads as claimed.** `checks/bundles.csv` is the clone's own
  register. Two clones that each build pages and each append to it conflict when merged, as two
  appends to `checks/decisions.csv` do; a page built on one and imported on the other is
  recorded as claimed, as a page built before the register is. Nothing marks a claimed decision
  in the record but its page's absence from the register, so a register row removed by hand
  turns that page's decisions into claimed ones.
- **A re-import is skipped by its answer, not by its file.** An answer is not written again where
  the record holds it already (`store._already`). An answer with no time of its own, from a file
  written by hand, is compared with the person's latest decision only: imported, superseded, and
  imported again, it is the latest once more. The page stamps every answer, so this needs a file
  it did not write.
- **The hook is a guard against an agent's ordinary commands, not against a deliberate
  evasion.** It reads a command's words as a POSIX shell and as Windows give them, and asks
  where the tool's name, `checker` and `import` stand in the text or in those words (so
  `imp''ort` is `import`), unless the command is plainly `checker build`, `status` or `recap`;
  so `checker status && git commit -m import` is asked too. A substitution, `<(`, `>(`, a
  word opening with `(`, `@(` or `{`, or a typographic quote is not read, and asked. A command that
  builds the tool's name or its verb at run time, `$v`, `eval "$(...)"` reading from a file, an
  alias defined elsewhere, a script file, is not recognised. `tests/test_hooks.py` holds the
  forms it does catch.
- **A page's file name can change when an author is added.** A name takes a suffix only while
  another name in `authors.yaml`, or in the run, folds to the same file name, so adding one
  gives the next page a new file. Answers match by the page's identifier, not its file, and the
  old file is not replaced, but a co-author may be sent a file of another name.
- **Authors who share a full name cannot use checker** until one of the names is written in a
  form of its own in `authors.yaml`. Nothing else tells two people apart in a record that keeps
  a name and never rewrites it.
- **The latest decision is the latest imported, not the latest given.** Among a person's answers
  about the item as it is now, the one imported last counts, whatever its `at` says, as before
  this register. Answers imported in another order than they were given count in that order.
- **A file rebuilt after the items changed loses a co-author's unsent progress.** The page keeps
  answers in the browser under a digest of the items' own digests and the person's name (not
  under its identifier, which digests the token too): a rebuild that changes nothing they were
  asked keeps their progress, and one that changes any item does not. So import what someone has
  before rebuilding a round they are part of, or that part of their reading is done twice.
  Nothing is lost that was saved and sent.
- **A sentence is split by punctuation, and the list of abbreviations is finite.** The split is
  a stop, a space, then a capital letter or an opening quote or bracket — except after a word with
  a stop inside it ("U.S.", "e.g.", "Ph.D.", "b.i.d."), after a word in `NOT_AN_END` ("et al.",
  "Fig.", "Suppl.", "No.", "St." and about thirty more) or after a single initial, and except where
  the piece that results carries no word of its own, which is joined back to the piece before it.
  The rules exist because of two shapes: "described by Okada et al. [@key]." cut at "al." left an
  item reading `[@key].`, and "sent to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration [@key]." cut at
  "U.S." left one reading "Food and Drug Administration [@key]." — in both, the subject of the
  claim on no item. A word with a stop inside it is a rule rather than a list for that reason. A
  word that ends in a stop, has none inside it and is not in the list still splits a sentence,
  and a reader is then shown a half of one; what holds is that no item is without a word of its
  own. A citation written after a sentence's stop and before another sentence ("…was small.
  [@key] A later study…") is read with the sentence after it; at the end of a paragraph it is
  joined to the one before. The earlier text here said "the rest of the sentence is in the file
  either way", and then that an item with no claim in it could not happen any more; both were
  false.
- **A claim is one sentence citing something.** An argument made across two sentences is asked as
  two questions, and a sentence citing three papers is one question about all three, which a
  person can only answer as a whole or decline. A paper whose claims need finer grain writes its
  own items.
- **The bibliography is read as fields, not as the format.** One small reader, everywhere: the
  fields as the file writes them, so `M{\"u}ller` reaches a co-author as typed, a `@string` macro
  unexpanded, a `#` concatenation with its hashes, and a biblatex extended name as its raw parts.
  It makes no entry of an `@` inside a value or of an `@comment`. pandoc read the format properly
  and was used where it was on the path, until it was measured: the two readers disagreed on 58
  of 58 references of a real bibliography, so a page built where pandoc was and imported where
  it was not refused every reference answer as about changed text, when nothing had changed; and
  pandoc dropped a particle ("von Elm, Erik" as "Elm, Erik") and lower-cased an unbraced title,
  proper nouns included. A digest that depends on the machine is not a digest of the paper, so
  pandoc is not used here. The built document's bibliography is still pandoc's reading of the
  same file under a style, so the page and the paper can print a reference differently.
- **No test runs the page's JavaScript.** The template is checked by reading it and by opening a
  built page in a browser by hand; its storage, its download, its dialog, its clipboard and its
  keyboard handling are held by nothing. A defect there reaches a co-author and not the suite.
- **"Any browser" means a current one.** The page uses `??` and `<dialog>`, so a browser older
  than about 2022 shows it wrongly or not at all. What a co-author sees then is untested.
- **The browser's storage is a convenience, not a record.** A note typed and not yet attached to
  an answer is lost on closing the tab, and everything unsent is lost where storage is refused —
  in a private window, for instance — with nothing said. What is saved and sent is the answers
  file.
- **The whole file must fit in mail.** A page is refused over 24 MB, and an image over 4 MB, since
  a mail server will usually carry no more. A project with many page images sends a round in parts
  rather than raising the limit.
- **Every page carries every author's details.** The author items hold each author's e-mail,
  ORCID, affiliations and competing interests, and every page carries every item, so a page sent
  to one co-author holds the others' details too. Within an author group that is what the title
  page will print; a page sent to anyone outside it should be built from an items file without
  the author group.
- **Some of what a co-author sees is outside the digest.** The digest covers the words: an item's
  title, facts, sentences and the text of its evidence. A table's outlined cell and an image's
  bytes are not in it, so an answer survives the outline moving to another cell or the image
  being replaced. A bound value is shown by its name (`[reported_incidence]`), so a changed
  `results.` or `lit.` value leaves the sentence, and an answer about it, as they were. A
  methods item is the exception: its values are filled in and in its digest, and so is what a
  cross-reference in it prints, "Figure 1". A figure placed before Figure 1 renumbers it, and
  the answers about every methods item that points at it go stale, though its words did not
  change.
- **A methods item's code is read from disk, and only what the step's digest holds.** The
  lines shown are the script as it is when the page is built, and a script whose digest is not
  the one its run recorded is said to be so on the page and by `build`; a fragment that records
  no digest of its script is said to leave it unknown. A module the script imports is not
  shown, nor followed, as G9's digest does not follow it; R gives the step's body only, and
  no function it calls. Under decision 1 (a) the comments are outside the digest: a comment
  rewritten to contradict the text, with the code unchanged, keeps a co-author's ok, and so
  does a step whose lines moved.
- **An "ok" given on code edited and not yet run again is about the old code.** Under
  decision 1 (a) a methods item's digest holds the code digest the run recorded. A page built
  after the script was edited and before the analysis was run again shows the edited lines,
  with the warning that they may not be what ran, while its digest holds the old run's; an ok
  given on it is recorded against that, and stays current until the run is made, when it goes
  stale if the code changed.
- **A cross-reference in a Methods item prints only where the count is exact.**
  `{{ref.figure.forest}}` is shown as the build prints it, "Figure 1", from G2's count of the
  displays; where that count is not exact (a display placed by hand, or sent as a file) the
  binding is shown by its name, `[ref.figure.forest]`, as an unresolved value is.
- **`impact` finds the answers of the other groups by a file's name.** A methods item records
  its file's path under `manuscript/` and is matched by it; a cited sentence or a value records
  the file's name alone, so a file of the main text and one of the supplement with one name
  match each other's answers in `impact`.
- **A project's own `methods` group is read, and no longer built.** A project whose
  `checks/items.json` declared a group `methods` before the toolkit had one has it refused by
  `checker build`, where earlier releases built the page: on purpose, since the page would send the
  project's items under the toolkit's question and none of the toolkit's, and the message says
  to rename it; `import` and `status` read it as before, leaving
  the toolkit's methods items out, with a line. Renamed, its items keep their ids and their
  recorded answers, but an item's digest holds its group, so each is asked again, its notes
  kept.
- **Answers about a group that could not be made are refused, not kept.** Where the Methods
  could not be read this run (a manuscript file G9 refuses, a results file that does not
  parse), `import` refuses each answer the page marks as the methods group's, and each `code`,
  with that reason, and `status` says the group is out; the files can be imported again once
  it reads. A page built before it wrote the group with each answer is known by `code` alone,
  so its ok, wrong and unsure on Methods items are recorded as about items gone.
- **An open Methods paragraph is known by its place.** It has no steps to be known by, so
  its identifier is its place among the open paragraphs of its file: one added above, or one
  given an anchor, moves those below, and their answers go stale (never onto another
  paragraph, since the digest holds the text). A claim's place among the claims of the same
  steps works the same way, which matters only where several texts point at one step.
- **`checker` is still refused for a LaTeX manuscript.** The methods producer reads
  `anchored`, which reads LaTeX, but the literature and claim producers read Markdown, and
  every verb draws its items from all of them.
- **Only comments are left out of the sentences.** A sentence a draft has commented out is not
  offered; one in a fenced code block or in the front matter is, if it cites something.
- **The highlighter can mark inside a character reference.** A marked word is found in the
  escaped text, so a short one that also spells part of an escape (`amp`, `lt`) is marked inside
  `&amp;` or `&lt;`, and the page shows the escape's characters.
- **The splitter's time grows with the square of a paragraph's length.** Each stop is judged on
  the text before it, taken from the paragraph's start. A paragraph of ordinary length is split
  at once; one of hundreds of sentences is not.
- **`checks/decisions.csv` and `checks/bundles.csv` are for this toolkit to write and a person
  to read.** Opened in a spreadsheet and saved again, one can come back in another encoding,
  which ends the next `status` in a `UnicodeDecodeError`, or as UTF-8 with a byte order mark,
  which takes the name of its first column (`when`, `built_on`) with it. A note opening with `=`
  is read by a spreadsheet as a formula.
  Read them in a spreadsheet; write them only with `checker import` and `checker build`.
- **The recap's chain shows a change only against a head kept elsewhere, and nothing is
  signed.** `checker recap --check` holds a recap to the record; whoever can write both can make
  them agree, and the chain carries no secret, so a rewrite of the record with every recap made
  again leaves no trace. What shows a change is a head recorded where that person cannot reach:
  an earlier recap kept in git, the pack's copy sent to a journal, a digest quoted in a message.
  The earlier recap a recap names is that recap's own word: its row count and head are read from
  the file being checked, so a recap edited to name another earlier head, or none, is held to
  that one, and passes `--check` where the rest is as made; `--check` says the line is
  unverified, and the next recap carries it forward. The root digest does not cover it.
- **`--check` names a line of the recap, not a row of the record.** The recap stores one head,
  so a row edited, deleted or moved is found to be among the first rows the recap counted, and
  the line named is the first of the recap the change moved: a table's row, a note, or the
  footer's head where nothing else moved. Which row of the record changed is found by holding it
  to a copy kept elsewhere, in git.
- **An item's digest in the recap is 64 bits.** The table gives each item's 16-hex digest, as
  the record does, and two items whose words collide in it would read as one. The root digest
  and the chain are SHA-256 in full.
- **The pack's copy leaves the notes out, and lists the names.** `coauthor-verification.md` says
  who verified and who flagged each item, and not what they said: a journal reading a flag
  learns that someone asked for a change, not which. It names every co-author who answered,
  claimed or not, and anyone who is not an author whose answer the record holds.
- **The record keeps a name as it was written.** `checker status` takes each person's latest
  answer by the name as recorded, and so does the recap: "Jane Doe" and "jane doe" are two
  rows, each with its own answers, and the second's wrong does not close the first's ok, nor
  her later ok her own flag given under the other spelling. An author's answer under another
  spelling is a row of its own beside the author's. The page writes the name `authors.yaml`
  gives; a file written by hand may not. Two names that differ only in inner spaces or in
  their Unicode form ("Jane  Doe", or "José" composed and decomposed) are two rows that print
  alike, since a cell's spaces are joined. `checker recap --check <project>` run from outside
  any project fails with the project's own error, not the hint to name the project first.
- **Two authors of one name share their row's counts.** The recap gives each author in
  `authors.yaml` a row and counts in it every decision recorded under that name, so two
  authors written alike each get a row counting both's decisions. `checker` refuses such
  namesakes before a round, so this is a record made before the second was added.
- **A header that repeats a column hides its first cell from the chain.** The chain reads each
  row as the CSV reader maps it to the header, so a `decisions.csv` whose header names a column
  twice keeps the last cell of the two, and an edit to the other leaves the head as it was.
  `checker import` never writes such a header; one made by hand is not refused.
- **`coauthor-flag-open` is held to the person, not to the item.** A flag stays open until the
  person who gave it answers again about the item as it is now, ok or not sure, or the item
  changes: a co-author's ok on someone else's flag does not close it, and an edit to the sentence closes it whether or
  not it did what was asked, until the item is sent again.

- **G1 fails only on the script that wrote a results file and on the inputs it declared.**
  The digests it compares are of the emitting script and of each path given to the emitter
  as an input. A module that script imports, or a file it reads without declaring it, can
  change and `check` still passes. The most it says is a warning, `analysis-newer`, for a
  source file under `analysis/` modified after the newest results file; a helper kept
  elsewhere gets none. `build` then writes the old values:
  seen on the example with a helper module holding the 1.96 of a confidence interval, changed
  to 2.58 with nothing run again. Listing the helper among the emitter's `inputs` makes its
  change an `input-changed` failure. `verify`, which runs the analysis again and compares
  every value, sees the change either way. Imports are not followed.
- **The environment is the lockfiles at the project root, and only a warning.** Both
  emitters record the digest of each of `renv.lock`, `uv.lock`, `poetry.lock`,
  `environment.yml` and `requirements*.txt` found at the root, and G1 warns
  (`environment-changed`) when one has changed, gone or appeared since a fragment was
  written: the numbers on disk are still the ones the analysis wrote, and a re-run may not
  give them. A lockfile in a subfolder, a package installed outside any lockfile, a system
  library, a compiler, and a lockfile that does not match what is installed are not seen.
  A lockfile is digested with its line endings left out, as a script is. One that is a
  link to a file elsewhere is recorded by R under the path it links to, and by Python under
  its own name. A fragment written before the emitters recorded the environment says
  nothing. When a
  re-run differs, `verify` says whether the analysis declares a seed: a parameter whose key
  holds "seed".
- **The figure-caption style reads one convention and nothing else.** The paragraph after a
  figure is set in `Figure Caption` (10 pt against 12 pt) when its text opens "Figure 1.",
  "Figure 4:" or "Figure S1."; the stop or colon has to come right after the number, so that
  prose resuming under a figure ("Figure 1 shows ...", "Figure 2.5-fold higher ...") is left
  as prose. A no-break space between the word and the number is read as a space. The cost: a
  caption written "Fig. 1.", "Figure one." or with a chapter-style number ("Figure 1.1."), a
  caption separated from its figure by a comment, and a caption under an image that shares its
  paragraph with other text are all left at body size. A figure that carries pandoc's own caption
  (`![caption](path)`) keeps `Image Caption`, which the reference document does not size
  either, and a caption inside a block quotation takes `Figure Caption` in place of
  `Block Text` and so loses the quotation's indent. The style is added to the author's own
  `reference.docx` from pandoc's user data directory when there is one, and skipped when that
  file already defines `FigureCaption`; table captions are untouched.
- **A build killed outright leaves its generated reference document in `build/.cache`.** Each
  build names its own `reference-XXXX.docx` there and removes it for as long as the process
  lives, whatever fails — an unreadable reference, a missing bibliography, pandoc itself. A
  process that is killed cannot run that removal, so the file stays until someone deletes it,
  and nor can a removal that the operating system refuses — a file held open for an instant by
  a scanner or a sync client — because the build reports what it was doing, not what tidying up
  it could not finish.
  Nothing reads it afterwards and the next build makes its own, so the cost is a stray file in
  a cache. Sweeping the directory instead would mean one build deleting a file another build
  is reading, which is the failure this naming exists to prevent.
- **After a range of tables, a comma goes on with the list.** It must, for "Tables S1-S3,
  S5", so "In Tables 1-3, 30 patients were excluded" reads Table 30: a pointer past the
  tables where they are counted, and a count G2 does not hold to the results
  (`test_a_count_after_a_range_of_tables_read_as_a_table_is_pinned`, round 3 of #256).
- **A quote of a revised sentence is compared with its Markdown.** Its `*`, backticks and
  comments are taken off, and nothing else: emphasis written with underscores, a
  citation, a link, a sub- or superscript or an escape in the sentence keeps a quote of it
  as it prints from matching, and G13 says the text does not read it
  (`test_a_quote_of_the_printed_sentence_against_its_markup_is_pinned`, round 1 of #266).
- **A number a summary gives is looked for by its key, and in a table or figure by its
  display.** A key printed in a table or drawn in a figure the paper places counts as
  reported when its display stands there as a number of its own, so a coincidence keeps the
  warning back: the example's figure draws a tick at 10, and a key whose display is 10 is
  reported by it. A figure with no text layer, a PNG alone, reports nothing, and neither
  does a table's caption. A section whose title names the Results in other words
  ("Outcomes", "Main results") is not read as the Results, and a conclusion written as a
  bold paragraph rather than a heading is not read as one. Literature values (`lit.`) are
  not looked for: an abstract may give the background it rests on.
- **G8 compares only values whose units agree.** A count of 56 and a share of 56.0% are two
  quantities, and keying on the unit is what tells them apart. The cost: one quantity emitted
  once with `unit="%"` and once with no unit, or with the unit spelt two ways ("percent" and
  "%", "years" and "y"), is no longer reported as written two ways.
- **G8 holds only the arithmetic an analysis declares.** `em.relation` and `em.flow` say
  which results are a sum, a difference, a ratio or an order of which, and G8 checks those.
  A subgroup total nobody declared is not checked, and nothing searches the prose for numbers
  that might add up. That is the price of checking nothing by guesswork.
- **A relation between values is exact, so a value emitted rounded fails it.** Whole numbers
  are compared exactly and floats to their last bits (1e-9 of the result, and 1e-9 of
  nought), so a result and its computed value both within 1e-9 of nought are equal,
  whatever the terms: 1e-12 passes as the sum of 1e-12 and 2e-12, and 9e-10 as 0.3 less
  0.3 (pinned by `test_terms_all_near_nought_are_equal_by_being_small`). A
  tolerance taken from the terms instead let a wrong ratio pass, its largest term being
  its denominator, and a difference of terms near a million rounded at the sixth place,
  and failed a true difference of two means summed two ways (#340). A script that emits
  `round(rate, 1)` instead of the rate
  breaks a ratio that holds, and is told to emit the value unrounded and let the display
  round it.
- **The printed arithmetic reads the first number of each display.** A display that is not a
  rounding of its own value ("<0.001", whatever its value, a rate printed per 1,000 of a
  value held per person, "1.2 × 10⁻³") is left out of it, and the relation is then held to
  the values alone. What Decimal arithmetic leaves in its last digits, 100 over 3 times 3
  being 99.99...9, is no rounding of the printed numbers (round 1 of #293). A
  share held as a fraction and printed as a percentage is read as a percentage. The warning
  is meant to fire routinely: percentages rounded one by one often miss 100, and the text
  may say so rather than change a number.
- **A flow's record is checked step by step, and nothing more.** "One study, several
  reports" (PRISMA 2020) is not a subtraction, so a flow stops at the reports and the studies
  are an `at_most` of them. Where one record can be excluded for several reasons, the step is
  named in `overlapping`, which waives the sum of that step's reasons but not its total; the
  reasons are still each at most what the step removed, and together at least that. The flow diagram is not yet
  drawn from the record: a figure script reads the counts from the results like any other.
  A flow two fragments record is the first's, as its counts are, and `duplicate-key` says so
  of the second's (round 1 of #293, where the second record was held to the first's counts).
  Python's `relation()` refuses an `of` that is one key written as a string, which it read
  as its letters (in R a string is a vector of one key), and either emitter refuses a name
  that is no results key. Python takes NumPy's whole numbers and its single truth values as
  its own, and the steps that overlap as a list or a NumPy array of whole numbers; R takes
  any numeric vector of whole values, or a single number, for those steps.
- **A UTF-16 input without a BOM is normalised as if it were 8-bit text.** Its 0x0D and 0x0A
  bytes can belong to ordinary characters, so an edit that swaps one such character for
  another (U+4E0D for U+4E0A) can leave the digest unchanged and pass G1. Exports that write
  UTF-16 carry a BOM; a file without one is taken for 8-bit text.
- **A blind document is read for the names `authors.yaml` gives, as they are written
  there.** A name written another way is not found: a nickname, a given name of several
  words reduced to its first, a family name alone, a name in a language's other script, or a
  user name in Word's author fields. An institution named by its abbreviation or its city is
  not found, nor is the funder or the ethics committee that would identify the authors as
  surely. A figure is read where it has a text layer; a raster figure, which the document
  most often holds, is read through the SVG or PDF the manuscript places beside it, when
  there is one. A journal that wants self-citations anonymised has its reference list
  unread.
- **Checking a declared input reads the whole file into memory.** Before input digests
  normalised line endings they were streamed; a 300 MB CSV now peaks at about 1.2 GB while G1
  checks it. The R emitter peaks at about twenty times the file (600 MB for a 28 MB CSV), since
  its line-ending masks are logical vectors of four bytes a byte. Large binary inputs are
  affected too, because the file is read before its suffix is tested.
- **One pandoc version is tested.** CI pins one, in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: the version
  the tests that assert on pandoc's output were written against. It refuses to run the
  suite with any other. An author's pandoc may be older or newer, and nothing here checks
  that the build and the import behave the same with it.
- **Digests are byte-level, so line endings are part of the guarantee.** `.gitattributes`
  pins `eol=lf` here, and `init` now writes the same file into every scaffolded project:
  without it Git stores LF and hands Windows CRLF, and every byte-level check reports a
  change nobody made. A *script's* digest is normalised in code as well (`source_digest`,
  mirrored by `mg_source_digest` in the R emitter), so G1 stays right on a repository that
  predates the scaffold or was not made by `init`. A *fragment's* digest is still byte-exact
  on purpose: it must be reproducible from any language that can emit results, and "hash the
  bytes you just wrote" is the only operation meaning the same thing everywhere. So a project
  that deletes its `.gitattributes` can still see `results-edited` on a clean checkout. Found
  by dogfooding — the same omission in the author's own paper repository, `.csv` missing from
  a normalisation set, reported 16 stale outputs including all seven figures, every one of
  which re-rendered pixel-identical.
- **A fenced block tagged with a language the lexer does not know is not read.** Only
  Python and R have lexers, so a ```stata or ```sql listing is reported as unread rather
  than checked. Saying so is the point; it is still a hole an author could tag their way
  into.
- **`verify` cannot hide from the code it runs.** The easy tells are gone — no
  `MANUSCRIPT_GUARD_VERIFY`, no `manuscript-guard-verify-` in the scratch path, and no
  `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE`, which was set for tidiness and was the same backdoor in
  miniature: readable by the script being checked, absent in an ordinary run, so two lines
  make an analysis honest under verification and dishonest everywhere else. A script can
  still notice it is running under the system temp directory. An analysis written to deceive
  its own toolkit defeats this; an author who edited a results file does not.
- **`verify` runs untrusted code, so its own machinery is part of the attack surface.** The
  child gets its own process group and the whole tree is killed on timeout — an analysis is
  usually a launcher, and killing the direct child left a grandchild holding the scratch
  directory open. Its output goes to files and is capped, because with pipes the reader was
  this process and a grandchild holding one open outlasted the timeout meant to enforce it.
  Directory junctions are skipped explicitly when staging the copy: `symlinks=True` stops a
  symlink loop but `os.path.islink` is False for a junction, so `copytree` walked into one
  and re-copied the tree at every level, reachable by any unprivileged `mklink /J`.
- **A figure render manifest is a drift detector, not a proof.** `<name>.render.json` sits
  beside the figures it vouches for and is writable by whoever holds the checkout: retouch
  the raster *and* rewrite its digest and G3 skips it again, exactly as a `.sha256` can be
  recomputed. It catches the ordinary case — a raster re-rendered on its own and left beside
  a fresh vector — which is how the wrong figure actually reaches a journal. There is no
  `verify` equivalent for figures, because re-rendering is not reproducible across
  plotting-library versions.
- **The other rendered keys in a manuscript's front matter are read by G2 and printed by
  nothing.** `subtitle`, `summary`, `keywords`, `short_title` and `running_title` are read
  because pandoc can print them, and the build strips the block and takes its header from
  `paper.yaml`. A number in one is checked and never printed, which is the safe direction,
  but the text itself is dropped without a word. Only the abstract is refused
  (`front-matter-abstract`), and only the title is compared with `paper.yaml`
  (`two-titles`).
- **The two titles are compared as typed, not as pandoc prints them.** The title in a
  manuscript's header is read as YAML reads it and set beside `paper.yaml`'s with the
  spaces, tabs and line breaks of each folded (`two-titles`). Pandoc then reads a title as
  Markdown, and two that it prints alike are still two to the comparison: `A *cohort*
  study` beside `A _cohort_ study`, a straight quotation mark beside a curly one, three
  hyphens beside a dash. So are two that differ by a no-break space, one pasted after the
  header's title for instance, where the warning shows a title that looks the same as
  `paper.yaml`'s; and a line separator or a next-line character in `paper.yaml`'s title,
  which the build folds for the document and the comparison does not. The other way, the
  comparison says nothing where pandoc would hold the two apart: a blank line or a hard
  break inside a block title, which the folding takes for a space, and a plain `yes` or
  `1.0`, a boolean and a number to pandoc and text here. A title that is a list or a
  mapping is warned of whatever it holds, and shown as its key's line; an empty one, and a
  title of nothing but a no-break space, is read as no title. A supplementary file's own
  title is compared with
  the paper's as well, and warned of: nothing prints it, since the supplement's title is
  made from the paper's. Its hint says that, and does not say to make the two agree. It is
  a warning, the document prints `paper.yaml`'s title in each of these, and deleting the
  title from the header ends it.
- **A front matter is composed at 15 to 20 seconds a megabyte.** PyYAML's pure-Python
  composer is linear but slow. The block is composed once, cached for the rest of the
  process: to decide that it is front matter, and for the abstract and the title in it.
  Until the title was read as YAML it was composed twice, the second time for the
  abstract, and with half a megabyte of front matter, which only a deliberately hostile
  manuscript has, `check` on the example took 30 seconds against the 20-second budget of
  `test_robustness.py`, and 24 without the second reading. The C composer is 40 times
  faster and overflows its stack on deep nesting, which is why the pure-Python one is
  used.
- **The search for a merged abstract or title is not linear, and runs on every block.**
  It follows merge keys, and each mapping that merges a list goes through the list again,
  so many mappings merging one long list cost the one times the other. Since the abstract
  and the title are taken from the one composing, the search runs on every block that is
  composed, a block in the body included, where `main` only composed those. A block built
  for it, 2,400 mappings merging one list of 24,000 items, 148 KB, takes 13 to 18 seconds
  in the body, against 1 to 2 before, about twelve times as long, and the same in the
  header, against 8 to 13. The lower figures are from a quiet machine and the higher from
  one running other suites. Nothing fails, and no manuscript has such a block. Going through a merged list once was tried in #168 and
  taken back: marked when the mapping that merged it was read, a list was passed over by a
  mapping reached first, under an earlier merge key, the search took a later mapping's
  abstract, and an abstract pandoc prints went unrefused by `check` and the build. The
  header that showed it is among the abstract's spellings in `tests/test_corruption.py`
  (`_MET_TWICE`). Putting the list itself on the stack, to be gone through where its
  members stood, keeps the order on the texts it was tried on, and is a change for a pull
  request of its own.
- **A YAML block later in a file is read as prose.** Pandoc takes any `---` block that
