  follows a blank line and holds a YAML mapping for metadata, wherever it sits, and prints
  none of it. The gates recognise only the block that opens a file, so a later one is read:
  its words count, and its closing `---` underlines the line above it into a heading. A
  block of `note: |` over an indented `Methods`, placed under `## Results`, gives G2 a
  Methods heading the document never prints, and `p < 0.001` after it passes as the alpha
  chosen in advance.
- **Nothing asks for a design round before the analysis stage.** One that was never
  held says nothing. A design round's request carries the plan and the feasibility results
  only: the reporting guideline and the journal's profile are not sent, and a plan's
  binding to a result that is not a feasibility one is sent as written. An unsigned
  override of a design-round major is a warning, at submission too, as a new warning
  starts.
- **A planned result is held to its key, not to what the paper says of it.** G12 checks
  that a key listed under Planned results is emitted and quoted, not that the sentence
  quoting it reports the result the plan described: a planned "adjusted ratio" listed as
  `ror.point`, the crude one, passes. Keys are read from the list items' first code spans
  only; a result the section describes in words is not checked, and a section with one key
  and ten results in words says nothing of the ten. A Deviations section that names a key,
  whatever it says of it, stands down that key's warning. A heading that names both,
  "Planned results and amendments", or a list nested under the Deviations heading, is
  read as the list and as the Deviations, so its items stand down their own keys' warnings
  (rounds 2 and 3 of #351; telling the two apart made other plans warned of).
- **A data dictionary says one condition, and reads its range by its type alone.**
  `applies_if` names one coded variable and the codes under which the variable is recorded;
  a variable asked where two conditions hold, or where a number passes a threshold, cannot be
  said, and is written without the condition. A `count`'s bounds are held to be numbers, not
  whole ones. A datetime's bounds are compared only where both or neither carry a time zone.
  What YAML reads as another value is found only where it is written plain; a value YAML
  reads as written but the author meant otherwise, `1.5` for the item "1.50", is not. A
  rule's `order` takes dates and datetimes as one family, so the data checks that read it
  have to compare a date with a datetime by the date, and it refuses an order between two
  times (round 1 of #382). A bound in the basic ISO form, `20200101`, or with a fraction of
  a second of other than three or six digits, reads on Python 3.11 and later and is refused
  on 3.10 (rounds 2 and 3 of #382). A sign YAML drops is a misreading in a code, an item and
  a condition's codes, not in a reporting item: `reporting: {STROBE: [+6]}` reads as item 6
  (round 3 of #382).
- **The plan names a variable by its backticks, and nothing else.** A covariate the plan
  writes in words, "adjusted for age", is not read, and an entry for it is said to be
  unused until the plan writes `age`. A name in backticks that is code and not a variable,
  `lme4` or `R`, is warned of as an undefined variable until it is written as code, `lme4::`
  or `R()`, or without the backticks, and so is a value other than the nine left out,
  `NA_real_` or a code written `M`. A heading with "deviation" in it is the Deviations, as G12
  reads the plan, so a subsection "Standard deviation of `bmi_kg`" is not read (round 1).
  A derivation cycle is said once for each group of variables derived from one another,
  not once for every cycle in it. A plan written in `#` sections with no title, opening
  with `# Amendment history` over a `## Version 2` that names a dropped variable, takes the
  history for a title and reads it, so the dropped variable is not said to be unused (round
  2; `test_a_history_at_the_title_s_level_is_read_as_a_title`). The other side of the level
  chosen: a title at level 2, or a setext title over `---`, that names an amendment is the
  Deviations of the plan, and nothing under it is read
  (`test_a_level_2_title_naming_an_amendment_is_read_as_the_deviations`). The generated
  plans all have a level-1 title, so only these tests hold the rule for a plan with none
  (round 3 of #393). A title followed by a
  heading at its own level is the Deviations of its text up to that heading, where it
  names an amendment. The Deviations are left out whole, so a variable named
  only there is unused even where the change kept it. That an entry is needed is all that
  is checked: not that the plan uses it as its type says, that the analysis's own
  `variable()` declarations agree with the dictionary, or that an instrument's `citation` is
  in `references.bib`. An entry for an existing dataset's column the study does not use
  needs its reason like any other.
- **The REDCap export writes what a data dictionary can say, and no more.** A missing code
  of a number is written in the field note, not as one of REDCap's missing data codes,
  which a project sets for itself, so a value of -99 is refused by the field's range until
  the project's codes are set. No field is flagged as an identifier, since the dictionary
  does not say which fields identify a person. A `pattern` is not written as a validation
  (REDCap's own are a fixed list), and is said. A name over 26 characters, which REDCap
  advises against and accepts, is written as it is. A code with a comma, a bar, a quotation
  mark or a space, or a label with a bar or a line break, is refused, since it would not
  read back from REDCap's choices (round 1); a code REDCap refuses for another reason,
  `N/A`, is written, and REDCap's import says so. A bound with seconds is truncated to the
  minute, and one with a time zone is written without it; a `count`'s bound is written as
  given, `0.5` included. A failure to write the second or third file leaves the first
  written (round 2). A name REDCap reserves for itself, or `<form>_complete`, which it makes,
  is not refused, and a definition holding an action tag, `@HIDDEN`, acts as one in the
  field annotation. The REDCap file has not been imported
  into a REDCap server by these tests: its columns, types, validations, choices and
  branching logic are held to the template as the packages above read it.
- **A statistic is held to what it belongs to by which bindings share its sentence, and by
  nothing else.** An estimate with intervals at two levels is asked to be quoted whole at
  each, though a paper quotes the one it means. An interval quoted whole only in a table the
  analysis emits is asked for again, since a table's cells are text and bind no key. A
  caption, a supplement or a Discussion that gives a P again on its own is warned of, as a
  sentence of the Results would be. And a key declared `same_as` the estimate stands for
  nothing of it here: "Overall it was {{results.headline}}, P = {{results.or.p}}" is quoted
  alone. All are warnings, and `test_what_quoted_alone_does_not_read_is_pinned` holds them as
  they are. And a sentence that really ends at "s.e." followed by a binding or a word in
  lower case runs on into the next, for the order of an interval's bounds as for the rest,
  so a bound restated before it can hide a reversal after it (round 1 of #343).
- **The feasibility results are asked for by their names only.** Any one result under
  `feasibility.` quiets `feasibility-not-run`: nothing checks that the counts cover the
  plan's variables or its selection steps, or that the script read the data the analysis
  will. G1 holds the results to the inputs the script declared, and no more. The question
  is asked at the `design` stage alone, so a project that starts at a later stage is never
  asked it.
- **G4's blanking of comments and fences is close to pandoc's reading, not the same.** A
  stray fence line inside a comment, or a fence directly under prose that is tilde or
  indented a space or more, hides what follows from the statement and abstract-heading
  searches while pandoc prints it, so a statement there is reported missing: a false alarm.
  A raw block, ```` ```{=openxml} ````, is blanked although pandoc passes its text into the
  document. An indented code block is not blanked, so a pattern written for a phrase can be
  met by a line of code; one anchored on a heading cannot.
- **A data statement is the first of two matching headings at one level.** A numbered
  Methods subsection on data sharing is read as the statement where the statement stands
  under a Declarations heading at the same level
  (`test_a_statement_heading_level_with_a_methods_subsection_is_pinned`, round 2 of #269).
- **A Word citation field with a DOI no entry has is matched to an entry with no DOI by its
  title.** The title has no minimum length, and the year and the first author are
  compared only where both give them, so a conference abstract filed without its DOI is
  taken for the paper of the same title and authors (round 1 of #350). An entry that has
  the field's DOI is always taken first, each DOI read as the gates read one: without the
  dressing `normal_doi` takes off (`doi:`, a resolver's address, a stop after it), in one
  case.
- **Some tests of the literature are narrower than the rule they hold.** The words beside a
  quoted value are drawn with each value once, between spaces, and never inside a word with
  a digit: a value quoted twice, or within "CYP3A14", and a quote in a script written
  without spaces, are held by corruption cases only, or not at all (round 1 of #278). A
  Zotero field in a returned document is tested in one shape, with its run properties and
  its result in one run: a field with no `rPr`, a result over several runs, a
  `w:fldSimple` and a `formattedCitation` are not (round 1 of #281). A narrative
  citation's name written as hex on the command line is tested with Latin names only
  (round 3 of #296).

Added by the adversarial review, verified and **not** fixed:

- **Re-signing still defeats G1**, and always will: the digest and the file it protects are
  both writable by whoever holds the checkout. What changed is that G1 is no longer the only
  answer. `manuscript-guard verify` re-runs the analysis into a scratch copy and compares
  the fragments value by value, and a result cannot be forged into existence the way a
  digest can be recomputed. It is a separate command because it executes the project's own
  code, which a gate must never do. It cannot make a non-deterministic analysis agree with
  itself; it reports the disagreement and says to set a seed.
- **Two models' rows are compared by their labels, within one language.** pandas numbers
  rows from 0 and R from 1, so a model fitted in Python and one fitted in R on the same
  data are always taken for different rows; and two data frames whose labels were reset
  between the fits are too. Rows that share a label are not told apart: where a frame's
  index repeats, a fit without the first of two such rows and a fit without the second
  record the same rows (`test_rows_that_share_a_label_are_not_told_apart`). A stratum
  fitted without its stratifier, beside the whole cohort's model with it, is two models of
  one outcome on different rows, one's terms among the other's, and is warned of as a crude
  model fitted on other rows, with advice for that. A count with a person-time denominator
  modelled with no offset is not yet read: it needs the rate the analysis declares, which
  nothing records. An R `lm` or `glm` records "model-based" standard errors whatever is
  done after the fit, so a modified Poisson regression whose sandwich variance is computed
  beside the fit (`sandwich::vcovHC`) is still warned; the hint says so. An R `lm` keeps no
  data, and its rows are found by their labels in the data its call names, looked up in the
  formula's environment, as that data is when the model is emitted: a label gone since the
  fit is refused, but data relabelled since (sorted and its row names reset, or new rows
  bound before it) is not detected where its new labels still cover the old, and its other
  rows are counted; a unit changed since the fit is counted as it now is. One outcome is the
  same variables, the same comparison or none, and the same expression, spaces aside: a
  space inside a quoted level counts for nothing (`I(group == "a b")` is `"ab"`), and any
  other difference in how it is written makes two (`> 5` and `> 5.0`, `'IV'` and `"IV"` in
  a Python formula; R writes double quotes).
- **Numbers written as words escape the tokeniser.** "four thousand and twenty-one" is not
  read. Vulgar fractions and enclosed digits now are. Number words are left alone on
  purpose: "one of the two arms", "a single centre" and "two-tailed" are ordinary prose, and
  a rule that flags them is a rule that gets the gate switched off.
- **A P is held to its statistic only in a sentence that writes both, for four kinds of
  test.** t, F, chi-squared and z are read; r, U, H, W and the rest are not. A test in a
  table, its statistic in one column and its P in another, is not read. A statistic takes
  the next P in its sentence, before the next statistic, so where each P stands before its
  own, "P = .022 (t(23) = 2.45); P = .40 (t(30) = 0.85)", the first statistic is judged
  with the second's P and reported (round 1 of #285, where this said such a P was not
  read; `test_a_p_written_before_its_statistic_is_read_as_the_next_one_s`). A number written
  with a comma for its point, "0,62", is not read at all, so a paper set that way has none
  of its tests judged (a middle dot, "0·62", is read as a point; see "Closed since"); a
  comma after a number with its point,
  "P = 0.40,12", is the sentence's (round 1 of #336), so in such a paper a point that groups
  thousands is read as a point, "1.234,5" as 1.234 (pinned by
  `test_a_point_that_groups_thousands_in_a_decimal_comma_paper_is_read_as_a_point`). A P above 1 is not judged. A sentence ends at a stop before a
  capital or a bracket, so "et al. (2019)" ends one, and a word before it that says the
  test is not the textbook one is not seen. Such a word stands the test down wherever it is
  in the sentence, about this test or not: "exact" or "corrected" said of anything, and
  "adjusted", so "adjusted for age, z = 2.10, P = .40" is not judged, though a Wald z of an
  adjusted model is the textbook one (pinned by
  `test_adjusted_said_of_anything_stands_a_test_down`). Dunnett's and Games-Howell's
  procedures are among those words; others are not. A quote two ledger values rest on is
  judged once. Degrees
  of freedom with a thousands separator, "F(1, 1,234)", are not read. Decimal degrees of
  freedom are read over their digits by the corners of that range, which is exact where the
  P moves one way with each. A t or a z is read as two-sided unless its sentence says
  otherwise, so a one-sided test the sentence does not call one is reported. A ledger quote
  and an audited paper are judged at 0.05; only `check` reads `param.alpha`.
- **An estimate is held to its interval only where a name for it stands before it.** OR,
  RR, HR, IRR, ROR, PRR and their names in words are ratios; MD, RD, SMD and "difference"
  are differences. "It was 2.6 (95% CI 2.1 to 3.2)" is not read, and neither is a second
  interval with no name of its own, "and 1.1 (95% CI 0.8 to 1.5) in women". A ratio's
  interval that is not a Wald one and does not say so, a profile-likelihood interval with
  one or two events in a group, is reported as lopsided. An interval and a P from different
  methods, a Wald interval beside a log-rank or chi-squared P, can fall on either side of
  the level near it, and are reported unless the sentence calls the test exact or
  likelihood-based, or the P adjusted for multiplicity. A word that stands an interval or
  its P down does so wherever it is in the sentence, as for the tests. A P given before its
  interval, or in a table column of its own, is not read. Each of these is pinned by
  `test_what_the_interval_reader_gets_wrong_is_pinned` (rounds 1 and 2 of #300):
  - a P in a later clause is taken as the estimate's, the search stopping only at another
    interval's name: in "OR 1.9 (95% CI 1.2-3.0) but not in women (OR 1.1, P = 0.40)" the
    first OR is judged with 0.40;
  - "HR" for heart rate, or "RR" for respiratory rate, is read as a ratio held to 1;
  - an interval whose level is not printed is taken as 95%, so a paper that states 90% once
    in its Methods is judged at 0.05;
  - "the difference in hazard ratios" is read as a hazard ratio;
  - a word that says a P is another's, "heterogeneity" or "interaction", stands it down
    when it stands between the interval and the P or follows the P within 40 characters,
    whatever it is about (round 1 of #336, where this said only after).

  An SMR, an SIR, a standardised mortality or incidence ratio and a ratio of means are not
  read, since their exact intervals need not be symmetric on the log scale. "SMR", "SIR"
  and "ratio of means" stop a "difference" before them, which is not read across them
  (round 2 of #300); a longer name keeps the two apart anyway, since a name and its
  estimate stand at most 24 characters apart. An en dash straight before an estimate's
  digits, after no digit, is read as its minus, "MD–0.4" and a log ratio's "–0.4" too,
  except glued to a ratio's name: "OR–1.9" is 1.9 (#336). After a ratio's name, glued to any
  letter it is a dash, so "log OR was–0.4", with no space, is read as 0.4, outside its interval, as on main
  (pinned by `test_an_en_dash_glued_to_any_word_before_a_ratio_is_a_dash`).
- **An n (%) is held to its denominator only where the table writes both, in one cell, in
  a pipe table or a Word table.** A grid or a simple Markdown table is not read, nor a
  count and its share in columns of their own, nor a share whose denominator only a caption
  or a note under the table states ("Values are n (%)", "of those with data"). A share of
  those with data, under a header that gives everyone, is listed: as uncertain where the
  row's label carries a footnote marker, as plainly off where it does not. A row whose
  shares add up to 100 across it is let off if they are shares of its total, so a wrong
  share in a row of two that happens to add up to 100 with the other, and fits the row's
  total, is not listed; and a row-percentage table with a Total column, whose shares add up
  to 200, is listed whole. Categories with nothing but their sum to say they are shares are
  read only where every row of their run adds up to 100: followed in the same run by the
  next characteristic, they are not read, and a wrong count among them is not listed
  (`test_categories_run_on_into_the_next_characteristic_are_not_read`); a whole-number mean
  in a run that adds up to 100 with it is read and listed. Both are the price of not letting
  a running sum say what is a share (round 3 of #314). Categories that add up to 100 are let
  off as shares of their own
  total in the same way. A group label's "n (%)" reaches every row with a count below it
  until a row without one, and a data row with no count in it is read as a header, so its
  "n = 980" becomes the denominator below it. A superscript unit in a label, kg/m^2^, reads as
  a footnote marker and makes the row uncertain. A group label that says only "%",
  "Smoking status, %", says nothing, so its categories are read only where their shares add
  up to 100, and one wrong among them leaves them all unread. A unit label with a footnote
  marker after it, or with no comma before its "%" ("SpO2 %"), is not a measure.
  Categories whose counts add up to an old denominator are let off as shares of it. "No. of
  patients (%)" and "% (n)" are not read as saying shares. A nested Word table is read as
  text in its cell. A measure in percent whose mean is above 100, "Predicted FEV1, % | 104
  (15)" under a header that says n (%), is read as a share and listed, since only a number
  up to 100 is barred as a measure. What may stand beside a characteristic's own label
  takes a lone "P", "<", "0" or "1", so a second header row "| Characteristic | | | P |" is
  read as a label, and refuses a negative SMD, a P with a footnote marker and "NS", beside
  which the label is read as a header (round 3 of #314). A span is held to the 63 columns a
  Word table has.
- **A mean of whole numbers is checked only where the author says it is one, and only
  as a mean.** `audit` reads only the table rows `--whole-numbers` names, and in them only a
  cell shaped as a mean, with its SD or not, a nought before its point or not (".47"); a
  mean in a sentence is not read, nor a median, nor a mean whose thousands are grouped. A
  cell that is a mean and names its n, "3.1 (1.0), n = 25", or any other cell of a row of
  means that names one, sets the n for the column below, and the means held to it are
  uncertain, whether its own row is read or not (round 1 of #336); a mean naming its n has a
  spread or a point, and is not in the table's first row, so a header "2019 (n = 120)" or
  "0.5 (n = 40)" in the first row is a header (#336). In a second header row, a decimal
  beside an n, "0.5 (n = 40)", is taken for a mean naming its n, though "2019 (n = 120)" is
  not: the n is right, and the means below are called uncertain (pinned
  by `test_a_header_of_two_rows_marks_the_means_below_uncertain`). Its n is its column header's, so a mean over those
  with data is listed as not fitting where its n is smaller; the message gives the nearest n
  it fits, and the reader decides. A mean of several items per person is read in `audit` as
  a mean of one number each: every mean possible for n is possible for n times the items, so
  this passes nothing wrong, but lists a mean that is right for its items (round 1 of #331,
  where this entry said the reverse). The ledger takes `items`. Whether an SD is possible for whole numbers with that mean and n is not
  checked. In the ledger, n is what the author records from the source; nothing reads it from
  the quote.
- **A name or a unit typed with pandoc's subscript and superscript signs was an unbound
  number.** G2 cuts an atom at the punctuation round it, so `CO~2~` was `CO~2`, which no
  term matched: `HbA1c` is a built-in term and `HbA~1c~` was reported, a declared `CO2` did
  not cover `CO~2~`, and `kg/m^2^` was reported where `kg/m²` never was. What passed was
  `terms: ['CO~2']`, sign and all, or the character itself (found 2026-10-04). Now a
  name is matched against the terms, built in and declared, with the signs of its
  subscripts and superscripts taken out, and the hint of a name that is not declared
  says how to declare it, `terms: [CO2]`. And an exponent on a unit is read as the
  superscript character is, as typography: one digit, with a sign or none, between
  carets directly after one to three letters, which takes in `m^2^`, `mm^3^`, `s^-1^`,
  `R^2^` and `χ^2^`, and the letter in italics, `*R*^2^`. `10^6^` stays a number, as
  `10⁶` does by its `10`. There is no list of formulae or of units: the terms are the
  list for names, and the shape is the rule for exponents (Basile, 2026-10-04).
  A sign is one where pandoc reads one: closed by another, with no space between. A
  tilde nothing closes is printed as a tilde, and stands for "about" or for a range. The
  first version took every `~` and `^` out, and the number after such a tilde joined the
  letters before it: `pH~2` was `ph2`, which holds the built-in term `h2`, and a pH, an
  effect of `HR~2`, a rise of `increased~2-fold` and the end of `1 week~2 weeks` passed
  `check` and the build (found by the review of the change). And read without its signs,
  a name is matched only by terms that open a word: `risk^1^`, a citation's number, was
  `risk1`, which holds the term `k1`.
  Where it stops. The terms have to account for every digit, as before, so a count typed
  hard against a name (`HbA~1c~7.2`), between the signs (`^412^`) or before a subscript
  (`412~patients~`) is reported. The hint says how to declare a term only of what reads
  as a name: it opens with a letter, its digits are all in its subscripts and
  superscripts, and it is no word with digits alone in a superscript (`shown^12^`,
  `year^-1^`). A term is still found anywhere in an atom as it is written, so `H2O` is
  accepted by the built-in `h2`, as before, and so is `H~2~O`, where `h2` opens the word.
  A symbol with a subscript that makes a term is that term: `b~1~`, `d~2~`, `k~2~`. An
  exponent of two digits or more, and one on a word of four letters or more, is a number:
  `year^-1^` and `mmHg^-1^` are reported, and are typed with the superscript characters or
  declared without their signs, `terms: [year-1]`. That is narrower than what is read for
  the characters themselves, on purpose:
  `shown^12^` is a citation's number typed by hand, and the caret is how it is typed. One
  digit after a word of one to three letters that is no unit, `it^2^`, `OR^3^`, `mg^7^`,
  is not read, as `it²` is not: a citation's number typed there is missed, and so is one
  after such a word in italics, `*et al*^3^`. Three shapes are read as names that are
  none. Digits in a superscript after a word that is the whole of a term's letters make
  the term, so a citation's number typed as `hepatitis B^12^` passes as vitamin B12,
  and `CD^19^` as CD19. A superscript letter before a number, `^b^12`, is read as `b12`,
  where `12^b^` is reported. And two tildes that pandoc reads as one subscript,
  `h~2/d~3`, are read as `h2` and `d3`. None is how a result is written. Leaving digits
  alone in a superscript in their signs was tried for the first, and it took declared
  names with it, which the review of that change found: an anion, `SO~4~^2-^` declared
  `SO42-`, a symbol with a subscript and an exponent, `R~adj~^2^` declared `Radj2`, and
  `year^-1^` declared `year-1`; so a name's superscripts are taken out whatever they
  hold. An isotope is declared by its mass and its element, `terms: [68Ga]` for
  `^68^Ga-DOTATATE`, and its hint does not say so: what opens with a digit is told
  nothing of terms, since a count typed between the signs opens the same way. Terms of
  one length came in the order of a set, so a name was a term on one run and a number
  on the next; they come in one order now, longest first and then by their letters. Two
  names typed with nothing between, `FiO~2~PaO~2~` and `PaO~2~FiO~2~`, are two terms
  in either order: a term counts where another ends (#438). A term that holds a
  superscript's digits counts only where it opens a word: read without its signs, a
  citation's number typed after a word with a capital inside stood hard against that
  capital, and "PharmD^2^" was `d2` and "ApoB^12^" `b12`, which a capital after a
  lower-case letter opens (#438). A term after a capital counts as written, "CD3+",
  "Th1/Th2", "CCR2" and "HLA-DRB1" being names, and after a lower-case letter only from a
  capital, "April-12" being a number (#438). `^99m^Tc` opens its word and stays a name, and a
  subscript is the name's own: `pCO~2~` is a declared `CO2`. Where terms overlap, the
  atom is a term if some of them cover its digits: `MERS-COVID-19` is `covid-19`. The
  terms were once gone through again for as long as one was taken out, which took time
  by the square of the atom and did not end for a declared term of one space; the atom
  is now read once from its end. The
  conventions still read the text with its signs in: `75th percentile` is a convention
  and `75^th^ percentile` is none, and under Methods `I² > 50%` is one where `I^2^ > 50%`
  leaves the 50% reported. Both allowances hold wherever the tokenizer and the classifier
  are used, and not only in a manuscript's text: in a figure's text, in `audit` and in a
  string value the analysis emits, where `^` and `~` are only characters, `m^2^` is no
  number either. A declared `CO2` covers `CO~2~` in a figure's text and in a table the
  analysis emits; `audit` and a string value the analysis emits are read with the
  built-in terms and not the project's, as before, so there `CO~2~` is reported and
  `HbA~1c~` is not. Listed in
  `tests/data/exemptions.yaml` as `unit-exponent`, with the test that types a number in
  each of those shapes.
- **`conventions:` and `terms:` in `paper.yaml` are self-service.** A pattern of `\d+` with a
  `why` of "house style" disables G2, and `terms:` needs no justification at all. The gate
  is a tool for an author who wants it, not a control over one who does not — so this stays.
  What has changed is that it is no longer *invisible*: every run reports how many numbers
  the project's own rules accounted for, and which rules did it, as `project-exemption`
  (a warning past a quarter of the numbers in the manuscript). Self-service and silent are
  different things, and only the first was intended. A convention may be given a name,
  `id`, by which that report and `explain` cite it, as `project:<id>`; without one it is
  cited by the first 24 characters of its pattern (Basile, 2026-10-03). A name is text on
  one line with something in it besides spaces; another is the schema's finding, and the
  convention is not read. Two conventions given one name each exempt what they match and
  are counted under it together, as two whose patterns begin alike are. Before the review
  of #153 the second one's matches replaced the first's, under either kind of shared name,
  and a number the first was written for failed as unbound.
- **A figure file is read for its pixels only where it is a PNG, JPEG or TIFF.** An EPS
  figure's text, lines and fonts are not read, nor is a raster inside an EPS, a PDF or an
  SVG's `<image>`. A figure the build places is the first of its files in the
  build's order, PNG first, and every file of it is held to the rules, so a figure kept as
  PNG and TIFF is held to the journal's limits twice. A JPEG whose JFIF header records no
  resolution, or a PNG with no `pHYs` chunk, is not said to shrink: how large it was drawn
  is unknown. A legend is the paragraph straight after the figure that opens with "Figure"
  and its number; a legend written above it, or in the figure, is not counted. A megabyte
  is 1,048,576 bytes, the larger of the two a journal may mean.
- **A PDF figure is read for its first page, and as far as its operators say.** A stream
  under a filter other than Flate is not read, nor is an encrypted PDF. A Type 3 font's
  `/FontMatrix` is not applied, so one drawn in other than a thousand units to the em is
  read at the size `Tf` gives; a text's rise and horizontal scaling are not read, nor are
  the lines a Type 3 glyph draws. A font is said where the page's or a form's resources name
  it, whether any text uses it or not.
- **An SVG's text and lines are read from its elements, not drawn.** A `<style>` rule is
  read where its selector is made of types, classes and ids joined as descendants or
  children; one with a pseudo-class, an attribute or a sibling is not, and `!important`
  wins nothing. A text is cut off only where its anchor is outside the `viewBox`; one that
  starts inside and runs past the edge, or is hidden by a `clipPath`, is not said. A line
  with `vector-effect: non-scaling-stroke` is widened all the same, a `<marker>` is not read,
  a `stroke-width` in percent is taken of the font size and not of the figure, and a text's
  `dx`, `dy` and `text-anchor` do not move its anchor. A `<use>` that refers to itself is
  followed sixteen deep.
- **A figure's alternative text is checked for being there, not for being right.** That
  it says what is drawn is the figure review's and a person's to read. It is read from the
  figure's guard file only: alternative text set in Word by a co-author, or in a PDF figure's
  own structure, is not read, and `import` does not bring Word's back into the guard file. A
  LaTeX manuscript's build writes none, and the check reads nothing there, since it finds
  the figures placed in the Markdown sources alone. A link's target, a URL, a citation key or
  attributes in the text are hidden by the prose's mask and printed by the build, so a number
  in one is not read, and a release typed across two numbers is said twice. The pack's `alt-text.md` names each figure by its
  key, not by the number the document prints. A figure the manuscript places twice is held to
  the main text's rule if either place is in the main text. The text's bindings are read by
  the document's stamp, the custodian's minimum and the synthetic-data check, as the
  manuscript's are; G2's other readings of bindings do not see it, so a value quoted there
  alone is still one the manuscript does not quote.
- **A figure's colours are read from its SVG or PDF, and compared all with all.** A raster
  figure's are not, nor an image inside an SVG or a PDF (a heat map matplotlib embeds as one),
  nor a gradient, a pattern, a shading, or a PDF colour in a separation, an indexed or a Lab
  colour space. A figure that draws a continuous scale is not compared at all, its series
  beside the scale included, and neither is one of more than 300 colours: both are said in a
  note, and left to the figure's review. A scale drawn with neighbours more than 10 apart, or
  through less than 10 of lightness (a colormap's narrow slice, a correlation map's pale
  middle under fixed limits), is no scale to the check, and its shades are compared as
  series; a rainbow colormap a deficiency scrambles is not said. The bands of one series at
  three opacities or more chain through lightness and are taken for a scale, so such a
  figure is not compared. A text drawn as glyphs is known for one where
  matplotlib (`text_` groups) or Cairo (`glyph` symbols) draws it so, and is a mark where
  another program does. A text's colour is left out, so data told apart only
  by coloured labels is not checked. Every colour painted is compared with every other, the
  background and the grid's among them: the check does not know which colours encode data, so
  a series and a grid line made one by a deficiency are said, and `allow_colours` is how a
  figure says that pair does not matter. A colour laid at an opacity is laid over white, not
  over what is under it. A PDF's CMYK is taken to RGB without its profile, and any colour
  space of three numbers is read as sRGB. The deficiencies are simulated at full severity
  only, the dichromacies; the anomalous trichromacies, commoner and milder, are not, and
  Machado's model is less sure of tritanopia than of the other two. The threshold of 10 is a
  convention, not a standard. A LaTeX manuscript's figures are not read.
- **A palette's verdict is the check's, at its threshold, on its colours as written.** The
  number of a set's colours that stay apart is counted in the collection's order for that
  many, so a set whose first colours are close is rated low though a figure could take
  others of it. A continuous map's lightness is judged at eleven points, so a wiggle between
  them is not seen. What a collection claims is copied as its file states it (MetBrewer,
  MoMAColors and NatParksPalettes) or as its makers' documentation states it (viridis,
  cividis, Crameri, Okabe and Ito), not tested. `figure_style` and `mg_theme` size text and
  lines to the journal's least or 7 pt and 0.5 pt, sizes many artwork guides give, which the
  journal's own guide may set otherwise; `size` overrides. `mg_theme` sets ggplot2's `line`
  and `rect`, and an element a base theme draws at a multiple of them keeps it: `theme_bw`'s
  minor grid is drawn at half the journal's least. A palette's colours are not
  checked against the figure that uses them: G3 reads the rendered figure.
- **`stage:` is declared, not detected.** Writing `stage: analysis` demotes every G2 finding
  to INFO. It is printed, counted and summarised — never hidden — but CI reading the exit
  code sees green.
- **A coding dictionary's release is read from a file only for MedDRA, and found typed only
  beside its name.** That `meddra_release.asc` opens with the version, as the first of its
  `$`-separated fields, is taken from published descriptions of the ASCII release; the
  format document itself comes with a MedDRA licence and was not read. A file that does not
  open with a version is refused, not guessed at. Every other dictionary's release is what
  the script says. G2 finds a release typed only where the dictionary's name, as its key
  writes it, stands within 60 characters before it on the same line: "coded with MedDRA
  version" wrapped onto the next line, a name written another way ("the Medical Dictionary
  for Regulatory Activities"), or the release written otherwise than declared ("B3 2025" for
  "Global B3 March 2025") is not found. `verify` reports a release that differs on a re-run
  as a difference, not as the environment: the dictionary is data.
- **G3 checks a number drawn in a figure for set membership, not identity.** A text node in
  an SVG is accepted if it equals *any* results display, not the one that belongs at that
  position — so a forest plot labelled with the right value against the wrong outcome passes.
  The gate cannot know which value a given text node is meant to be; nothing in the artefact
  says. The real protection is one level up: `figure-script-ignores-results` requires the
  script to read the results file, and a figure whose labels are drawn from results cannot
  carry another outcome's number. Set membership is the backstop for the figure nobody
  scripted, and should be read as "no number here is a stranger", not as "every number here
  is the right one".
- **A figure that estimates is found by the names of the calls it makes.** Only the calls in
  `data/figure_estimates.yaml` are read, by the last part of their name: a function of the
  script's own that wraps one, a call through an alias (`bar = sns.barplot`), seaborn's
  `catplot` and `relplot`, which estimate only under some `kind`, and a density estimate
  (`kdeplot`) are not. A method of the same name on another object is taken for one: any
  `.sample(` or `.std(`. Any seed call in the script (`np.random.seed`, `default_rng(7)`,
  `random.seed`, `set.seed`) is taken to settle every random call in it, though
  `np.random.seed` does not seed Python's `random` module. A draw from a generator the script
  made, `rng = np.random.default_rng()` and then `rng.normal()`, is a method of that object
  and not under `np.random.`, so it is not read even unseeded; a test pins it. The figure's
  sheet lists what is allowed under `allow_estimates`, and a section there that is no list
  allows nothing. A seaborn bootstrap is settled
  only by its own `seed=`. `geom_smooth`, `stat_summary` and `dropna` have no argument that
  quiets them: each needs a reason under `allow_estimates`, or the computation moved into
  the analysis.
- **The source-of-truth invariant does not survive a co-author round in Word, and a real
  paper is the proof.** This toolkit rests on "Markdown is the permanent source of truth and
  the .docx is a disposable build artifact". Run against a submitted pharmacology paper, the
  main text turned out to be a `.docx`: the project began markdown-first, twelve rounds of
  tracked changes happened in Word between May and July, none were back-ported, and the
  markdown was eventually deleted as the losing copy. The supplements, which never went
  through Word, are still markdown and still built from the pipeline.

  So the invariant held exactly where the review loop did not touch it. `import` and the
  paragraph round trip exist to prevent this and were built after the fact; whether they
  actually hold a manuscript together through a real co-author round is untested, because no
  paper has yet been through one with them in place. Until then, `audit` — the weaker
  question, asked of a document nobody bound — is not a fallback for awkward cases. It is the
  command that meets the situation a real paper is most likely to be in.
- **`import` compares only paragraphs that carry an identifier.** Table cells, headings,
  captions, list items, block quotes, definitions (the term of a loose definition list is
  one paragraph and keeps its identifier), footnote text, code, and anything the co-author
  newly wrote carry none. Those edits are not merged and not refused. Outside tables they
  are listed - reworded, deleted or reordered - and import exits 1; inside a table only the
  count of what went unexamined is printed, which is a report rather than a fix. A number
  corrected in a table is the case that matters, because that is where a stale number is
  likeliest to be. A document built before identifiers moved off lists and quotations comes
  back listing them as changed even untouched: the fresh build it is compared with sets
  them out as lists and quotations, where it had run them into paragraphs, and names the
  run-on paragraphs it carries as not compared, because no paragraph goes by their
  identifier now. Nothing is applied, and a current build sent out ends it. Lists and quotes are on the list by choice: a
  marker in front of one rewrote it, and a marker inside its first item would let `import`
  splice that item over the whole block (see "The round trip carries prose"). Comparing
  them needs an identifier per item and a merge that puts the list marker back, and neither
  exists.
- **A design's sections are found by the words of their headings.** "Comparator" is any
  heading that holds the word, so a plan with "Choice of comparator drug" under its Exposure
  has the section, and one that answers the question under a heading of its own words has
  not. Seven designs are named; a design outside them (a cross-sectional study, a
  diagnostic accuracy study, a target trial emulation as a design of its own) names none and
  keeps the seven sections. The self-controlled designs have no reporting guideline, and
  their sections come from the methods literature. G5 holds the paper's guidelines to the
  design, and not the protocol's (SPIRIT, PRISMA-P). A guideline is matched by the start of
  its name, so a name that begins as another does ("STROBE-anything").
- **Which blocks are paragraphs is decided by pattern, not by pandoc.** `tag` runs where
  pandoc may be absent, so it reproduces pandoc's rules — two spaces after "C." before it is
  a list, the inline HTML tags a paragraph may open with, what can interrupt a paragraph —
  and is checked against pandoc in `tests/test_pandoc_agreement.py`, which CI runs against
  the pandoc it installs and pins, 3.9.0.2. Where the patterns are unsure they leave a block
  unmarked, which costs a comparison and corrupts nothing. Known cases: a paragraph opening with a TeX command
  (`\noindent`), one holding a line of nothing but dashes and pipes, one starting "p. 12"
  (pandoc's abbreviation rule, not reproduced), and a paragraph whose unescaped braces do
  not pair. And the scan for raw content does not know where pandoc reads a `<!--`, a
  verbatim tag such as `<pre>`, or a `\begin{x}` inside something it closes first. Found
  so far: inline code, inline or display maths, `\verb|...|`, an indented code block, a
  fence written under a line of its block rather than after a blank one, a fence opening
  a list item on its marker's line, a fence in a block quote or indented four columns or
  more, a link's destination or title, an image's destination or title, an autolink, the
  attributes of a tag, a span, a heading, a div, a link, an image or a code span, a table
  cell, a list item, a block quote, a line block, a definition, a YAML block in the body
  and any value in the front matter. `<pre>`
  and `\begin` are misread in link text, an image's alt text, an inline note and a
  citation's locator too, and `<!--` and `<pre>` in a TeX command's argument. There the
  opener is taken for real. The paragraphs from the one holding it to the one holding its
  closer go unmarked, though pandoc prints them: the closer is the next `-->`, the tag's
  own end tag (`</pre>`, `</script>`), or the `\end{x}` matching it by name. With no closer
  later in the file, nothing is hidden. The document looks right; an edit made to one of
  those paragraphs in Word comes back listed as not compared, to be carried over by hand.
  For a `<!--` anywhere but inline code, a fence and the front matter, `check`'s comment
  scanner hides the text from the opener to the closer as well, and G2 reads no number
  there (see "The comment scanner knows code spans, fences and the front matter"). No way
  around it is given here: each tried, a fenced block, an empty comment after the opener,
  an escape, `%3C` or `&lt;`, fails or changes the printed words somewhere the others
  work, and the reviews of #97 list where. Raw TeX other than an environment is not
  followed across a blank line. When the blank line falls inside braces, the blocks either
  side are refused by the brace count, since `\footnote{One.\n\nTwo.}` is one paragraph
  to pandoc; a block wholly inside
  such a group, the middle of a `\newcommand` with two blank lines in its body, gets a
  marker, and pandoc drops raw TeX from the .docx so the identifier names nothing, which
  `import` already tolerates. When it falls inside an optional argument,
  `\cite[p.~5\n\nmore]{key}`, the braces pair on each side and both halves are marked:
  pandoc then prints the halves as literal text. The document shows it and `import` stays
  consistent with it, and counting brackets instead would refuse every paragraph quoting an
  interval such as `[0, 1)`. Every review round on these patterns found holes in the
  version before it,
  each by running pandoc on a construct the table did not yet hold, so the table is
  evidence for what is in it and no more. The HTML block tags are pandoc 3.9.0.2's, taken
  from its source; a later pandoc that takes another tag for a block marks a paragraph it
  splits, until the agreement test is run against it.
- **A caption or a definition is told from a paragraph by its opening alone.** A block
  opening `Table:`, `table:` or a colon is a caption beside a table. A line that is `: ` or
  `~ ` and text, or a colon or a tilde alone, makes a definition of a single line above it,
  with or without a blank line between; under a paragraph of two lines or more it is more of
  that paragraph, or a paragraph of its own after a blank line. The tagger sees one block at
  a time, so it leaves every block that opens so, or holds such a line second, without an
  identifier. The merge escapes any such opening a co-author types. A rewording that brings
  a kept `:` or `~` up to a paragraph's second line, by joining the lines above it, is
  refused by #69's check: the next build would give it no identifier. A paragraph written
  that way in the `.md` is never compared.
- **A brace an earlier version wrote back is half a pair now.** Before a `}` was escaped,
  `import` wrote a co-author's `{a, b}` as `\{a, b}`. Only unescaped braces count now, so
  such a paragraph has an unpaired `}` and no identifier: it builds as before, but an edit
  to it in Word is reported as not compared and not applied, so it can be edited only in
  the `.md`. Adding the missing backslash, `\{a, b\}`, gives it its identifier back.
- **A rewording that splits a brace pair across a number or citation is refused.** A brace
  from Word is written escaped, so where a rewording leaves a bare brace from the `.md` on
  one side of a number or citation and its partner comes back from Word - edited, moved or
  typed anew - or is deleted there, the braces no longer pair and the paragraph is refused
  and named. So is a brace typed in Word that pairs with nothing. `main` before #72 wrote a
  `}` from Word bare and merged many of these correctly, 212 of 4,174 in #72's round-3
  differential; written bare, a brace can complete what pandoc reads as attributes after a
  `]`, a link, an autolink or a value, and #90's three review rounds found each (see "The
  writer and the tagger have to read an opening the same way"). Braces inside code count
  too, though pandoc pairs none there. The edit is made in the `.md`.
- **A line pandoc does not call blank still ends a block for the numbering.** A line
  holding only a non-breaking space, an em or ideographic space or a form feed ends a block
  for the identifiers' numbering, while pandoc reads one paragraph across it. Marked, the
  first half's bookmark sat on the joined paragraph and `import --apply` wrote the second
  half twice; both halves are now left unmarked and never compared. Renumbering would fix
  it and would move every identifier after them. Over two stacked lines of dashes, such a
  line is a setext heading to pandoc and the second line opens a table; the table rules
  lose the line, take the heading's underline for the opener, and a paragraph inside the
  table can be marked.
- **A YAML block in the body is followed only where a block starts with it.** Pandoc tries
  every `---` in column 0 with text straight under it as YAML, up to the first `---` or
  `...` in column 0, and a marker at the start of a line inside turns its quiet fallback (to
  a rule, a table or prose) into a parse error that fails the build. So everything it tries
  is left unmarked, mapping or not. Two cases are not followed, and neither corrupts the
  source. A `---` that opens mid-block, straight after a code fence, straight under a
  table's closing rule or inside a fenced div with no blank line before it, fails the build
  when its YAML holds a blank line. An attempt that opens in one source file
  and stops in the next - each file is tagged on its own and the build joins them - builds,
  with the second file's paragraphs read into a table whose bookmarks `import` ignores, so
  their edits go uncompared.
- **A block that opens on a line of dashes is taken for a table whatever surrounds it.**
  When the line has text straight under it, `tag` leaves everything up to the table's
  closing line of dashes unmarked; with a blank line under it, the line is a rule and opens
  nothing. Pandoc reads no table there when the line continues a list item, sits inside a
  fenced div after a blank line, or follows a no-break-space line inside a paragraph. The
  paragraphs in between then go uncompared although pandoc reads them as paragraphs, and
  nothing is corrupted. Lines of three dashes or more had these cases already; since two
  dashes can open a table, `--` has them too.
- **A table that opens mid-block is followed only under the lines it was seen to open
  under.** Pandoc 3.9 opens one straight under a code or div fence, a whole line of
  block-level HTML, a setext underline, a grid table's border, a pipe-table row, a line
  opening on `|`, `\end{...}`, a comment's closing `-->` or a YAML stop, and under a
  heading or a one-line comment when the dashes hold two runs or more; `tag` follows it
  from there. Under prose, a list item, a quote, a definition, a caption, a TeX command, an
  image or a one-line reference definition it opens none: over a line of dashes, most of
  those are a simple table's header. A line of any other kind is taken to open none, among
  them a reference definition whose title continues on the next line, a line block's
  continuation and an HTML tag split over two lines. A table pandoc does open under one
  gets a marker in its rows, visible in the document; `import` then reports that paragraph
  as deleted in Word and leaves the source alone. The other way round costs only
  comparisons. A line taken for one of these that pandoc does not end a block under, over
  a line of dashes with text under it, hides the paragraphs down to the next line of
  dashes. Such lines sit inside code, a comment or a table's rows, or in prose such as
  `A -->`, `\end{x}`, `...` or a line opening on `|`. The block where that span ends is
  read again as any block is - below its first line when it starts inside code, since
  that line is code - so a real table the span runs into is still followed. Read only for tables opening further
  down it, the block missed a real table's own top rule, and the table's rows were marked.
  Four layouts are still not covered, all contrived. A span that ends on the underline of
  a header split by a blank line leaves the table's rows marked. A span that ends on a line
  of dashes inside a YAML block scalar leaves a marker in the YAML, and the build fails. A
  real table that pandoc ends on a line of dashes inside a code block pairs every later
  fence differently from `tag`, so a paragraph after it can be marked inside code; that
  one is older than this reading. And a block a span hides is not read for raw content, so
  a comment or an environment opened in a paragraph the span hides, and closed after the
  span, goes unfollowed: a paragraph inside it is marked, and the identifier names nothing
  in the document.
- **Code fences are paired by `text/fences.py`, not by pandoc.** Where the two pair them
  differently, a paragraph can be marked inside code, and the marker prints there, and a
  table under such a fence can go unfollowed. Every case found so far, an opener whose info
  string pandoc rejects (`python title="x"`, `{code-cell} ipython3`), a `~~~` straight under
  a paragraph line, a fence line inside an HTML comment, is refused by `check`
  (`unclear-fence`) or by the build's comparison of listings, so no document is built from
  one; the entry stands because `tag` still pairs fences itself.
- **A heading with its first paragraph directly under it is one block, left unmarked.**
  `# Methods\nWe did X.` is a heading and a paragraph to pandoc, and since the block starts
  with `#` the paragraph never carries an identifier and its edits are never compared.
  Marking it would mean placing the identifier after the heading line. This was already so
  before identifiers moved off lists.
- **A review point anchored to a list or a quote before identifiers moved off them names
  nothing.** A `where:` recorded from a document built earlier can hold the identifier the
  flattened list carried. That block is no longer tagged, so G13 reports the paragraph as no
  longer in the manuscript rather than checking the response against it.

Recorded by review, judged contrived or rare by the reviewer that found each, and left
(2026-10-19). Each is named so that it is not trusted beyond it:

- **Review panels and their records.** A provider is judged by its name, so a router such as
  OpenRouter or a local Ollama, which serves models of several families under one name, is
  warned of as one provider (`round-one-provider`) though its models are not one family. A
  remit that speaks of "chart review" or "medical charts" is taken to ask for the figures.
  A superseded round's own new warnings are not lowered, only `review-stale` and
  `review-uncovered`. An unreadable plain record drops the overrides of the named readings
  beside it, and is called "a record". A design reading by a reviewer not on the panel, and
  a design round folder with no panel, are passed over; a design reading is superseded by its
  reviewer and reader, not by its remit, and a stale plain record only by a later plain
  one. An override's digest is of the finding and the reason, not of `where`, `ask` or
  `overridden_by`. A named design reading is opened at the path its name gives, so a file
  system that tells case apart reads one filed under other capitals as missing, and two
  files under one slug go unsaid (G11 finds both in a manuscript round); a misfiled reading is named by its slug where its overrides are
  listed. A reader named O'Brien makes the printed hint unparsable. The design remit is
  looked up outside the record's lock, and a panel that is a YAML list raises. `review
  --design` passes over `--digest` and `--files`, and says nothing for a project with no
  design round. The plan sent and its `plan_sha256` come from two reads.
- **Sign-offs and approvals.** One authorisation is given per provider, so a cloud model
  added later to a provider already authorised goes unasked, and a `-cloud` model added to
  a local provider voids the sign-off with the message of any other change. No test calls
  the backstop with a model that has no sign-off standing. The text "manuscript-guard
  approve" in a search draws an extra prompt. An approval that cannot be parsed stops
  `submit` after the pack is written, and one that breaks the schema is printed as a
  failure and not acted on. Approvals are not guarded against `cp` or `rm` from a shell.
  Two authors of one name with neither ORCID nor e-mail share a file, an e-mail differing
  only in characters outside `[\w.@-]` folds into another, a duplicate ORCID is not
  flagged, and a very long name or a device name (`Con`, `Nul`) can make no file. The
  unsigned checklist in the pack does not say whether a sign-off was void or never made.
- **The literature and its lookups.** Citation keys that differ only in case are filed
  apart or not found, by the file system. `[x?]+` in pages takes Roman page numbers for a
  placeholder; a Crossref `component` always fails, a cited supplementary item included;
  `\textregistered` and `\textdegree` keep their names in a title, `{\'\i}t` reads as
  `\it`, a footnote letter in `<sup>` joins the word before it, and a kind of notice
  Crossref adds later passes. A quote in Chinese, Japanese, Korean or Thai, written without
  spaces, counts one or two words and is always too short; a value quoted from a table row,
  with no sentence, is warned of. A quotation in the prose with a citation or a binding
  inside its marks, a block quotation's `>`, an unpaired straight `"` (5' 10") or
  mismatched curly marks can be warned of wrongly. A data statement's DOI is cut at `<` in
  a SICI DOI, and a closing `'`, `’` or `_` is kept on it.
- **What `impact` reads.** Figure scripts are found in the scripts folder only, not below
  it, figures only where a `results.` key exists, and a figure file, where no render record
  names it, only by its script's stem and as `.svg`, `.pdf`, `.png`, `.tif`, `.tiff`, `.jpg`
  or `.eps` (not `.jpeg`, `.gif` or `.webp`); answers are matched by file name, and readings G11 does not judge are
  listed. `--since` placed before `--` can carry an option. A folder named lists only the
  readings of the whole manuscript, and a file name that is not UTF-8 is shown with
  replacement characters on Linux.
- **Typed releases of a dictionary.** Any number equal to the release within 60 characters
  after the dictionary's name is taken for it, and a second release overlapping the first
  ("2025" in "Global B3 March 2025") draws a second finding. A slug with a doubled or
  trailing underscore ("MedDRA®") is never found. A `release_file` is an input, and R
  looks for a relative one where it looks for any (see "The emitters").
- **Figure estimates.** `def std(values):` is read as a call; an `.Rmd` or `.qmd` is lexed
  as R throughout, its Python chunks missed and "sample (" in its prose read; a form feed
  counts as a line break for one count and not the other. `stripplot` is not marked seeded,
  `geom_jitter(position = "jitter")` passes quietly, and R's `rt`, `rchisq`, `rlnorm`,
  `rnbinom`, `rweibull` and `sample.int` are not among the draws.
- **Figure files.** With no `widths_mm` in the profile and no `print_width_mm` beside the
  figure, resolution, height and shrinking are not checked;
  72 dpi written as a placeholder gives an absurd shrink, and EXIF's resolution is not
  read. Any "Figure N" paragraph after the placeholder counts as its legend, a figure
  placed twice is reported twice, the whole file is read for its header, a size, height or
  shrink rounded for print can show the limit itself, and a header of zero pixels gives no
  finding.
- **Figures drawn as SVG or PDF.** In SVG, `rem` of an inherited size, `visibility` and
  `opacity` that hide text, a `tspan`'s tail, and a width of 100% with no `viewBox` (read
  as 16 units) are not read as a browser would; `@media` and `@supports` apply always, a
  child combinator matches as a descendant, and `font-size` and the `font` shorthand are
  not ordered. A run of `{` before one `}` is read again from each brace. In PDF, a
  `MediaBox` written as a number or a name, which page is first, an inline image's `EI`
  inside its data, and a form decoded once per use are not handled.
- **Study designs and their plan sections.** A section is found by words of its heading:
  "Trial monitoring" answers interim analyses, a bare "Measures" answers the measure, and
  "Risk interval", "Events of interest", "Definition of cases", "Case-finding",
  "Comparison", "Reference database", "Control group", "Background population", "Signal
  definition", "Cases/controls" (which finds controls and not cases) and "Case/control
  selection" are not found. A guideline counts by its name's start, so PRISMA-P or an
  abstracts checklist counts for PRISMA, and a trial protocol that declares SPIRIT 2025 is
  told to declare CONSORT.
- **Planned results.** A nested subsection also titled "Planned results" is read twice, a
  dotted code span (`data.table`, `table1.csv`) is taken for a key, and a key copied with
  its braces is skipped. At the analysis stage every planned key not yet emitted warns, by
  design. A feasibility fragment that fails its schema is dropped, and the warning says
  nothing was emitted.
- **Checklists transcribed from a paper.** A `jats-table` recipe with no `rows_sha256`
  transcribes unchecked; `table:` is read for a Word recipe too; an `.xml` fetch accepts a
  page with `<article` in its first 4096 bytes; a recipe's name is matched in its case on
  Windows. In a JATS table, a column span over an earlier row span, a nested table, rows of
  `tr` outside `tbody`, a footnote's superscript in a cell, a byte-order mark or a
  single-quoted PUBLIC literal before an external DOCTYPE, `<!DOCTYPE` inside CDATA or a
  comment, and a NUL in the first kilobyte (called "not UTF-8") are not read as they are.
  `transcribe` does not catch a source that cannot be read for its permissions or is a
  folder.
- **A journal's quoted rules.** "twenty-four" states 4, "3 500" states 3, "123 456" states
  456, and a quote in Chinese or Japanese, or before a footnote digit glued to it, is
  refused. An HTML entity, a soft hyphen or a word broken across lines in the stored page
  is not folded. A page that is not UTF-8, or a folder, is called not stored. An empty
  `abstract_headings` needs its quote where an empty `required_sections` does not, and a
  negative limit is not held to its quote. A profile is not checked against its schema
  before its target is read, and `journal --reread` says an unreadable profile names no
  journal and diffs a missing page as empty. `references: "x"` raises in `style`, which the
  schema already fails. A style named `x.yaml` would share a path with another's record.
- **Journals on the shortlist.** A nine-character ISSN that is no ISSN ("1234 567X") is
  kept, fails its schema and stops the lookup.
- **Citations inserted in Word.** A narrative `@a` and a suppressed `[-@a]` share one
  identity, and both are left out of the record when both appear; a field whose end lies in
  a deletion and whose start does not is never closed; nested `EN.CITE` fields lose the
  outer XML and a field split across paragraphs is not seen. Without the build's record,
  the build's own Zotero fields are reported as a co-author's. Corporate, TeX-accented and
  particled names lose the key suggestion, titles in NFC and NFD do not match, and deeply
  nested CSL JSON could raise. `--csl` is passed over for a document built offline by
  default or live. More than about 500 narrative citations make the command line too long
  for Windows. A release before this one reads a record with `citations` as no record.
- **Text structure.** On Linux, `Main.MD` is said to be an `.md` file that is not read. Of
  several files, the Methods heading is chosen by name within each file, so an earlier
  file's "Overview of existing methods" wins over a later "# Methods". A Lancet "# Summary" with no `abstract_title` is taken for the title, and a
  Discussion's "Findings in context" or JAMA's "### Findings" reports. A pointer "in
  Appendix 1" or "in Supplementary Material" after its number is not read as the
  supplement's, "S" carries only across a range, and a reference-style image, a one-column
  pipe table, a table set as an image and `\begin{tabular}` are not seen as placed by hand;
  a caption directly under a heading line counts as a citation. The audit takes "VII.
  References" or "A. Bibliography" for prose, where G4, G14 and the recycling check know the
  list by it. G4 counts a figure placed by hand where it is an image with a caption alone in
  a paragraph of its own; one in a list, a block quotation or a div, or written by
  reference, `![caption][ref]`, is a figure pandoc numbers and G4 counts none.
- **Placeholders.** "47,XXX reports" (a count in the forty thousands) is read as a
  karyotype, the karyotypes 69,XXX and 92,XXXX as gaps; a bracketed translated title that
  opens with an instruction's verb, or holds a to-come word in capitals, fails in a cited
  entry; "[Your ...]" is not read in a caption, nor "fill in later" or "replace later"
  followed on its line by anything but a stop, a bracket, a colon, a semicolon or a comma: a
  pipe table's `|`, "?", "!", a quotation mark, a dash or an asterisk.
- **Scripts the gates do not read.** Front matter and image captions are not counted; a
  citation key that opens with a CJK character is counted as prose; 々, 〆, 〇, CJK Extensions
  G to I, the compatibility supplement, Hangul Jamo Extended A and B and half-width Hangul
  are not among the blocks.
- **The submission pack.** "Abstract screening" is taken for the Abstract's heading; an
  e-mail autolink is refused as a link with words of its own.
- **Blinding.** "J.-P. Example", "Van der Berg" at a sentence's start and an APA "A.
  Example, 2019" in the text are not read as written; a figure in the supplement only is
  reported against `manuscript.docx`; an SVG with an internal subset is read as empty with
  no warning; a malformed `styles.xml` is `docx-unreadable` rather than read as
  "Bibliography".
- **Revision rounds.** With `paths.manuscript` at `.`, the submitted copy is part of the
  manuscript; the copy is written after the round, so a manuscript that is not UTF-8 fails
  once the round exists; a "Results" sub-heading in the Abstract answers `section:
  Results`.
- **Hooks.** An `attested.yaml` that cannot be read gives no prompt, and an Edit whose
  `old_string` uses curly quotes may pass unasked (not confirmed live).
- **The emitters.** R lists lockfiles in their case on Windows (`Requirements.txt` is not
  seen); an empty lockfile's digest has not been compared between R and Python, nor R's
  `validUTF8` with Python's decoder on overlong, surrogate and out-of-range forms. R reads
  a relative input from its working directory where a file of that name is there, and
  Python always from the project root, so an analysis run from another folder that holds
  one may read and record another file in R; and on Windows `~` is R's home (Documents) and
  the user's folder to Python. An input's path is collapsed as text inside the project
  (round 1 of #409): `data/linked/../x.csv`, where `data/linked` is a link, is recorded as
  `data/x.csv`, while on Linux and macOS the file read and digested is the one beside the
  link's target. Python expands `~name` as well as `~`, so a project folder named `~raw`
  is read elsewhere, and R records a path when it is added and digests the file at
  `write()`, so a `setwd()` between the two may digest another file of that name (round 2
  of #409). On Windows a path is recorded in the case it was written in, so one file
  spelt in two cases is two inputs, and a path in another case than the disk's names no
  file in a clone on Linux. A `.txt` input is digested as its bytes, so a copy checked out
  with CRLF line ends reads as changed.
- **Inputs kept by Git LFS or git-annex.** Results written from an analysis run on an
  unfetched pointer read as `input-changed`; a pointer's size written as "²" raises; a
  large input is hashed twice.
- **Assurance and verify.** A gate stopped by an unreadable manuscript is said to have read
  nothing rather than not to have run, and G0's and the build's findings fall in no
  dimension. Verification is stale against results fragments only, not scripts or data;
  round folders are counted without their panel, the last round is not said stale, a folder
  named with a superscript digit raises, and an error writing `build/verify.json` is a
  traceback after `verify` printed. A results fragment whose `values` is a list raises
  after the report, which its schema check fails already.
- **The plugin's own tests.** A code-shaped string in a skill's text counts as a code it
  names, a description's list of codes is read by shape, `--yes` is looked for in one
  fragment, only `pip install` counts as an install, `venv/` is not skipped and `build/` is
  at any depth, and `Invoke-Expression (...)` called on a download,
  `WebClient.DownloadString`, `sudo -E bash` and `| python3` are not among the forms of a
  download run. A grader's keys are checked against every type's together, a hook's refusal
  messages are checked for the commands they name without the `mguard` alias, an
  `input_match` is not required of every Skill grader, and the last sentence is found only
  after ". " before a capital. The frozen-plan loop test is skipped where `git ls-files`
  fails, and from an sdist inside another repository it copies nothing.
- **Skills copied for other agents.** `--remove` takes away a user's folder identical to a
  skill `install-skills` recorded; a link to a file counts as its target's content, and a
  link to a folder or an empty folder inside a skill is not in its digest; an error partway
  through `--remove` does not list what went; `--verify`
  prints the remover's version for a stamp kept; an older release calls such a stamp newer.
- **Test fixtures.** `_keeps_data`, called twice, writes `data_custodian` twice under
  `roles:`; the generator always draws a P beside the subtypes' label, the bare label held
  by a corruption case only; a header row of a bare "P", "<", "0" or "1" passes as a P
  column, while a negative SMD, a P with a footnote and "NS" are refused; a docx `gridSpan`
  has no upper bound.

Open, recorded as each change landed:

- **A figure review does not survive a change of plotting library.** The digest normalises
  render timestamps and generated element ids, but not the drawn path data, and a different
  matplotlib or font stack produces different paths for the same figure. CI found this: the
  committed review of the example read as stale on Ubuntu and macOS. Arguably correct — the
  bytes did change — but it means a review cannot be shared across machines with different
  rendering stacks, only re-stamped after re-rendering.
- **Raster figures cannot be inspected for numeric text.** Reported as a warning. No longer
  silent when a vector export sits beside them: the pairing has to be recorded by
  `render.record()`, and an unrecorded one is `figure-render-unproven`.
- **G10 verifies that a review happened, not that it was right.** A review recorded without
  looking is worse than none, because it makes an unexamined figure look examined.
- **Changing the digest algorithm invalidates every stored review.** There is no version
  field on `content_sha256` yet.
- **The supplementary files are joined into one document.** Every Markdown source under
  `manuscript/supplementary/` is built into one `supplementary.docx`, apart from the paper.
  A journal that asks for each additional file on its own gets them as one.
- **A verified quote does not mean the value was read correctly.** The chain proves the
  sentence is in the source and the number is in the sentence. Whether that number means
  what the manuscript says it means is a judgement, and belongs to the review panels.
- **Nothing checks that a stored source is the work the citekey names.** Saving the wrong
  PDF under the right name passes, provided the quote is in it.
- **A locator is checked for being there, not for being right.** The schema refuses a blank
  `locator`, and nothing reads the one that is written: "Table 2" on a quote taken from the
  abstract passes. It is for the person checking the value, who is sent to the place it names.
- **A field the literature schemas call blank is one of white space only.** Their `\S` is
  any character that is not white space (a space, a tab, a line break), and a zero-width
  space (U+200B) or a byte-order mark is one:
  `attested_by` made of either passes as a signature that shows nothing. Nobody types one by
  accident, and a name that is there but wrong passes as well.
- **A PDF is read as its reader gives it, less a short table of foldings.** Curly quotes,
  the dashes, the hyphens U+2010 and U+2011, the ellipsis and the ligatures fi, fl, ff, ffi
  and ffl are folded before a quote is looked for. Anything else one reader spells out and
  another does not is compared as it comes: a quote typed with "oe" is not found in a source
  read as "œ". A quote copied from the source, which is what the hint asks for, is.
- **What a failed quote is said to nearly be is read by words, not by meaning.** A word is a
  run of letters and digits, so "2.6" is the words 2 and 6, and a quote whose number differs
  in one digit is a quote with one word retyped. Words more than twelve apart are not read
  as the quote's, so a quote broken by a long footnote is said to be partly there. A source
  that holds the quote's words in order in two places is read at the one with the most of
  them, then the fewest interruptions, then the fewest words in them, which need not be
  where the author copied from. A soft hyphen inside a word fails the quote, as it always did, and is said to split
  it. Only the first two interruptions are named, and the rest counted.
- **An ellipsis set against a value hides it.** The ellipsis is folded to three full stops
  and a value is not read with a full stop before it, so a quote holding `…14 per 100 000`
  does not state 14 and is reported `value-not-in-quote`. With a space after the ellipsis
  it does.
- **Retrieval is not automated.** The skill drives Chrome by hand; there is no DOI-to-PDF
  pipeline, deliberately, because publisher access varies and bulk fetching is not
  something this tool should make easy.
- **A journal profile's quotes prove words are on the stored page, and no more.** The page is
  what someone saved as text: that it is the journal's page, of the date recorded, rests on
  them. A rule read from the right words in the wrong way (a limit for letters given to an
  original article) passes. A limit's number is found as digits, with or without a separator
  of thousands, or as a word up to twenty: "three hundred words" fails its limit's check
  until the quote holds the digits. A limit of none or one is not held to its quote's number
  at all, only its quote to the page: "may not include figures", "Figures: none" and "a
  single table" were each read wrong by a rule that tried, one way or the other.
- **A rule left out of a journal profile entirely is not seen.** Nothing reads the stored
  page for rules that are neither a field nor under `manual:`: which sentences of a page are
  rules is the reader's judgement, and a heuristic that guessed it would warn of every
  sentence it misread. `journal --reread` shows a rule the page added a year on only as a
  line of the difference, for the author to read. A profile without quotes is warned of,
  not failed. The checklist of `manual:` rules is signed as a whole: a sign-off says the
  corresponding author checked every rule on it, not which. It is bound to the rules and the
  page, not to the paper: a cover letter or a title page edited after it stays signed.
- **No real journal profile is distributed**, and no transcribed checklist text. Recipes for
  thirteen checklists are, so a user needs only the official document. Journals get a
  different answer, and deliberately: an annotated template
  (`manuscript-guard journal --template <slug>`) plus the `journal-profile` skill, which
  chooses the journal *with* the author and then reads that journal's own guidelines page to
  fill it. Shipping profiles for named journals was considered and rejected — author
  guidelines change without announcement, so a distributed profile would eventually be wrong
  and would be wrong silently, which is the failure mode this whole toolkit exists to
  prevent. Every field in the template says what to do when the page is silent, and the
  answer is always to delete the line.
- **One licence is all-rights-reserved: TRIPOD.** Free to read, no Creative Commons terms,
  not deposited in PMC. Everything else is settled: RECORD, STROBE, ARRIVE, PRISMA 2020 and
  RECORD-PE are CC BY (the last two through their statement papers, not their websites);
  CONSORT and SPIRIT explicitly permit download and copying with notices retained; READUS-PV
  is CC BY-NC. Nothing is redistributed either way. See [ATTRIBUTION.md](ATTRIBUTION.md),
  which quotes the operative sentence for each.
- **The gates read English text.** Measured 2026-10-14 on a copy of the example with its
  scripts run, `check` clean before the edit:
  - G2: Chinese puts no space between words, so in
    "结果见表1，比值比为{{results.ror.point}}（95%置信区间…）。" the tokens "结果见表1，比值比为" and
    "（95%置信区间" are read whole and match no rule, and the sentence fails with every result
    bound; in English it passes. Numbers written in Chinese numerals, "共纳入四千份报告，
    其中一百二十三份为肝损伤，比值比约为三点四", are not read as numbers, and nothing is
    found in that sentence. Full-width digits in English prose ("Of ４０００ reports") are
    read as digits and caught.
  - G4: words are counted between spaces, so six short Chinese paragraphs added 18 to
    `main_text_words`. A journal that publishes in Chinese counts characters, and the limits
    mean nothing for Chinese text.
  - G6 and G14: the phrasing, the abbreviations, the declared terms and the spelling are
    lists and rules of English.
  - `reworded`: a number in numerals is no fact, so one changed passes.

  Japanese and Korean fare the same where they are written without spaces or in numerals.
  Each manuscript file whose prose holds Han, Hiragana, Katakana or Hangul is said
  (`script-not-read`, a warning and never a failure, since an English paper may quote a
  title or a name in another script), with how many characters of each and what was not
  checked in them. Reading those languages is weeks of work, for word splitting, their
  conventions and numerals, and counting characters against a limit, and waits until
  somebody writing in one of them asks.
- **A typed pointer is held to the number of a placement, not to its key, and only where
  every placement is a binding.** "Table 2" passes wherever the main text places two tables,
  whichever two they are: the check sees the numbering, not which table a sentence means.
  `{{ref.table.<key>}}` names the table, and is the way out.
  A paper that writes any of its tables or places any of its figures by hand has no
  pointer of that kind checked, only a note; one that sends some as files of their own and
  does not declare them in `paper.yaml` (`displays`) has a pointer past the bound ones
  failed as pointing at nothing. A pointer
  in a heading, or in a caption typed above its table ("**Table 2.**"), is checked for a
