- **An interleukin is a term, and other names with digits are not.** The shipped terms hold
  the interleukins HGNC names, abbreviated with a hyphen and written out with one: "IL4",
  "interleukin 4" and a chemokine such as CXCL10 are numbers to G2 and to the audit alike.
  A project declares them in `terms:`; the audit reads no `paper.yaml`, so for it they stay
  numbers. A term counts where it opens a word, where another term ends, after a capital,
  or where its first letter as written is a capital after a lower-case letter: "sIL-2R",
  "ppFEV1", "CD3+", "Th1/Th2", "CCR2", "HLA-DRB1" and, with CO2 declared, "pCO2" are
  terms, and "April-12" and "Brazil-3" numbers, not `il-12` and `il-3`. A name written in
  lower case after a lower-case prefix, "sil-2r", is a number. A word in capitals is read
  as "CCR2" is, so "BRAZIL-3" holds `il-3` and "WEEK1" `k1`, and their numbers go
  unchecked, as they did when a term was found anywhere in an atom; a capital is all that
  tells "CCR2" from them. And a word with a capital after a lower-case letter is read as
  a name from that capital, so "preCO2", with CO2 declared, is a term, and so is a word
  that ends in a term's letters after one, "MyIL-2".
  A term holding a subscript's place counts where a word opens, at a capital after a
  lower-case letter, or directly after another term, so that "pCO~2~", "EtCO~2~" and
  "ppFEV~1~" are terms; "PharmD~2~" is a capital after a lower-case letter too, and reads
  as `d2`, a term, where main reported it. Told from "EtCO~2~" it would be by its word
  opening with a capital, and from "pO~2~", with O2 declared, by the one capital before the
  subscript, and either rule refuses a name an author writes.
- **A term counts directly after any other.** "PaO2FiO2" and "CD8CD4" are two terms each
  because the second counts where the first ends, and that holds after a term with no
  digit as well: with MeSH among the terms, "meshd2" is `mesh` and `d2`. Holding the second
  to a first that itself opened a word or at a capital changes nothing for it, "mesh"
  opening its word; and "MESHD2" is `d2` after a capital in any case, as "CCR2" is `r2`.
- **An e-mail address is one whose domain ends in letters.** "name@host" with no dot, or an
  address at a bare IP number, is read as a number.
- **`set` writes five settings, and only as values.** It cannot take a key out, so a stage,
  a journal or an English once set is changed and never unset; that is an edit by hand. It
  refuses a whole file for an anchor or an alias anywhere in it, even one in a setting it
  does not touch, and for settings written as one mapping between braces; the author writes
  those out first, and for a line separator YAML reads (U+0085, U+2028, U+2029) anywhere,
  inside quotation marks too. A list with a comment among its entries is refused rather
  than written with the comment lost. A commented example is taken only at the left margin and only where
  it is the one such line; an indented `  # stage: …` is left, and the key added at the end.
- **The guard on `set` reads shell commands only, and asks more than it must.** An agent
  that edits `paper.yaml` itself and lowers `stage:`, takes a guideline out or changes the
  journal is not asked, nor is one that passes a stage to `check --stage` for a run. It asks
  of every command it does not read exactly, so `manuscript-guard set stage analysis && git
  status`, a quoted guideline name, or a forward move inside a script is asked, and so is any
  command that merely names the tool, `set` and a key, as `echo set stage` after `stages`.
  On Windows a backslash in a plain word is read as a folder's separator, as PowerShell reads
  it; Git Bash takes it as an escape, so `cd papers\a` there names `papersa`. After `&&` that
  `cd` fails and nothing runs; after `;` the guard reads the folder a failed `cd` leaves as
  well, so what is left unread is a folder `papersa` that holds another project.
- **The guard on `set` is for an agent's ordinary commands, not a deliberate evasion.** It
  reads a command's words as a POSIX shell and as PowerShell give them, its quotation marks
  taken out, typographic ones included, so `st''age`, `s''et` and `mgu''ard` are seen and
  asked. A command that builds the tool's name, `set` or the key at run time is not
  recognised: a variable (`$v`), `eval "$(…)"` of a file's text, an alias defined elsewhere.
  `tests/test_set.py` holds the forms it catches.
- **A change of English or of study type is not asked.** Either changes what is asked of
  the paper, G14's spelling or G12's plan sections, and could clear a failing finding as a
  journal change can; they are left free because each is a statement about the paper an
  agent is usually told outright, and asking at every one would teach the author to wave
  the question through.

- **Left by round 2 of #452 (2026-10-28), to fix later.** Each is small, and none is a
  regression against main.
  - The printed view folds an accent beside a letter command from the unfolded mask, so
    `\L{}\'od\'z` loses its Ł there; the words view reads "Łódź".
  - The second backslash of `\\` is read as the start of an accent: `a\\`Text'` prints
    "T̀ext".
  - Inside `tabbing`, `\=`, `\'` and `\`` are tab commands, read as accents.
  - A heading's title is not folded: `\section{Caf\'e}` prints "Cafe" in the printed view.
  - An accent at a line's end does not take the next line's letter, as TeX does (as on main).
  - A `\par` inside `\verb` or a group ends the paragraph for the pairing of quotation marks.
  - `classify._names_covering`'s docstring says "PharmD~2~" is no term with D2 declared; it
    is one, as DESIGN says.
  - Declaring R2 makes "HR~2~" and "OR~2~" terms (as on main).
  - G5 reads the rows of a Markdown simple or multiline table as one sentence, so a row that
    names an undeclared guideline can be joined to another's claim.
  - G8r takes "(Spring and Summer 2019)" for a citation, and one season name in a group of
    citations leaves the whole group as words.
  - `build` sets aside `supplementary.docx`'s staleness when the supplement's folder holds any
    file, though it builds one only from Markdown there.
  - A `docx-unreadable` from the live-field check says the journal's review is blind.
  - With `--skip-checks`, the count of failing checks `build` prints is one short of `check`'s
    when `manuscript.docx` is stale.
  - ci.yml's comment on setup-pandoc names a step that is gone.

- **The boxes a journal prints beside the abstract (2026-10-28), what G4 does not read.**
  - A box's words count towards the main text's word limit, as any section's do: a journal
    that counts its highlights apart is held to a count that includes them.
  - A box is read in one file: a heading in one file and its items in the next, or a LaTeX
    box's heading over an `\input` that holds its list, is a box of no items.
  - A citation or a footnote in an item is measured as written (`[@key]`, `[^1]`, `^[...]`,
    `\footnote{...}`), not as the style prints it, which can make `box-item-long` fire or
    pass falsely; a LaTeX command the mask prints nothing of (`\,`) joins the words beside
    it, a character short.
  - A Markdown box's sub-heading is read as a paragraph of it where it is underlined, and so
    as an item of a box with no list.
  - A box has one quote, and each of its numbers is looked for anywhere in it:
    `items_max: 3` passes against "3 to 5 highlights, 85 characters". Holding each number
    near the word for it ("highlights", "characters") was not exact: pages write "3 to 5
    bullet points", "85 characters, including spaces, per highlight" and "characters: 85",
    and a reading of the nearest word fails a right profile. A quote for each number
    (`boxes.<id>.<field>`) would be exact, and is a change of the profile's shape.
  - A LaTeX box's list is read by `itemize`, `enumerate` and `description`, and by the box's
    environment: an `\item` of another list environment (`compactitem`, `inparaenum`) nested
    in an item is counted as an item of the box.
  - `file: separate` is recorded and not acted on: the build still prints the box in the
    manuscript, and the submission pack writes no file of it.
  - The graphical abstract's rules and the sharing policy are recorded and not read; the
    `communicate` commands are to read them.

- **What `audit` reads of a LaTeX paper, its words and its references (Task 3, PR 1,
  2026-10-28).** Each limit, as built:
  - A number an author's macro prints where it is used is not read there, as in G2; nor is a
    table `\csvautotabular` or pgfplotstable draws from a file. A `longtable`'s caption is read
    as a row of it, and a head it repeats with `\endhead` is read once, where it is typed.
  - A reference list BibTeX or biber makes from a `.bib` is not counted: only a typed
    `thebibliography` is, and the report says so where the paper cites and has none.
  - A folder's `.tex` with `\documentclass` is an entry however it is used: a standalone
    figure's file is read as a paper of its own, and so is a file whose `\documentclass`
    stands in a `\verb` or a `comment` environment.
  - G6 and G14 run on a project made for each paper, so an abbreviation defined in the main
    text and used in a supplement given beside it is undefined in the supplement. Nothing of
    a `paper.yaml` is read but the English: no journal profile, no `language:` settings, no
    accepted spellings. A .docx's lines are those of the text pandoc converts it to.
  - The census holds citations to a list only where the entries carry their numbers, or in a
    .docx whose list one Word numbering counts 1, 2, 3 from its first entry, by each entry's
    place in its count. A count that a paragraph with words above the list is numbered in
    too (the same abstract numbering and level, or the same numbering where it restarts the
    level), a numbering linked to a numbering style, a level not resolved for sure, or one in
    another format or from another start, is taken for none, and such a list is counted and
    not held to the text's numbers. Only the count is compared: a lower level above the list
    that restarts it is not looked at. A citation in superscript, `^3^`, or in parentheses,
    `(3)`, is not read; a bracketed number that is no citation, an equation's `[2]`, is read
    as one. Two lists each numbered from 1 are read as one. A Markdown entry wrapped over
    lines with no blank line between entries is one entry only where each starts with its
    number. A list found by its entries' shape alone, with no heading, is not counted.
  - A paragraph in a table's cell is given no count, though Word numbers it: one numbered in
    the list's count above the list does not stop the list being numbered by place, and the
    entries after it are numbered as though it were not there (fix-only round of #463).
  - `--lookup` asks about the first DOI and the first PMID of an entry, and nothing about one
    with neither: `lookup`'s search by title is not run. A record kept with
    `--lookup-cache` is used however old it is, until the identifiers it was asked for
    change. `--strict` counts no finding of G7's, in the census or from a registry.
  - `--strict` counts what it counted before, a number in no output, a stretch not read and
    an audit that read no number, and nothing new: the sums and flows that will count come
    in the PRs after this one.
  - In a folder given, a `.tex` with `\documentclass` is audited as a paper beside the
    Markdown or Word one: a pandoc template or a LaTeX export of the paper is read as a paper
    of its own, its numbers are not found in the outputs, and the reader's refusals in it are
    counted, so `--strict` can fail where the paper alone passes. A `.tex` that cannot be read
    counts as an entry. Name the paper's own file, not its folder, to audit it alone (round 1
    of #463).
  - A table whose rows a tabular `\input`s from another file, as xtable and esttab write
    them, is read nowhere as cells: its numbers are read where they stand, as text, and no
    n (%) or mean in it is held to its denominator (round 1 of #463).
  - A citation that encloses the number before it, `2 studies [1,3]`, is read as an
    interval after its value and no citation, so the entries it cites can be reported as
    cited nowhere (round 1 of #463).

- **A table's totals are read in English, as partitions, a line at a time** (Task 3, PR 2,
  `stats/margins.py`).
  - Only Total, All and Overall, alone in their cell, make a total: "Gesamt", "Totale",
    "All patients" and "Subtotal" total nothing, and their lines are not read.
  - A total is taken to be the sum of the counts above it or before it. One that is not, a
    "Total" of patients with any of several events that overlap, or rows that are subtypes
    of the row above them, is said to be off when it is right (`sum-off`, a false alarm).
  - A row of whole-number measures, a median of 24 months printed bare, under a Total
    column is read as counts unless its label names the statistic.
  - A total header spanning several columns, the "n | %" pairs under one, totals none of
    them.
  - A characteristic's categories are a line under their column's header n only where they
    stand under a label of their own; a table that is one characteristic with no such label
    has no header line.
- **A count held back is worked out a line at a time** (Task 3, PR 2). Each line, a total
  and its counts, is read alone: a cell that only its row and its column together pin down,
  a count worked out from two tables, from a table and a sentence, or from another
  publication of the same data, is not found. A count held back is taken to be anything from
  0 to its bound, so a cell that must be at least 1 (a category no row can lack) has a wider
  range than it does, and a count that this would disclose is not said: the 0 errs to
  silence. A sum or a flow is read only where every key of it is bound; one printed as a
  typed number beside the bound ones is not seen. `deposit` reads the tables of the results
  files it carries, and the values in them through `deposit.counts`, not their sums.
- **A deposit is staged, not sent.** `deposit` uploads nothing in this version: the Zenodo
  and OSF clients, the receipts and the DOI written to `paper.yaml` are the next pull
  request's. arXiv and medRxiv have no interface to send through, so what they accept, their
  TeX Live, their moderation and their scope, is theirs; the sheets name their rules as
  written down, and the tool checked none of them. A plan deposited by the tool is a file with
  a date, not an entry in a registry of studies, and "deposited before any results were
  written" rests on there being no `design/plan.frozen.yaml`, which a project whose results
  were written before the emitter kept one also lacks.
- **What a bundle holds beyond the package is not in the crate.** VERIFICATION.md and .json,
  the dictionary's exports and the checklist tables are files of a release that
  `ro-crate-metadata.json` and the package's MANIFEST.yaml do not list; the release's
  SHA256SUMS lists every file. VERIFICATION reads `build/verify.json`, which is the
  checkout's, so a release made in another checkout says no run of `verify` is recorded.
  CITATION.cff calls a plan a dataset, having no word for a plan, and .zenodo.json a
  publication of type "other".
- **A preprint's documents are built again, and the arXiv archive holds one document.** The
  medRxiv bundle builds the `.docx` offline into `build/`, over the last build, and a LaTeX
  manuscript's PDF with TeX: a `build/manuscript.docx` built with live Zotero fields is
  replaced by one whose citations are citeproc's text, with no field in it, until the next
  `build` makes it again. The `.docx` is dated 1980-01-01 so that its bytes repeat, and
  `build/manuscript.docx` keeps that date until the next `build`; another pandoc, or a zlib
  that compresses otherwise (zlib-ng), writes other bytes, which the custodian then signs
  again. A LaTeX manuscript's PDF is signed by the
  folder it is compiled from and the tool's version, not by its bytes: the custodian's
  sign-off holds for a PDF another TeX installation compiles from the same folder, which
  may differ from the one they saw, and the tool sets no date for that compile. A
  restricted input is found in a bundle by its name, by the file it is and by its bytes, so
  one the LaTeX build reads in part or rewrites (a table cut from it, a file re-encoded) is
  not found, and an empty one is not looked for. The Data availability statement is read
  for the sheet as its own passage: a footnote or a reference link it uses that is defined
  elsewhere stops it being printed, by the bracket left, and no generated input holds the
  statement's rule in `tests/test_properties.py`; it is the abstract's rule, read through
  pandoc. The arXiv archive leaves out the supplement and keeps every other file of the folder, one
  only the supplement uses among them. Neither sheet counts pages. A dry run of a preprint
  builds its documents, and writes nothing under `build/deposit/`.
- **What a bundle's sign-off leaves out** (round 2 of #460). MANIFEST.yaml is left out of
  every bundle's signed list by its name, so an arXiv source file of that name would go
  unsigned. What MANIFEST.yaml says besides the files, the title, the DOI and the list of
  what is withheld, is never signed, as in `package`. And a restricted input that `\input`
  pulls into the LaTeX source is written into the `.tex` itself, where neither its name nor
  its bytes find it.

- **`next` is advice, and its order is a rule.** It puts what is upstream first, and a
  project whose author knows the journal's reviewers will read the figures first may want
  another order; `check` is the gate, and nothing `next` says makes a finding pass. A choice
  is due by a rule as well: from `drafting` for a journal, an English and a guideline that
  are not set, wherever for a study design, so a paper that follows no listed design is
  offered one at every call.
- **A prefix or a gate names a coarser skill than a code's own.** `registration-` goes to
  analysis-plan for every registration code, and a code no route names goes to its gate's
  skill with `check`. The command a route gives is the command that shows or does the work
  (`verify`, `bind`, `journal`), not one that puts the finding right.
- **`next` runs every gate at every call.** 5 to 10 seconds on the example, and more on a
  long paper; there is no cache, by choice (see "`next` says what to do now").
- **`next` shows no co-author checker for a LaTeX manuscript**, nor offers a page or the
  proof check, since neither command reads LaTeX yet.
- **The journals offered are only those the project knows.** `set target_journal` takes a
  journal with a stored profile or a shortlist candidate's `profile`; another one is offered
  as a profile to start, and how current the offer is depends on the shortlist and the
  profiles kept.
- **Showing the command and asking is an agent's to keep.** `who` says `ask-author` for
  `review --run`, `bind --apply`, `set stage` and another journal or English, and `author`
  for what only a named person may answer; the hooks enforce only `approve`, `sign`,
  `review --run --yes`, the submission guard and `set`'s; that an agent puts a choice to the
  author rather than picking is the skill's guidance, not a check.
- **A code made at run time is routed only by its prefix.** The walk of the source reads
  strings, names, conditionals and helpers' tuples; a code built from data (a table of
  codes read elsewhere, a whole f-string) is seen only where a gate reports it on the
  fixtures the test runs, and otherwise goes to its gate's skill with `check`.
- **Tier 10 lists only the commands there are.** Depositing the package and communicating
  the paper join it as their commands are added, and the co-author checker's fields in
  `next --json` are those `checker status` reports now.
- **`next` quotes a command for `cmd.exe`, not PowerShell, and leaves `%` as it is.** A word
  holding a space or one of `& | < > ^ ( )` is put in double quotes, but `cmd.exe` still
  expands `%NAME%` inside them, so a path holding two `%` can be shown as another path. A
  word holding `"` beside one of those is refused, and only `argv` is said. In PowerShell a
  bare word holding `,` is an array and one starting with `@` splats, and the command shown
  is not written for it. `argv` is what an agent runs, and is right on both.
- **A G15 warning only a sign-off closes is offered as `models`.** `model-few-events` is
  closed by the statistician's `manuscript-guard sign`, and `next` sends it to methods-writer
  with `models`, the agent's; `sign` is never offered, since the person who signs is the
  statistician the hint names and not an option `next` can fill.
- **One person-only warning makes its skill's group the author's.** Warnings go one action
  to a skill, so a person-only code among them (an attestation that is thin, say) makes
  every warning of that skill `who: author`, those an agent may put right among them.

- **That the guide asks before it runs is the skill's guidance, not a check.** The skill
  and `AGENTS.md` tell an agent to show a command, to put a choice to the author and to wait
  for a yes; nothing holds an agent to it but the hooks, which ask for `approve`, `sign`,
  `checker import`, `review --run --yes` and a `set` that moves the stage back, takes a
  guideline away or replaces the journal, and hold a submission to its check. `bind --apply`,
  a forward `set stage` and every other command `next` marks `ask-author` go through on the
  agent's word. An agent tool that reads neither the skill nor `AGENTS.md` is told none of it.
- **Projects made before the guide have no paragraph on conversation.** `init` writes
  `AGENTS.md` once and never over an existing one, and `rules_to_add` prints the rules only
  where the file does not name manuscript-guard. An older project's `AGENTS.md` keeps the
  rules it had, and an agent tool that reads `CLAUDE.md` where there is one reads
  `AGENTS.md` only where that file imports it.
- **The status line's "Next:" is the first action's title and no more.** Its options, its
  command and who runs it are in `next`; a status line that has to say a choice is due says
  only its title, "Name the study design", and an agent that acts on the line alone has not
  seen the options.
- **At `submission` the line says "Next: Have the review panel read the paper" every
  time.** From `internal-review` on, with nothing failing, the review panel is the first of
  the optional steps (tier 10) whether or not a round has been read, so once a paper is clean
  at submission the status line names it at every session start, after the last round as
  before the first. It is `next`'s rule, which offers the optional steps without asking what
  is already done, and not the status line's.

Closed since, and why each mattered (an open gap goes above this line):

- **A masked cell recovered by subtraction was not looked for (Task 3, PR 2, 2026-10-28).**
  `deposit`'s preflight called `gates.custodian.recoverable_cells`, which found nothing, so a
  bundle whose results let a reader subtract their way to a small count was deposited. It
  reads each table carried now, and G2 the tables, sums and flows the manuscript binds; see
  "A table's totals, and a count held back that they give away".

- **`audit` refused a LaTeX paper (Task 3, PR 1, 2026-10-28).** A `.tex` named was refused,
  and a folder of them had nothing to audit, so a LaTeX paper outside a project had its
  numbers, its tables and its references checked by nothing. It is read through its include
  tree now; see "Reading anything, and what needs no outputs".

- **`document-stale` blocked the build that would clear it.** At `internal-review` the
  gate fails, `build` refused while anything failed, and `--skip-checks` wrote
  `manuscript.UNCHECKED.docx` beside the stale document, which then went stale in its turn:
  a second finding no build cleared. The Word build now leaves `document-stale`, and only
  it, out of what it refuses for and of what names a document UNCHECKED, since the document
  it writes is the one that clears it; a checked build that writes `manuscript.docx` takes
  away the UNCHECKED copy of an older source; and a build given its name by `--output` no
  longer says the document is named UNCHECKED (`test_cli.py`,
  `test_a_stale_document_does_not_block_the_build_that_clears_it`). A LaTeX build writes
  PDFs, which clear no stale `.docx`, and still counts it. It left every `document-stale`
  out at first, so a stale `build/x.docx`, which no build rewrites, and `manuscript.docx`
  under a build that `--output` sends elsewhere were passed without a word: only the
  documents this build writes over in `build/` are left out now, the paper under its
  checked or UNCHECKED name where no `--output` is given, the supplement where there is
  one, the annotated copy for an annotated build (round 1 of #452;
  `test_the_build_sets_aside_only_the_staleness_of_the_document_it_rewrites`).
- **The submission pack lost an abstract and passed a document it could not read.**
  `**Keywords**` and `**Keywords.**`, bold with no colon as the abstract's own labels are
  written, went into `abstract.txt`; they end the abstract now, as a label with a colon did,
  and a sentence that opens with the word, emphasised, plain or all in bold, does not. An
  abstract heading inside a Div was looked for among the text's own blocks only, and the
  abstract was left out without a word: it is found inside a Div, to the Div's end, and
  where the gates read an Abstract section and pandoc reads no heading naming it, the pack
  says why `abstract.txt` is not written. And `build` exited 0 where the blind check could
  not read its own document (`docx-unreadable`): it exits 1 and says not to send it, as it
  does for a name it read (properties over `keyword_paragraphs` and `abstract_trees`).
- **A heading straight under a captioned `{{table.x}}` was printed inside the caption.** The
  build wrote the caption as a paragraph after the table, a heading on the next line does
  not interrupt a paragraph, and the document lost the heading G2 read. `render_table`
  writes a blank line after the caption, as the example leaves one.
- **The build styled only captions opening "Figure 1."** `figure_caption.lua` set "Fig. 1."
  and "eFigure 1.", which G2 holds as captions, in the body font. It takes the three forms
  now, a stop or a colon after the number as before (a property over `figure_captions`, with
  pandoc).
- **A minus sign in a PDF figure was not the hyphen in its sidecar.** A figure saved with its
  text kept as text (matplotlib's `pdf.fonttype: 42`, or an SVG) holds the U+2212 matplotlib
  draws before a negative tick, and a sidecar entry `"-1.0"` did not allow it:
  `figure-number-unbound`. G3 writes U+2212 as a hyphen in the figure's numbers, the
  results' displays and the sidecar's entries alike before comparing them, so either sign
  allows either; a number allowed only with the opposite sign is still another number (a
  property over `signed_ticks`).
- **A PDF figure whose forms named each other in a ring raised RecursionError.** The fonts
  of forms whose resources name each other, of two or more, or the page's own through
  another form, were followed until Python's recursion limit. `_fonts` reads each
  resources dictionary once, and lists the fonts found in the ring.
- **The skills, the README and a pack's manifest told an agent to run `check --submission`.**
  The submission guard holds that to the check it names and refused it in a failing project,
  so an agent was refused once before being told the other spelling. The project-setup,
  review-panel, submission-pack and word-roundtrip skills, the README, `docs/` and the
  `MANIFEST.yaml` of a pack assembled with `--skip-checks` write `check --stage submission`
  now, and `test_plugin.py` holds that no skill or page tells an agent to run the other.
  What the guard matches is unchanged, as decided (Basile, 2026-10-02); what still writes
  the old spelling is above.
- **An abstract `init --from` did not find in Word's metadata was set aside.** pandoc reads
  the Abstract style as metadata only straight after the Title, Author and Date paragraphs,
  and an abstract elsewhere on the title page went into the comment with it, its numbers
  read by no gate. `init --from` reads the document a second time with its styles
  (`docx+styles`) and, where that reading is the first block for block, puts the title
  page's paragraphs in the Abstract style in the section `# Abstract`, after any pandoc
  read as metadata. What it cannot match exactly it leaves as before (above).
- **The stop counted what an editor or the system leaves as a change.** Only hidden files
  and `__pycache__` were passed over, so Word's `~$main.docx`, there whenever the document
  is open, Emacs's `#main.md#` and `main.md~`, and Windows' `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`
  counted, and the line followed a turn that changed nothing the gates read. Those names
  are passed over now, and compiled Python outside its cache with them, and a test holds
  that every name the reproducibility package leaves out as no one's work is passed over
  too. The list is the hook's own and not imported from `deposit/plan.py`, which brings in
  the gates, half a second or more at the end of every turn. A name with a `#` or a `~`
  inside it, `#1 notes.md` or `a~b.json`, is the author's and still counts.
- **A JSON file with the mark of UTF-8 in front was refused in the parser's words.** A
  results fragment saved as Notepad's "UTF-8 with BOM", or written by Windows PowerShell 5's
  `Out-File -Encoding utf8`, stopped `check` with "cannot parse: Unexpected UTF-8 BOM
  (decode using utf-8-sig)", where YAML with the same mark was always read. The mark is
  passed over in JSON too now, by `read_structured`, which every structured file of the
  project is read through. The bytes are not changed, so a digest of the file is as it was.
- **A headingless reference list knew two styles of entry.** Where no heading says where the
  list is, the audit knows an entry by its shape, and only a journal article in the
  numbered styles with a full stop before its year, or in the author-year styles with one
  after it, had a shape. A book, a chapter, a web page, an article online first, the BMJ's
  entry ("BMJ 2021;372:n71", no full stop before the year) and a Harvard entry with no full
  stop after "(2019)" were read as prose, and their years, volumes and pages were reported
  among the findings. Each is now known by an ending a caption or a sentence does not
  have: the BMJ's by a capitalised word that is no month's before the year, with the volume
  and pages and nothing after them but a note, as before; a book by "Place: Publisher;
  2019." and perhaps its pages; an article online first by its year, or "Published online"
  and a date, after the journal's full stop and then a DOI, a PMID or an Epub note; a web
  page, whose author may be an organisation, by "[Internet]" or "[cited ...]", by
  "Accessed March 5, 2021." and the address at the end, or by "Available at:" and the
  address at the end, perhaps with the date it was read; and Harvard's year by a title in
  capitals or quoted after it, where "(2019) found" is a sentence. The lookalikes the tests
  hold to being none include "Dec 2019;2:14." and "Accessed on 412 sites in 2019".
- **The audit took an interval after a comma-written value for a citation.** A bracket of
  whole numbers after a value is an interval where it encloses the value, and the value was
  read as digits with a point, so `12,5 [10-15]`, `1,204 [1,100-1,300]` and `45 % [40-50]`
  were filed as citations and their bounds never compared. A decimal comma and a spaced
  percent sign, a no-break space included, are read now, and a value grouped in thousands
  is read as one, with bounds that may be grouped too: `1,204 [1-3]` stays a citation,
  where a decimal comma's reading would take 1.204 to lie inside it.
- **The audit masked HTML comments in Word and figure text.** A `.docx` and a figure print
  `<!--` as typed, but their text went through the mask Markdown does, so a paragraph that
  mentioned both markers hid everything between them from the comparison and from the
  tests of a statistic against its P. Their text is masked with every `<!--` made to open
  nothing, so the other regions, an address for one, are masked as before.
- **A .docx with no heading styles gave its reference list no end.** The cut ran from the
  paragraph "References" to the end of the body, and a figure legend, a statement or a
  table after the list was never audited. A list under a paragraph that is no heading now
  ends where `check` ends one under no heading in Markdown (`text/reference_lists.py`):
  at a caption of a figure, a table, a box or an appendix, at a back-matter title standing
  alone, "Funding" or "Figure legends", and at a table. A list under a styled heading runs
  on to the next heading, as one under `# References` does. What is left is above.
- **A subscripted index after capitals read as a term.** A term holding a subscript's place
  counted wherever any term does, after a capital among them, so "HR~2~" and "OR~2~" were
  `r2`, and G2 and the audit passed their numbers, where main reported them. Such a term
  counts now where a word opens, at a capital after a lower-case letter, or directly after
  another term, and not after a capital that ends no term: "HR~2~" and "OR~2~" are unbound
  numbers, and "CO~2~", "pCO~2~", "HbA~1c~", "ppFEV~1~" and "PaO~2~FiO~2~" names
  (`test_a_subscripted_index_after_a_capital_is_a_number`). "PharmD~2~" is still a term,
  above. Held there alone, a term the project declares lost the names that put capitals
  before it: with CO2 declared, "ETCO~2~", "PCO~2~" and "VCO~2~", which main read as CO2,
  each gave an unbound 2. A declared term holding a subscript's place counts after
  capitals as well, where nothing but capitals stands between it and its word's start; a
  built-in one does not, so "HR~2~" is a number and, with CO2 declared, "ETCO~2~" a name
  (`test_a_declared_term_with_a_subscript_after_capitals_is_a_name`). A project that
  declares R2 has "HR~2~" read as R2, as it would have had "HR2" typed.

- **"Methods: data sources" and "Methods of the study" were no Methods to G2 and G15.**
  `classify.METHODS_SECTIONS` took "Methods" alone or joined to another part's name by
  "and", so under such a title G2 reported a threshold the analysis chose as an unbound
  number, and G15 read no model's name. "Methods" followed by a colon, a stop or a dash and
  what the section holds, or by "of" and words, is the Methods now; a title that also names
  what was found, "Methods: main results", is not, as "Methods and results" is not
  (`test_the_methods_named_with_what_they_hold_are_the_methods_to_g2`).

- **A divisor after a space was not read after a binding.** Written, "mg kg-1" was read as
  its first symbol and said to differ from an emitted "mg/kg"; emitted, it was compared
  with nothing. A divisor after a space with its power below nought, typed ("kg-1",
  "kg^-1^", with a minus sign) or in superscript characters ("kg⁻¹"), is read now, among
  the symbols and the one-letter ones a power below nought tells from a word ("mg L-1",
  "µg m-3"), and compared as the same divisor after a slash, both ways
  (`test_what_the_unit_reading_gets_wrong_is_pinned`).

- **The plan's sections.** A heading "### Standard deviation of the dose" was read by G12
  as a Deviations section, since "deviation" anywhere in a title named them, so a plan with
  no word on what changed after it was agreed was said to have one. "deviation" after
  "standard" names no Deviations now; "Protocol deviations" and "Deviations from the plan"
  still do (`test_a_standard_deviation_is_no_deviation_from_the_plan`).

- **A test set with a middle dot for its point was not read.** "t(23) = 2·45, p = 0·40", as
  the Lancet sets numbers, was refused as a decimal comma is, so such a paper had none of
  its tests judged by the reading of a P against its statistic (G8, the
  audit and the literature check). A middle dot between digits is a point now, in the
  statistic, its degrees of freedom and its P, and a middle dot before a power of ten is
  still a multiplication sign, "6·8·10^-4^". Degrees of freedom with a thousands' comma,
  "F(1, 1,234)" or "df = 1,234", were read as two numbers and the test dropped; a comma
  that can be either is read the way that gives the test as many degrees of freedom as it
  has, "F(1,234)" as 1 and 234 and "t(1,234)" as 1,234, and where both ways do, nothing is
  read (`test_a_p_that_does_not_follow_from_its_statistic_is_found`). The decimal comma is
  still open, above. The P of an interval's sentence is read by the same pattern, so a P
  written "0·03" after an interval is read now, though the interval's own numbers with a
  middle dot are not (`stats/intervals.py`).

- **An escaped backtick opened a code span for G2's escapes.** `import` writes a backslash
  before every backtick typed in Word, and the pattern that paired backtick runs took the
  escaped ones for delimiters, so in `` (\` ROR \> 2 \`) `` the `\>` was read as a
  backslash code prints, and the threshold pandoc prints was an unbound number.
  `masking._code_spans` reads the runs once now: a backtick after an odd run of backslashes,
  outside code, is printed and opens nothing, the rest of its run opening as pandoc's does;
  inside code a backslash prints, so a run after one still closes the span, as pandoc
  reads `` `a\` `` (`test_an_escaped_threshold_between_escaped_backticks_is_still_a_convention`).
- **A part the paper placed by `\includestandalone` or `\subfile` was read loose.** A
  `standalone` picture was read under no heading and warned of as a file nothing inputs,
  and `\subfile` was refused, failing BUILD, though LaTeX prints both where they stand, as
  the maintainer asked to have them read (2026-10-27). Each command is now an input of the
  file it names (`commands.PLACED`), past `\includestandalone`'s options. A file in the
  `standalone` or the `subfiles` class is read past its preamble, opening the heading and
  the environments the command stands in at its `\begin{document}`, so a picture placed in
  a `figure` is the figure's; what its preamble loads, inputs, declares or comments is not
  the paper's, and its preamble and what follows its `\end{document}` are TeX's to pass
  over, so the submission folder writes its body alone in the command's place. What is
  still open, a part placed nowhere and the options the folder drops, is above.
- **A preamble's `\input macros` was not followed.** TeX's form without braces named no
  file to the reader, so an author's `macros.tex` was read as a file nothing inputs, warned
  of, its definitions unknown where they were used. In the preamble the name up to a space,
  a brace, a command or a comment is now the path, as a class's is read
  (`mask._BARE_PATH`), and a name the folder lacks is the distribution's as before
  (2026-10-27).
- **G2 read a typed `thebibliography` as prose.** Its years, volumes and pages were
  `unclassified-number`, where a Markdown project's reference list, which the build makes,
  is never read. G2's LaTeX view, which `explain` and `bind` read too, now blanks each
  reference list the reader records, a binding typed in one excepted; G6, G8r, G14 and the
  printed view already passed over it, and no gate needs its numbers read as the text's
  (2026-10-27).
- **"Table 2 in Supplement 1" was the main text's Table 2.** JAMA's form names its
  supplement by number, and G2 read only "in the Supplement" after a pointer as the
  supplement's, so such a pointer before the main text's Table 1 was cited out of order,
  and a journal profile that writes the form was `pointer-form-unread`. "in" or "of"
  "Supplement" and a number after a pointer now put it in the supplement, in Markdown and
  in LaTeX (2026-10-27).
- **A LaTeX quotation left open was not ended at `\par`.** A ``` `` ``` that nothing closed
  before a `\par` was closed by a straight `"` after it, which made the two paragraphs one
  quotation for G7. A `\par` TeX reads now ends the quotation as a blank line does; one in a
  comment or in what TeX passes over, and the letters after `\\`, do not (2026-10-27).
- **G8r read a claim within one line.** A claim whose verb and guideline a hard-wrapped
  source put on two lines, "prepared following the / PRISMA statement", was not read, and a
  guideline the paper said it followed went unreconciled with paper.yaml. A sentence now
  runs over single line breaks, in Markdown as in LaTeX, and stops at a blank line, before
  a Markdown heading or a table's row, and at a typed table's line ends, so that a table of
  checklist items is not one claim (2026-10-27). It ran from one item of a list into the
  next, so "- Outcomes were reported by sex" over "- STROBE flow diagram in Figure 1" said
  the paper followed STROBE: a line that opens with a list's marker (`-`, `*`, `+`, `1.`,
  `1)`) ends the sentence before it, and so does an `\item` (round 1 of #452;
  `test_g8r_reads_each_item_of_a_list_as_a_sentence_of_its_own`).
- **An accent command lost its mark in the printed view, and its word in G14's.**
  `Chr\'etien` printed "Chretien", so a quote copied from the PDF was not found by G13, G8
  or G7; and a word an accent command, a letter typed as a command or `\-` split was not
  read by G14 or G15 at all, so `co\-lor` was no American spelling and `logis\-tic
  regression` no model typed. The printed view now writes each accent command whose letter
  it reads as the accented letter, composed as Unicode composes it, and a letter typed as a
  command beside a letter it reads as that letter; the words view writes such a word whole,
  as LaTeX prints it, from where it starts, `\-` dropped (`words.folded`). The printed view
  already printed LaTeX's dashes and `\ldots` as the characters (2026-10-27). Where Unicode
  composes no letter of the two, `Erd\H{e}s`, `\'{x}`, `\t{o}` or `\v{J}`, the letter and
  its combining mark were both written in the command's first place, the view was a
  character longer from there on, and every stretch of the file after it was read one
  place off: a quote of the words after such an accent was not found. The mark now goes in
  the place after the letter (round 1 of #452). G14's message for a word it does not read
  says it holds an accent over no letter, the one case left, and no longer names `\-`.


- **G4 read the main-text files in path order, and the build prints them in another.** The
  build puts `main.md` first and sorts the rest by file name; G4 joined them as their paths
  sort, so an `abstract.md` beside a `main.md` written in `##` headings made the whole paper
  abstract as far as G4 could tell, over the abstract's limit, and an unclosed comment or
  fence at the end of the file it read first hid the next file's statements. `main_text`
  now takes the files in the build's order (`gates.numbers.printed_order`), as the paragraph
  record does (`test_g4_reads_the_main_text_files_in_the_order_the_build_prints_them`).

- **Two keys for one work went unfound where the file wrote the DOI or the title in TeX.**
  A DOI was compared as `references.bib` writes it, so `10.1000/abc\_def` and
  `10.1000/abc_def`, or a resolver's `%28` and `(`, were two works to G7; `sync-sources
  --from` looked for the PDF under `10.1000_abc__def`, and the registry lookup asked for the
  DOI with its backslash. A title's TeX accents were read as letters, `Caf\'e` as two words.
  `identifiers.normal_doi` now reads TeX's escape of `_`, `%`, `&`, `#` and `$` as the
  character and a printable ASCII character's percent-encoding as the character, for every
  reader of a DOI, and `duplicates.title_of` takes TeX out of a title as the registry lookup
  does (`test_a_doi_is_compared_as_it_is_registered_however_the_file_writes_it`,
  `test_a_title_in_tex_is_the_title_in_unicode`). A preprint and its article are still not
  found, above. A percent-encoded space, `%20`, was read as a space, and the DOI then
  called malformed: an escape is read as its character only where that character prints
  and is no space, so `%20` and `%7F` stay as written (round 1 of #452).
- **A placed part's preamble defined commands for the whole paper.** The commands a part
  that `\subfile` or `\includestandalone` places defines in its preamble, which TeX passes
  over, were told to every file of the tree: one defined there with delimited parameters
  had main's own command of that name refused, and a `\providecommand{\keywords}` made
  main's `\keywords` the author's. Only what the part's body defines is told now, and its
  preamble's input encoding is no longer the paper's (round 1 of #452;
  `test_a_placed_part_s_preamble_defines_nothing_for_the_paper`).
- **r-interop's R stood still while its cache was warm, and pytest might run under conda's
  Python.** The conda environment was cached on its package list alone; its key now holds
  the ISO week, so R follows conda-forge's releases as setup-r followed CRAN's. The tests
  run in a login shell, where the environment comes first on PATH: they are run by
  setup-python's interpreter, named, and the step prints which Python is first (round 1 of
  #452; `test_r_interop_s_environment_moves_with_the_week_and_pytest_runs_on_setup_python_s`).

- **G6's em-dash rate counted the dashes in a simple or a multiline table.** The threshold
  was measured on papers read with their tables left out, and a table pandoc writes from
  Word marks "not applicable" with a dash, so a paper with such a table warned for its
  cells. The `em-dash` rule now leaves tables out as the bold rate does (`in_tables: false`).

- **A number before a heading's name hid the reference list from G4 and G14.** "VII.
  References", "7. References" and "**References**" were read as typed, so G4 counted the
  list's words as main text and G14 read its authors' initials as abbreviations, where the
  recycling check, which reads the title as printed, set the list apart. `Section.
  is_references` reads the title as printed now (`section_names.plain`), and
  `NOT_METHODS_SECTIONS` takes a Roman number before a part's name as `METHODS_SECTIONS`
  does, so "III. Results" is set aside as no Methods. A later file's "# Methods" still
  loses to an earlier file's "Overview of existing methods", above.

- **An earlier paper's citation by author and year cut a passage the manuscript repeats.**
  "(Smith et al., 2019)" was three words the manuscript did not have beside its citation key,
  so the words before it, where fewer than a shingle, were not reported. Such a citation in
  parentheses is blanked before the earlier paper's words are compared, its line breaks
  kept (`recycling.without_author_year`): names with a capital, "et al." or "and" between
  them, a year with a letter after it, several joined by semicolons, "e.g." before and a
  page after; not a date, "(January 2019)", nor words in lower case before a year.

- **A display item counted only where a binding placed it.** A LaTeX figure placed with
  `\includegraphics` and captioned, and a Markdown figure placed by hand, `![caption](file)`
  alone in its paragraph, are numbered figures in the document the journal counts, and G4
  counted none of them, so a paper over a limit on display items passed. G4 now counts each
  display a LaTeX float's caption numbers, as G2's pointers count them, and a binding where
  no caption numbers its float, once a float however many pictures it places
  (`gates.journal.latex_displays`); and a Markdown image with a caption alone in a paragraph
  as a figure (`text.sections`). What is still counted by its bindings only, and the title
  page's count, are above.


- **BOUND.md read no LaTeX manuscript.** It listed nothing a LaTeX paper binds and warned
  (`package-bound-not-read`) on every LaTeX project. Its rows are read now by `bound_rows`
  (`deposit/bound.py`), from a Markdown file as `placeholders.parse` reads it and from a LaTeX
  one as the gates' reader does, each binding with the nearest heading over it and whether
  the supplement prints it; the warning is kept where a row stands past a part the reader
  refuses, and that row says no heading is known
  (`tests/test_ro_crate.py`).

- **A paper that declared no English heard nothing of its journal's.** Since `english_variant`
  became optional, G4 compared a journal's English with the paper's only where the paper
  declared one, so a paper spelt in British English and sent to a journal that asks for
  American was told nothing by G4, and G14 held it to its British majority. G4 now gives a
  note, `english-variant-undeclared`, where the journal's profile names `en-GB` or `en-US`
  and `paper.yaml` declares none: it names the English the journal asks for and says that
  declaring it holds the paper to it. It is a note and fails no stage, as the author decided
  (Basile, 2026-10-23): an English nobody declared is no rule broken, and the author is the
  one to say which English the paper is in. A paper that declares the other English is
  `english-variant-mismatch` as before. That nothing compares the journal's English with the
  one the paper's words are in is still open, above.

- **A LaTeX `\crefrange` cited nothing, and a range of `\ref`s cited its ends only.** G2
  said a figure that `\ref{a}--\ref{b}` or `\crefrange{a}{b}` took in, cited by itself only
  later, was cited out of order, and one cited only by a `\crefrange` not cited at all; the
  reader did not know cleveref's ranges and printed their labels as words. A range cites
  every display from its first end to its last now, as a typed one does in Markdown, and the
  floats of a `subfigures` or a `subtables` are one display, in the group's file or in files
  it inputs (corpus round, 2026-10-23, and fix round 1).

- **A dataset's name was not held to the record of data sources.** The name was meant to be
  the id of its source in `design/data_sources.yaml`, and nothing said where it was not: an
  analysis could read another source than the one the record chose, or name the chosen one
  otherwise, with every gate green. G12 now warns of a dataset the results declare whose
  name is none of the ids under `decision.chosen` (`dataset-not-chosen`), and names it and
  the ids chosen. The comparison of coverage is still open, above.
- **One file had as many inputs as it had spellings, and R and Python recorded it apart.**
  Python's `add_input` compared the text of the path as given, so a file declared by
  `dataset()`, which names it from the project, and by `add_input` spelt in full was two
  entries, and G1 reported a change to it twice. R's compared the text too, recorded the
  path through `normalizePath`, which follows links (a git-annex input is one), and wrote
  the full path of a file outside the project, where Python wrote "../" or stopped at
  `write()`; and a path R was given as a factor lost its `restricted` mark. Both now record
  an input once, by its path from the project with "." and ".." collapsed as text and no
  link followed, and mark it by that path (the review of 76880fc3, #392;
  `test_r_and_python_record_a_file_however_spelt_as_one_input_alike`). Read only as text,
  a path from the home folder, `~/proj/data/x.csv`, or one written through a folder that
  links to the project, as a home folder on a cluster can, was recorded as written, since
  the root is resolved (round 1 of #409). So `~` is expanded, and where the path as written
  leaves the project, the folder it is in is resolved and its name kept; an input is
  digested where the analysis read it.
- **A reply in Word with no author was listed again as a co-author's comment** (round 1 of
  #367), since the import's comment reader named such a comment "an unnamed reviewer" and
  the reader of replies did not. Said twice, it would now have been filed as a comment to
  answer. The import reads threads now (`filed_comments.threads_of`), and leaves out a
  panel's comment, and the replies in its thread, by its author and the digest of its words
  as Word holds them, which is how `suggestions.decisions` knows it.

- **A suggested edit beside emphasis, code or a link was not offered.** `import` merged an
  accepted suggestion as any rewording, rebuilding its stretch from Word's text, so an edit
  in a stretch that also held markup was dropped by `review --suggestions` rather than
  flattened at import. In a paragraph with an italic *P*, or one with no value and *E. coli*
  anywhere, that was every edit. An accepted suggestion is now written into the source where
  its words were, and only the rest of the paragraph is merged (Basile, 2026-10-20; "An
  accepted suggestion is written, then the rest is merged"). An edit inside emphasis is
  offered too, and the new words keep it.
- **The header's title was read by line, and the warning of two titles was wrong on any
  header but the plainest.** Nobody saw the warning until #165. Shown, it took what stands
  after the first `title:` in the block, at any depth and on that line alone, less every
  quotation mark and apostrophe at either end. So it warned of two titles that agreed where
  the header's had a comment after it, an apostrophe doubled between single quotation marks
  (`'Crohn''s disease'`), a quotation mark or a backslash escaped between double ones, a
  mark of its own at either end, a second line or a folded block, or an author's
  `title: Dr` above it; and where `paper.yaml`'s own was a folded block, whose closing line
  break YAML keeps. An author who made the two agree by copying `paper.yaml`'s line, as
  `init` types it for a title with TeX (`"IFN-$\\gamma$ release assays"`), kept the
  warning. And it said nothing of two that differed where the header's title began under
  its key, was written `title :` or `"title":`, or was written twice. The header's title
  is now read as its abstract is: by the key pandoc knows, its own or merged in, and the
  last of one written twice. Both are taken from the one composing that finds the header.
  The abstract had a second composing of its own, and the title was at first read from
  that: a header nested just as deep as the first composing could take, about 480 levels,
  then raised `RecursionError` out of the second, one call further down the stack, and
  `import` ended in a traceback where it had answered (the review of #168). The two
  titles are compared with their spaces, tabs and line breaks folded, and the warning
  names the line of the header's title. Pandoc is asked for the title it keeps from each header of the
  table that holds this (`AS_YAML_READS_IT` in `tests/test_corruption.py`), and agrees on
  every row but the one Known gaps names. `init` types a header for more titles as a
  consequence (Basile, 2026-10-04): one that begins or ends with a quotation mark or an
  apostrophe, `the patients'`, is held between the other kind. A title that neither kind
  gives back is still left without a header: one holding both kinds, or a backslash and
  an apostrophe, `TNF-$\alpha$ inhibitors in Crohn's disease`.
- **The warning of two titles was shown by no command.** Assembling compares the title in a
  manuscript file's header with `paper.yaml`'s and makes a warning where they differ
  (`two-titles`). `build` and `submit` printed what assembling found only when that held a
  failure, and `check` does not assemble, so the warning was made and nobody was told: with
  the title changed in `paper.yaml` and the header left as it was, `check` listed nothing
  and `build` printed the name of the document. That document carried `paper.yaml`'s title,
  the one meant, so nothing wrong was printed, while this file said the build warned. Found
  in the work on #162. `check` now gives the warning at every stage, from the gate that
  already refuses what assembling would refuse; the stage decides which failures are due,
  and a warning is not one. `build` and `submit` print what assembling warns of, once and
  before the document is made (Basile, 2026-10-04). `import` rebuilds a document already
  sent and says nothing of it, as before. How the header's title was read was left as it
  was then; the entry above is what became of it.
- **An abbreviated `--submission` was not seen by the submission guard.** argparse reads any
  prefix of an option that names one option only, so `manuscript-guard build --subm` was a
  submission build and `review --subm` a review at submission standard, and the guard's
  marker is the whole word: in a project that fails, `build --subm --offline` was let
  through by the guard. `build` then refused on its own account, as it does while anything
  fails; with `--skip-checks` it built, and that build is what the guard missed. Found in
  the review of #131 and true before it. No command reads an abbreviated
  option now (Basile, 2026-10-02): `build --subm` exits 2 with `unrecognized arguments:
  --subm`, and so does `--off` for `--offline`, which is the cost, paid by someone typing a
  short form by hand. No document, skill or test in the repository wrote one. The marker was
  not widened to the prefixes instead, because it would then have to be kept in step with
  the parser by hand: on `review`, `--su` already stands for `--summary` as much as for
  `--submission`. argparse's setting belongs to each parser, and on the top one alone it
  leaves every command abbreviating, so it is set by the class the commands are made from.
  `tests/test_cli.py` takes the commands that have the option from the parser and holds
  every prefix of the word to one rule, that a spelling read as a submission is one the
  guard's pattern matches; a second test fails for a command added with abbreviations on.
  Before any command, `manuscript-guard --vers` is an error too, though the message is
  argparse's for the missing command and does not name the option.
- **A backslash before raw markup was not read.** `<!--`, `\begin{x}` or `<pre>` after an
  odd number of backslashes is text to pandoc, and `import` writes what a co-author types
  in Word so: a `<!--` typed there comes back as `\<!--`. `_blocks` took it for an opener
  all the same, and where a `-->` followed further down the file, that paragraph and every
  one up to the `-->` went without an identifier. A co-author's next edit to them was
  dropped with "nothing came back"; since #69, `import` refused the rewording that typed the
  `<!--` instead, though it was safe to make. A `\<div>` in a paragraph did the same to that
  paragraph alone. An opener, a LaTeX `\begin` or `\end` and a block-level tag now count
  only where no backslash escapes them (`_backslashed`): an odd run makes them text, an
  even one escapes itself. Inside a comment or a verbatim element pandoc reads no escapes,
  so `\-->` and `\</pre>` still close them. Braces were left to #72, which merged with this:
  `_untagged` counts only unescaped braces, and `import` escapes a `}` as well as a `{`, so a
  lone `{` typed in Word, written `\{`, keeps its paragraph's identifier, and so does
  `\{\{results.x\}\}`, a binding typed as text (see "The writer and the tagger have to read
  an opening the same way").
- **Front matter closed by `...` took the body with it.** YAML, and pandoc, close a header
  with `...` as well as `---`, and the build's pattern took only `---`. It ran on to the
  next `---` line in the file, a horizontal rule, and the Introduction above the rule
  vanished from the document, from `import` and from G13, with no warning. The build now
  uses the pattern the gates use, which closes on the first `---` or `...` line, the file's
  last line included, and the line straight after the opening, where an empty header had
  run on to the next rule the same way. And it counts a block as front matter only where pandoc keeps it as
  metadata: a mapping, or nothing. A list or a sentence between two delimiters prints, so
  it is no longer stripped or masked. A header never closed before a later rule, with prose
  in it, is not YAML, and pandoc refuses the file. The build had stripped it into one that
  built without the Introduction. Now G2 and the build stop on it and name the YAML's
  error, as they do for any header pandoc cannot read. Leaving such a header in the body for
  pandoc to refuse was not enough: the identifier in front of its first paragraph made it
  prose, so the build printed the YAML as text, and a `# Methods` in it let `p < 0.001`
  pass G2 as the alpha chosen in advance. A header behind a byte-order mark or a blank first
  line is found too, as pandoc finds it, and tabs are expanded before the YAML is read, as
  pandoc expands them. Left in the body, such a header's title never met the two-titles
  warning, and G2 read its keys as prose.
- **A token straight after inline code stopped `import` for the whole manuscript.** The
  bookmark around a binding or citation is raw inline code, and against a code span's
  closing backtick its own backtick joined that run. Pandoc read the code and the bookmark
  as one raw span and wrote the code into the marked build as XML: `` `age<65`{{x}} `` made
  that build unreadable, and `import` exited 2 over a file the author had never seen. An
  empty comment now keeps the two apart, which the Word writer drops, so the paragraph
  still takes a rewording. And a marked build that cannot be read no longer stops the run.
- **G8 went quiet exactly when two keys had diverged.** It fires when two quoted keys hold
  the same value with different displays, so a duplicate was caught while it still agreed
  and missed once it did not — a paper could carry `ror.point` at 0.95 and `ror.abstract`
  at 3.84 and nothing said a word. `same_as` records the author's intent, and G8 fails when
  a declared pair disagrees. A declaration rather than an inference, because the question
  *is* about intent: `ror.point`, `ror.ci_low` and `ror.ci_high` share everything a
  heuristic could see and are supposed to differ. The limit is honest — it protects the
  pairs someone thought to declare — but a declared pair cannot drift in silence.
- **`p < 0.05` was a convention everywhere.** The same characters mean two things: where a
  paper describes its own method it is the alpha chosen in advance, and in the Results it is
  a finding. A significance claim the analysis never produced therefore passed the gate that
  carries the invariant. A rule can now be marked `methods_only`, and G2 reads the chain of
  headings enclosing each number — a chain rather than the nearest heading, because
  `### Sensitivity analyses` under `## Methods` is still Methods. Only G2 passes a section:
  a figure legend has no Methods section to sit in and its `p < 0.05` is a legend
  convention, so figure text and the audit keep every rule. One entailment: a display may
  now carry a comparator, since a reported p-value has to be emittable and "<0.001" is the
  honest rendering of a number too small to state. The value must be on the stated side of
  it — `display="<0.001"` on a value of 0.4 is refused.
- **`build --skip-checks` left a document that could pass for a checked one.** Revert the
  source afterwards and `check` passes while the stale `.docx` still holds the wrong
  number — the check and the artefact disagreeing silently, with nothing on disk recording
  which was skipped. An unchecked build is now written as `manuscript.UNCHECKED.docx`, and
  a submission pack assembled with `--skip-checks` says so in its own `MANIFEST.yaml`,
  which is the file whose entire purpose is to be the thing you can tell from.
- **Sidecar exemptions took a value with no reason.** `why` was optional in the code and
  mandatory in every message these gates print, so `- value: '1'` on its own exempted a
  number with no argument recorded anywhere. An entry without a reason is now ignored
  rather than honoured: an exemption nobody justified is one nobody can review.
- **`{{results.x}` was neither a binding nor malformed.** The loose pattern required `}}`,
  so a single missing brace travelled into the built document as literal text, in the place
  where a number was supposed to be. One typo, worst available outcome.
- **A `.jl` figure script produced an empty report**, which reads as "checked and clean".
  The lexer has no Julia entry; it now says the source was not read.
- **A point estimate outside its own confidence interval passed `check`.** `interval()`
  refuses it, and `interval()` was the only thing that did — the results fragment is a
  contract with three other writers (`value(bounds=…)` called directly, the R emitter, a
  hand-edited file), and none of them went through that helper. It is the one arithmetic
  error a reader catches by eye in the first sentence of the Results. Bracketing is now
  checked where every producer meets: at the fragment, by G2, along with an inverted interval,
  a bound of an estimate nobody published, and two bounds claiming the same end.
- **The reversed-interval check was disabled by restating a bound, and invented reversals
  that were not there.** The guard meant to keep the *first* mention of each end tested
  `value.bound in seen` while the keys were `"{bounds}:{bound}"`, so it never matched: the
  last mention won. "2.10 to 7.02, and a lower bound of 2.10 excludes unity" was reported as
  reversed, and a genuinely reversed interval that named its upper bound again went
  unreported. A false positive on ordinary writing is the worse half — an author whose only
  recourse is to delete a true sentence learns to distrust the gate.
- **One estimate could carry only one interval.** A 90% CI beside the 95%, or a credibility
  interval beside a frequentist one, is ordinary in a disproportionality paper and was
  inexpressible: `interval()` wrote one fixed pair of key names, and declaring a second pair
  by hand became a duplicated bound the moment bracketing started being checked — so closing
  that hole closed a door too. A bound now carries a `level`, `interval()` takes one and
  derives the key from it (`"90%"` → `ror.ci90_low`), and omitting `point` reuses the estimate
  rather than publishing it twice: two keys holding one number is what `same_as` is for and
  what G8 watches. Bounds are compared within a level and never across, because a 90% interval
  nested inside a 95% one is correct rather than a contradiction — in the fragment and in
  prose alike, since "3.84 (95% CI 2.10 to 7.02; 90% CI 2.51 to 5.87)" is one sentence and two
  intervals. The slug is derived identically in both languages, or a manuscript's bindings
  would depend on which language its analysis was written in.
- **The example's figure had a different digest on Windows and on Linux.** matplotlib writes
  an SVG through a text stream, so the same picture came out CRLF on one and LF on the other,
  and everything downstream hashes the bytes: re-running `figures/forest.py` on Windows
  invalidated the figure's own review record and its render manifest, and reported a change
  nobody had made. The committed manifest was therefore right only on the machine that wrote
  it. Exactly the trap `writeLines` set for the R emitter, in the Python path, in the example
  a new user copies from. The script normalises the file before recording it.
- **Supplementary material was welded into the manuscript.** There was no way to say a file
  was a supplement, so it went into `manuscript.docx` after the Discussion — counted against
  the journal's word and display-item limits, declared in that count on the title page,
  arriving as pages an editor has to find the end of, and impossible to upload to the
  "supplementary material" slot every submission system has. An author's only recourse was to
  keep the supplement outside the project, which is also the only place the gates cannot see
  it. `manuscript/supplementary/` builds as its own document, reaches the pack as its own
  file, is still read by every gate that reads prose, and is still in scope for review.
- **The pack answered "attach your completed checklist" with YAML.** It copied
  `reporting/*.yaml` and nothing else, which is a serialisation rather than a checklist. A
  table now goes beside the record — generated, so it cannot drift from the file the gate
  checks, and built from the *published* item list rather than the completion, so an item
  nobody answered appears with the answer blank instead of vanishing from what the journal
  receives.
- **`audit` reported a third of a real paper's citation markers as unexplained numbers.**
  Pointed at a submitted pharmacology paper — 580 numeric tokens, 94 output files — it called
  232 of them "not found in any output". Reading the list rather than the count: 25 were
  Vancouver citation markers (`rejection[1,2]`, each dragging the preceding word in, because
  an atom runs to the next space and only *author-year* citations had a rule); 29 were
  confidence intervals written as ranges, matched as a single string `0.72–0.82` against
  outputs holding the two bounds separately; 15 were `§3.1` section references, since only
  the word form was recognised and its number was undotted, so "Section 4.2" failed too; and
  14 were the ORCIDs and postcodes in the author block. Fixing those four took 232 to 151 on
  the same paper.

  The count was never wrong; it was unreadable, which is the same thing. A list where two in
  three entries are the tool's own noise does not get triaged, it gets abandoned — and the
  intervals are the sharpest case, because an interval is the paper's actual result and the
  audit was worst precisely there. What remains at 151 is mostly the paper's own vocabulary
  (`3-core`, `top-1%`), which is what `terms:` is for and is correctly reported as "this tool
  does not know these words".

  The same paper's supplements — still markdown, 1766 tokens — added one more: `n=8,393`
  written closed up is a single atom that no longer looks like a number at all, so thirty
  counts sitting in the outputs were reported unexplained. With spaces, `n = 8,393` is
  already two tokens and always read correctly, which is why nobody had noticed. A label of
  up to three letters is stripped before the number is read; 278 → 248 on those files.
  Deliberately *not* fixed there: forty-three four-digit-hyphen-four-digit tokens, which in a
  bibliometrics paper are ISSNs. They have the same shape as a plain range — that paper also
  writes `2000-3999` for a Scopus code band — so a rule for them would be a rule matching a
  shape rather than naming values, which is the mistake this file records six times already.
- **A claim published through the results file came out green.**

      em.value("conclusion", "The drug causes liver failure and should be withdrawn")

  resolved, passed every gate, and the annotated copy painted it *traced* — green, over its
  own key and "emitted by 01_disproportionality.json", the strongest reassurance that document
  offers — on a sentence the author typed into an analysis script and nothing verified. And it
  is the one route by which text escapes everything that reads text: the writing gate reads
  manuscript sources, and this sentence is not in one.

  Judged on whether the display carries a digit, not on whether it reads like a sentence — a
  rule about the shape of the text would be the wrong kind of rule. `label=True` already means
  "a name, not a measurement", so it is both the way out and a declaration on the record: a
  drug name or a cohort label stays green, because it really is traced to the analysis.
  Unlabelled prose is a defect in the annotated copy and a `prose-as-value` warning in
  `check`. A warning rather than a refusal, because the toolkit does not get to decide that
  keeping a name in one place is wrong.
- **A value printing display maths split its paragraph in Word.** Identifiers are given to
  the source before bindings are substituted, and a paragraph with `$$` in its source gets
  none. `em.value("model.formula", "$$y = 2.1 x$$")`, bound in the sentence that ends a
  section, put `$$` into a paragraph that had one. Pandoc gave the equation a Word paragraph
  of its own, and only the part before it carried the identifier. A co-author who swapped
  that part with the paragraph above had the whole sentence moved in the .md, exit 0, and
  `check` said nothing: the digit kept even the prose warning quiet. G2 now refuses a value
  whose display holds what, typed into the source, would have kept the identifier off the
  paragraph (display maths, a LaTeX environment or an HTML block tag), and a line break,
  after which a blank line, a fence or a `<div>` ends the paragraph. Leaving such a
  paragraph untagged was the other way, and it was not taken: the identifiers would then
  depend on the results as well as the source, and `import` reads them from the source.
- **A p-value of 3.2 × 10⁻⁹ was published as "0.00".** `digits=2` on any number smaller than
  half a unit in the last place gives a string of zeroes, and nothing objected: an explicit
  `display` has been checked against its value since round two, but a *derived* one was
  checked against nothing at all. So the one field a reader looks at first could carry a
  number that is not the number, silently, from a single ordinary call. A rounding that turns
  a non-zero value into zero is now refused, and the message says what to write instead.

  What to write instead had to exist first. `display="<0.001"` already worked; scientific
  notation parsed only as `3.2e-9`, which no journal prints — so an author wanting the value
  stated precisely had the choice of a programmer's notation or `digits=`, and `digits=` was
  the trap above. `3.2 × 10⁻⁹`, `3.2 x 10^-9` and `3.2*10**-9` are now readings of the same
  number, superscripts included, and each is still checked against the value it claims to
  render: `3.2 × 10⁻⁸` on a value of 3.2e-9 is refused, and so is `3.2 × 10⁻⁹` on a value
  of 3.2 — which would previously have parsed with `10⁻⁹` as a *unit*.

  Mirroring it in R exposed a live divergence in the cross-language contract: R's tolerance
  was computed from the mantissa alone, which the Python side had already fixed. R therefore
  accepted a display of `9.99e-6` for a value of `1.2e-6` while Python refused it. The parity
  harness missed it because not one of its cases carried an exponent — "both emitters have to
  be exercised on the same input, or mirrors is only a claim", written in that file's own
  comments, and true again.
- **`bind --apply` was all or nothing.** It replaced every literal that matched exactly one
  published value, in one go. But a match is a suggestion and never evidence — the gate
  refuses a number *because* it matches one, since nothing may pass by coincidence — so a
  `12` that happens to equal a published count while meaning twelve months of follow-up was
  applied along with the nine correct ones, and the only way to avoid it was to decline all
  ten and retype them. `--only manuscript/main.md:42` accepts one suggestion; naming an
  ambiguous one is refused rather than treated as permission to guess, and an unmatched
  selector is an error rather than a silent no-op. The command now also names every
  replacement it made — "replaced
  7 literal(s)" said nothing about which seven, and each of them rewrote a sentence.
- **The submission pack left out the response to reviewers.** `respond` wrote the letter into
  `build/` and nothing collected it, so a resubmission pack held the revised manuscript and no
  answer to the reviewers — the document a resubmission is judged on as much as the paper, and
  the only artefact whose claims G13 actually checks. It is generated at pack time from the
  revision records rather than read out of `build/`, by the same function `respond` calls: two
  renderers would drift, and the drift would be invisible because both produce something that
  looks like a letter. A stale letter is worse than an absent one — a checked set of claims
  and an unchecked document making them. The manifest now also says which submission the pack
  is, because "which version did the journal get" is a question about a round as much as about
  a checksum.
- **Two gates blocked the work and had no command behind them.** G11 refuses a submission
  until a panel exists and every reviewer has filed a record; G10 refuses until every figure
  has been read. Both asked for a SHA-256 the toolkit computed and never printed — G10's is a
  digest of the figure's *content*, so it could not be obtained at all. An author who reaches
  a gate and finds no way through does not hand-write the YAML; they reach for
  `--skip-checks`, and the gate has then made the project worse than having no gate.
  `review --record` and `--record-figure` write the file, fill in the digests, extend the
  panel (carrying a reviewer's remit into a later round), and leave the findings to a person.

  What they deliberately do not offer is a way to re-stamp a record after the manuscript has
  changed. That one flag would turn the review system into theatre: the digest is the only
  thing separating "somebody read this version" from "somebody read a version". Recording
  twice is refused and says to record a further round instead. For the same reason the
  verdict is required rather than defaulted — a record written before the reading is a claim
  that somebody looked — and a figure's checks are written `ok: false` with the question each
  one asks, so the file is a to-do list the gate reads back rather than a row of ticks.
- **R could not express an interval at all.** The R emitter had `value()` and no
  `interval()`, and its `value()` took no `bounds`/`bound`, so an R analysis published three
  keys that no gate could know were one estimate — `interval-reversed` simply could not fire
  on an R project, with nothing saying so. The results fragment is a cross-language contract,
  and a rule enforced on one side only is a rule an author steps around by switching language.
- **"According to the medical record" claimed adherence to RECORD.** The guideline names were
  matched case-insensitively, and several of them — RECORD, ARRIVE, CONSORT — are ordinary
  English words. The gate therefore warned about an unfollowed reporting guideline on the
  Methods section of essentially every observational paper: a false positive about the
  paper's own conduct, which is the fastest way to teach an author that this output is noise.
  Guideline names are published in capitals; the match now requires that casing.
- **The annotated figure sheet always said no values were exempt.** It read a
  `presentational` section; the sidecar's sections are `allow` and `allow_source`, and no
  schema, gate or example has ever written the other name. So the one page whose whole job is
  to show what was exempted claimed nothing was — including for the shipped example, which
  declares five axis ticks. Wrong precisely when it mattered, and untested, which is why it
  survived.
- **`fetch --save-url` wrote inside the installed package.** `_recipe_paths` falls back to the
  recipes shipped in `src/`, and `--save-url` wrote back to whatever it returned: on a normal
  pip install the command edited a file in site-packages — invisible to git, lost on upgrade,
  applied to every other project on the machine, a `PermissionError` traceback on a
  system-wide install. It also round-tripped the YAML through `safe_dump`, dropping every
  comment; in those files the comments *are* the licence reasoning. The URL now goes into the
  project's own recipe, edited line by line.

- **The emitter had no invariants.** `display` was returned verbatim, so one call could
  publish a fabricated estimate *and* a fabricated interval; table cells were `str()`-ed and
  compared to nothing, so "tables are emitted, not written" was satisfied by calling the
  emitter while the numbers stayed typed. A display must now render its own value, and a
  numeric cell must be a number. A composite cell — "3.84 (2.10 to 7.02)" — stays a string,
  but every *claim* in it must be a value the analysis published, with the manuscript's own
  classifier deciding what counts as a claim so "Age 18-44" is a label in a table for the
  reason it is one in a sentence. `em.cell("{} ({})", n, (pct, 1))` covers "n (%)", because
  an f-string reaches `table()` indistinguishable from a typed string and the API has to be
  the thing that tells them apart. Both are now in the R emitter too, and neither depends on
  it: see the section below on where the rule actually lives.
- **`script-newer` compared mtimes, and `touch` sets those.** The fragment now records the
  analysis script's digest. Fragments written before the field existed fall back to the
  mtime test, so an older project degrades rather than breaking.
- **Inline code and fenced blocks were masked but render.** Both are read now. The argument
  for masking them — not nagging a Methods section about `n = 42` — turned out to be an
  argument about READMEs: G2 reads `manuscript/` only. Word counting keeps its own answer,
  since "what would a journal count?" and "where is a digit not a claim?" are different
  questions that were sharing one mask.
- **A figure with no text layer was counted as checked.** matplotlib draws text as outlines
  unless `svg.fonttype` is `'none'`, so an SVG full of annotations read as empty — and
  because a figure yielding no atoms is also not "drawing numbers", the script's results
  check dropped from FAIL to WARN at the same time. Both halves, one setting. An empty text
  layer now fails, and a figure that could not be read no longer softens its script's check.
- **A raster beside a vector was skipped on the strength of its filename.** Render both
  honestly, re-render only the PNG from elsewhere, and the retouched figure went into the
  .docx while G3 read the correct SVG. `manuscript_guard.render.record()` writes a manifest
  of what one run produced, and the raster is skipped only when the manifest says the two
  came out together and both still match their digests.
- **The offline build applied no journal style unless `--csl` was given.**
  `manuscript-guard style` keeps the style the journal's profile names in
  `profiles/journals/styles/`, and the offline build formats citations with it
  (item 51). What is left: a style that is not in the CSL style repository, a build
  before `style` has been run, or a kept style edited since it was fetched still needs
  `--csl`; without it the build uses pandoc's default and says so.

## Still open

- Who reviews additions to the per-project convention allowlist, and whether entries need
  a written justification. The schema already requires a `why`; nothing enforces review.
- Cross-platform hook portability. Only Windows is available for testing, so CI runs
  Ubuntu and macOS.
- Zotero group library support, and behaviour when a citation key is pinned in one library
  and absent from another.

Resolved 2026-08-03: the pre-analysis design gate **warns rather than blocks**, so
exploratory work stays possible.

Resolved 2026-09-24: after a revision, **a later complete round supersedes the outdated
rounds before it**, chosen over requiring every round to be re-read, over superseding only
across a journal's revision, and over leaving it as it was. See "Review panels" above.
